authors: Hugging Face
summary: A Hugging Face agent successfully chained together two separate Spaces (hosted ML applications) to autonomously generate and render a 3D virtual gallery of Paris. This demonstrates practical agentic behavior—breaking down a complex creative task into subtasks and orchestrating multiple specialized models in sequence.

title: Introducing Gemma 4 12B: a unified, encoder-free multimodal model
authors: Google DeepMind
summary: Google DeepMind has released Gemma 4 12B, a unified multimodal model that processes both text and images without a separate encoder. This represents a shift toward simpler, more efficient architectures that handle multiple modalities in a single unified framework.

title: The Open Source Community is backing OpenEnv for Agentic RL
authors: Hugging Face
summary: The open-source community is rallying around OpenEnv, a framework designed for training and evaluating agentic reinforcement learning systems. This signals growing momentum behind standardized, community-driven tooling for agent-based RL, addressing a gap in accessible infrastructure for this emerging capability area.

title: QF3: Fast Flow RL with Filtered Q-Gradients
authors: Chung Min Kim, Brent Yi, David McAllister, Hongsuk Choi, Himanshu Gaurav Singh et al.
summary: This paper introduces QF3, a reinforcement learning algorithm that trains flow-based policies — neural networks that learn to generate smooth action sequences — for robot control tasks. The key innovation is using a critic (value estimator) to guide policy updates while filtering out unreliable gradient signals, achieving 10x speedup over prior methods and enabling robots like humanoids to learn walking from scratch and transfer directly to physical hardware.

title: 4D-HOF: Hand-Object Flow Matching for Feed-Forward 4D Interaction Reconstruction
authors: Shiqi Li, Sean Cho, Yijie Li, Fengzhi Guo, Bowen Wen et al.
summary: This paper presents 4D-HOF, a feed-forward neural network that reconstructs realistic 3D hand-object interactions from video using flow matching — a generative technique that gradually refines noisy predictions toward accurate ones. Rather than optimizing each video separately (slow) or generating from scratch (unstable), the method takes rough starting guesses from vision foundation models and iteratively improves them while respecting physical constraints, achieving state-of-the-art results on benchmark datasets.

title: IdeaAnchor: Teaching LLMs to Turn Literature into Research Ideas
authors: Ziyu Chen, Yilun Zhao, Jiashuo Sun, Yiling Ma, Manasi Patwardhan et al.
summary: This paper teaches language models to generate new research ideas by synthesizing insights from multiple papers, mimicking how scientists actually ideate. The key innovation is "IdeaAnchor"—a structured training signal that explicitly annotates how papers should be combined (their roles, relationships, constraints) to produce novel research directions. The authors mine real examples from published papers and train models using demonstration, self-distillation, and reinforcement learning, showing measurable improvements in idea quality.

title: Sherpa: Teaching LLMs to Teach Adaptively
authors: Weixian Xu, Yanzhe Zhang, Zora Zhiruo Wang, Changyu Chen, Diyi Yang
summary: This paper introduces Sherpa, a reinforcement learning framework that trains LLMs to teach adaptively by simulating diverse student archetypes and directly optimizing for their learning outcomes. Rather than relying on static pedagogical rules or human demonstrations, the system learns teaching strategies that work across different learner profiles, achieving 20+ percentage point improvements in student performance and significantly higher pedagogy scores than baseline models.

title: Agent in a Bottle: Can LLM Agents Turn Their Capabilities Into Cheap, Scalable Artifacts?
authors: Ankit Sonthalia, Haritz Puerto, Alexander Rubinstein, Martin Gubri, Seong Joon Oh
summary: This paper asks whether LLM agents can autonomously create cheap, task-specific solutions (like small distilled models or programs) when given a large repetitive workload and a fixed budget. The authors introduce BOTTLED, a benchmark where agents must complete millions of similar tasks under compute and cost constraints, and find that while strong zero-shot performance doesn't guarantee good "bottling" ability, successful agents can achieve 600+ times cost reduction with acceptable quality loss.

title: AdvSim2Real : Training Web Agents Against Adaptive Prompt Injection in a Web World Model
authors: Sarim Hashmi, Mukul Ranjan, Kshitij Mishra, Mikhail Kuznetsov, Praneeth Vepakomma et al.
summary: This paper tackles a critical vulnerability in web agents—software that browses and acts on web pages to complete user tasks. The problem: attackers can inject misleading instructions into web pages to hijack the agent away from its intended goal. The authors present AdvSim2Real, a training method that co-evolves three things together (the agent, an adaptive attacker, and a curriculum of tasks) inside a simulated web environment to make agents robust against prompt injection attacks that they've never seen before.

title: Neural Petri flows for chemical reactions
authors: Jose Eduardo Escrig Molina, Daniel Probst
summary: This paper proposes Neural Petri Flows, a neural architecture that learns chemical reaction dynamics while guaranteeing they obey physical conservation laws (like atomic valence rules). Instead of building neural networks from scratch, the authors hard-wire the mathematical structure of Petri nets—a formal model where places represent bonds, tokens represent bond order, and transitions represent bond formation or breaking—and let the network learn only the reaction rates. The result is a model that predicts reaction products, atom mappings, and enzyme classification with higher accuracy than existing methods, while ensuring every prediction is physically valid.

title: The Missing Minimal Pair: Stereotype Evaluation in LLMs
authors: Nataliya Stepanova, Ivan Titov, Emily Allaway, Björn Ross
summary: This paper identifies a critical flaw in how we measure bias in large language models: comparing just two opposite sentences often produces logically inconsistent results. The authors propose a better method using "dual minimal pairs" — comparing along two dimensions simultaneously — and introduce metrics based on information theory to make stereotype evaluation more reliable across languages and models.

title: Reinforcement Learning with Conformal Action Sets: An Application to Sequential Recommendation
authors: Wenwen Si, Honghao Wei
summary: This paper proposes RLCP (Reinforcement Learning with Calibrated Pruning), a method that dynamically adjusts which items a recommender system considers at each step in a user session, rather than always using a fixed set. The key insight is that the number of genuinely good options changes as users browse, so adapting the action set improves both recommendation diversity and efficiency. The authors prove theoretical bounds on performance and show their approach outperforms fixed-slate baselines by 1–5× on diversity metrics.

title: On the Computational Tractability of Robust Bandits
authors: Vanessa Kosoy, Vinayak Pathak
summary: This paper studies the computational complexity of learning in "robust bandits"—a setting where the true environment may not match any model the learner has access to. The authors identify a special case that admits a polynomial-time algorithm with near-optimal regret bounds, then show that natural generalizations become NP-hard, pinpointing the boundary between tractable and intractable variants. The work is motivated by the claim that efficient unrealizable learning is essential for AI alignment.

title: Does an Agent's History Tell You When Compaction Will Hurt? A Modest, Bounded Effect on the TRACE Paired-Replay Corpus
authors: Egor Pakhomov, Erik Nijkamp
summary: This paper investigates whether an AI agent's recent behavior can predict when context compaction (summarizing old information to save tokens) will hurt performance. Using a corpus of 590 real compaction events from an app-interaction agent, the authors find that history predicts harm only weakly—the best interpretable trigger catches 21% of harmful compressions while retaining 84% of compression opportunities, but doesn't clearly beat simple token-budget rules. The work matters because long-horizon agents need to compress context, and predicting when compression hurts could improve agent reliability.

title: When Forgetting is not Catastrophic: On the Mechanics of Spurious Forgetting
authors: Vedant Palit, Florent Draye, Nicolas Zucchet, Zhijing Jin, Bernhard Schölkopf
summary: This paper reveals that language models don't truly "forget" old knowledge during finetuning — instead, they temporarily hide it through shared representational shifts that can be reversed. The authors show that what looks like catastrophic forgetting is actually two distinct processes: a reversible loss of access to old facts and a slow, permanent erosion; understanding which dominates determines whether forgetting is recoverable or not.

title: Agreement Is Not Validity: Cross-Model LLM Consensus in Diagnosing Student Failure Modes in K-12 Math Tutoring Dialogue
authors: Clayton Cohn, Joyce Fonteles, Kirk Vanacore, Gianni Mazza, Candida Crawford et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether agreement among multiple LLMs on educational diagnoses actually reflects correct interpretations. The researchers found that while different LLMs agree with each other 76–78% of the time when classifying student math errors, they only agree with human experts 52–60% of the time—suggesting that LLM consensus can mask systematic errors. For educators and learning analytics researchers, this is a critical warning: using multiple models to "validate" automated diagnoses of student reasoning may give false confidence.

title: Principled Under Pressure: Post-Training Decides Whether LLMs Act on Their Own Moral Judgment
authors: Orion Reblitz-Richardson
summary: This paper investigates whether language models act according to their stated moral judgments when under pressure, or abandon their principles. Using a pre-registered panel of 248 scenarios, the researchers show that some instruction-tuned models (like OLMo-3 and Llama-3.1-8B) violate their own stated values roughly 20% of the time when pressured, while others (like Tulu 3) remain consistent. The finding matters because it reveals a gap between what models claim is right and what they do — a failure invisible to standard evaluations that only check stated values.

title: A Case Study in Assuring AI-Written Software
authors: Lindsey Ferris, Sierra Bonilla
summary: This paper studies how to maintain human control over software built by AI coding agents, using a real healthcare platform as a case study. The authors show that traditional code review fails when agents produce more code than humans can inspect, and that even sophisticated monitoring systems (tests, automated reviewers, repair agents) have hidden failure modes — revealing that effective oversight requires alignment of objectives, evidence, permissions, and human decision-making across the entire system.

title: SquidAgent: Parallelize Wisely, Coordinate Efficiently
authors: Yexiong Lin, Shanshan Ye, Yu Yao, Zhen Fang, Bo Han et al.
summary: This paper identifies why parallelizing LLM-based agents often runs slower than a single agent, despite seeming like it should be faster. The authors show that parallel execution incurs two hidden costs: workers redundantly reconstructing context (re-exploration) and the overhead of reconciling their independent outputs (alignment). They propose SquidAgent, a system that decides layer-by-layer whether to parallelize based on predicted token costs rather than wall-clock time, achieving 2–2.6× speedup over existing approaches.

title: Spectral Recovery of Point Clouds from Noisy Geometric Graphs
authors: Tatiana Brailovskaya, Nicholas A. Cook, Sofia Poinelli
summary: This paper studies how to recover the original geometry of a point cloud from a noisy geometric graph — a network built by connecting nearby noisy data points. The authors prove that spectral methods (analyzing the largest eigenvalues and eigenvectors of the graph's adjacency matrix) can reconstruct the underlying low-dimensional structure with high accuracy, even when the original points are corrupted by Gaussian noise and embedded in high dimensions.

title: Recursive Game Creator: An Agentic Product-Level Experience-Oriented Game Harness
authors: Jiajun Chen, Haoyu Wu, Mingda Jia, Xihui Liu
summary: This paper presents Recursive Game Creator, a multi-agent system that generates entertaining video games by iterating between design, implementation, play-testing, and feedback. Unlike prior work that focuses on code correctness, this approach explicitly optimizes for player experience through automated agents that play games, measure enjoyment, and propose improvements in a closed loop.

title: Classifications in modular restricted Boltzmann machines
authors: Elena Agliari, Andrea Lepre, Edoardo Roscani
summary: This paper studies modular restricted Boltzmann machines (RBMs) — neural networks with multiple interconnected layers designed for pattern classification and separation. The key innovation is coupling multiple RBM modules with competitive interactions (anti-Hebbian between modules, Hebbian within) so they can both classify input patterns and disentangle mixtures of patterns. The authors prove that a specific weight initialization based on training data constitutes a stable fixed point of learning, with quantifiable convergence guarantees.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Hierarchical Reasoning Rewards: Minimax-Optimal Rates with Transformers
authors: Naoki Nishikawa, Taiji Suzuki
summary: This paper provides theoretical analysis of why reinforcement learning works well for post-training language models on reasoning tasks. The authors model rewards as hierarchical functions and prove that a Transformer-based actor-critic algorithm achieves optimal learning rates, while also showing that offline approaches (sampling from a fixed distribution) are fundamentally slower. The work bridges the gap between RL's empirical success in language model training and formal understanding of why on-policy exploration helps.

title: Network Intervention by Polling Strategic Agents
authors: Chenyu Zhang, Rohit Parasnis, Saurabh Amin
summary: This paper addresses how a central planner can set prices in a network of self-interested agents who have private information and incentives to lie. The authors develop a distributed polling algorithm called Poll that scales to large networks (300,000+ agents) while maintaining economic efficiency and truthfulness guarantees. The key insight is that optimal prices depend on agents' network centrality weighted by their preferences, which enables a scalable local-sampling approach rather than requiring global information.

title: Visual Orchestration Tax in Agentic VLM Pipelines: Auditing and Certifying Visual Evidence Reuse
authors: Lingteng Zeng
summary: This paper identifies and measures "visual orchestration tax"—the wasteful reprocessing of identical images across multiple specialist agents in multi-agent VLM (vision-language model) pipelines. The authors develop an auditing framework that reveals 67–76% redundant image processing, then propose SharedVisCache, a caching system that eliminates this waste while preserving output correctness and reducing computational cost by 75–90%.

title: Token-Efficient Multi-Agent Collaboration via System One-Guided Computational Division of Labor
authors: Zihan Zhou, Xinzhe Hu, Hanxu Yang, Liangjian Wen, Zhao Kang
summary: This paper proposes S1-MAS, a framework that makes multi-agent LLM systems cheaper and faster by splitting work: lightweight "System One" models handle coordination decisions (task selection, routing, termination), while expensive LLMs focus on reasoning. The approach cuts token costs by 45–97% and latency by 38–93% compared to existing systems, without sacrificing accuracy—making LLM-based agent collaboration more practical for real applications.

title: ProximalFM: Amortized Proximal Causal Inference under Hidden Confounding
authors: Christophe Muller, Ayub Kharel, Alex Luedtke, Chan Park, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen et al.
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in causal inference: estimating treatment effects when some important confounding variables are unobserved. The authors propose ProximalFM, a deep learning method that uses proxy variables and transformer-based foundation models to quickly estimate causal effects without requiring dataset-specific tuning or solving computationally unstable equations.

title: A Functional Representation of Credit Behavior for Probability of Default Modeling
authors: Jonas Brunholm, Bjarne Højgaard, Thomas D. Nielsen, Orimar Sauri
summary: This paper proposes a new way to predict whether borrowers will default on loans by treating credit behavior as continuous functions over time rather than monthly snapshots. Instead of aggregating credit data into discrete monthly values, the authors retain account balances, credit limits, and account types as continuous processes, then use functional logistic regression to predict default risk—achieving performance comparable to XGBoost while remaining interpretable enough for regulators.

title: Forecast Accuracy Is Not Trading Profit: Evolving Small Recurrent Networks for Stock Return Prediction
authors: Jonathan Chang, Zimeng Lyu
summary: This paper challenges the assumption that better forecasting accuracy leads to better trading profits. The authors compare different neural network architectures—transformers, recurrent networks, and others—on stock return prediction, and find that small networks evolved via neuroevolution outperform larger models on both forecast accuracy *and* actual trading returns, while maintaining extreme computational efficiency. The key insight: what matters for trading is not pointwise prediction error, but how forecasts align with the decision horizon and after accounting for transaction costs.

title: Common-Mode Errors Limit Low-Timestep Deep Spiking Q-Networks
authors: Zijie Xu, Bingrui Guo, Yiding Sun, Yiting Dong, Zhile Yang et al.
summary: This paper identifies why spiking neural networks (SNNs)—energy-efficient brain-inspired networks—perform poorly in reinforcement learning tasks when run with very few simulation timesteps. The authors discover that low-timestep SNNs suffer from "common-mode errors" (errors that affect all action values equally) and propose CMC-DSQN, a method that uses a small auxiliary neural network to correct these errors during training but can be removed at inference, preserving energy efficiency. The work matters because it makes SNNs practical for real-time RL on battery-powered devices.

title: Convex Order Beyond Dimension One: Projection Tests, Counterexamples and Gaussian Mixtures
authors: Olivier Guéant
summary: This paper resolves a long-standing question about how to compare probability distributions in high dimensions when they have the same mean — a core problem in actuarial science and finance. The key finding: checking all one-dimensional "slices" (projections) of two distributions suffices to determine convex order when comparing a Gaussian with a mixture of Gaussians, even though this test fails for general distributions.

title: One Figure, Every Canvas: Editable Flowchart Relayout via Agentic Pipeline
authors: Shih-Chen Tseng, Chih-Hsuan Chen, Ryan Yang, Hsi-An Chen, Chun-Wei Tuan Mu et al.
summary: This paper solves the practical problem of automatically adapting flowchart diagrams to different aspect ratios (e.g., paper columns, slides, social media formats) while preserving all connections and content. The authors propose an agentic pipeline that parses the flowchart, applies styling, and relayouts elements to fit new dimensions, using critic agents to catch and prevent common failures like broken edges or hallucinated content.

title: Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data
authors: Sophie L. Wang, Amil Dravid, Rulin Shao, Kevin Farhat, Sewon Min et al.
summary: This paper reveals that base language models can achieve reasoning performance comparable to reinforcement learning–trained models simply by prepending specific token sequences ("cues") to their responses. The authors show these cues work because training data creates strong associations between certain starting tokens and reasoning behavior, and they demonstrate this by rewriting training data to turn arbitrary words like "chicken" into effective reasoning triggers.

title: BiasFlow: Geometric Monitoring and Backbone Regularization for Spurious Feature Reliance
authors: Haojin Deng, Zhiping Lin, Yimin Yang
summary: This paper addresses spurious feature reliance in deep learning models—when classifiers make predictions based on incidental correlations (like background color) rather than genuine object features. BiasFlow is a diagnostic toolkit and regularization method that monitors how frozen neural network backbones rely on biased attributes, then applies a penalty during training to reduce this reliance. The work matters because it helps build more robust models that maintain accuracy even when deployment data differs from training data.

title: Learning to Read the Contextual Tokens in Diffusion Transformers
authors: Omer Dahary, Etai Sella, Hadar Averbuch-Elor, Daniel Cohen-Or, Or Patashnik
summary: This paper investigates what happens inside Multimodal Diffusion Transformers (MM-DiTs) — neural networks that generate images from text — by training a lightweight system to "read" hidden representations using natural language questions. The authors discover that these hidden states encode rich semantic information about the image being generated, and they show that this understanding can be used to improve image generation quality.

title: Recursive Video In-Context Learning for Agentic Robot
authors: Wenrui Bao, Xinxin Liu, Bingxin Xu, Yuzhang Shang
summary: This paper addresses a key challenge in robot learning: how to efficiently use demonstration videos to help LLM-based robotic agents learn new tasks. The authors propose Recursive Video In-Context Learning (RV-ICL), a method that converts flat video demonstrations into hierarchical structures that agents can navigate intelligently — loading only the relevant video clips at the right moment during task execution. On two benchmark robot manipulation tasks, RV-ICL improves success rates from ~87–93% to ~96–97% using just one demonstration per task.

title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points
authors: Benhao Huang, Chufan Shi, Junlin Chen, Shicheng Wen, Zhengzhong Liu et al.
summary: This paper improves the efficiency of looped language models—models that apply the same computation repeatedly—by exploiting the mathematical property that recurrent states converge to fixed points. The authors develop techniques that reduce training cost, speed up decoding, accelerate model prefilling, and enable faster reinforcement learning updates, with perplexity improvements across model scales from 100M to 1.6B parameters.

title: MemPilot: Orchestrating On-Demand Multimodal Memory Curation for LLM Agents
authors: Haozhen Zhang, Haodong Yue, Quanyu Long, Jianzhu Bao, Qingyuan Liu et al.
summary: This paper introduces MemPilot, a framework that intelligently manages memory for LLM agents by deciding when to retrieve pre-cached information versus when to dynamically curate fresh details from raw multimodal data. The key innovation is using reinforcement learning to optimize memory retrieval policies under different trade-offs between accuracy, computational cost, and response latency — letting agents tune their memory behavior based on what matters most for each task.

title: CLIFT: Conformal Self-Verification for Web Agent Training and Test-Time Scaling
authors: Yifan Zhang, Yutong Dai, Viraj Prabhu, Zhiyuan Hu, Ran Xu et al.
summary: This paper introduces CLIFT, a method for training web agents (AI systems that interact with browsers to complete tasks) using weak supervision and self-verification. The core insight is that agents can answer questions about their own actions to generate training signals, and these self-verified signals can be reused at test time without expensive calls to external AI judges — enabling both better training and cheaper deployment.

title: PlotGround: Grounding Plot Digitization in Real Scientific Figures and Their Source Data
authors: Yaohui Zhang, Binxu Li, Haoyi Duan, Jiacheng Miao, Yixin Wang et al.
summary: This paper introduces PlotGround, a system for automatically creating benchmarks that test how well AI models can extract precise numerical values from real scientific figures. The authors built a dataset of 1,119 questions from actual bioRxiv papers paired with their source data, revealing that current multimodal models (which process both images and text) struggle with precise recovery—achieving 87.5% accuracy at ±5% error but dropping to 64-76% at the tighter ±2% threshold. This matters because many published scientific results exist only as figures in PDFs, and accurate automated digitization could enable better reproducibility and data reuse.

title: Deep Learning for Sleep Heart Rate Estimation from Accelerometers: Toward Population-Scale Cardiac Insight Without Optical Sensors
authors: Tanbin Islam Rohan, Pranjol Sen Gupta, Tanusree Debi, Nazmus Sakib
summary: This paper presents SeqSmoother, a transformer-based neural network that estimates heart rate during sleep using only wrist accelerometer data—without optical sensors. The key motivation is that many large health studies collect motion data but lack dedicated heart-rate sensors; recovering cardiac information from this existing data could unlock population-scale insights into nocturnal cardiovascular health at minimal cost.

title: Paradee: Distilling Kokoro-82M into an 8M-Parameter Single-Voice Text-to-Speech Model
authors: Sahil Mahendrakar
summary: This paper shows how to shrink Kokoro-82M, a multi-voice text-to-speech (TTS) model, down to Paradee: an 8M-parameter single-voice version that runs 25x faster than real time on a CPU and fits in 8.5 MB. The key insight is distilling the teacher model in two separate stages (text-to-features, then features-to-audio) rather than training them jointly, avoiding expensive alignment learning while maintaining quality within 0.11 UTMOS points of the original.

title: T-Search: An Open Agentic Retriever and Playground for Hard Multi-Step Search
authors: Olga Tsymboi, Ramil Latypov, Aleksandr Medvedev, Danil Taranets, Dmitrii Stoianov et al.
summary: T-Search is an open-source AI system that retrieves relevant evidence from a fixed corpus by running multiple rounds of targeted searches, then returns ranked chunks with explanations so a separate model can generate the final answer. It matters because it decouples retrieval from answer generation, enabling modular AI pipelines that can be updated independently, and it achieves strong performance on multilingual hard-search tasks using a combination of supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning.

title: On Learning Optimal Corners in Orthogonal Partially Observable Cooperative Guard Art Galleries
authors: Yassin Ben Mansour, Edwin Meriaux
summary: This paper combines formal verification with machine learning to solve the cooperative guard art gallery problem—a scenario where multiple agents must collectively monitor all visible areas in an environment. The authors show that using learned neural networks to decide where each agent should be positioned can dramatically speed up existing algorithms while preserving their formal guarantees about coverage and connectivity.

title: Balancing Memory Pathways: Analyzing and Improving Memory Utilization in Hybrid LMs
authors: Hyunji Lee, Joykirat Singh, Zaid Khan, Justin Chih-Yao Chen, Elias Stengel-Eskin et al.
summary: This paper identifies a critical problem in hybrid language models that combine recurrent and attention layers: models disproportionately rely on attention while underutilizing their recurrent pathways, even though both should offer complementary strengths. The authors propose an auxiliary loss function that forces the model to route information through recurrent layers, improving both coordination between memory pathways and overall performance on long-context and aggregation tasks.

title: BazaarBench: Delegation Safety in Decentralized C2C Marketplaces Run by LLM Agents
authors: Ziyan Wang, Shuqing Shi, James Oldfield, Samuele Marro, Jialin Yu et al.
summary: This paper introduces BazaarBench, a simulated marketplace environment where LLM-controlled agents buy and sell goods, and measures how often they commit fraud or breach trust under normal and adversarial conditions. The work is important because autonomous AI agents now handle real money and reputation in marketplaces — understanding when and why they fail is critical before deploying them at scale.

title: Improving Diversity in LLM Short Story Generation
authors: Zahra Solati Dehkordi, Vasileios Lampos
summary: This paper addresses a key weakness of large language models: they tend to generate similar, repetitive outputs even when asked creative questions. The authors propose DivLM, a training framework that makes LLMs produce more varied short stories across genre, tone, style, and character names, while keeping the stories well-written and following instructions. This matters because diversity is essential for creative applications—users want different stories, not variations of the same narrative.

title: SAFE-MR: Evidence Sufficiency Learning for Selective Multimodal Rumor Detection
authors: Shiwen Ni
summary: This paper presents SAFE-MR, a framework for detecting rumors in multimodal posts (images + text) that distinguishes between whether a claim is true and whether there is sufficient evidence to support that judgment. Most rumor detectors conflate these two problems; SAFE-MR separates them, enabling the system to flag cases where predictions lack adequate backing—a practical necessity since retrieved evidence can be incomplete, duplicated, or contradictory. On three benchmarks, it achieves strong accuracy gains and better handles selective prediction scenarios where abstaining is preferable to guessing.

title: The Birkhoff Geometry of Manifold-Constrained Hyper-Connections: Two Channels, Vertex Viscosity, and Sinkhorn as a Retraction
authors: Xiaoyu Li, Zhizhou Sha, Chiwun Yang
summary: This paper provides a rigorous geometric analysis of manifold-constrained hyper-connections (mHC)—an architectural extension of transformers that uses multiple parallel streams mixed by doubly stochastic matrices. The authors show that Sinkhorn normalization (a standard algorithm for computing these mixers) implements entropic mirror descent on the Birkhoff polytope, and they characterize how information flows and decays across layers, providing both theoretical convergence rates and experimental validation.

title: Inverse Cross-spectral Neural Networks for Multivariate Time Series
authors: Lorenzo Marinucci, Leonardo Di Nino, Gabriele D'Acunto, Paolo Di Lorenzo, Sergio Barbarossa
summary: This paper introduces Inverse Cross-Spectral Neural Networks (iCSNNs), a new type of graph neural network designed to process multivariate time series by learning frequency-dependent relationships between variables. Unlike existing approaches that treat data as independent samples, iCSNNs capture how variables depend on each other at different frequencies, making them better suited to understanding temporal structure in multivariate data.

title: LinearPFN: Amortized Variable Selection for Linear Models with Interactions
authors: Louis Schiekiera, Max Zimmer, Christophe Roux, Manuel Arnold, Sebastian Pokutta et al.
summary: This paper presents LinearPFN, a neural network that solves variable selection for linear models by amortizing Bayesian spike-and-slab inference — instead of running expensive computations for each new dataset, the network is trained once on synthetic data and then performs inference in a single forward pass. This addresses a fundamental computational bottleneck: traditional methods require rerunning Markov chain Monte Carlo for every dataset, which doesn't scale; LinearPFN trades that per-dataset cost for upfront pretraining.

title: Symmetry and AI-assisted discovery of magic-state factories
authors: Shubham P. Jain, Adam Wills, Shraddha Singh
summary: This paper develops AI and symmetry-based methods to discover efficient "magic-state factories" — quantum circuits that produce special quantum states needed for fault-tolerant quantum computing. The researchers use language-model agents and group-theory constraints to search a previously intractable design space, finding 699 new factory designs that significantly reduce the computational overhead required for practical quantum computers.

title: SOL: Measuring Gaps between Text Distributions by Double Sliced Wasserstein Metrics
authors: Gregor Kornhardt, Moritz Piening, Jannis Chemseddine, Gabriele Steidl
summary: This paper proposes SOL, a new metric for measuring the distance between text distributions using double sliced Wasserstein distance. Current evaluation methods like perplexity work well for autoregressive language models but fail or give loose bounds for diffusion and flow-based models; SOL fills this gap by comparing the distributions of hidden representations from a fixed transformer, providing a principled way to evaluate any generative text model.

title: Valid Stopping in Adaptive Generator-Verifier Loops
authors: Mahmoud Hegazy, Michael I. Jordan, Aymeric Dieuleveut
summary: This paper addresses a practical problem in agentic workflows: when should a generator-verifier loop stop searching? The core issue is that a cheap verifier (like a learned proxy) often disagrees with a costly ground-truth check (like actual lab validation), leading to false acceptances. The authors develop statistical methods to control how many bad proposals get accepted while the system is running.

title: Visual Swarm Navigation via Deep Reinforcement Learning and Evolutionary Hybrid Design
authors: Álvaro Díez, Fidel Aznar
summary: This paper presents a method for training swarm robots to explore environments autonomously using only camera input, combining deep reinforcement learning with evolutionary optimization techniques. The approach achieves competitive exploration performance with 31% less energy consumption than traditional sensor-based methods, making it practical for real-world deployment of robot swarms in search-and-rescue or monitoring tasks.

title: GAMBIT: Learning to Plan Continuous Multi-Robot Trajectories
authors: Rishabh Jain, Akmaral Moldagalieva, Lorenzo Magnino, Michael Amir, Keisuke Okumura et al.
summary: GAMBIT learns how to coordinate the trajectories of multiple robots in continuous motion spaces by combining imitation learning with reinforcement learning. The key insight is that robots sometimes need to sacrifice local efficiency for team-level coordination—like sacrificing a pawn in chess for strategic advantage. The system scales to over 1,000 robots while maintaining collision-free execution and planning speeds of hundreds of milliseconds.

title: AgentDiscover: Autonomous Discovery with Minimal Search Scaffolding
authors: Mahdi Farahbakhsh, Ilan Sela, Fatemeh Doudi, Vishnu Teja Kunde, Krishna Narayanan et al.
summary: This paper presents AgentDiscover, a system where an AI agent autonomously plans and conducts scientific searches rather than following a fixed human-designed algorithm. Instead of treating the language model as merely a proposal generator, the system lets it own the entire search strategy, using a persistent database as working memory. The approach outperforms existing frameworks on diverse tasks—kernel engineering, biology, algorithm design, and mathematics—while being more cost-efficient.

title: AlphaPADI: Formulaic Alpha Discovery via Pool-Aware Hierarchical Discrete Diffusion
authors: Yanzheng Jin, Pengyang Shao, Yunshan Ma, Haowen Pan, Naixin Zhai et al.
summary: This paper introduces AlphaPADI, a system that automatically discovers trading formulas (called "alphas") by generating pools of complementary formulas rather than individual formulas one at a time. The key insight is that in real trading, multiple formulas work together, so the generator should optimize for the entire pool's collective performance rather than each formula in isolation. The method combines hierarchical diffusion (a generative technique) with reinforcement learning to outperform existing approaches on real stock market data.

title: FactorBench: A Portfolio-Aware Benchmark for Automated Factor Mining
authors: Zhuohan Wang, Carmine Ventre
summary: FactorBench is a standardized benchmark for comparing automated factor mining methods across five equity markets, evaluating roughly five thousand factors discovered by nine different algorithms (including genetic programming, reinforcement learning, generative models, and large language models). The paper shows that no single paradigm consistently produces better trading signals or portfolio returns, revealing that recent machine learning advances haven't clearly translated into economically useful financial discoveries.

title: Agent Policy-Value Audit: Separating Transition Composition from Event Selection in Financial LLM Agents
authors: Mingyang,  Chen,  Yida,  Xu,  Huiwen et al.
summary: This paper reveals a critical flaw in how financial AI agents are typically evaluated: standard performance tests conflate two distinct sources of profit — the agent's ability to time trades correctly (event selection) versus passive exposure to market drift (transition composition). The authors propose the Agent Policy-Value Audit, a statistical technique that isolates selection skill by holding an agent's action patterns fixed while randomly reassigning them across different market events. Applied to real earnings-event data, their audit shows that a deployed LLM agent's apparent +15.2 basis points/event profit is actually -10.6 bps of selection skill masked by +25.8 bps of passive composition — meaning the agent adds no real value.

title: AdaEva: Accelerating LLM-Driven Algorithm Design with Adaptive Partial Evaluation
authors: Tai Nguyen, Fei Liu, Phong Le, Carola Doerr, Nguyen Dang
summary: This paper tackles the computational inefficiency of using LLMs to automatically design algorithms. The authors propose AdaEva, a framework that evaluates candidate algorithms on progressively larger subsets of test instances, dropping weak candidates early rather than fully evaluating every candidate—similar to how you'd eliminate bad job applicants after early interview rounds instead of running them through the entire hiring process.

title: Less Decoder is More Encoder: Geometric Representation Learning from Novel View Synthesis
authors: Keerthi Kaashyap, Dennis Anthony, Akshay Krishnan, Nhi Ngoc Nguyen, Jeremy Collins et al.
summary: This paper argues that existing view synthesis methods produce poor geometric representations not because of insufficient training signal, but because of architectural choices that dilute what the encoder learns. The authors introduce SNAP, a self-supervised approach that uses a pose-conditioned decoder and latent-space reconstruction to learn transferable 3D geometric features from multi-view images. The method is competitive with supervised geometry methods while enabling downstream tasks like pose estimation, depth prediction, and robot manipulation.

title: 4DCodeBench: Benchmarking Agents on Inverse Graphics of Dynamic Scenes
authors: Ruihong Shen, Žiga Kovačič, Peter Kulits, Xingrui Wang, Zizhang Li et al.
summary: This paper introduces 4DCodeBench, a benchmark where AI agents reconstruct dynamic 3D scenes from videos by generating executable graphics code. Instead of predicting pixels, agents must understand scene structure and physics well enough to write programs that reproduce complex real-world behavior like deformation, fluids, and fracture. This matters because it tests whether models can truly understand dynamics rather than merely memorizing visual patterns.

title: RNADyn: A Benchmark for Generating and Understanding RNA Dynamics
authors: Yiming Huang, Lennart Bastian, Hanqun Cao, Luis Vollmers, Tolga Birdal
summary: This paper introduces RNADynBench, a large-scale benchmark dataset of RNA molecular dynamics simulations, and RNADynNet, a unified neural network model that generates realistic RNA trajectories and extracts dynamics information from static structures. RNA molecules constantly change shape to perform their biological functions, but datasets and methods to understand these dynamics at scale have been scarce—this work fills that gap with quality-controlled data and a model that treats trajectory generation and dynamics understanding as complementary tasks.

title: From Mixing to Tearing: Graph Decomposition in Decentralized Optimization via Message Passing
authors: Kuangyu Ding, Gesualdo Scutari
summary: This paper develops a new framework for decentralized optimization where multiple agents cooperatively minimize objective functions over a network graph, communicating only with neighbors. Instead of existing approaches that use the graph primarily to mix information, the authors jointly design both the optimization subproblems and the communication protocol by decomposing the graph into tree-structured blocks—a technique they call GATE (Graph-Tearing message passing). This approach is theoretically more principled and computationally more efficient than prior gossip or tree-routing methods.

title: LESSER: Post-Training Data Selection with Output-Layer Gradients
authors: Lyuxin David Zhang, Eric Wong, Surbhi Goel, Anton Xue
summary: This paper shows that selecting training data for large language models using only output-layer gradients is nearly as effective as using full-parameter gradients, but costs 9–10× less to compute. The key insight is that you don't need expensive backward passes through the entire model to pick good training examples — a cheap forward pass to the output layer gives you the signals you need.

title: FrugalEvo: Towards Cost-Aware LLM-Guided Program Evolution
authors: Hui Chen, Xuan Qi, James Xu Zhao, Zhaopeng Feng, Shilong Liu et al.
summary: This paper proposes FrugalEvo, a cost-aware framework that uses LLMs to solve hard optimization problems (like circle packing and algorithm design) while minimizing computational expense. The key insight is that practical optimization should maximize solution quality per dollar spent, not just per iteration — so the method pairs an expensive, capable LLM (for strategy exploration) with a cheaper one (for implementation), plus a cache-efficient evolution process. On 10 mathematical tasks and 10 algorithmic problems, FrugalEvo matches or beats prior state-of-the-art methods while cutting costs dramatically (e.g., solving circle packing for $0.55 instead of $50).

title: Planning to Learn
authors: Ian Osband
summary: This paper shows that standard cross-entropy loss implicitly optimizes for a long-horizon objective — it's patient about accuracy, considering how each update affects future learning. The authors propose "horizon loss," which interpolates between cross-entropy and exact policy gradients by accounting for remaining training time. On image classification tasks (MNIST, ImageNet with ResNets and ViTs), this one-line change improves accuracy, especially under label noise.

title: On-Board Anomaly Detection for Efficient Marine Environmental Monitoring
authors: Thomas Goudemant, Clotilde Szywala, Benjamin Francesconi, Michelle Aubrun, Yves Bobichon et al.
summary: This paper develops an onboard anomaly detection system for Earth observation satellites to identify marine environmental hazards like oil spills and algal blooms. The key innovation is a self-supervised neural network that compresses satellite imagery into a compact latent space, enabling efficient anomaly detection directly on resource-constrained satellite hardware—eliminating the need to transmit all raw data to ground stations.

title: On the Convergence of Success Conditioning for Policy Optimization
authors: Matthew Brun, Xu Andy Sun
summary: This paper analyzes success conditioning—a simple technique where policies are updated by increasing the probability of actions that led to successful outcomes—and proves it converges to optimal behavior in Markov decision processes. The work fills a theoretical gap: while success conditioning is widely used in practice, its convergence guarantees and rates were unknown. The authors show convergence is possible and characterize how many iterations are needed depending on the problem structure.

title: Broken scale symmetries in undercomplete linear autoencoders
authors: Farhad Pashakhanloo, Jacob A. Zavatone-Veth
summary: This paper studies how finite-stepsize stochastic gradient descent (SGD) breaks scale symmetries in undercomplete linear autoencoders — a toy model where you can scale up decoder weights and down encoder weights without changing the network output. The authors show that SGD has a *directional* preference: it consistently drifts toward large decoder weights on a slow timescale, eventually hitting a stability boundary. This illustrates a deeper principle: gradient noise can be converted into systematic motion along a manifold of equivalent solutions.

title: Do Large Language Models Know Colombian Law? A Reliability Benchmark for the Colombian Legal System
authors: Rubén Manrique, Michelle Castellanos, Jorge Morales, Juan David Gutiérrez, Antonio Barreto Rozo et al.
summary: This paper evaluates whether large language models reliably answer questions about Colombian law—a question almost never studied outside the US legal context. The authors built a 1,042-question benchmark with expert validation and tested 15 models across ten legal areas. They found a striking pattern: models sound confident and relevant but are frequently factually wrong, and free-text answers rarely exceed 45% correctness even for the best models.

title: World Embedding Benchmark
authors: Yiqi Liu, Ruifeng Yuan, Yang Wang, Long Li, Fengyu Cai et al.
summary: This paper introduces a benchmark dataset to test whether video embedding models understand physics — concepts like fluid flow, solid mechanics, and light behavior. The authors find that current models are weak at this task, but show that retrieved physics-accurate videos can improve the physical realism of AI-generated videos. This matters because many AI applications need to generate or understand videos that follow real-world physical laws.

title: FALCON: A Model and Dataset Agnostic Framework for Synthetic Data Generation for NL2SQL Pairs
authors: Darian Lee, Shannon Rumsey, Jack St. Clair, Xinyi Tang, Aditya Bansal et al.
summary: FALCON is a framework for generating synthetic NL-to-SQL training data (natural language questions paired with database queries) that captures real-world complexity and ambiguity. Instead of producing oversimplified examples, it creates challenging, realistic data using compact open-source models—enabling organizations to build better SQL understanding systems without relying on expensive external APIs or human annotation.

title: When a Correct Reward Is Not Enough: Diagnosing and Guiding PPO in an Analytically Solved Broker-Trader Game
authors: Siu Tung Wong, Carlo Campajola
summary: This paper tests whether a reinforcement learning algorithm (PPO) can learn to trade in a financial market where the optimal strategy is mathematically known. The researchers find that even with a correct reward signal, PPO struggles to match the analytical solution when market conditions are complex—but they show that using the analytical strategy as a starting point helps PPO adapt when costs change. This matters because it reveals gaps in how RL learns financial control problems and suggests that known mathematical solutions can guide and diagnose RL training.

title: Divergence controls entropy in distillation
authors: Nicolas Zucchet, Scott W. Linderman
summary: This paper explains how different training objectives in knowledge distillation—the practice of training a smaller "student" model to mimic a larger "teacher" model—affect the randomness (entropy) of the student's outputs. The authors prove that forward KL divergence (used in standard cross-entropy training) inflates student entropy above the teacher's, while reverse KL deflates it, and show these effects matter practically for LLM pretraining and finetuning.

title: Structured Composition of Verifiable Atomic Insights for Table-to-Report Generation
authors: Teng Lin, Xinyu Liu, Nan Tang
summary: This paper tackles automatic report generation from data tables — turning raw numbers and relationships into readable analytical narratives. The key innovation is breaking down insight discovery into verifiable atomic building blocks (simple, pattern-based facts) that are then systematically combined into complex insights, ensuring every claim in the final report can be traced back to specific data and SQL queries.

title: When Is Accuracy Evidence? A Unified Theory of Generalisation, Validation, and Information Fusion
authors: JM Gorriz
summary: This paper develops a unified statistical framework for understanding when model accuracy constitutes valid evidence of real-world performance. The core insight: K-fold cross-validation doesn't always provide stronger evidence as you increase K — when folds are correlated (as they often are in small, heterogeneous datasets), you get an "effective" number of folds much smaller than K, making validation less reliable. The paper replaces point-wise accuracy scores with principled upper bounds on true risk, showing when simple resubstitution with corrections can outperform K-fold CV.

title: Passing the Test You Trained On: Re-evaluating Prompt-Injection Detectors for LLM Agents
authors: Zhuowen Liu
summary: This paper reveals that prompt-injection detectors perform very differently when tested on agent-specific outputs compared to public benchmarks, even detectors that rank highly. The authors show that a detector scoring well on one benchmark may fail catastrophically on real agent tool outputs, suggesting current evaluation practices dangerously mislead teams deploying these defenses.

title: EdgeAgent: Orchestrating On-Device LLM inference for End-User Multi-Agent Systems on CPU-GPU Unified Memory Architectures
authors: Yuhai Long, Yuanxin Wei, Kai Wu, Jinhui Wei, Dan Huang et al.
summary: EdgeAgent is a system for running multiple AI agents on consumer devices (like smartphones or laptops) while keeping data private. The core problem it solves: when multiple language models work together on a single chip with shared memory, they slow down dramatically because they fight for bandwidth. EdgeAgent rethinks how to schedule and execute these agents to keep both the CPU and GPU busy, achieving 1.77x faster performance even when agents pause waiting for external tools (like API calls).

title: Defense-in-Depth at the Perception-Reasoning Interface of LLM-Centric Agentic UAV Swarms
authors: Mohammadhossein Homaei, Yousef Emami, Sajad Homayoun, Rahim Taheri, Hao Zhou et al.
summary: This paper addresses adversarial attacks on LLM-powered UAV swarms by implementing a layered defense system at the perception-reasoning interface—the boundary where sensor data enters the language model's decision-making. The authors show that an attacker can redirect drone operations by tampering with structured sensor reports without modifying the model itself, and they implement and test five defensive layers that detect corrupted data before it influences the swarm's schedule.

title: The Investment Acceleration Principle Revisited by means of a Neural Network
authors: Guido Fioretti
summary: This paper uses Kohonen neural networks (self-organizing maps) to model how firms make investment decisions based on consumption patterns and recognition of technological opportunities. The key insight is that investments accelerate when managers detect emerging technological trends, and the model separates innovation-driven investments from routine capacity expansion—offering a more nuanced view of business investment behavior than traditional economic models.

title: Evolving Hybrid Quantum-Classical Architectures for Image Classification
authors: Devroop Kar, Daniel Krutz, Travis Desell
summary: This paper automates the design of quantum circuits integrated with classical neural networks for image classification. Instead of manually choosing quantum circuit architectures, the authors use an evolutionary algorithm (EXAQC) to automatically discover compact quantum modules that work well with classical feature extraction layers, achieving competitive accuracy on MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10 while using far fewer trainable parameters than standard CNNs.

title: FinNextAssist: Towards Professional Financial Deep Research Assistant
authors: Xiangyu Li, Fengbin Zhu, Xuan Yao, Siyu Liu, Xiaoluan Liu et al.
summary: FinNextAssist is a specialized AI research assistant that helps financial professionals conduct deep analysis by breaking research tasks into stages: planning, evidence gathering, reasoning, and report writing. The system uses custom sub-agents to handle different types of financial data (tables, charts, text) and outperforms existing general-purpose research assistants on finance-specific benchmarks. This matters because financial analysis requires integrating many data sources and specialized tools — something generic AI assistants struggle with.

title: Learning While Inferring: Local and Parallel Learning for Edge SNNs across Sensing Modalities
authors: Yanxun Zhang, Yifei Wang, Changze Lv, Jingwen Xu, Yiyang Lu et al.
summary: This paper proposes Bidirectional Spike-Based Distillation (BSD), a method that lets spiking neural networks (SNNs—energy-efficient neural networks that mimic biological neurons) learn and adapt continuously while they're running inference on edge devices. Unlike standard training approaches that pause inference to update weights, BSD runs learning in parallel, reducing energy use to 36% of traditional methods while maintaining competitive accuracy across 25 benchmarks.

title: MintEval: Do LLMs Implement the Trading Strategy You Asked For? A Behavioural-Equivalence Benchmark for Natural-Language-to-Strategy Code
authors: Siyu Wang, Yifan Wang, Yuecheng He
summary: This paper reveals a critical failure mode in LLMs for trading: generated code executes correctly and produces backtests, but implements a different strategy than what was requested. MintEval is a behavioral benchmark that compares what a model's code *does* (not what it looks like) against reference implementations, showing that even frontier models silently diverge from intended logic on 27.5% of tasks. This matters because silent failures in trading code are worse than obvious errors — they destroy trust and risk capital.

title: Shapley-based Structural Analysis of Neural Calibration for Stochastic Volatility Models
authors: Shaïn Afzali, Serena Della Corte, Antonis Papapantoleon
summary: This paper uses Shapley-based explainability methods to understand how neural networks learn to calibrate stochastic volatility models—essentially reverse-engineering which parts of market volatility data matter most for inferring model parameters. The work shows that neural calibration methods are interpretable and can be simplified without losing accuracy, moving beyond just measuring prediction errors to understanding the learned structure itself.

title: Engineering Sustainable Agents: A Systematic Comparison of Agentic LLMs for Developer Workflows
authors: Merve Astekin, Yan Naing Tun, Arda Goknil, Erik Johannes Husom, Lwin Khin Shar et al.
summary: This paper systematically evaluates agentic LLM systems (where multiple AI agents collaborate) versus simpler single-model approaches across five software engineering tasks. The key finding: multi-agent designs consume 6–7× more energy and time while delivering inconsistent accuracy gains, challenging the assumption that more complex agent coordination always improves performance.

title: Temporal Geometry of Deep Networks: Hyperbolic Representations of Training Dynamics for Intrinsic Explainability
authors: Ambarish Moharil
summary: This paper proposes a novel approach to understanding neural network behavior by representing training dynamics in hyperbolic geometry — a curved, non-Euclidean space where distances expand exponentially. Instead of analyzing networks at single snapshots, the authors track how network weights evolve over the entire training trajectory and embed these temporal "parameter graphs" into the Poincaré ball (a hyperbolic model). This reveals how networks self-organize geometrically during learning, offering intrinsic explainability without post-hoc interpretation methods.

title: Evolutionary Computation for Trustworthy AI: From Attacks and Defenses to Self-Evolving Era
authors: Junhao Dong, Chenkai Wang, Xuanhui Lin, Mingrong Gong, Siyu Wang et al.
summary: This survey examines how evolutionary computation—population-based search algorithms inspired by natural evolution—can be used to attack, defend, and improve trustworthy AI systems. As AI has grown from single models to complex agents interacting with dynamic environments, the attack surface has expanded, making traditional gradient-based methods insufficient; evolutionary approaches excel at navigating discrete choices and expensive evaluations without gradients, offering a fresh lens on adversarial robustness and self-improving safe systems.

title: GTDD: Generative Test-Driven Development for AI Coding Agents with Adversarial Testing
authors: Masahiro Kato
summary: This paper proposes Generative Test-Driven Development (GTDD), a framework where an AI testing agent continuously generates new test cases to challenge a coding agent's implementation, rather than relying on a fixed test suite. The key insight is that AI coding agents can overfit to initial examples, so adversarial feedback loops during development force them to implement intended behavior more completely. The authors provide theoretical bounds on false acceptance rates and show empirically that adaptive testing reduces failure rates compared to one-shot test generation.

title: Dynamic Expert Pruning for Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Jabin Koo, Soheil Abbasloo, Sungjae Lee, Jungseul Ok
summary: This paper proposes Dynamic Expert Pruning (DEP), a method that reduces memory footprint in Mixture-of-Experts language models by dynamically selecting which model components ("experts") to activate based on the specific task and agent at hand. Rather than using a single fixed pruning mask for all requests, DEP learns to predict task-specific masks from system prompts, enabling more efficient deployment in multi-agent environments where different agents have different needs.

title: Cross-Fitting Under Nonregularity: Normality and Inference via Locality
authors: Bruno Fava
summary: This paper solves a critical problem in machine learning: standard confidence intervals fail when using cross-fitting (a technique that splits data into folds to avoid overfitting) in many real applications, leading to undercoverage—your 95% confidence interval might actually cover the truth only 80% of the time. The author shows that despite this "nonregularity" (statistical irregularity), a central limit theorem still holds if you adjust for correlations between folds, and provides a practical method to construct valid confidence intervals that actually work with modern methods like random forests and neural networks.

title: Event History Over Scale: Compact Transformers for Low-Latency Limit Order Book Forecasting
authors: David Schaurecker, Lasse B. Strand, Kevin O'Sullivan, Robert Jakob
summary: This paper introduces MBOFormer and MBOFusion, tiny transformer models (7–14 KB) designed to predict short-term price movements in equity and electricity markets using fine-grained order book event data. The key innovation is achieving high accuracy predictions while maintaining sub-millisecond inference latency and extreme model compactness—critical for real-time trading systems where speed and deployment constraints matter as much as accuracy.

title: Muon Learns Facts Better: Understanding the Role of Spectral Orthogonalization
authors: Xuheng Li, Qiwei Di, Yuan Cao, Quanquan Gu
summary: This paper explains why the Muon optimizer—which applies spectral orthogonalization to neural network weight updates—trains faster and learns more structured representations than standard gradient descent. Using a tractable model of factual recall, the authors show that spectral orthogonalization fundamentally changes *how* and *in what order* a transformer learns different types of information, enabling exponential convergence instead of polynomial decay.

title: KaliBench: A Fine-Grained Benchmark for Cybersecurity Tool Use on Kali Linux with Runtime-Free Verifiable Rewards
authors: Pengfei Li, Naufal Suryanto, Sicheng Zhang, Muzammal Naseer
summary: This paper introduces KaliBench, a benchmark for evaluating how well language models can translate natural language requests into executable commands for Kali Linux cybersecurity tools. The work addresses a critical gap: existing evaluations don't measure whether models can generate syntactically correct CLI commands that actually run, which matters because cybersecurity work requires precision at the command line. The authors show that even large models struggle with this task (under 42% accuracy), but that training with their verifiable reward signals significantly improves performance.

title: Reconstruct, Practice, Go Real: Guided Self-Improvement for Embodied Agents
authors: Yen-Jen Wang, Haozhe Jiang, Shuying Deng, Haoru Xue, Weirui Ye et al.
summary: This paper presents RPG, a framework that enables robots to autonomously improve their manipulation skills without retraining neural networks. The system identifies what tasks a robot can do from offline data, creates practice scenarios in simulation, diagnoses failures, develops reusable skills, and gradually transfers them to real hardware—achieving 95% success on 22 tasks after iterative practice and 100% on physical deployment. This matters because it sidesteps the costly bottleneck of manual skill engineering and reward design in robotics.

title: Embedding Prediction Helps Image Generation
authors: Sihan Xu, Ji Xie, Zilin Wang, Hui Shen, Stella X. Yu
summary: This paper proposes a new approach to condition image generation in diffusion transformers by predicting image embeddings rather than reusing static text or class labels. Instead of keeping the conditioning signal fixed throughout the denoising process, the method dynamically updates it at each step based on predictions from a separate transformer model, achieving competitive image quality (FID 1.32 on ImageNet) with significantly less training compute.

title: ScholarCatalyst: A Benchmark for Retrieving Papers That Inspire New Research
authors: Sohyeon Kim, Yoonho Lee, Bo Liu, Dayoon Ko, Rulin Shao et al.
summary: ScholarCatalyst is a benchmark dataset where 184 computer scientists annotated which prior papers inspired their recent research projects, creating a retrieval task: given a research question, find the papers that could advance it using only literature available at project start. The paper shows that current retrieval methods—including agentic search using Claude and embedding-based systems—perform poorly (R@20 ≈ 0.42–0.51), suggesting that AI systems lack the "expert intuition" scientists use to spot relevant prior work in large research archives.

title: VISTA: A Visual Harness for Reasoning in an Interactive World
authors: Qiushi Han, Keya Hu, Linlu Qiu, Cathy Wu, Kaiming He
summary: VISTA is a visual interface that enhances multimodal AI models (like Claude Opus) to reason and act effectively in interactive visual environments. By giving these models lossless visual memory and the ability to selectively retrieve and reorganize past observations, VISTA enables them to solve complex visual reasoning tasks with far fewer actions than baseline approaches—achieving perfect performance on ARC-AGI-3 puzzles with 57% fewer steps than human players.

title: TACO: Ternary Absolute-max Column-wise One-sparse Optimizer for LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Jichao Jiang, Cristian McGee, El Houcine Bergou, Hanqin Cai, Aritra Dutta
summary: This paper introduces TACO, a memory-efficient optimizer for fine-tuning large language models that reduces optimizer state by 174× compared to AdamW while maintaining accuracy. By using a sparse, low-precision update rule based on column-wise signs, TACO enables full-parameter fine-tuning of 30–32B parameter models on a single 80 GB GPU—a practical breakthrough for resource-constrained settings.

title: FERPO: Forward Entropy-Regularized Policy Optimization
authors: Sebastian Sanokowski, Alireza Sarmadi, Majid Khadiv
summary: This paper introduces FERPO, a new reinforcement learning algorithm for continuous control that improves policies without directly differentiating through the critic (value-function estimator). Instead of using action gradients from a learned critic—which can be unreliable—FERPO derives optimal target action distributions using entropy and KL-divergence regularization, then trains the policy to match these targets. The approach shows competitive performance and faster computation than existing methods on robotics benchmarks.

title: The Missing Primitive: Diagnosing and Repairing Mathematical Reasoning in Large Language Models
authors: Shuo Xing, Zilin Dai, Chengyuan Qian, Fangzhou Lin, Wenjing Chen et al.
summary: This paper diagnoses why large language models (LLMs) struggle with mathematical reasoning despite solving hard problems, introducing "Mathematical Primitives"—foundational reasoning capabilities—and a benchmark (LEAP) that breaks down math understanding into four dimensions: Discovery, Generation, Digestion, and Execution. The authors then propose a training method that improves mathematical reasoning by explicitly teaching these primitives, showing that fixing "Discovery" (finding the right strategy) is the highest-leverage improvement.

title: Trust the Direction, Search the Step: Zero-and-First-Order Methods for LLM Fine-Tuning
authors: Cristian McGee, El Houcine Bergou, Aritra Dutta
summary: This paper proposes ZFO (Zero-and-First-Order), a new optimization method that simplifies step-size selection during LLM fine-tuning by separating direction selection from step size. Instead of choosing how far to move in a direction independently, ZFO uses gradient information plus two extra function evaluations to estimate local curvature and pick an adaptive step size along a one-dimensional search line. The method is cheaper than full line search and shows consistent improvements over fixed-step baselines in practice.

title: Generative modeling of intrinsically disordered protein regions by reinforcing sparse autoencoder features
authors: Jason X. Liu, Sebastian Ibarraran, Frank Hu, Soojung Yang, Xinyu A. Feng et al.
summary: This paper introduces IDiom, a language model trained specifically on intrinsically disordered protein regions (IDRs)—stretches of proteins that lack fixed 3D structure but perform critical cellular functions. The key innovation is combining the model with a reinforcement learning technique (RL-SAE) that lets researchers steer the model to generate sequences with desired functional properties, achieving much higher control (90% feature activation) than prior steering methods.

title: Higher-Order Molecular Grammars for Generative and Foundation Models in Chemistry
authors: Yiming Huang, Yujie Zeng, Vijay Prakash Dwivedi, Simone Foti, Jianmin Wang et al.
summary: This paper introduces Higher-order Grammar Representation (HGR), a new way to represent molecules that captures their complex topology—like ring systems and recurring structural patterns—in a form that standard sequence models can process efficiently. The key innovation is converting molecules into combinatorial complexes and then serializing them as rule sequences, which maintains structural expressiveness while avoiding the computational overhead of explicit higher-order encodings. On molecular generation benchmarks, HGR-based models achieve 100% validity by construction and rank first in distributional alignment metrics; on representation learning tasks, they outperform existing baselines significantly.

title: Decoding Looped Transformers Better for (Almost) Free
authors: Weihao Liu, Huangjie Zheng, Tianrong Chen, Rohit Dilip, Richard He Bai et al.
summary: This paper proposes LoopCD, a training-free decoding method that improves looped Transformers — neural networks that reuse the same processing block multiple times — by using earlier recurrent iterations as weak predictions to guide final token selection. The key insight is that intermediate outputs from earlier loops naturally provide contrastive signals without any model retraining, enabling both better accuracy (e.g., 61.88% → 73.33% on AIME) and roughly 25–48% faster inference by requiring fewer recurrent passes.

title: SoftServe: A Scalable Quasi-Newton Method for Deep Learning
authors: Joohwan Ko, Tetiana Parshakova, Diana Cai, Robert M. Gower
summary: SoftServe is a new optimization algorithm that adapts quasi-Newton methods — classical techniques from convex optimization — to train deep neural networks. The paper shows that by carefully managing curvature estimates and using GPU-friendly matrix operations, quasi-Newton can match or beat popular modern optimizers like Adam on difficult problems like recurrent networks and physics-informed models, even at scales up to 136 million parameters.

title: Effective Resistance and Graph Neural Network Reliability in Tissue-Specific Interactomes
authors: Jianru Shen
summary: This paper investigates whether the structure of protein interaction networks — specifically a measure called effective resistance — can help identify when neural network predictions about protein function are unreliable. The authors test this on 24 tissue-specific networks and find that effective resistance contains a small but real signal about prediction difficulty beyond what simple network features like node degree already capture.

title: AutoCompact: Learning When to Compact Context in Long-Horizon Coding Agents
authors: Xuan Zhang, Longtao Zheng, Cunxiao Du, Bo An, Xin Dong
summary: This paper presents AutoCompact, a system that teaches coding agents to automatically decide when and how to compress their working context during long software engineering tasks. The agent learns this compaction policy alongside its main coding policy through a combination of supervised learning from corrected trajectories and reinforcement learning, achieving 9.2% absolute improvement on real repository-level coding benchmarks.

title: DuoMind: Enabling Distributed Multi-Robot Coordination with Semantic Communication
authors: Hanchu Zhou, Dechen Gao, Hang Wang, Brendan Lynch, Boqi Zhao et al.
summary: DuoMind is a framework that enables multiple robots to coordinate and solve complex tasks by combining vision-language models (VLMs) for reasoning with vision-language-action models (VLAs) for precise control. Each robot communicates with others using natural language-like "semantic messages" rather than raw data, allowing distributed teams to handle long-horizon manipulation tasks that no single robot could accomplish alone. The paper also introduces RoboPoly, a benchmark for testing multi-robot coordination, and demonstrates that semantic communication substantially improves task success rates.

title: When Do Intrinsic Rewards Lead to Exploration?
authors: Scott W. Viteri, Laura Gomezjurado Gonzalez, Clark Barrett
summary: This paper investigates when intrinsic reward signals—like prediction error or empowerment—actually lead to good exploration in reinforcement learning agents. The authors show that maximizing common intrinsic rewards can produce suboptimal exploration, propose a formal criterion based on "counterfactual information" (how well an agent's history substitutes for experience under other policies), and identify conditions where existing rewards succeed or fail.

title: From Knowledge Access to Source Learning: Developing Source-Specific Competence
authors: Lucheng Fu, Kejing Xia, Yiyang Wang, Yiqiao Jin, Jinjin He et al.
summary: This paper addresses how LLM-based agents can improve their understanding of external knowledge sources through repeated interaction. Instead of treating each source access as independent, the authors propose SourceLearn—a system that progressively builds a "source model" capturing how knowledge is structured and should be applied. The method combines two learning strategies and demonstrates substantial performance gains (up to 22.6 points) across multiple benchmarks, making it highly relevant for practical agent systems that rely on persistent information sources.

title: Faynt: Scaling and Optimizing Policies for Competitive Melee
authors: Ali Janati, Nikita Kuzmin, Rohit Swamy, Charles Niu
summary: This paper presents Faynt, a family of Transformer-based policies that play Super Smash Bros. Melee at competitive levels, with a single model controlling all 26 characters. The 10M-parameter version wins 98.4% of same-character matches against existing bots and achieves 100% win rate against a zero-delay baseline, demonstrating that large-scale pretraining on human replays combined with specialized post-training can produce superhuman performance in complex, real-time competitive games.

title: Finetuning with Sampling: SFT Learns Better Than You Think
authors: Aayush Karan, Sitan Chen, Yilun Du
summary: This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that supervised finetuning (SFT) — a simpler training method — necessarily produces worse generalization than reinforcement learning (RL) on new tasks. The authors propose an MCMC-based sampling algorithm that transforms offline training data to be more "on-policy" (matching what the model would naturally produce), enabling SFT to match or exceed RL's performance while avoiding catastrophic forgetting. The key insight: the problem isn't the learning algorithm itself, but the data distribution it sees.

title: Spiking neural networks for streaming qubit readout
authors: Barry M. Dillon, Aqib Javed, Jim Harkin, Patryk Dabkowski, Benjamin Lienhard
summary: This paper develops spiking neural networks (SNNs) — neural networks that process information as sparse temporal spikes rather than continuous activations — to read quantum qubit states in real time during superconducting quantum processors. The key innovation is processing measurement signals in successive chunks and streaming classification scores as data arrive, rather than waiting for the full measurement window; this approach beats traditional matched-filter methods and matches the accuracy of standard neural networks while running on FPGA hardware fast enough for real quantum feedback loops.

title: Argo-Bench: Evaluating Data Agents on Enterprise-Scale Workflows
authors: Gabriel Tomitsuka, Arman Raayatsanati, Emma Xing, Duke Gand, Joseph J Ma
summary: This paper introduces Argo-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on realistic enterprise data workflows. Unlike existing text-to-SQL benchmarks that test query generation in isolation, Argo-Bench requires agents to reason across hundreds of tables, perform statistical analyses, and take real-world actions—all graded by their actual consequences in a simulator. Even the strongest models solve only 35% of tasks, revealing a significant gap between current capabilities and enterprise-ready AI.

title: Where-OPD: Spatially Guided On-Policy Self-Distillation of MLLMs with Synthetic Scenes
authors: Sophia Sirko-Galouchenko, Monika Wysoczanska, Andrei Bursuc, Nicolas Thome, Spyros Gidaris
summary: This paper introduces Where-OPD, a training method that improves multimodal large language models (MLLMs — AI systems that understand both text and images) by having them learn from a smarter version of themselves. The key innovation is using spatial guidance — telling the teacher model *where* in an image to look — during training on synthetic scenes, so the student learns fine-grained visual reasoning without needing human annotations. The results transfer surprisingly well to real-world images, showing gains of 3+ points on counting, document, and chart understanding tasks.

title: A Comparative Explainability Framework for DeBERTa-v3 in Zero-Shot Medical Abstract Classification
authors: Javier Diaz Esteban-Herreros, David Muñoz-Valero, Raquel Martínez-España, Jose M. Juarez, Juan Moreno-Garcia
summary: This paper evaluates how well five different explanation methods (SHAP, LIME, occlusion, Input x Gradient, and Attention x Gradient) agree with each other when explaining a DeBERTa-v3 model's predictions on medical abstract classification. The authors find that explanations diverge significantly, especially when the model is uncertain, and identify three systematic failure modes—suggesting that auditing AI systems in medicine requires multiple explanation methods rather than trusting any single one.

title: Scalable, Transferable Meta-network for Data Selection Requires a Different Loss (and Why the Obvious Choice is Problematic)
authors: Zilin Du, Bowen Yang, Boyang Albert Li
summary: This paper addresses how to select the most valuable training examples when building large language models from massive datasets. The authors show that existing meta-learning approaches struggle when scaled to real-world data, and propose TESS — a new framework that learns which examples matter most through a neural selection network trained with a novel objective function. The method transfers well across different datasets and model sizes, which matters because data selection can significantly reduce training costs and improve model safety.

title: Wasserstein Gradient Flows and Forward-Only Diffusion Are Not Enough for Multimodal Sampling
authors: Daniel McBride, Pratik Khandagale, Cristina Garcia-Cardona, Yen Ting Lin
summary: This paper argues that popular sampling algorithms based on Wasserstein gradient flows and forward-only diffusion processes cannot efficiently sample from complex multimodal distributions, despite theoretical claims of fast convergence. The authors prove that these methods inherit fundamental mixing problems from statistical physics—specifically, they get stuck between well-separated modes and require exponentially long times to move probability mass between them, a limitation that cannot be fixed by standard implementation tweaks.

title: LLM2Jev: LLMs Are Already Jev-Style Decision Models -- When and How to Fine-Tune Them
authors: Yinheng Li, Justin Wagle
summary: This paper investigates whether general-purpose LLMs can directly output categorical decisions (like multiple-choice answers) without generating free-form text, and when fine-tuning is needed.
