The authors present LLM2Jev, a framework that extracts calibrated decisions from a model's token probabilities, showing that modern LLMs are already effective decision models out-of-the-box — but fine-tuning helps primarily for weaker models and specific tasks like intent routing.

title: Form and Void: Entangled Composition through an Autonomous AI Agent
authors: Shiwen Wang, Jian Yang, Xu Wang, Xincan Wang, Weiming Dong
summary: This paper introduces FaV-A, an AI agent that generates images with sophisticated positive-negative space composition—where foreground objects and background empty space are intentionally designed to work together visually. Current text-to-image models struggle with this because they must coordinate two interdependent concepts that share a boundary. FaV-A solves this by breaking the task into stages: first generating a base object, then analyzing it to find complementary negative space, then composing them together—outperforming single-pass prompting.

title: Typological Alignment of Stack-Based Language Models on Mildly Context-Sensitive Artificial Languages
authors: Nadine El-Naggar, Tatsuki Kuribayashi, Ted Briscoe
summary: This paper investigates why certain grammatical structures (like word order patterns) appear more frequently across human languages by testing how stack-based language models learn artificial languages with varying complexity. The authors find that models with limited working memory struggle less with cross-serial dependencies—nested grammatical patterns that represent the upper limit of human language complexity—suggesting this constraint might explain why natural languages tend to avoid such patterns.

title: CARM: Cancellation-Aware Response Masking for LLM Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yafei Zhang, Songshuo Lu, Sicong Liao, Zhi Chen, Yaohua Tang
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem in LLM reinforcement learning: when policy updates happen during training, some sampled responses become "off-policy" (generated under an older policy) and shouldn't fully guide learning. The authors show that standard masking approaches can mask problematic policy drift because positive and negative probability changes cancel each other out. They propose CARM, a better masking rule that prevents this cancellation and improves performance on math reasoning and code generation tasks by 2–3 percentage points.

title: Old Ideas, Novel Problems: The Instability of LLM-Based Novelty Evaluation
authors: Noy Sternlicht, Simra Shahid, Peter Jansen, Daniel S. Weld, Pao Siangliulue et al.
summary: This paper investigates how well large language models can judge whether research ideas are novel — a task that's increasingly used to evaluate automated ideation systems. The authors find that LLM-based novelty judges are unreliable: small changes to prompts flip their verdicts on identical ideas more than half the time, and specialized novelty evaluators often perform worse than simple baselines. This matters because many papers now claim their systems produce novel ideas, but those claims rest on unstable evaluation foundations.

title: Controllable Multi-label Video Safety Detection via Adaptive Tversky Policy Optimization
authors: Guangyu Yang, Jingbiao Mei, Mingsheng Sun, Jinghong Chen, Yingtong Bu et al.
summary: This paper addresses automated detection of unsafe content in videos by treating it as a multi-label classification problem rather than binary (safe/unsafe). The key innovation is Adaptive Tversky Policy Optimization (ATPO), a reinforcement learning framework that lets content moderators adjust the trade-off between catching unsafe content (recall) and avoiding false alarms (precision) — a control that existing systems don't provide.

title: Mem++: Non-Destructive Memory for Long-Term Organizational LLM Agents
authors: Ahmad Yehia, Aly O. Abdelkareem, Islam Ahmed, Hesham Omran, Khaled Alashmouny et al.
summary: This paper introduces Mem++, a memory system for LLM-based organizational agents that preserves full document history rather than compressing information at write time. The key insight is that organizational decisions evolve over time—newer documents revise older ones—so the system must track which version was "current" when a question is asked. Mem++ outperforms existing memory baselines by 8-13 percentage points on organizational benchmarks because it keeps all versions and lets the answering model choose the right historical context.

title: Mingbird: A Local-First Agent Harness Enabling Small Open Models to Complete Real Tasks
authors: Hao Wang, Ting Huang
summary: Small language models (2–9B parameters) can run on consumer laptops but fail to complete real tasks when wrapped in standard agent frameworks designed for cloud-scale models. This paper argues that many failures stem from the harness itself—not the model—and introduces Mingbird, a redesigned local-first agent framework that fixes specific failure modes like context overflow, infinite loops, and premature task abandonment. On controlled benchmarks, Mingbird achieves 88.6% completion versus 63% and lower for competing harnesses.

title: Universal Byte-Level Encoding: UTF-8/UTF-16 Routing to Reduce Cross-Script Token-Budget Disparities
authors: Hyunsik Kim, Youngmoon Jung
summary: This paper addresses a fairness problem in multilingual language models: non-English scripts require more tokens to represent the same information because their characters are encoded inefficiently. The authors propose Universal Byte-Level Encoding (UBE), a tokenization method that selectively routes characters through different Unicode encoding schemes (UTF-8 vs UTF-16) to equalize token costs across languages while preserving efficiency for English.

title: TRACE: Tackling Real-World Resource Assignment Problems via Agentic Heuristic Design
authors: Jose A. Ayala-Romero, Andres Garcia-Saavedra, Xavier Costa-Perez
summary: This paper presents TRACE, a system that automatically designs scheduling rules for allocating computational tasks to servers in real-time. The key innovation is combining evolutionary algorithm-based heuristic generation with AI agents that analyze system logs to understand *why* certain rules work better—filling a gap where existing methods only see a performance score without understanding the underlying system behavior. The work bridges the gap between theoretically optimal ML schedulers and practical industrial systems that need human-readable, auditable rules.

title: Token Communication-Assisted Collaborative Embodied Artificial Intelligence: Concepts, Framework, and Opportunities
authors: Peng Yi, Ying-Chang Liang
summary: This paper proposes token communication (TokCom) as a unified interface for multiple physical robots or embodied agents to cooperate effectively in shared environments. Instead of transmitting raw sensor data (images, videos, sensor readings), agents compress task-relevant information into compact tokens—discrete semantic units—that can be efficiently transmitted over wireless networks and processed by foundation models. The work matters because collaborative robotics requires both communication bandwidth and semantic understanding; TokCom addresses both simultaneously.

title: SoK: Decentralized Agent Economic Infrastructure
authors: Rui Sun, Xihan Xiong, Qin Wang, Fei Gao, Zelin Li et al.
summary: This paper systematizes security and economic failures in decentralized agent task workflows—where multiple separately-designed protocols are chained together to accomplish work. The authors show that even when each step appears correct, the overall outcome can fail: a worker might deliver what was approved, but that approval doesn't prove the work actually satisfied the task. They map 17 security properties across six workflow stages and test 12 real systems to expose recurring gaps where valid work goes unaccepted or evidence is ignored.

title: After Cooperation Is Learned: Gradient Routing and Optimizer-Dependent Maintenance in Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Chaoyuan Hao, Wentao Yue, Tianyou Lai, Hongji Li, Jiayi Zhou et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether cooperative policies learned by multiple agents remain stable when training continues—a question overlooked in prior work that focuses only on learning cooperation from scratch. The authors isolate how value gradients flowing through shared actor networks affect cooperation maintenance, and show the risk is conditional on scale and gradient routing, not universal critic failure.

title: Continual Reinforcement Learning with Neuroevolution
authors: Eleni Nisioti, Andrea Cossu, Kathrin Korte, Sebastian Risi
summary: This paper investigates whether neuroevolution—an optimization approach that evolves neural networks through mutation and selection rather than gradient descent—can better handle continual learning tasks where an agent must adapt to changing environments without forgetting prior knowledge. The authors compare evolution strategies and genetic algorithms against state-of-the-art reinforcement learning methods and find that evolution strategies consistently achieve better stability-plasticity trade-offs, suggesting that weight-space perturbations may be a fundamentally better approach for learning across shifting tasks.

title: The hidden advantage of mask resampling: a theory of masked autoencoders
authors: Jorge Medina Moreira, Lorenzo Bardone, Lenka Zdeborová
summary: This paper explains why masked autoencoders (MAEs) — neural networks trained to reconstruct hidden parts of input data — learn better representations than standard autoencoders that see all the data. The authors prove theoretically that masking helps recover underlying structure in high-dimensional data, especially when noise varies across features, and show that varying which parts are masked improves learning efficiency.

title: Managing Context and Communication in Distributed Agentic UAV Swarms
authors: Andrea Iannoli, Ivan Zyrianoff, Angelo Trotta, Lorenzo Gigli, Marco Di Felice
summary: This paper tackles a core challenge in distributed UAV swarms: how to keep each drone's onboard language model reasoning sharp while avoiding communication overload. The researchers propose an architecture where UAVs selectively share information based on what matters to each neighbor, rather than broadcasting everything. In a simulated search-and-rescue scenario with ten drones, their approach completes missions where naive message flooding fails, while cutting inference costs roughly in half.

title: Social welfare and price discovery in double auction markets
authors: Teemu Pennanen
summary: This paper explains why double auctions (a common trading mechanism where buyers and sellers simultaneously submit bids and asks) tend to drive prices toward competitive equilibrium — a phenomenon observed in lab experiments but never rigorously proven. The author shows mathematically that when agents bid based on their true preferences, repeated double auctions converge to Walras equilibria (prices where supply equals demand), proving the mechanism works as economic theory predicts.

title: Controllable Stochastic Quantization Encoding for Adversarially Robust Spiking Neural Networks
authors: Yujia Liu, Peiyu Liu, Yajing Zheng, Tiejun Huang
summary: This paper proposes a stochastic quantization encoding method to improve adversarial robustness in Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) — neural networks inspired by biological brains that process information as discrete spike events. The key insight is that adding controlled randomness during the input encoding stage makes SNNs harder to fool with adversarial attacks (tiny, crafted perturbations designed to cause misclassification). The method works as a general framework encompassing both Poisson encoding and direct encoding, and can be combined with other defense strategies.

title: Langevin-Informed Transfer Learning: Replacing Target Samples by Black-Box Feedback
authors: Vladimir R. Kostic, Karim Lounici, Hélène Halconruy, Timothée Devergne, Michele Parrinello et al.
summary: This paper presents Langevin-Informed Transfer Learning (LITL), a method for learning the underlying dynamics of complex systems (like molecular simulations or generative models) when you only have access to biased or incomplete samples and black-box feedback. The key insight is that many scientific systems evolve along low-dimensional manifolds governed by stochastic (randomized) dynamics, and LITL recovers the essential spectral structure of these dynamics without needing direct access to the target trajectories themselves.

title: No Model Required: Text Entropy Rate Filtering Mitigates Iterative Fine-Tuning Collapse
authors: Lewis Mitchell
summary: This paper addresses model collapse — the phenomenon where iteratively fine-tuning language models on synthetic data causes output to become increasingly repetitive and narrow — using a model-free approach based on information theory. The authors show that filtering training data using the Kontoyiannis entropy rate estimator, computed directly from raw text without access to the model itself, outperforms existing methods and reduces repetition by 19% while increasing vocabulary diversity by 30%.

title: A Multi-Agent LLM Framework for Personalized Health Checkup Interpretation and Guidance
authors: HyungJun Kim, Taehan Lee, Soojin Cheon
summary: This paper presents a multi-agent LLM system that interprets personalized health checkup results by breaking down complex queries into specialized subtasks, executing them in parallel, and synthesizing the outputs. The system outperforms single-agent baselines on compound health queries, improving answer quality across usefulness and consistency metrics, though at the cost of higher latency and computational expense.

title: Optimal Transport Meets Reinforcement Learning: A Survey
authors: Yujie Zhu, Charles A. Hepburn, Matthew Thorpe, Giovanni Montana
summary: This survey examines how optimal transport — a mathematical framework for measuring the cost of transforming one probability distribution into another — can be integrated into reinforcement learning algorithms. The key insight is that optimal transport handles cases where probability distributions overlap weakly (a common problem in imitation learning and offline RL) better than standard divergence measures, by explicitly modeling the geometric cost of moving probability mass between distributions.

title: LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Control for Skill-Based Smart Manufacturing
authors: Kay Köhle, Darko Anicic, Thomas A. Runkler, René Graf
summary: This paper demonstrates how large language models (LLMs) can control manufacturing systems by pairing each factory module with an LLM-based agent that both plans production sequences offline and handles real-time faults online. The key innovation is showing that LLMs can coordinate across distributed factory modules using standardized communication protocols (MQTT, OPC UA) and emerge fault-diagnosis behaviors without explicit programming, making smart factories more flexible for custom, small-batch production.

title: Verify Claims, Not Scores: Evidence-Based Verification of Modular Agents
authors: Ali Atiah Alzahrani
summary: This paper proposes a new way to evaluate modular AI agents by auditing the *evidence* behind their decisions rather than just looking at overall performance scores. The approach tracks what each component (planner, actor, verifier) contributes to outcomes and whether those contributions are actually justified, using a portfolio-allocation agent as a test case. This matters because swapping one component for another in an agent gives you no insight into which part broke, what the agent is actually checking, or whether improvements are real or just artifacts of how you measured them.

title: PPO-HRAP: Proximal Policy Optimization with a Hybrid Regime-Aware Policy for Risk-Controlled Trading
authors: Duong Hien Chi Kien, Thanh Trung Huynh
summary: This paper proposes PPO-HRAP, a reinforcement learning method that teaches trading agents to balance profit-seeking with drawdown control by blending learned policies with market regime information. The method achieves strong risk-adjusted returns (0.64 Sharpe ratio) on S&P 500 futures while cutting maximum drawdown nearly in half compared to buy-and-hold, addressing a core challenge in RL for finance: most profit-focused agents either become overly passive or take excessive risks during volatility spikes.

title: MASkillBlender: Decentralized Whole-Body Coordination for Multi-Humanoid Loco-Manipulation via Skill Blending
authors: Yifan Hu, Luhang Hong, Mingkang Long, Danning Wang, Chengfeng Jia et al.
summary: This paper presents MASkillBlender, a framework for coordinating multiple humanoid robots to perform complex manipulation and locomotion tasks together. The key innovation is learning a shared high-level policy that blends pre-trained single-robot skills, allowing decentralized decision-making without task-specific reward engineering. This matters because multi-robot coordination is essential for manufacturing, construction, and rescue operations, but current methods require heavy manual tuning.

title: Can AI Scientists Coordinate at Runtime?
authors: Zijian Liu, Yangzhixin Luo, Junyu Lu, Yi Li, Yu Chen et al.
summary: This paper asks whether AI agents can coordinate dynamically during task execution rather than following fixed workflows designed beforehand. The authors introduce Runtime Agent Coordination (RAC), a system that lets multiple AI scientists select each other, divide work via contracts, and verify results on-the-fly. Testing on three benchmarks shows runtime selection improves performance, though adding verification mechanisms can reduce gains under tight budgets—highlighting a real tradeoff in multi-agent coordination.

title: VeriHarness: Scaling Agentic Verification for Long-Horizon Tasks
authors: Caiqi Zhang, Rujun Han, Zifeng Wang, Zoey CuiZhu, Nigel Collier et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical challenge: how to verify whether LLM-based agents have correctly solved complex, multi-step tasks without access to ground-truth answers. The authors propose VeriHarness, a system that turns the same LLM generating solutions into a verification agent by equipping it with tools, workspace, and reusable verification skills. The approach shows 6+ point improvements over single-rollout baselines on five benchmarks, and the authors release 26,000 rollouts to enable future research.

title: ActiveSaddler: Automated Curriculum Learning for Agent Harness Optimization
authors: Sungho Park, Wonjoong Kim, Jue Zhang, Wook-Shin Han, Pengfei Gao et al.
summary: This paper introduces ActiveSaddler, a system that automatically improves LLM agents by adapting which training scenarios to use during optimization. Rather than fixing training data upfront, the method treats curriculum design as a dynamic bandit problem—continuously discovering failure patterns in the agent's behavior and prioritizing which ones to target for improvement. On two benchmarks, it improves agent performance by 4–8 percentage points over methods that use a static training curriculum.

title: HakiCC: LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Design and Optimization of Concurrency Control Protocols
authors: Farzad Habibi, Juncheng Fang, Faisal Nawab
summary: This paper presents HakiCC, a system that uses large language models (LLMs) and multiple AI agents working together to automatically design database concurrency control protocols tailored to specific applications. Instead of forcing all applications to use generic protocols like 2PL or OCC, HakiCC generates custom protocols optimized for particular workloads, then further improves them through an evolutionary optimization loop—achieving 50–92% throughput gains on real benchmarks.

title: Kepler: Auditable World Models for ARC-AGI-3
authors: Wensen Wu
summary: Kepler is a system for building and validating executable world models — computational simulations of game rules — to solve ARC-AGI-3 tasks, which require agents to infer hidden objectives from interactive environments. Using a single frozen Claude Opus 5 instance, it achieved perfect scores on all 25 public games with minimal action usage, offering a transparent, auditable alternative to black-box problem-solving and revealing that naive performance metrics hide important evaluation failures.

title: Increasing Width Allows Greedy Layer-wise Training to Rival End-to-End Backpropagation in Self-Supervised Learning
authors: Syon Mansur, Joel Zylberberg
summary: This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that end-to-end backpropagation is necessary for training deep neural networks. The authors show that in sufficiently wide networks, greedy layer-wise training—where each layer optimizes locally without coordinating with other layers—can match or even outperform standard backpropagation in self-supervised learning tasks. The finding suggests that network width can compensate for the lack of global error coordination, opening new possibilities for alternative training algorithms that may be more biologically plausible or computationally efficient.

title: Neuromorphic Pseudo-Random Number Generators with a Low Power Hardware Implementation
authors: Jafar Shamsi, Navid Akbari, Sonia Sennik, Aaron Gruber, Wilten Nicola
summary: This paper shows how spiking neural networks—brain-inspired computers that mimic how neurons fire—can generate high-quality random numbers while using very little power. The researchers built a neuromorphic random number generator that runs on low-power hardware (FPGAs) and consumes only 3.24 milliwatts, matching or exceeding the quality of traditional random number generators while being much more efficient.

title: Meta-Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Fast Adaptation of Interactive Policies with Applications to Autonomous Driving
authors: Huiwen Yan, Kyriakos G. Vamvoudakis, Mushuang Liu
summary: This paper develops a meta-multi-agent reinforcement learning (meta-MARL) framework that lets teams of agents quickly adapt their strategies to new situations by learning across many similar tasks. Unlike prior work that handles single agents or assumes fixed opponent behavior, this approach models the problem as a game where agents' strategies depend on each other, and it demonstrates faster adaptation than standard methods on autonomous driving tasks.

title: Beyond Supra-Competitive Outcomes: Collusive Behaviour in Deep Reinforcement Learning for Optimal Execution Games
authors: Christos Spyridon Koulouris, Carlo Campajola
summary: This paper shows that two independent AI agents trained on a stock liquidation game learn to collude—achieving costs better than competitive benchmarks by punishing each other if one tries to cheat. The key finding is that when one agent deviates, the other responds by accelerating its own selling in a way that hurts the deviator more than it helps itself, a hallmark of collusive behavior in economics.

title: Multi-agent Auditory Scene Analysis: Improved Localization Speed and Robustness by Multi-beamformed Speech Quality Feedback
authors: Caleb Rascon
summary: This paper improves real-time auditory scene analysis—the task of locating, separating, and classifying sound sources in noisy environments—by modeling it as communicating multi-agent systems. The key innovation is replacing single quality estimates with sets of multi-beamformed estimates across different spatial locations, which creates a clearer optimization landscape and dramatically speeds up sound source localization while maintaining real-time performance.

title: Ranking-Aware Prompt Optimization for Multimodal Clinical Diagnosis
authors: Tian Xia, Minghao Liu, Yiqing Liang, Laixi Shi, Jiayun Wang
summary: This paper addresses a critical flaw in how multimodal language models (MLLMs) are optimized for clinical diagnosis: standard accuracy metrics are useless on heavily imbalanced medical datasets where a trivial predictor can score 90%. The authors introduce Ranking-PE, a prompt optimization method that instead optimizes for AUROC (a ranking-based metric that correctly handles class imbalance), and show it dramatically outperforms accuracy-based approaches on real clinical tasks—gaining +16 points on some models.

title: Semifactual Credit-Augmented Policy Optimization
authors: Junshu Pan, Zhizhang Fu, Shulin Huang, Yiran Ding, Zifan Cheng et al.
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in reinforcement learning for language models: when models learn to solve reasoning tasks, they often become overly sensitive to irrelevant prompt features (like wording changes that don't affect the problem). The authors propose SCAPO, a new training method that assigns credit to individual tokens based on their stability under prompt variations, improving mathematical reasoning accuracy by 4–6 percentage points on competitive benchmarks.

title: Removing Timing Shortcuts Improves Non-Invasive Brain-to-Text
authors: Dulhan Jayalath, Oiwi Parker Jones
summary: This paper exposes a critical flaw in a high-profile brain-to-text decoding method: the neural network was learning word *durations* from overlapping time windows rather than actually decoding information from brain signals. By processing windows independently instead of jointly, the authors remove this "timing shortcut" and achieve substantially better performance (36.6% word error rate), approaching invasive decoding results. This work demonstrates that careful experimental design is essential when claiming neural signals contain semantic information.

title: Image Classifiers are Efficient Self-Supervised Video Representation Learners
authors: Owais Iqbal, Sudipta Sarkar, Shyam Marjit, Omprakash Chakraborty, Anirban Chakraborty et al.
summary: This paper shows that standard image classifiers can learn effective video representations without being explicitly trained on video data. The key insight: you can represent a video as a grid of sampled frames ("super image"), apply spatial and temporal masking separately, and train a Vision Transformer to align these two views—achieving better results than specialized video models while using 32–160× fewer training epochs.

title: EvoDuet: Bilevel Co-Evolution of Web Searching and Task Solving for Scientific Discovery
authors: Young-Jun Lee, Jinheon Baek, Soyeong Jeong, Minki Kang, Seungyeon Jwa et al.
summary: This paper presents EvoDuet, a method that improves how language models solve complex scientific problems by co-evolving both candidate solutions and web search queries together. The key insight is that a model should dynamically decide when to search for new information, reuse old documents, or proceed without retrieval — rather than blindly fetching pages as solutions change. On 21 optimization tasks, EvoDuet increases discovery gains by 3-21 percentage points compared to baseline approaches.

title: Is Weight Tying Still Beneficial for Decoder-Only LLMs in Private Settings Under DP-SGD?
authors: Razan El Mais, Ali Chehab, Ibrahim Issa, Razane Tajeddine
summary: This paper examines whether weight tying — a parameter-sharing technique used in many language models to reduce memory — remains beneficial when training LLMs with differential privacy (DP), a mathematical guarantee that protects individual data during training. The authors find that untying the shared weights actually improves both accuracy and memory efficiency under privacy-preserving training, suggesting that standard architectural choices need reconsideration in privacy-constrained settings.

title: Turbo Harness: Instance-Adaptive Harness Optimization
authors: Tunyu Zhang, Hao Wang, Kai Xu, Dimitris N. Metaxas
summary: This paper introduces Turbo Harness, a framework that customizes agent "harnesses" (the prompts, tools, and execution parameters that guide an AI agent) for individual task instances rather than using a one-size-fits-all approach. The key insight is that a harness optimized to work well on average may be suboptimal for specific instances, so the authors train a "harness editor" that reuses information from prior global optimization to generate instance-specific patches. The method shows consistent improvements across diverse agent tasks including interactive environments, code generation, and long-horizon planning.

title: WorldAuditBench: Interactive 3D World Auditing with Multimodal Agents
authors: Ziyan Jiang, Jingbo Yang, Jiabao Ji, Yujian Liu, Qiucheng Wu et al.
summary: This paper introduces WorldAuditBench, a benchmark for evaluating multimodal AI agents (systems combining vision and language understanding) on their ability to detect anomalies in 3D simulated environments—like floating objects, unrealistic walls, or scene inconsistencies. The work reveals a significant gap: current frontier models succeed only 6.6–42.3% of the time, far below human performance of 83.4%, highlighting fundamental challenges in coupling action (navigating) with visual reasoning (detecting problems) in interactive 3D worlds.

title: Cogentic: Multi-Agent Orchestration for Automated Proof Discovery
authors: Yang Cai, Vineet Gupta, Yanchen Jiang, Christopher Liaw, Aranyak Mehta et al.
summary: Cogentic is a system that uses multiple AI agents working together to discover mathematical proofs on unsolved research problems. Instead of asking a language model to solve a hard problem in one shot, the system orchestrates competing proof strategies, verifies results against each other, and builds on confirmed intermediate progress—like a team of mathematicians collaborating across long, complex investigations. The approach has already produced novel verified results on open problems in online learning, auction theory, and mechanism design.

title: MatLoom: Layered Text-to-Material Generation in a Compact Program Space
authors: Anson Y. Lam, Shuqing Li, Michael R. Lyu
summary: MatLoom generates 3D material textures from text descriptions by producing compact, human-readable programs rather than raw images. The key innovation is representing materials as layered compositions with explicit rules — making the "how it was made" part of the output, not just the final appearance. This matters because it enables users to understand, edit, and refine generated materials, rather than treating them as black-box outputs.

title: Scaling Laws for Looped Mixture of Experts
authors: Yanbei Chen, Anirudh Goyal, Raghuraman Krishnamoorthi
summary: This paper derives the first unified scaling laws that jointly model recurrence (looped inference) and sparsity (Mixture-of-Experts) in transformer models, alongside model size and data. The work shows that recurrence and sparsity are complementary efficiency axes — combining them yields ~2–3× parameter efficiency gains — and provides a principled framework for designing efficient models under compute budgets.

title: cua-speedrun: Standardized Benchmarking of the Speed of Computer-Use Agents
authors: Pranjal Aggarwal, Lawrence Keunho Jang, Sean Welleck, Daniel Fried, Ruslan Salakhutdinov et al.
summary: This paper introduces cua-speedrun, a standardized benchmarking framework for evaluating the speed and efficiency of computer-use agents (CUAs) — AI systems that interact with graphical user interfaces to complete tasks. While CUAs have recently matched or exceeded human performance on many benchmarks, their practical adoption is limited by speed and cost; this work provides reproducible infrastructure and metrics to measure and optimize these critical dimensions.

title: Belief-Aware Multi-Agent Path Finding under Map Uncertainty
authors: Viraj Parimi, Shao-Hung Chan, Han Zhang, Jingkai Chen, Brian Williams
summary: This paper tackles multi-agent path finding when the environment map is partially unknown and changes unexpectedly. Instead of treating each new obstacle discovery as an isolated event, the authors propose MAGIC — a framework that infers the traversability of nearby unseen locations from sparse observations, allowing teams of agents to plan smarter detours before they hit obstacles. The approach scales to hundreds of agents and reduces total travel costs by ~30% compared to existing methods.

title: Large Language Model-Guided Evolutionary Discovery of Native Neural Architectures for Spiking Sequence Modeling
authors: Ruoyu Zhao, Jiaqi Wu, Chenyu Zhu, Zhichao Lu
summary: This paper proposes OpenArchEvo, a system that uses large language models to automatically discover new neural network architectures optimized for spiking neural networks (SNNs)—a type of brain-inspired network that uses sparse, event-driven computation for energy efficiency. The key innovation is searching over executable code in an open program space rather than predefined configuration spaces, enabling discovery of fundamentally new architectural mechanisms. The discovered architectures achieve 50× better energy efficiency than standard transformer baselines.

title: Decision-Oriented Recommendation Reranking: An Empirical Study of Jev
authors: Hanjia Lyu, Yinglong Xia
summary: This paper investigates whether decision-oriented LLMs like Jev can serve as an efficient alternative to standard large language models for recommendation reranking—the task of reordering candidate items to present the best options first to users. The authors conduct an empirical comparison across Amazon review datasets, finding that Jev maintains competitive recommendation quality while showing better latency scaling than pointwise LLM approaches, though it remains slower than recommendation-specific models.

title: PhantomEnvironments: Training LLM Agents in Fictional Worlds
authors: Anmol Kabra, Swathi Saravana Selvam, Albert Gong, Chao Wan, Christian Belardi et al.
summary: This paper shows that LLM agents can be trained effectively using entirely rule-generated fictional environments instead of expensive human-curated or LLM-generated data. The key finding: agents trained in these "phantom" worlds—where they search templated articles to answer multi-hop questions—transfer surprisingly well to real-world benchmarks, often beating models trained on actual data. This matters because it solves a major bottleneck in LLM agent training: the cost and complexity of creating good environments.

title: MemLife: Curating and Reasoning over Long-Term Egocentric Video Memories
authors: Guangzhi Xiong, Xinyuan Zhang, Xiao Yang, Hyokun Yun, Kai Zhang et al.
summary: MemLife is a system that helps AI assistants understand long-term egocentric video (hours-long first-person video footage) by converting it into searchable text memories instead of reprocessing raw video every time. The key innovation is using entity-grounded episodes (text summaries tied to specific people/objects) and a time-indexed retrieval system, plus a reinforcement learning method called MemOpt that automatically improves how memories are written to be more faithful and retrievable.

title: From DNA Design to DNA Slimming: Auditable Agentic Discovery of a Deletion-Only Designer
authors: Joel Shor
summary: This paper tackles DNA sequence design by removing unnecessary bases while maintaining biological function — a "slimming" problem distinct from traditional sequence design. The authors use an AI agent (ERA) to automatically discover and modify DNA designers, producing GRADASLIM, which outperforms simpler baselines at compressing regulatory DNA elements while preserving transcription-factor binding activity. The work matters because compact DNA saves synthesis costs and reveals which sequence features actually drive function.

title: Amortized Bayesian Inference on Multilevel Models of Arbitrary Structure
authors: Daniel Habermann, Andreas Bulling, Stefan T. Radev, Paul-Christian Bürkner
summary: This paper presents a method to automatically build neural networks that perform Bayesian inference on complex hierarchical statistical models. Instead of running expensive sampling algorithms each time you need to make predictions, the method trains a neural network once that can then instantly produce probabilistic estimates—and it does this while staying true to the original model's mathematical structure.

title: Mid-Harness: Scaling Actions Between Model and Harness for Terminal Agents
authors: Minki Kang, Ryo Hachiuma, Shaokun Zhang, Subhashree Radhakrishnan, Yonggan Fu et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem in terminal agents (AI systems that interact with computer environments via commands): even when a language model can generate good actions, execution failures often derail progress. The authors propose Mid-Harness, a technique that samples multiple candidate actions and verifies them before execution, without changing the underlying model or environment interface. They show this approach significantly improves task success rates — for example, raising performance from 50% to 68% on a benchmark — and that stronger verifiers can extract better alternatives from the same generator.

title: AIMS: An Agentic AI Framework for Sim-to-Real Multi-Modal ISAC
authors: Yijie Bian, Kai Zhang, Wei Guo, Zixin Wang, Shenghui Song et al.
summary: This paper introduces AIMS, a framework that uses multiple AI agents to automatically configure and adapt machine learning models for integrated sensing and communication (ISAC) systems across sim-to-real deployment scenarios. The key problem: training ISAC models requires real-world data, which is expensive and scarce, so researchers use simulations—but existing simulations don't transfer well to real deployments because of mismatches between simulated scenes, sensor readings, and wireless characteristics. AIMS solves this by having agents automatically generate deployment-specific synthetic data and configure learning systems through natural-language requests.

title: Solving Multi-Agent Sokoban via LaCAM
authors: Keisuke Okumura
summary: This paper presents Sokoban-LaCAM, a planning algorithm for Multi-Agent Sokoban — a puzzle where multiple agents must cooperatively push boxes onto target locations. The key insight is that recent advances in multi-agent pathfinding (MAPF) can be adapted to handle the harder problem of coordinating both task assignment and collision-free movement, scaling to dozens of agents while guaranteeing solutions will eventually be found.

title: BayesNDE: Bayesian Generative Modeling for Neural Density Estimation
authors: Chenglin Li, Qiao Liu
summary: BayesNDE proposes a new method for density estimation—computing the probability that data comes from a particular distribution—using Bayesian generative models. Instead of requiring complex invertible neural networks, it uses posterior inference to adaptively focus computation where it matters most, then combines multiple samples to estimate densities accurately. The method works well on complex, multi-peaked data and improves anomaly detection in real applications.

title: Safety of Latent Communication in Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Muhammad Huzaifa, Sina Mavali, Thorsten Eisenhofer
summary: This paper reveals a critical safety vulnerability in multi-agent systems that communicate through latent (internal) representations rather than text. Even when individual agents are safety-aligned, the lightweight neural links connecting them can be exploited or accidentally trained to increase harmful behavior — and the authors show attackers can weaponize this with reinforcement learning to raise harmful compliance from 28% to 77% without modifying the agents themselves.

title: BAM! Bayesian Anything Model: a foundation model for generative computational imaging
authors: Alessio Spagnoletti, Charlesquin Kemajou Mbakam, Jonathan Spence, Andrés Almansa, Marcelo Pereyra
summary: This paper introduces BAM (Bayesian Anything Model), a lightweight foundation model that performs physics-aware image reconstruction in a few steps without requiring likelihood approximation or task-specific training. The key innovation is making the model condition on instrument physics at inference time rather than during training, allowing a single 36M-parameter network to handle diverse computational imaging tasks like deblurring, inpainting, and super-resolution across different datasets and camera systems.

title: Mitigating Representation Gaps in Amortized Bayesian Inference with Auxiliary Supervision
authors: Hans Olischläger, Svenja Jedhoff, Šimon Kucharský, Aayush Mishra, Stefan T. Radev et al.
summary: This paper addresses a practical problem in amortized Bayesian inference — a technique where neural networks learn to approximate posterior distributions directly, enabling fast inference on new data. The authors show that these networks often get stuck in "representation gaps" (local optima) that hurt accuracy, and propose using auxiliary supervision losses on internal network representations to fix this. The work matters because it makes amortized inference more reliable without requiring problem-specific tuning.

title: CAMOS: Coupled Oscillatory State-Space Model for Multimodal Clinical Time-Series
authors: Maxx Richard Rahman, Mostafa Hammouda, Wolfgang Maass
summary: This paper introduces CAMOS, a neural state-space model designed to handle multimodal clinical time-series data that is irregular, incomplete, and heterogeneously sampled. Unlike standard linear models that treat missing data as simple masking, CAMOS allows the transition dynamics themselves to adapt based on which measurements are actually present, enabling it to capture interactions between modalities. The work is clinically motivated by real datasets like ADNI where half of imaging visits lack certain modalities.

title: QuantCode Model: Specializing Language Models for Executable Algorithmic Trading Code
authors: Alexey Chernysh, Orkhan Ekhtibarov, Dmitry Zmitrovich
summary: This paper develops QuantCode, a specialized language model trained to generate executable algorithmic trading code from natural language strategy descriptions. The key innovation is combining continued pretraining on trading framework code with supervised fine-tuning on validated strategy-to-code pairs, which the authors show significantly improves both single-turn code correctness and multi-turn agent-based code repair success rates on their new 400-task benchmark.

title: Null-model treatment of the sensory-motor boundary changes an evolutionary connectome comparison
authors: Gyujeong Park
summary: This paper questions how we evaluate whether biological neural circuits matter by comparing evolved agents with fruit fly brains against randomized control brains. The key finding: standard randomization methods accidentally create direct shortcuts from sensory inputs to motor outputs that don't exist in the real fly brain, which biases conclusions about whether the biological wiring actually provides an advantage. The result suggests that how we design control experiments fundamentally shapes what we can conclude about evolution.

title: Evolutionary foraging in grids: Intermittent search dynamics emerge in finite, depletable landscapes
authors: Shailendra Bhandari, Alex Szorkovszky, Anis Yazidi, Pedro G. Lind
summary: This paper studies how search strategies evolve when agents forage in finite environments with limited resources. The researchers simulate evolution of movement traits (step lengths, velocities, turning angles) and find that evolved foraging follows "intermittent search" dynamics — local exploitation with occasional long jumps — rather than the pure power-law "Lévy walk" patterns often assumed in nature. This matters because it reveals how constraints like resource depletion shape optimal search behavior, with implications for understanding animal foraging and designing efficient exploration algorithms.

title: T-Router: Learning Thalamic Routing for Reasoning with Parameter-Efficient Reinforcement Learning
authors: Liuxian Ma, Jiale Dai, Jiaqi Li, Lu Mi
summary: This paper introduces T-Router, a parameter-efficient method for improving reasoning in large language models through reinforcement learning. Instead of retraining the entire model, T-Router adds only 0.47% new parameters—a small "routing" layer that learns which computations from earlier layers to reuse and how much to weight them—achieving stronger performance on math reasoning tasks than much larger adaptation methods.

title: Self-Evolving Algorithm-Design Agents: Escaping In-Context Evolutionary Stagnation via Population-Curated Policy Optimization
authors: Chen Lu, Ke Xue, Siyuan Xu, Mingxuan Yuan, Chao Qian
summary: This paper addresses a critical limitation of in-context learning in language model agents: evolutionary algorithms designed within a single context window quickly plateau and fail to improve. The authors propose Population-Curated Policy Optimization (PCPO), a method that allows agents to learn from their own generated algorithms by fine-tuning the underlying model on high-quality self-generated solutions. The approach is validated on algorithm-design tasks (learning rate schedules for chip placement, GPU kernel optimization) where it outperforms pure in-context methods while drastically reducing inference cost.

title: Behavioral Persistence and Incomplete Functional Transfer of Co-evolved Communication in Evolutionary Robotics
authors: Fernando Montes-Gonzalez
summary: This paper investigates whether communication protocols learned by two robots through evolutionary co-adaptation can transfer from simulation to physical robots without retraining. The authors find that transfer is incomplete and asymmetric—one robot succeeds rarely while the other fails entirely—revealing that successful knowledge transfer requires not just preserving the learned signals but also matching the physical and environmental conditions in which those signals evolved.

title: Simulating Synchrony Loop Networks in the Open Source RISP Neuroprocessor
authors: Jackson Mowry, Patrick Abbs
summary: This paper demonstrates how to run Synchrony Loop Propagation (SLP) networks—a sophisticated spiking neural network approach—on the RISP neuromorphic processor, a specialized hardware platform designed for event-driven computation. The authors show their implementation achieves comparable accuracy to standard clustering algorithms while running 10× faster and using far less power, suggesting that complex learning tasks can work efficiently on neuromorphic hardware despite the constraints of spiking architectures.

title: Skill-Space Shooting for Autonomous Robot Policy Improvement
authors: Zihang Rui, Renhao Wang, Haoxu Huang, Yang Gao
summary: This paper presents skill-space shooting, a method that helps robots improve their policies by learning from their own failures without requiring constant human supervision. The key insight is that many corrections robots need are reusable skills (short, recognizable behaviors) that foundation models can understand and reason about—so the paper shows how to explore these skills systematically and convert successful trials into policy improvements that transfer across tasks.

title: Imagine3D-LLM: Teaching MLLMs to Imagine 3D Scenes Before Answering
authors: Jaewoo Jung, Hyeonseo Yu, Honggyu An, Jisang Han, Mungyeom Kim et al.
summary: This paper teaches multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to reason about 3D scenes by first "imagining" a compact 3D representation before answering questions. Rather than relying on pixel-level geometry details, the model learns to assemble a coarse 3D layout of a scene from multi-view images—mimicking how humans reason spatially—then grounds its answers in this internal 3D model. The approach consistently improves performance on spatial reasoning and 3D understanding benchmarks.

title: Cropland PAtteRNS: Parallel Dimensional Attention Networks and Attention to Dataset Disparity for Crop Segmentation in Satellite Imagery Time Series Data
authors: Joseph Metcalfe, Sara Sharifzadeh, Fabio Caraffini
summary: This paper presents PAtteRNS, a hybrid transformer-convolutional model for identifying crop types in satellite imagery over time. The key innovation is using separate attention mechanisms for temporal, spectral, and spatial dimensions of multispectral satellite data—rather than treating all dimensions together—which reduces computational cost while improving accuracy. The authors also expose a critical problem: datasets for this task are built inconsistently (different tile sizes, flawed class groupings), making it impossible to fairly compare different models.

title: Pretraining Latent Information Feedback Transformers with Teacher Supervision
authors: Dor Tirosh, Ido Amos, Mor Geva
summary: This paper introduces LIFT (Latent Information Feedback Transformer), a new architecture that allows language models to feed internal representations backward through layers during generation, breaking the feed-forward constraint of standard Transformers. Using teacher supervision during pretraining — where a pretrained model's state predictions guide learning — the authors show that models with this recurrent feedback consistently outperform standard Transformers at similar computational budgets, while remaining fully parallelizable during training.

title: Thinking Before Thinking: Scaling Agentic Inference Through Meta-Reasoning
authors: Paras Dahal, Anton Bakhtin, Taco Cohen, Zhengxing Chen, Carole-Jean Wu et al.
summary: This paper introduces a meta-reasoning framework for AI agents that explicitly structures how agents decide what to do next during long, complex tasks. Instead of agents blindly pursuing actions, a controller examines progress, explores options, and allocates remaining computational budget before each step. The approach shows consistent gains on hard tasks like program reconstruction and theorem proving, especially as problems get longer.

title: Learning Meta-Skills for Agent Harness Design in Test-Time AI4AI
authors: Cheng Qian, Kunlun Zhu, Beibin Li, Zhenhailong Wang, Heng Ji
summary: This paper studies how one AI system (a Builder) can learn to design better execution environments for another AI system (a Target) without changing either model's weights. The key idea is that the Builder learns reusable "meta-skills"—principles about when to provide support and what resources to give—from feedback on development tasks, then applies these skills to new unseen tasks. The approach shows significant performance gains, suggesting AI systems can improve themselves by learning to construct better environments for their own reasoning.

title: AdviSD: Learning to Advise Frontier LLMs via Targeted Multi-Turn Self-Distillation
authors: Rishabh Agrawal, Hejie Cui, Shasha Li, Shanchan Wu, Sercan Ö. Arık
summary: This paper introduces AdviSD, a method for training a small "advisor" model that steers frozen large language models (like Gemini or Claude) using natural-language guidance. The key insight is that not all feedback corrections are equally valuable for learning — some can mislead future decisions — so the method selectively learns from corrections that actually change the executor's behavior. AdviSD outperforms baselines by 4–6 points on standard benchmarks and generalizes to new tasks and different model families.

title: Breaking the Uniformity Trap: Scaling Video Diffusion Model via SplitMoE
authors: Yu Xu, Yuxin Zhang, Xiao Yang, Haotian Yang, Yizhi Wang et al.
summary: This paper proposes SplitMoE, a new architecture for scaling video generation models using a split expert pool that avoids uniform routing constraints. Current Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) systems treat all tokens identically, causing semantic information to scatter across experts—but video data has natural semantic structure and temporal redundancy that gets lost. SplitMoE separates experts into "semantic" and "generic" roles, letting tokens cluster by meaning rather than arbitrary load balancing, resulting in faster training and better video quality.

title: Multi-Agent Flow Matching with Decoupled Generative Guidance
authors: Ruoyu Lin, Magnus Egerstedt, Fabio Pasqualetti
summary: This paper introduces DeGG-Flow, a framework that uses flow matching (a generative modeling technique) to generate multi-agent systems while guaranteeing they satisfy hard constraints. The key innovation is "decoupled guidance"—each agent can independently determine how to steer the generation process toward satisfying requirements, without needing to coordinate with other agents in real time. The work matters because generative models are powerful but typically make no promises about constraint satisfaction; this bridges that gap for multi-agent scenarios.

title: IMPACT: Modeling Socially Interdependent Movement in a Generative Multi-Agent Simulation of a Pompeian Household
authors: Tianqi Liu, Nayoung Kim, Julia Sebastien, Kathryn Gleason, Caitlín Eilís Barrett et al.
summary: This paper presents IMPACT, a multi-agent simulation architecture that models how people in a Roman household coordinate their movements and activities based on social roles and relationships. Rather than simulating independent agents, IMPACT captures how individuals wait for, prompt, and constrain each other's behavior through socially defined dependencies—demonstrating this through a five-hour simulation of a Pompeian dinner party where social hierarchy and obligations shape who moves where and when.

title: How Local Mixing Encodes Relative Position in Global NoPE Attention
authors: Cutter Dawes, Nick Alonso, Tom Figliolia, Beren Millidge
summary: This paper explains how transformer models can work without explicit position encodings (like RoPE) when they combine local attention layers (like sliding window attention) with global attention layers. The key finding: local mixing layers create a "recency bias" in the model's internal representations that carries position information forward, allowing global attention to implicitly track sequence positions. This matters because it challenges the assumption that explicit position encodings are necessary and suggests a path toward position representations that could generalize to longer sequences.

title: Do LLM Agents Execute the Plans They Declare? From Planning-Mode Declaration to Pattern-Specific Execution
authors: Subba Reddy Oota, Francisco Herrera, Jordi Cabot Sagrera, Marcos López de Prado, Shadab Khan
summary: This paper examines a critical gap in LLM-based agent systems: agents often fail to execute the plans they declare, even when the plans are sound. The authors propose Planning-as-Routing, where agents explicitly choose a planning mode (Predefined, Sequential, Hierarchical, or Search) and a specialized executor enforces that structure, dramatically improving task success rates across multiple benchmarks.

title: Correct Answers, Invalid Traces: What Verifiable Grade-School Math Reveals About Chain-of-Thought Traces
authors: Ratish Puduppully, Pranabendu Misra, Paarth Iyer, Durgesh Kalwar, Vardhan Palod et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether chain-of-thought traces—the step-by-step reasoning that language models generate—actually reflect how models solve problems or are just post-hoc rationalizations. Using a specially designed math benchmark (iGSM) where correct solutions can be mechanically verified, the authors discover that models frequently produce correct answers with logically invalid reasoning traces, even when those traces pass surface-level checks. This matters for AI safety: if we can't trust model reasoning to be genuine, we can't rely on interpretability methods for debugging or auditing AI systems.

title: Explore Broadly, Reason Sharply: Push Small Models toward the Frontier via Sampling
authors: Panagiotis Theodoropoulos, Nan Jiang, Xintong Duan, Ali Hasan, Yuriy Nevmyvaka et al.
summary: This paper proposes Parallel Power Tempering (PPT), an inference-time method that improves reasoning in smaller language models without expensive retraining. Instead of using reinforcement learning to update model weights, PPT runs multiple copies of the model in parallel at different "sharpening" levels — some explore diverse reasoning paths while others exploit the most likely correct answers — allowing small models to match frontier model performance on complex reasoning tasks.

title: Effective Dense Retrieval using Only In-Context Examples
authors: Nour Jedidi, Abdul Basit Ali, Hang Li, Jimmy Lin
summary: This paper shows that large language models can be turned into effective dense retrievers—systems that find relevant documents by comparing numerical representations—without any training, using only a few example queries and documents as context. The method, called RICE, works by prompting the LLM with in-context examples that teach it how to encode both queries and documents consistently, making it practical for teams that can't afford to fine-tune models.

title: Traversing the solution space of neural networks with Hessian Null Space Continuation
authors: Ann Huang, Mitchell Ostrow, Zhouyang Lu, William T. Redman, Leo Kozachkov et al.
summary: This paper introduces Hessian Null Space Continuation (HNC), a method for exploring the weight space of trained neural networks while preserving their output behavior. The key finding is that near any trained solution, there exist many radically different internal representations and computational mechanisms — far more diversity than previously known. This matters because it reveals that neural network solutions are not isolated points but regions full of hidden variation, with implications for understanding how networks compute, merging models, and editing their learned behaviors.

title: Latent Inference-Time Guidance of Time Series Foundation Models
authors: Chloé Hashimoto-Cullen, Amaury Durand, Laurent Bozzi, Benjamin Guedj, Yannig Goude et al.
summary: This paper presents a method to improve time series forecasts by intelligently combining predictions from multiple foundation models (large pre-trained neural networks) at prediction time. Rather than picking a single "best" model configuration, the approach uses a latent variable model to learn how to weight different forecasts together, adapting across time — and it does this without modifying the foundation models themselves, keeping them as plug-and-play tools.

title: Gender bias across LLMs is common and highly heterogenous
authors: Edoardo Bolzoni, Valerio Capraro
summary: This paper systematically audits ten recent large language models (LLMs) for gender bias using two empirical paradigms: whether models attribute stereotyped phrases to the "correct" gender, and whether they judge harmful acts differently depending on the victim's gender. The researchers find that gender bias is widespread across models, but the direction and magnitude varies dramatically—some models favor men, others favor women, and some show no pattern at all. This heterogeneity suggests that bias evaluation can't be done once and forgotten; it requires ongoing monitoring across multiple vendors.

title: Brain-SAD: A Brain-Inspired Safe Autonomous Driving Control Framework with Dynamic Fear-Oriented Constraint on Dual-Policy
authors: Huan Rong, Chao Yin, Anouar Imel, Yijie Xia, Tinghuai Ma
summary: This paper proposes Brain-SAD, a safe autonomous driving framework that uses dynamic, fear-based constraints instead of static safety rules. The key insight is that danger varies moment-to-moment based on the immediate driving scene—so constraints should adapt in real-time rather than stay fixed. The approach uses dual policies (one for normal driving, one for emergency avoidance) and outperforms existing safe reinforcement learning methods in collision avoidance and task completion.

title: Identifiability Guarantees for Drivers and Dynamics of Delayed Physical Systems
authors: Julien Boussard, Antoine Débouchage, Théo Saulus
summary: This paper develops a method to identify the underlying drivers and dynamics of delayed physical systems (stochastic differential equations with time lags) from observed data, with mathematical guarantees. Unlike physics-informed neural networks or symbolic regression approaches that lack identifiability guarantees, this work proves that under reasonable assumptions, you can uniquely recover the true dynamics — a critical requirement for trustworthy scientific modeling.

title: A neural network that maintains and retrieves memories based on context
authors: Hayoung Song, JeongJun Park, Qihong Lu, Giacomo Vedovati, Monica D. Rosenberg et al.
summary: This paper shows how a recurrent neural network (RNN) with memory can learn to use context—inferred from visual scenes—to both maintain working memory and retrieve episodic memories, much like the human brain does. The model's activity patterns match fMRI recordings from humans watching movies, and it retrieves memories faster and more accurately when context modulation is included, suggesting a computational principle underlying how context shapes memory in naturalistic settings.

title: RLTL;DR: Self-improvement by Internalizing Self-generated Feedback
authors: Michael Kirchhof, Eleonora Gualdoni, Andrew Szot, Khashayar Gatmiry, Aryo Lotfi et al.
summary: This paper tackles a hard problem in self-improvement: teaching agents to solve tasks where success is extremely rare or impossible initially. The authors introduce RLTL;DR, which lets a policy generate its own textual insights after each failure, then conditions future attempts on these insights. The key finding is that by "internalizing" the task-to-insight mapping through backpropagation, the model learns to solve hard problems without needing the insights at test time—suggesting a new training paradigm for difficult generalization.

title: Rational Clarification by Assistive Agents via Value-of-Information Reasoning
authors: T. Duy Nguyen-Hien, Yee Whye Teh, Wee Sun Lee, Tan Zhi-Xuan
summary: This paper addresses a practical problem: when users make ambiguous requests to AI assistants, should the assistant ask clarifying questions or just act on its best guess? The authors propose REVOIR, a reasoning method that decides whether to clarify by estimating how much an answer would improve the task outcome, balancing question-asking costs against the risk of misalignment. On two tasks, REVOIR outperforms existing approaches while asking far fewer questions.

title: RAVEN: Receiver-Conditioned Action-Value Encoding for Finite-Alphabet Multi-Agent Communication
authors: Shuwei Sun, Chenxi Wang, Jian Huang, Weiyun Ru, Hui Cao
summary: This paper addresses a core problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning: how to compress messages between agents so that they retain only the information each receiver actually needs to make good decisions. The authors propose RAVEN, a method that encodes messages as short 4-symbol sequences (2 bits each) by learning what distinctions in value matter to each receiver given its own private context—and show it outperforms recent communication methods that use 12–1,000× more bits.

title: Physical Muon: Orthogonalization as an Equilibrium Computation
authors: Yuren Hao
summary: This paper redesigns Muon, an optimizer for neural network training, to work on analog hardware by replacing dense matrix operations with a continuous-time flow that can be approximated using only matrix-vector products and local updates. The key insight is that orthogonalization — a core step in Muon — can be computed as the equilibrium state of a dynamical system rather than through explicit matrix inversion, making it feasible for physical neural networks and in-memory computing devices.

title: PowerMarketJax: A JAX Benchmark Suite for Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning in Power Markets
authors: Zhanhua Pan, Xin Qin, Xiao Liu, Zhilong Cao, Jianhong Wang et al.
summary: PowerMarketJax is a GPU-accelerated benchmark for training multiple learning agents to bid in realistic electricity markets. The paper shows that agent bidding strategies vary dramatically depending on market rules, and demonstrates 33× speedup by implementing the entire simulation and training pipeline in JAX, enabling large-scale study of how competitive learning shapes real-world power market outcomes.

title: Hybrid Joint-Selective Optimization: Reduced-Space Levenberg-Marquardt Refinement of Low-Dimensional Parameters of Interest
authors: Muhammad Luthfi Shahab, Gabriella Alfa Indahsari, Imam Mukhlash, Hadi Susanto
summary: This paper proposes a hybrid optimization strategy (HJSO) that combines first-order gradient descent on all parameters with targeted second-order refinement on a small subset of "parameters of interest." It's useful when you have a huge neural network but only care deeply about getting a few specific outputs right — like option prices in financial models or specific eigenvalues in matrix problems. The method trades off computational cost for accuracy in the dimensions that matter most.

title: FlowMAS: Learning Multi-Agent Workflow Topology via Information-guided Generative Flow Network
authors: Haitao Wang, Chenjing Liang, Haipeng Zhang, Jiawei Hu, Sicheng Wang et al.
summary: This paper proposes FlowMAS, a method for automatically designing the topology (structure and connections) of multi-agent workflows without manual specification. It uses Generative Flow Networks—a machine learning technique that treats workflow design as a guided exploration problem—to discover effective collaboration patterns between agents, and shows improvements over existing search and text-based approaches on benchmark tasks with large language models.

title: Evolving Towards Better Codes: LLM-Guided Search for High-Distance Binary Linear Codes
authors: Amal Seddas, Vladyslav Shashkov, Maryna Viazovska, Emmanuel Abbe
summary: This paper shows how large language models (LLMs) can discover better binary linear codes — mathematical structures used in data transmission and storage — by searching over possible code-construction programs. The approach found seven new record-breaking codes that beat the current best-known constructions, suggesting LLMs can guide search in classical mathematics problems where exhaustive solutions are infeasible.

title: Multi-Depth Temporal Fusion for Feedforward, Locally Trained Spiking Neural Networks
authors: Aidin Attar, Eleonora Cicciarella, Michele Rossi
summary: This paper presents a new spiking neural network (SNN) architecture that processes images and event streams using biologically-inspired spike timing. The key innovation is Multi-Depth Temporal Fusion (MDTF), which combines early and late temporal features intelligently rather than replacing them, and trains the network using only local learning rules (STDP). The work matters because it achieves strong image classification while remaining efficient and trainable without backpropagation — important for neuromorphic hardware and energy-constrained systems.

title: A Spread-Gated Hawkes-Flocking Model for Best Bid and Ask Dynamics, with an Application to Limit Order Placement
authors: Hyoeun Lee, Kiseop Lee
summary: This paper models how best bid and ask prices move together in financial markets using a spread-gated Hawkes-flocking model—a statistical framework that captures how quote updates on one side of the market influence the other. The authors apply this to real stock data and derive optimal strategies for placing limit orders, showing that understanding these joint dynamics improves trading decisions.

title: Introducing the CZAR Loss: A Tailored Objective Function for Financial Log-Return Predictions
authors: Joel Pfeffer, J. M. Diederik Kruijssen, Florian Stecker, Steven N. Longmore
summary: This paper identifies a fundamental problem in financial machine learning: standard loss functions (like mean squared error) treat zero as near-optimal for predicting stock returns, because returns naturally cluster around zero. The authors propose CZAR, a custom loss function that rewards models for getting the *direction* of returns right, even when noisy, and show it dramatically improves directional accuracy in real bitcoin trading data.

title: Telescopic Language Models
authors: Zhilin Guo, Boqiao Zhang, Hakan Aktas, Kyle Fogarty, Nursena Koprucu Aslan et al.
summary: This paper introduces Telescopic Language Models (TLMs), a training method that produces a single neural network capable of operating at any computational budget—from shallow to full depth—without retraining. The key insight is using stochastic prefix supervision during training: randomly truncating the model's depth on each step while keeping a full-capacity forward pass as the target. This yields a single trained artifact that works as a valid language model at every layer depth, reducing the efficiency loss typically seen in fixed-exit approaches by 43–44% while costing ~12% less to train.

title: Learning Native Reflection in Unified Models with Interleaved Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yijia Fan, Ziqi Huang, Zhongang Cai, Yan Li, Zimo Wen et al.
summary: This paper introduces UMM-Reflection, a method that teaches unified multimodal models to diagnose and repair their own image generations through iterative reflection and revision. The key insight is that a single model can both generate images and write reflection text about what's wrong with them, creating a self-improvement loop — but learning this requires reinforcement learning over full reflection trajectories, not just supervised fine-tuning, because whether a revision actually helps is only known after rendering the new image.

title: TokenCast: Forecasting Token Consumption During LLM Agent Execution
authors: Chaoqian Ouyang, Ling Yue, Libin Zheng, Huanghui Guo, Shengxiang Xu et al.
summary: This paper presents TokenCast, a system that predicts how many tokens an LLM agent will consume during task execution. Token consumption is highly unpredictable because agents take different paths based on tool feedback, and context grows with each step—making costs vary by 10× or more across runs. TokenCast learns lightweight "cost representations" for each execution segment and composes them to forecast total consumption, updating predictions as the run unfolds without needing extra LLM calls.

title: Scaling Long-Form Story Generation via Narrative State Tracking
authors: Zhennan Wan, Jianfei Chen
summary: This paper introduces Narrative State Tracking Agent (NstAgent), a framework that helps large language models (LLMs) write much longer stories — up to 100,000 words — while keeping the plot and characters consistent. The key insight is that by explicitly tracking structured information about characters, past events, and future plot requirements, LLMs can maintain coherence across full-length novels, solving a major limitation of current story-generation systems.

title: Neural Harmonic Measure Operator
authors: Jinjin He, Sinan Wang, Yuchen Sun, Bo Zhu
summary: This paper presents Neural Harmonic Measure Operator (NHMO), a neural network method for solving elliptic partial differential equations (PDEs) on domains with varying shapes. The key insight is that the solution to certain PDEs depends only on the domain's geometry and boundary conditions—not on the specific source term—so the authors train a single neural operator that can be reused across different boundary values and source terms without retraining. NHMO outperforms existing neural PDE solvers on standard benchmarks.

title: How to Loop MoE: Flatten the Experts, Untie the Attention
authors: Shouren Wang, Chuang Ma, Mohsen Hariri, Debargha Ganguly, Wang Yang et al.
summary: This paper proposes Foil, a method for designing mixture-of-experts (MoE) models that reuse layers multiple times ("looping") to improve computational efficiency. The key insight is to flatten the expert structure — halving expert layers while doubling experts per layer — and give each loop pass its own attention parameters. The approach achieves better pretraining loss and downstream performance at the same parameter and compute budgets.

title: KV-streams for Efficient Compaction in Agentic Reinforcement Learning
authors: Emiliano Penaloza, Dane Malenfant, Dheeraj Vattikonda, Roger Creus Castanyer, Siddarth Venkatraman et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical bottleneck in scaling language model agents: fitting long context traces into GPU memory during training. The authors propose KV-streams, a technique that streams the key-value cache forward instead of repeatedly recomputing it, achieving 2.6–5x speedup in training throughput while maintaining or improving performance. This matters because agentic LLMs need long horizons to plan and reason, but memory constraints have forced painful tradeoffs between context length and training efficiency.

title: Towards Communication-Efficient Social Intelligence in Language Agents
authors: Linxiao Gong, Yijie Xu, Tianfu Wang, Yin Wu, Yili Wang et al.
summary: This paper tackles a practical problem: how can AI agents communicate with humans and other agents efficiently—saying just enough to achieve their goals without wasting words or attention. The authors propose Teacher-Assisted Communication Training (TACT), a method that trains agents to negotiate and coordinate better while using fewer tokens, tested on social interaction benchmarks where it achieves strong goal completion with substantially reduced communication costs.

title: Improving Test-Time Scaling with Adaptive Looped Transformers
authors: Yichen You, Tianyu Fu, Aosong Feng, Xingtai Lv, Xuefei Ning et al.
summary: This paper improves how language models scale during inference by introducing TaH2, a method that makes "looped transformers" (which reuse layers to save parameters) more efficient at test time. The key finding is that not all tokens benefit equally from extra computation iterations—by selectively routing tokens that need it, the model achieves 53% better accuracy-per-compute trade-offs on hard math benchmarks while staying parameter-efficient.

title: Copy the Same, Distill the Difference: Initializing Linear Vision Transformers
authors: Huaiyuan Qin, Muli Yang, Gabriel James Goenawan, Shiqi Huang, Min Kass Chong et al.
summary: This paper addresses how to efficiently initialize linear Vision Transformers (models that replace expensive attention mechanisms with faster linear-complexity alternatives) by reusing weights from pre-trained standard Vision Transformers. The key finding is counterintuitive: attention weights cannot be simply copied between the two architectures, but MLP (feedforward) weights can be, and attention's behavior can be recovered through knowledge distillation. This enables linear ViTs to match or exceed the performance of their slower Softmax-based counterparts while remaining computationally efficient.

title: FinAutoRubric: Expert-Guided Automatic Rubric Generation for Evaluating Financial Research Agents
authors: Hoyoung Lee, Suyeol Yun, Jack Haverty, Yunju Cho, Meesong Kim et al.
summary: This paper presents FinAutoRubric, a system that automatically generates evaluation rubrics for assessing financial research agents by combining expert guidance with AI-driven workflows. Rather than manually creating fixed rubrics for each financial benchmark task, experts provide reusable evaluation principles that agents use to generate query-specific scoring criteria, review them, and validate results—solving a critical problem in building trustworthy evaluations for AI systems operating in high-stakes financial domains.

title: Shockingly Simple Self-retrospection Improves Agentic Models Without RL
authors: Jonathan Light, Christopher Zhang Cui, Jeonghye Kim, Roger Creus Castanyer, Emiliano Penaloza et al.
summary: This paper shows that language model agents can improve their problem-solving performance by simply training on explanations of their own past attempts — without reinforcement learning or external rewards. The method, called Retrospection-Only Fine-Tuning (ROFT), has a language model agent attempt a task, generate a written explanation of what happened, and then fine-tune itself on predicting those explanation tokens. On software engineering benchmarks, ROFT matches or exceeds reinforcement learning baselines while being simpler and faster to train.

title: Harness Learning Enables Generalizable Test-Time Adaptation
authors: Alvin Zhang, Xuecheng Liu, Zixuan Wang, Fahim Tajwar, Daman Arora et al.
summary: This paper introduces harness learning, a method that trains AI agents to automatically revise their own execution programs (the "harness" — the code that orchestrates model calls and tool use) based on task feedback, without updating model weights. The key insight is that different tasks benefit from different ways of organizing computation, and the agent can learn to adapt this organization at test time to generalize to unseen problems.

title: X-Reset: Scaling Object-Centric Reinforcement Learning via Cross-Embodiment Resets
authors: Prithwish Dan, Chenyang Ma, Wei Zhan
summary: This paper introduces X-Reset, a method for training robot manipulation policies in simulation by using human hand-object demonstrations as a source of good starting states (resets) for reinforcement learning, rather than as trajectories to imitate. The key insight is that kinematically retargeting human demonstrations to robot embodiments and filtering for simulation stability creates a diverse, exploration-friendly reset distribution that helps RL policies learn dexterous manipulation of many objects without task-specific reward engineering.

title: Reinforcing Agentic Creativity in Scientific Ideation with Night Science
authors: Priyanka Kargupta, Silviu Cucerzan, Shweti Mahajan, Allen Herring, Jiawei Han et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical limitation of large language models: they tend to produce safe, predictable outputs that are poorly suited for open-ended scientific discovery. The authors introduce AI Night-Scientist, a reinforcement learning framework that teaches models when and how to explore creative, unconventional reasoning paths. The result is substantially more diverse and novel research proposals, with improvements in citation impact and originality.

title: Rethinking Personalized Generation: Test-Time Alignment via Factorized Ranking Models
authors: Qiyao Ma, Junshan Zhang, Zhe Zhao
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem: large language models trained with standard alignment methods optimize for an "average" user and ignore the diversity of real preferences. The authors show that personalized generation—tailoring outputs to individual users—can be tackled efficiently at test time using lightweight ranking models rather than expensive reward models. They propose a million-parameter MLP-based ranker that scores candidate outputs 10,000× faster than billion-parameter reward models while delivering better personalization across nine datasets.

title: Denoising Multi-Robot Trajectories
authors: Yuhao Zhang, Keisuke Okumura, Ajay Shankar, Amanda Prorok
summary: This paper presents D4orm, a diffusion-denoising framework that solves multi-robot trajectory planning by iteratively refining candidate paths to be collision-free and dynamically feasible. Rather than using traditional optimization, it leverages massive parallel sampling on GPUs to efficiently generate high-quality solutions, scaling from small robot teams to 100+ robots and real-world quadrotor deployments.

title: EvE: An Alternate Optimizer to Adam
authors: Shashank Raj, Kalyanmoy Deb
summary: This paper introduces EvE (Evolutionary Explorer), a new optimizer that combines differential evolution with targeted gradient descent to speed up neural network training and hyperparameter search.
