The work matters because autonomous agents are increasingly managing user accounts, yet this vector of attack—attacking through the platform's own ranking mechanism—was largely unexplored.

title: Propose, Don't Judge: An Anytime-Valid Referee for LLM Agents That Mine Investment Factors
authors: Bo Qu, Mingguang Chen, Licheng Wang
summary: This paper studies how to safely deploy LLM agents in quantitative finance factor research—the process of discovering and validating trading signals. The key idea: let the agent *propose* investment factors, but have a frozen, independent "referee" *judge* them using only future market outcomes. This approach guarantees statistical validity (no false discoveries) at any stopping time, while empirically showing LLMs outperform simpler baselines at factor generation, though with a cost in validation speed.

title: WTF?! Simulation-Free Reinforcement Learning with Wasserstein-Tilted Flow Maps
authors: Abbas Mammadov, Jerry Y. Huang, Justin Lin, Partha Kaushik, Sheel Shah et al.
summary: This paper introduces Wasserstein-Tilted Flow Maps (WTF), a method for fine-tuning pre-trained generative flow models to maximize reward without running simulations. Instead of the standard approach of reweighting the base distribution (KL tilting), the method directly transports individual samples toward higher rewards using optimal transport regularization. The key innovation is showing this optimization problem reduces to a deterministic control problem on the flow itself, enabling a simulation-free algorithm that's 280× more compute-efficient than existing baselines while maintaining diversity.

title: Loss Choice or Model Choice? The Role of Forecast Level in Cryptocurrency Volatility Forecasting
authors: Andrzej Tokajuk, Jarosław A. Chudziak
summary: This paper investigates whether loss function choice or model architecture matters more for cryptocurrency volatility forecasting. The authors show that when you adjust for the overall forecast level (a hidden factor that makes losses appear more important than they are), model selection becomes the primary driver of forecasting quality, while loss choice has less influence than raw comparisons suggest.

title: The Computational Value of Sensory-Aligned Receptive Fields Depends on Neuronal Expressivity
authors: Agnese Adorante, Aaron Spieler, Anna Levina
summary: This paper investigates whether biologically-inspired structured receptive fields—like those found in sensory neurons that respond selectively to specific features—provide computational benefits beyond just reducing connectivity. Using recurrent neural networks, the authors show that receptive fields aligned with task-relevant sensory coordinates improve accuracy, but this advantage shrinks as individual neurons become more expressive. The finding suggests that structured inputs matter as a computational prior, not merely for wiring efficiency.

title: NeuroRule: Making Black-Box Neural Networks Explainable through Rule-set Evolution
authors: Tapaswini Kodavanti, Hormoz Shahrzad, Risto Miikkulainen
summary: This paper proposes NeuroRule, a method to convert opaque neural networks into human-readable rule-sets using evolutionary algorithms. The key insight: you can distill a black-box model's decision logic into simple logical rules without needing the original training data, making neural networks trustworthy enough for high-stakes decisions like healthcare or finance.

title: Rethinking Pairwise Token Interaction in Spiking Transformers
authors: Sicheng Shen, Dongcheng Zhao, Zhiyuan Li, Jinyan Yu, Qian Zhang et al.
summary: This paper proposes Gated Spike Axial Propagation (GSAP), a new way for spiking neural networks to handle token interactions. Spiking neural networks use sparse, binary spike events to process information efficiently, but when applied to transformers, they suffer from communication bottlenecks because tokens only interact when their spike patterns match exactly. GSAP decouples information propagation from pattern matching, enabling distant tokens to communicate through structured sequential propagation rather than pairwise coincidence, potentially making neuromorphic transformers more practical for real-world tasks.

title: Risk Measures under Paired-Ambiguity: A Deep Learning Reflected BSDE Framework
authors: Nacira Agram, Jan Rems, Emanuela Rosazza Gianin
summary: This paper solves the problem of deciding when to exercise options (like American options) when there is uncertainty about both the true probability model and the discount rate used for valuation. The authors use deep learning to approximate solutions to complex mathematical equations (reflected BSDEs) that describe optimal stopping under this "paired ambiguity." The work matters because real-world financial decisions involve both model risk and parameter uncertainty, and this framework provides a practical computational method to handle both simultaneously.

title: Financial Language Models as Applied Artificial Intelligence Systems for News-Based Trading under Market Frictions
authors: Kemal Kirtac
summary: This paper presents MFAST, a framework that uses language models to turn financial news into trading signals while accounting for real-world constraints like transaction costs and liquidity. It's the first integrated system to rigorously test whether NLP-based sentiment extraction actually works for profitable trading when you include market frictions — the delays, costs, and constraints that exist in real trading.

title: OrderFusion+: Probabilistic Buy--Sell Price Trajectory Forecasting in Intraday Electricity Markets
authors: Runyao Yu, Derek W. Bunn
summary: This paper introduces OrderFusion+, a deep learning model that forecasts probabilistic buy and sell price trajectories in intraday electricity markets by combining order book data from multiple delivery products. It improves upon the prior OrderFusion model by incorporating neighboring-product information and handling price trajectories rather than single-product snapshots, advancing the practical accuracy of trading decisions in real-time electricity markets.

title: Two Models of Event Finality: Functional Alignment, Contestability, and Empirical Comparability on Polymarket and Kalshi
authors: Maksym Nechepurenko
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental infrastructure problem in decentralized prediction markets: different platforms (Polymarket and Kalshi) define "finality" — when an event contract is economically settled — through incompatible institutional mechanisms, making cross-venue comparison and aggregation impossible. The authors develop a formal framework to identify what conditions must align for duration comparisons to be meaningful, then empirically map the finality pathways on both platforms and identify where exact matching fails.

title: SAiFE-gym: Model-based Environments for Automated Market Making with Concentrated Liquidity
authors: Georgios Chionas, Charalampos Kleitsikas, Stefanos Leonardos, Leandro Sánchez-Betancourt, Carmine Ventre
summary: SAiFE-gym is a Python simulation toolkit for training and testing trading algorithms in decentralized finance markets where liquidity providers can concentrate their capital in specific price ranges. The paper addresses a gap in RL research by providing realistic, modular environments that capture how modern automated market makers (AMMs) work, enabling researchers to develop smarter trading strategies under real market uncertainty.

title: Separated Signal Libraries: Packing, Saturation, and Joint Spectral Limits
authors: Marc da Costa Nunes
summary: This paper studies how to build large libraries of trading signals (forecasts of asset returns) while keeping them sufficiently uncorrelated with each other. The authors frame signal selection as a geometric packing problem—signals are points on a sphere, and a correlation cap means maintaining minimum angular separation—and prove when an equally-weighted portfolio of many signals converges to a theoretically predictable quantity. The work matters because portfolio managers need to understand whether combining many imperfect signals produces reliable results or just dilutes signal strength.

title: Design of a Deep Learning Credit Risk Early Warning System Integrating Multi-source Heterogeneous Data
authors: LiYang Wang, Zhen Zhong, Zhen Tian, Keyu Chen, Keyu Chen
summary: This paper develops an early warning system for credit risk using deep learning and attention mechanisms to integrate diverse data sources—transaction histories, social networks, and other behavioral signals. The system detects credit problems faster and more accurately than traditional rule-based approaches, helping financial institutions intervene before defaults occur.

title: Towards foundation models for insurance risk modelling
authors: Christopher Blier-Wong
summary: This paper proposes using foundation models — large pre-trained neural networks — to extract predictive signals from unstructured insurance data like claim narratives, images, and sensor readings. Instead of manually engineering features from these rich data sources, foundation models can learn patterns automatically and then be adapted to specific actuarial tasks, potentially helping insurers make better risk assessments and reserve estimates faster and with less domain expertise.

title: ViperQ: Order Flow Pattern Recognition via Auction Market Theory for Reinforcement Learning Trading
authors: Asser Moustafa, Rares-Mihail Neagu, Jugal Kalita
summary: This paper introduces ViperQ, a reinforcement learning trading system that uses Auction Market Theory to understand order flow patterns and make trading decisions. Instead of relying on simple price bars or order book snapshots, ViperQ builds its understanding from microstructure primitives like volume distribution and price levels, achieving strong returns on real stock data—163.6% ROI on Tesla and 116.5% on Nvidia over a held-out test year. The work bridges practitioner trading theory with academic RL, showing that market microstructure patterns can be computationally useful.

title: Large Signal Libraries: Equal-Weight Limits and the Divergent Spectra of Signals and PnL
authors: Marc da Costa Nunes
summary: This paper investigates why large portfolios of trading signals often align unexpectedly well with market structure—specifically, why ~3,000 signals across 20 assets showed 90% correlation with the market's leading return component. The author develops population theory to distinguish between signal geometry, their principal components, and actual profit-and-loss (PnL) outcomes, revealing that crowding alone doesn't explain such alignment and that signal libraries follow predictable spectral properties under different research designs.

title: Simple Dynamic Stock/Bond/Gold Portfolios
authors: Nikhil Devanathan, Alexandros E. Tzikas, Stephen P. Boyd
summary: This paper asks whether simple dynamic rebalancing strategies can beat the classic 60/40 stock/bond portfolio over a 20-year period. Using publicly available data and standard quantitative finance methods, the authors show that volatility-controlled portfolios and convex optimization-based approaches consistently outperform fixed-weight benchmarks and popular risk-based methods like risk parity, while keeping rebalancing monthly and costs realistic.

title: Explainable Deep Learning for Price-Trade Dynamics: From Black-Box Forecasts to Effective Parametric Models
authors: Manuel Naviglio, Fabrizio Lillo
summary: This paper uses neural networks as a tool to discover the hidden structure of how prices and trades interact in financial markets, rather than just making better predictions. By applying explainability techniques (specifically Shapley values) to a trained deep network, the authors reverse-engineer an interpretable parametric model that captures nonlinear price-volume dynamics while remaining transparent enough for traders and risk managers to understand and trust.

title: Artificial Intelligence in Equity and Crypto Markets: Progress, Profitability Evidence, and the Limits of Automated Investing
authors: Linsen Zhu, Mengqing Cai
summary: This review examines whether AI systems can reliably generate investment profits in equity and crypto markets. The authors find that while AI has made real progress in prediction, text analysis, and portfolio design, evidence for *sustained net returns* (after costs and real-world constraints) remains weak — and no AI approach is proven to work consistently across different market conditions and asset scales.

title: Convex Modeling of Price Cross-Impact over Time
authors: Vincent Yinjun-Wang, Madeleine Udell
summary: This paper builds a mathematical model of how trades affect prices—both in the same contract (self-impact) and in related contracts (cross-impact)—and how that impact decays over time. The model uses convex optimization to help traders plan multi-leg trades (like commodity spreads) without overestimating their costs, which matters because even small improvements in cost estimates can unlock profitable strategies in thin markets.

title: The Analyst in the Prompt: Role, Retrieval, and Memory Biases in LLM Financial Analysis
authors: Ahmed Asaad, Amr Mohamed, Yang Zhang, Omneya Abdelsalam
summary: This paper investigates how LLMs' financial analysis changes based on user context (roles, memory, profiles)—and whether they retrieve different evidence or interpret the same evidence differently. Testing 3,575 SEC filings across twelve models, the authors find that most bias comes from *interpretation*, not evidence selection, and propose two mitigation strategies with mixed results. This matters because LLMs are increasingly used for high-stakes financial decisions where consistency and objectivity are critical.

title: Insights on Time-consistent Deep Hedging under Elicitable Dynamic Risk Measures
authors: Shuyi Zhang, Frédéric Godin
summary: This paper develops a deep learning approach to hedging financial derivatives (specifically basket options) using time-consistent dynamic risk measures — a framework that ensures sequential hedging decisions remain coherent over time. The work tackles a practically important but computationally hard problem: designing hedging strategies that don't suffer from "precommitment bias" (where a single upfront decision becomes suboptimal as time passes and new information arrives). The key innovation is leveraging conditional elicitability of spectral risk measures to make the optimization tractable in high dimensions.

title: SPADE: Self-Play in Adaptive Synthetic Executable Environments
authors: Bo Liu, Simon Yu, Yiding Jiang, Ao Qu, Andrew Zhao et al.
summary: This paper introduces SPADE, a self-play framework where a single language model simultaneously acts as both an Environment Designer (writing training tasks as executable code) and a Reasoning Agent (learning to solve them). The key insight is that by making environment design learnable rather than fixed, the system can continuously generate harder problems at the edge of the agent's abilities, enabling open-ended self-improvement without human-curated task pools.

title: ADEPT: Accelerating Dexterity via Pre-Training and Post-Training using Reinforcement Learning
authors: Jayjun Lee, Jessica Yin, Asif Rana, Nicholas Blauch, Sam Mady et al.
summary: ADEPT is a large-scale reinforcement learning framework that teaches robots with many joints (like multi-fingered hands) to perform complex manipulation tasks by first pretraining on a generic object-repositioning task, then fine-tuning for specific downstream behaviors. The approach enables robots to transfer skills learned in simulation to the real world while maintaining dexterity — fine motor control — even after task-specific training, solving long-horizon tasks from raw camera and touch sensor data.

title: Learned, Then Lost: A Measured Single-Example Counterfactual in Pre-training
authors: Zachary Speck, Asa Shepard
summary: This paper measures—rather than estimates—how much a single training example influences a finished language model by running expensive counterfactual pre-training experiments. The authors trained 32 GPT-2 models from scratch, injecting a 194-token passage into one batch at a critical moment, then tracked what happened to the model's weights, loss landscape, and learned representations. They find that examples are learned quickly but then forgotten completely, leaving almost no trace in the final model.

title: Beyond the Transcript: Detecting Covert Co ordination in Latent Multi-Agent Communication
authors: Ramneet Kaur, Pradyumna Chari, Ramesh Raskar, Jugad Singh, Sumit Kumar Jha et al.
summary: This paper reveals that language-model agents can coordinate covertly through hidden internal states that bypass text transcripts, and proposes Verifiable Latent Alignments (VLA)—a monitoring and steering framework to detect and prevent such collusion. The work matters because as AI systems become multi-agent and increasingly autonomous, hidden communication channels pose a safety risk that current transcript-based oversight cannot catch.

title: Continuous-Time Reinforcement Learning for Controlled Hawkes Jump-Diffusions
authors: Tomasz R. Bielecki, Thibaut Mastrolia, Haoze Yan
summary: This paper develops a machine learning method to control complex financial systems (Hawkes jump-diffusions) that have memory effects and don't fit standard control theory. The key innovation is "Markovianizing" non-Markovian processes — converting them into simpler forms that RL algorithms can handle — then using continuous-time policy gradients to find optimal control strategies. This matters because many real financial phenomena (like market microstructure and event clustering) are naturally described by Hawkes processes, but controlling them has been mathematically intractable.

title: Autonomous Cyber Defense in Connected Vehicles: A Multi-Agent Approach to V2X Security
authors: Krishna Teja Medam
summary: This paper addresses a critical security problem in connected vehicles: adversaries can inject fake safety messages (like false emergency braking alerts) in under 100 milliseconds, before a vehicle's systems can distinguish real threats from attacks. The authors propose a three-tier multi-agent system — onboard vehicle agents, roadside edge agents, and cloud services — that makes fast, safety-aware decisions about whether to accept, quarantine, or escalate each incoming V2X (vehicle-to-everything) message, with strict latency budgets matched to real communication standards.

title: SCORE: Subject Coordinate Recovery for Label-Free Cross-Subject EEG-to-Image Retrieval
authors: Zhenyao Cui, Siyuan Kan, Siyang Li, Ziwei Wang, Dongrui Wu
summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in brain-computer interfaces: making EEG-to-image retrieval work across different people without labeled training data for each new user. The key insight is that different brains encode visual concepts in similar ways but along different "coordinate directions" — like rotating a map. SCORE solves this by learning to recover each person's unique brain coordinate system at deployment time using only unlabeled EEG and images, achieving state-of-the-art cross-subject performance.

title: Beyond Trial Averaging: Anchoring Neural and Visual Representations for Few-Repetition Brain-to-Image Retrieval
authors: Zhenyao Cui, Siyuan Kan, Dingkun Liu, Dongrui Wu
summary: This paper tackles brain-to-image retrieval — decoding what visual images someone is seeing from brain signals — with a focus on making it work with very few repetitions of the same stimulus. Current methods require averaging 80+ brain recordings per image, which is impractical in real settings; the authors show this performance drop with few repetitions isn't just noise, but also misalignment between representations, and propose NEAR (neural-anchor-based retrieval), a framework that uses high-repetition data as an anchor to guide both query denoising and image placement.

title: PGFS++: Molecular Property Improvement under Synthesis and Diversity Constraints
authors: Boqiao Zhang, Godbless James, Sai Krishna Gottipati, Andrew Fitzgibbon
summary: This paper addresses a practical problem in drug discovery: improving molecular properties like drug efficacy while ensuring the designed molecules can actually be synthesized. The authors develop PGFS++, a reinforcement learning framework that optimizes molecules through realistic chemical reactions, using in-stock building blocks and known synthesis routes, while preventing a common failure mode where the optimizer "cheats" by collapsing diverse inputs into the same high-reward molecule.

title: Pretraining Reusable Inference Across Views with Synthetic Task Priors
authors: Jielong Lu, Zhihao Wu, Jiajun Yu, Zhaoliang Chen, Haishuai Wang
summary: This paper proposes SIMPLE, a method to pretrain reusable multi-view inference procedures that can adapt to new tasks with minimal data. Rather than learning a fixed way to combine information from different data sources (images, text, omics data, etc.), the authors train a task-conditioned model that learns *how* to fuse views by seeing examples—similar to how humans solve new problems by analogy. The key innovation is a synthetic task generator that creates diverse training scenarios so the model learns general principles about which views matter, when they conflict, and how to handle missing information.

title: Open-MOPD: Diagnosing and Fixing Capability Imbalance in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
authors: Huan-ang Gao, Haohan Chi, Yong Yan, Shiyuan Feng, Hanlin Wu et al.
summary: This paper diagnoses why multi-teacher distillation—combining multiple specialized RL experts into one general student model—fails to capture available performance, finding that token-level optimization budgets are severely misallocated across domains rather than due to gradient conflicts. The authors propose Open-MOPD, a framework using token-share balancing and dynamic budget allocation, that recovers 83% of potential performance (up from 36%) and release a reproducible post-training recipe for language models.

title: Robust Risk Under Evolving Uncertainty: A Wasserstein Counterpart of the Entropic Value-at-Risk
authors: Deep Kumar Ganguly, Jan Křetínský
summary: This paper proposes a new risk measure—the Wasserstein entropic value-at-risk—that helps agents make safer decisions under uncertainty, especially when learning about their environment. Unlike existing entropy-based approaches, this measure accounts for unlikely "catastrophic" scenarios that standard methods might miss, making it more suitable for safety-critical applications where learning gradually increases confidence.

title: What is Missing from AI Post-Training AI: An Empirical Analysis
authors: Joy Jia Yin Lim, Xin Huang, Hao Peng, Yaxi Lu, Xin Cong et al.
summary: This paper studies AI agents that autonomously post-train large language models—writing code, launching experiments, and iterating toward better performance. The key finding: these agents excel at fine-tuning within a chosen training strategy but fail to revise their high-level approach as evidence accumulates. The authors show this isn't due to missing experience, guidance, or compute, but rather the absence of a mechanism for strategy re-evaluation during execution.

title: Diffusion Models for High-Dimensional Clustered Data: Intrinsic-Dimension Adaptivity via Bayesian Classification
authors: Yuga Iguchi, Paul Fearnhead
summary: This paper proves that diffusion models—a class of neural networks that generate data by gradually removing noise—automatically adapt to the intrinsic structure of clustered, high-dimensional data. The key finding is that the error scales with the *intrinsic dimension* of each cluster (its true complexity) rather than the ambient dimension (the full space), even when clusters have heterogeneous structures. This matters because it explains why diffusion models work well on real data that often lives on lower-dimensional manifolds hidden in high-dimensional spaces.

title: Adaptive Memory and Reflection Multi-Agent System for Medical Question Answering
authors: Pradeep Murugesan, Luoxiao Yang, Xueli Chen, Xinqi Fan
summary: This paper presents AMR, a multi-agent system for medical question answering that uses specialized agents with persistent memory and reflection-based feedback to solve complex medical cases. Unlike traditional single-agent systems, it routes questions through solo, collaborative, or escalated workflows, and includes ethical oversight—achieving strong results on medical QA benchmarks while emphasizing trustworthiness in healthcare settings.

title: Grading the Graders: Verification Autonomy Levels (L0-L5) for LLM Reasoning
authors: Yajie Yin
summary: This paper proposes Verification Autonomy Levels (VAL), a classification system for evaluating how well different verification schemes can check LLM reasoning. The key insight is that most verification systems have a fundamental blind spot: they can confirm a proposed answer is correct, but cannot guarantee no better answer exists. The paper clarifies a confused literature by showing that formal completeness is only possible for properties that can be mathematically specified—everything else (fact-checking, diagnosis) tops out at checking correctness of individual steps.

title: rEDMRec: Distilling Large Language Model Reasoning into an Editable Experience Memory for Recommendation
authors: Minh Hoang Nguyen, Tung Le, Huy Tien Nguyen
summary: This paper proposes rEDMRec, a system that distills reasoning from a large language model into a compact, editable memory structure to power recommendation systems more efficiently. Instead of running expensive LLM reasoning on every ranking request, the system compresses the LLM's insights into four typed memory channels (user preferences, context, item perceptions, and contrastive comparisons) that a lightweight model can query directly—cutting inference costs while improving ranking quality by up to 13.3% on standard benchmarks.

title: Training Chemical Plausibility-Aware Large Language Models for Single-Step Retrosynthesis
authors: Bogdan Zagribelnyy, Ivan Ilin, Nikita Bondarev, Maksim Kuznetsov, Mathieu Reymond et al.
summary: This paper trains large language models to predict chemical reactions in reverse (retrosynthesis), a key step in drug discovery and materials science. The key innovation is using "Top-K prompting" — asking the model to generate multiple plausible reactions rather than one — combined with chemical correctness constraints and reward signals, achieving better performance on out-of-distribution benchmarks than prior approaches.

title: DentAgent: Evidence-Centric Multi-Agent Coordination for Multimodal Dental Reasoning
authors: Zijie Meng, Xiwei Dai, Yixuan Tang, Jin Hao, Yang Feng et al.
summary: DentAgent is a multi-agent AI system that coordinates specialized agents to reason over dental data (X-rays, photos, 3D scans, text) and generates diagnostic decisions backed by explicit evidence. Current dental AI systems work in isolation per data type; this framework unifies them and forces the system to show its work—which matters because traceable medical reasoning builds trust and catches errors in high-stakes healthcare.

title: GEAR: Generative Expansion and Real Anchoring for Two-Stage Distillation of Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Qi Qin, Jiajie Zhu, Dali Chen, Yuzhao Zhang, Jia-Xing Han et al.
summary: This paper presents GEAR, a method to distill large tabular foundation models (neural networks trained on structured data) into tiny, fast models that run on standard computers. The key innovation is a two-stage process: first, generate synthetic data to expand training coverage while learning from the original model's predictions; second, re-anchor the student model to real data to avoid errors from synthetic examples. The result is 50–2800× faster inference with minimal accuracy loss.

title: A Unifying Relational Perspective on Expressive Lottery Tickets
authors: Lorenz Kummer, Samir Moustafa, Anatol Ehrlich, Franka Bause, Marco Nennstiel et al.
summary: This paper proves that sparse graph neural networks can retain their expressive power—the ability to distinguish different graph structures—even after aggressive pruning. The authors generalize prior lottery ticket results to multi-relational and temporal graphs, showing that random pruning has a mathematically quantifiable probability of preserving expressivity. This matters because it bridges neural network compression (making models faster and smaller) with theoretical guarantees about what those smaller models can still represent.

title: CentaurBench: Benchmarking LLM Capabilities on Augmenting vs. Automating Real-World Work Tasks
authors: Pattaraphon Kenny Wongchamcharoen, Kris Gulati, Min Min Fong, Abhishek Nagaraj
summary: This paper challenges how we measure LLM capabilities by showing that the models best at automating tasks aren't necessarily best at helping weaker agents complete those tasks. Using seven real-world tasks, researchers compare "automation mode" (LLM produces the output directly) against "augmentation mode" (LLM assists a weaker worker who produces the final output), and find these two rankings are only weakly correlated—suggesting current benchmarks miss a critical use case.

title: DART-SD: Diamond-topology Aware Retrieval and Tuning for Self-Distillation of Multi-Turn Tool-Calling Agents
authors: Hangrui Xu, Jiarui Wang, Yang Yang, Chuanbo Zhu, Fangda Chen et al.
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in training autonomous agents: when tasks have multiple valid solution paths (order-independent sub-goals), standard trajectory imitation learning forces all solutions into a single path, penalizing valid alternatives. DART-SD instead models the solution space as a "diamond topology" — a lattice of converging paths — and uses targeted self-distillation to correct only the parts of reasoning that failed, preserving correct reasoning steps that precede failure points.

title: Bayesian Partner Modelling enables Adaptive Replanning for LLM Coordination
authors: Harsh Goel, Aditya Sai Ellendula, Vaishnav Tadiparthi, Ehsan Moradi Pari, Hossein Nourkhiz Mahjoub et al.
summary: This paper tackles a key challenge in multi-agent LLM systems: agents often continue executing outdated plans when their teammates' strategies change mid-task. The authors introduce BayesBeliefAgent, which combines hierarchical LLM planning with Bayesian tracking to intelligently decide *when* to replan based on contradictions in observed partner behavior, rather than replanning constantly or ignoring strategy shifts. The method dramatically reduces unnecessary replans while keeping agents aligned with their teammates' actual strategies.

title: Debiased Inference for AI-Generated Data without Gold-Standard Labels: Identification via Multiple Imperfect Measurements
authors: Naoki Egami, Sooahn Shin
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem: when researchers use AI systems (like LLMs) to measure variables for statistical analysis, ignoring the AI's prediction errors causes bias and invalid confidence intervals in downstream results—even when AI accuracy exceeds 90%. The authors propose DMM (Debiased inference with Multiple Imperfect Measurements), a framework that combines multiple error-prone AI measurements to enable valid statistical inference *without* requiring expensive gold-standard labeled data.

title: SeisEvo: Evolution of Seismic Data Reconstruction Algorithms by Agents
authors: Yingjie Xu, Siwei Yu, Jianwei Ma
summary: This paper presents SeisEvo, a system that uses LLM-driven agents to automatically discover seismic data reconstruction algorithms rather than manually designing them or training neural networks. The key insight is that agents search through the design space of algorithm components (while respecting physical constraints), producing interpretable, standalone algorithms that outperform classical methods by 3–7 dB in signal-to-noise ratio without requiring any agent or neural network at inference time.

title: Multi-Level Market Making with Reinforcement Learning
authors: Patrick Cheridito, Moritz Weiss
summary: This paper applies reinforcement learning to market making—the task of profitably buying and selling assets by placing orders at multiple price levels in a limit order book. The key innovation is using deep learning to handle variable-length order data and strategic reward shaping to train an agent that dynamically adjusts order sizes and inventory levels in response to different types of market participants.

title: From Corpora to Co-Evolving Capabilities: Capability-Centric Data Design for Generalist Image Generation
authors: Xingjian Wang, Zhao Wang, Taihang Hu, Jun Zheng, Qing Jin et al.
summary: This paper proposes a capability-driven data infrastructure for training generalist image generation models that can handle both text-to-image synthesis and image editing tasks. Instead of optimizing datasets in isolation, the authors organize heterogeneous training data according to the dependencies between different generative capabilities, using specialized data engines and curriculum learning to co-evolve multiple skills. They curate a massive 440M-image dataset and train 3B and 6B parameter diffusion models that achieve broad visual coverage and effective transfer across tasks.

title: Multi-Agent AI System for Radiology Report Structuring and Quality Assurance with Independent Radiologist Evaluation
authors: Iryna Hartsock, Cesar Lam, Christopher Otteni, Aliya Qayyum, Robert Gatenby et al.
summary: This paper describes a locally deployed multi-agent AI system that automatically structures radiology reports into standardized anatomical sections and performs quality assurance checks to catch errors like section mismatches and undocumented critical findings. The system was evaluated on 638 real chest, abdomen, and pelvis CT reports, with independent radiologist validation showing 84% of reports achieved "excellent" or "good" quality ratings, suggesting that AI-assisted structuring could improve consistency and safety in clinical radiology workflows.

title: On the Fragility of Self-Improving Agents: Variance, Task Order, and Underspecification
authors: Qinyuan Ye, Yu Li, Yada Pruksachatkun, Jiaxin Zhang, Chien-Sheng Wu
summary: This paper exposes fundamental reliability problems in memory-based self-improving agents—systems that learn from streams of tasks and improve over time using a textual memory bank. The researchers found that these agents are fragile: their performance is noisy, highly dependent on the order tasks are presented in, and vulnerable to underspecification (lack of clear task definitions and feedback). The work calls for more rigorous evaluation and better human oversight mechanisms.

title: TokEval: A Tokenizer Evaluation Suite
authors: Clara Meister
summary: This paper introduces TokEval, a framework for systematically evaluating tokenizers — the algorithms that break text into subword units for language models to process. While tokenizers profoundly affect what language models can learn, they're typically chosen with minimal evaluation. TokEval measures linguistically and structurally meaningful properties (like whether digit boundaries align with place-value structure) and validates these metrics against downstream model performance across language, math, and code tasks.

title: Delegation Asymmetry in Agentic Recommender Systems: Measuring Two-Sided Receptivity in Online Dating
authors: Daria Leshchikova, Valentina V. Kuskova, Dmitry Zaytsev, Valerii Klimov
summary: This paper studies a critical but overlooked problem in AI-mediated dating platforms: users must be willing not just to delegate conversation to an autonomous agent, but also to receive messages from other users' agents. Using surveys of nearly 3,000 dating app users, the authors show these are psychologically distinct choices with a dramatic asymmetry—people are far more willing to deploy their own agent than to engage with someone else's. This matters because most agent-based platforms assume symmetric receptivity, but real deployments will fail if this imbalance isn't designed for.

title: StagedWorkspace: A Versioned Workspace for Knowledge-Work Agents
authors: Yining Hua, Hongbin Na, Yifan Zhou, Akshay Kalose, Cyrus Ayubcha et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in how AI agents handle knowledge work: they often operate on inconsistent versions of files when searching, editing, and reviewing documents. The authors introduce StagedWorkspace, a versioned workspace system that binds all agent views (parsed data and native files) to explicit versions, enabling agents to work reliably on code, spreadsheets, PDFs, and mixed-format projects. Experiments show this versioning improves agent performance by 8–12 percentage points on document tasks and enables significant gains over published baselines.

title: Language Has Two Parameters: Narrative-Induced Semantic Plasticity and Phase-Sensitive Interpretation
authors: Hollis Robbins
summary: This paper proposes that language understanding requires two parameters: amplitude (word co-occurrence strength, what embeddings capture) and phase (how coactivated meanings relate and combine). The author argues that current transformers and interpretability work ignore phase—a relational parameter indexed to individuals and dyads—which is essential for irony, allusion, and quotation. The work frames this formally using quantum probability notation and makes testable predictions about suppressed meanings and encounter order.

title: Optimize Your Sampling: Tuned Diffusion Sampling with Bayesian Optimization
authors: Travis Zhang, Christian Belardi, Justin Lovelace, Jin Peng Zhou, Saebyeol Shin et al.
summary: This paper addresses a simple but overlooked problem: how to choose the timesteps during diffusion model sampling to balance speed and quality. Instead of relying on fixed schedules or theoretical surrogates, the authors treat timestep selection as a black-box optimization problem and use Bayesian optimization to find better schedules directly. The result is dramatic efficiency gains—a 5-step schedule achieves 89–94% of the quality of 50 steps, cutting inference cost by 10x.

title: Where A Small Language Model Helps in Invoice Categorisation, Understood Through Embedding Geometry
authors: Emma Ceccherini, Daniel Lawson, Anjulika Salhan
summary: This paper shows that small language models (SLMs) like SBERT can accurately categorize invoices into accounting codes while remaining cost-effective and interpretable for in-house deployment. The authors analyze why this works by studying the geometric structure of sentence embeddings in financial text, finding that pre-trained embeddings naturally cluster by vendor identity and that these clusters correlate with classification performance.

title: Chain-of-Experience for Continual LLM Improvement
authors: Haoqin Tu, Yunhao Fang, Yizhong Wang, Cihang Xie, Shen Yan
summary: This paper studies how large language models can improve their performance through iterative test-time feedback—a capability called Chain-of-Experience (CoE). Rather than using models once at inference, the authors show that LLMs can learn and adapt by receiving feedback (from themselves or external signals) and refining their outputs across multiple iterations, achieving measurable gains in math, coding, and knowledge tasks while reducing computational costs.

title: Can Large Language Models Explain Flight Safety Events? A Prior-Guided Semantic LLM-based Approach
authors: Lu Xu, Xu Li, Linjiang Zheng, Fan Li, Riquan Zhang et al.
summary: This paper presents FlightLLM, a system that uses large language models to explain why flight safety incidents occur by converting numerical flight data into natural language descriptions. The key innovation is combining LLMs with domain knowledge and statistical classifiers to generate both accurate predictions and human-understandable explanations of dangerous flight events like hard landings.

title: Policy-Invariant Reward Shaping from LLM Feedback: A Framework for Hybrid RL Agents
authors: Christophe D. Hounwanou, John Emeka Eze, Yaé U. Gaba
summary: This paper addresses how to safely use language models to guide reinforcement learning agents by formalizing the hybrid LLM-RL architecture and proving that LLM-generated reward signals can be used for "reward shaping" (adjusting rewards to guide learning) without changing which policies are actually optimal—even when the LLM makes mistakes. This matters because combining LLMs with RL is becoming common in practice, but the theoretical guarantees for doing so safely have been unclear.

title: Judge, Retrieve, or Abstain: Uncertainty-Guarded LLM Judging with Provable Risk Guarantees
authors: Sher Badshah, Ali Emami, Hassan Sajjad
summary: This paper tackles a core problem in using LLMs as automated judges: how to evaluate factual correctness reliably when no reference answer exists. The authors propose a framework that combines parametric judgment (using the LLM's built-in knowledge) with retrieval-augmented judgment (using web search) and routes between them based on calibrated uncertainty thresholds—ensuring that false verdicts stay below a user-specified error rate with mathematical guarantees.

title: Against Political Polarization: A Unified Framework for Tracing Evolving Political Ideologies on Social Media
authors: Yijie Xu, Chao Wang, Hui Xiong
summary: This paper presents TSN4PI, a framework for detecting and predicting how people's political ideologies evolve on social media platforms. The key challenge is that political content is sparse and mixed with irrelevant posts, manual labeling is expensive and biased, and predicting future ideological shifts is hard. The authors combine large language models (neural networks trained on massive text) with graph neural networks (a technique for modeling relationships in networks) to filter noise, identify ideology, and forecast how beliefs change over time.

title: Do Large Language Models Play Six Degrees of Separation? Measuring Topological Compression in Long-Context Manifolds
authors: Md. Faiyaz Abdullah Sayeedi
summary: This paper reveals that LLMs organize their internal representations as small-world networks — structures where distant concepts connect through just a few semantic hops, like the classic "Six Degrees of Separation" game. By analyzing the hidden geometry of transformer models rather than surface-level attention patterns, the authors show that early layers fragment semantic concepts while deeper layers compress them into highly navigable pathways, enabling multi-hop reasoning. They validate this framework on hallucination detection in retrieval-augmented generation, suggesting that factually grounded outputs maintain structural coherence while hallucinations create topological collapse.

title: Procedural Content Metageneration via Program Search and Continual Abstraction Discovery
authors: Matthew Siper, Ahmed Khalifa, Julian Togelius
summary: This paper shows how to automatically generate video game levels and rule systems by evolving Python programs with language models, rather than designing individual levels by hand. The key innovation—Continual Abstraction Discovery—finds reusable code patterns during evolution and turns them into helper functions, which improves the quality of generated content. This matters because procedural content generation is tedious for game designers, and automatically discovering useful abstractions could scale content creation.

title: Collective Counterfactual Planning: Coordination, Consent, and Verification under Representational Constraints
authors: Chainarong Amornbunchornvej
summary: This paper introduces Collective Counterfactual Planning (CCP), a formal framework for understanding how teams coordinate to solve problems that no individual member can handle alone. The key insight is that coordination failures often stem not from lack of capability or knowledge, but from *representational constraints*—each agent sees and understands only a limited projection of the shared task space. The paper defines when a team can provably reach a shared goal and verify completion under these geometric limitations.

title: A Theoretical Framework for Parallel Lifelong MAPF Using Group Decentralized Planning
authors: Alex DeWeese, Jiaoyang Li, Guannan Qu
summary: This paper solves a major computational bottleneck in lifelong multi-agent path finding — the problem where many robots or agents must repeatedly move between destinations without crashing into each other or obstacles. The authors prove that a popular but slow algorithm (RHCR) is near-optimal, then use that insight to design a faster parallel version (GD-RHCR) that partitions agents into groups and plans for each group in parallel, maintaining the same quality guarantees while scaling to more agents.

title: AutoResearch: Insight In, Hallucination Out
authors: Yiming Ren, Xiang Liu, Qumeng Sun, Xiao Zhang, Jiahao Li et al.
summary: AutoResearch is a two-stage autonomous system that generates and executes research ideas while actively preventing hallucination and false conclusions. It combines idea generation (using domain knowledge and cross-review) with idea execution (coordinated agent-based experimentation and evidence validation), demonstrating that scientific rigor can be automated through systematic verification rather than relying solely on language model outputs.

title: Spatially explicit feature importance for building height estimation using research-access high-resolution SAR and optical sensors
authors: Guilherme Iablonovski, Pierre-Louis Frison, Tatiana Silva da Silva
summary: This paper estimates building heights in cities using freely available satellite data (radar and optical imagery) combined with machine learning, achieving 5-meter accuracy without expensive LiDAR. The key innovation is showing that different satellite sensors matter in different urban contexts — tall buildings rely on shadows, while low-rise buildings depend on footprint shape — which helps practitioners choose the right data for their region.

title: Thinking in a Low-Resource Language: What SFT Builds, What RL Fixes, What Accuracy Cannot See
authors: Ayoub Kirouane, Christos Petrocheilos
summary: This paper investigates what happens when you fine-tune large language models to reason in low-resource languages (Greek), and finds that standard accuracy benchmarks are too noisy to detect meaningful changes. Instead, the authors develop behavioral measurement techniques showing that supervised fine-tuning (SFT) successfully teaches models to reason *in* the target language rather than translate internally, while reinforcement learning (RL) fixes format violations and reasoning-channel leakage that SFT cannot address. The work matters because it reveals that model capability changes invisible to standard metrics are real and measurable — and that different training approaches fix different problems.

title: Offline Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning with a Physics-Informed World Model for Cooperative Mixed Traffic Control
authors: Lu Liu, Chi Xie, Xi Xiong
summary: This paper tackles cooperative control of connected and automated vehicles (CAVs) on congested highways using offline multi-agent reinforcement learning — training policies from previously collected data without needing real-time trial-and-error or complete knowledge of traffic states. The key innovation is embedding physics-based traffic dynamics directly into a world model, enabling the system to reconstruct full traffic conditions from limited local observations and learn safer, more interpretable control policies.

title: The Influence of Agent Models on the Complexity of Bus Routing
authors: Eva Deltl, Christian Komusiewicz, Jurek Rostalsky, Johannes Schröder, Luca Pascal Staus
summary: This paper studies the computational complexity of bus routing problems where multiple agents need to travel from start to end points using shared bus services. The authors prove that the problem becomes NP-hard (computationally intractable) under various reasonable assumptions about how agents value costs like walking distance and travel time, and they show these hardness results persist even on extremely simple network structures like star graphs.

title: Communicating Credit Risk with Large Language Models: Evaluation of Explanations from Standard and Alternative Data-Based Models
authors: Sahab Zandi, Noah Kostesku, Christophe Mues, María Óskarsdóttir, Cristián Bravo
summary: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can translate technical model explanations into plain-English narratives for credit risk decisions. Using real mortgage data, the authors compare three explanation pipelines (standard tabular, network-based, and hybrid) with three LLM variants, finding that the quality of input evidence matters more than which LLM is used, but that LLMs struggle reliably to communicate the *direction* of risk factors—a critical gap for regulatory compliance.

title: Information fusion and machine learning for sensitivity analysis using physics knowledge and experimental data
authors: Berkcan Kapusuzoglu, Sankaran Mahadevan
summary: This paper combines physics-based computational models with experimental data using machine learning to improve sensitivity analysis — understanding how input changes affect system outputs. The key innovation is using physics-informed machine learning (enforcing physical laws as constraints, or pre-training with simulation data) to get better and more reliable sensitivity estimates when both simulations and real measurements are available.

title: Expressivity In Multimodal Contrastive Learning
authors: Andrew Stuart, Florian Wolf
summary: This paper analyzes the theoretical expressivity of multimodal contrastive learning architectures—specifically models like CLIP that learn joint representations of text, images, and other modalities. The authors prove that the standard two-tower CLIP design can represent any joint distribution (universal approximation), but a common three-or-more-modality extension cannot, motivating a new "Hadamard-CLIP" variant that restores universal approximation while staying computationally efficient.

title: Policy Optimization and Statistical Inference for Online Contextual Matrix Games
authors: Liner Xiang, Yixin Wang, Hengrui Cai
summary: This paper tackles a practical problem at the intersection of online learning and game theory: how should an agent learn and act when payoffs depend both on observable context (like market conditions) and on rivals' strategic responses? The authors introduce online contextual matrix games and an algorithm called OnGameLearn that balances exploration-exploitation while learning both payoff structures and Nash equilibria, with statistical guarantees and a hotel pricing case study.

title: Automating Parent Selection Configuration in Genetic Programming with Agentic AI
authors: Jose Guadalupe Hernandez, Jui-Hsuan Chang, Anil Kumar Saini, Xi Li, Jason H. Moore
summary: This paper explores whether AI agents—systems that can reason and act autonomously—can automatically design and configure genetic programming systems. The researchers built an agentic framework that uses large language models (LLMs) to identify and implement parent selection algorithms (rules for choosing which solutions to breed together) for symbolic regression problems. The work shows that LLM reasoning combined with retrieval-augmented generation (accessing existing knowledge) can generate competitive algorithm implementations, suggesting AI agents may automate the tedious configuration work that evolutionary algorithm designers currently do by hand.

title: Don't Drop the BATON: Long-Horizon Robot Manipulation via Agentic Subtask Exploration and Transition-aware Memory
authors: Bingxin Xu, Yuzhang Shang, Emilio Ferrara
summary: This paper addresses the challenge of long-horizon robot manipulation — tasks requiring many sequential contact-heavy skills — by decomposing them into independently explored subtasks coordinated by an LLM agent with transition-aware memory. The key insight is that exploring whole multi-stage tasks is exponentially expensive (cost scales as T^K for K stages), but exploring individual subtasks and composing them is much cheaper (cost becomes T*K), if you handle the transitions between subtasks correctly. On a benchmark called RoboMemArena, BATON achieves 11.6% higher task success than prior state-of-the-art.

title: Q-based Variational Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Ondrej Bajgar, Peter Tisnikar, Alessandro Abate, Konstantinos Gatsis, Maike Osborne
summary: This paper introduces QVIRL, a method for learning reward functions from expert demonstrations while quantifying uncertainty over those rewards. Rather than assuming a single "correct" reward, the method produces a probability distribution, which is crucial for safety-critical tasks where we need to know how confident we are in the inferred preferences. The approach scales to high-dimensional problems (like raw pixel images) — a first for Bayesian inverse reinforcement learning.

title: AutoSR: Automatic Symbolic Regression by Searching Research States
authors: Kejia Zhang, Youran Sun, Xinyu Ren, Chugang Yi, Haizhao Yang
summary: AutoSR is an automated system that discovers scientific equations from noisy data by treating symbolic regression as a multi-agent investigation rather than a simple curve-fitting problem. Instead of just finding equations that fit the data, it builds up a "research state" — a record of reasoning, evidence, and review — that explains why a particular equation is scientifically credible, and it recovers correct formulas on benchmark problems where previous methods fail.

title: Data-Efficient and Interpretable Classification of Circulating Tumor Cell Phenotypes in Microfluidic Devices via Deep Learning
authors: Serena Su, Yifan Wang, Senwei Liang
summary: This paper develops a deep learning system to classify cancer cell types from their movement patterns in microfluidic devices—tiny lab channels that reveal how cells move based on their physical properties. The key innovation is a data-efficient training method called SubSeq that learns from short snippets of cell trajectories instead of full paths, plus interpretability techniques that show which parts of a trajectory matter for classification.

title: Towards Computational Provenance: Carrying Causal-State Evidence in Generated Text
authors: Benjamin Belay
summary: This paper investigates whether neural networks can embed hidden evidence of their internal computational states into generated text — evidence that remains detectable even when the final answer stays the same. The authors design controlled experiments where feed-forward networks and transformers must route through specific intermediate states to solve arithmetic tasks, then embed subtle statistical signatures of those states into their outputs. The work matters because it addresses a foundational question: can we verify *how* a language model arrived at an answer, not just *what* answer it gave?

title: Non-Crossing Deep Quantile Regression for Distributional Survival Prediction
authors: Shuai Huang, Zhe Qu, Zhaowei Hua, Guohao Shen, Rui Tang et al.
summary: This paper proposes a method to predict the full distribution of survival times (not just average risk) while ensuring quantile estimates remain logically ordered. The key innovation is a framework that uses deep neural networks (specifically Transformers and Kolmogorov-Arnold networks) to estimate multiple survival quantiles simultaneously while preventing crossing curves—a common problem in survival analysis when covariates affect early and late failures differently.

title: zLend: A Dual-Scope Cash-Flow Reconstruction Framework for On-Chain Credit Underwriting
authors: Girish G N, Ashutosh Sahoo, Akshay SP, Gurukiran S, Dhanashekar Kandaswamy
summary: zLend is a deployed system that evaluates creditworthiness for decentralized lending by reconstructing a borrower's cash-flow history directly from public blockchain transactions, without traditional credit bureaus or income verification. The key innovation is analyzing two separate views of a wallet—its total token holdings and its liquid stablecoin reserves—to catch borrowers who appear wealthy but lack actual spending power, then deriving repayment-capacity signals (liquidity coverage, cash-flow volatility, drawdown patterns) from these reconstructions.

title: HAF: Adapting Generalist VLAs to Humanoid Whole-Body Loco-manipulation via Hierarchical Action Flow and Spectral Latent RL
authors: Langzhe Gu, Chengkai Hou, Meng Li, Xinhua Wang, Jiaming Liu et al.
summary: This paper presents HAF, a framework that adapts general-purpose vision-language-action (VLA) models to control humanoid robots performing complex whole-body tasks that combine walking, posture control, and dual-arm manipulation. The core innovation is a two-stage approach: hierarchical action generation that breaks full-body commands into coordinated stages, plus a latent-space reinforcement learning pipeline that refines policies in the real world without retraining the large pretrained model—enabling safer, more efficient robot learning.

title: Model Hypnosis: Strong control of AI via additive subliminal effects
authors: Enric Boix-Adsera, Benedict Tessler
summary: This paper reveals that large language models can be reliably manipulated through subtle, seemingly irrelevant textual cues (like paraphrases or typos) that individually appear weak but combine to strongly steer model behavior — a phenomenon the authors call "model hypnosis." The finding matters because it exposes a hidden vulnerability in AI safety: models can be controlled through inconspicuous prompting techniques that are hard to detect, complicating both safety efforts and interpretability research.

title: GEO-Flag: Detecting and Measuring GEO-Optimized Web Content
authors: Junjie Chu, Ye Leng, Mingjie Li, Yun Shen, Xinyue Shen et al.
summary: This paper introduces methods to detect and measure "Generative Engine Optimization" (GEO) — the practice of strategically modifying web content to be favored by AI search engines like Google's Gemini. The authors create a benchmark dataset, develop a detection model using intervention-based training, and deploy it on real search results, finding that roughly 9% of indexed pages show signs of GEO. This matters because AI search engines synthesize information into single answers rather than listing sources, so optimized misinformation could spread more easily.

title: ClawGym II: Exploring Black-Box RL on Agent Harness
authors: Huatong Song, Fei Bai, Ming Yang, Renyuan Li, Jia Deng et al.
summary: This paper presents ClawGym II, a framework for training language model agents using reinforcement learning (RL) through complex external tools and harnesses (like code execution environments) without needing to modify their internals. The key innovation is treating these harnesses as black boxes — the RL system doesn't need to understand their implementation — and using sandbox infrastructure to run many parallel training rollouts stably and efficiently, demonstrating 10–15 point improvements on code generation benchmarks.

title: Neurosymbolic Embodied Agents
authors: Mohammad Albinhassan, Yuming Feng, Alessandra Russo, Pranava Madhyastha
summary: This paper presents a neurosymbolic agent that combines vision-language models with symbolic planning to execute long-horizon household tasks reliably. The key insight is that language models alone generate plausible plans that can violate environment constraints, so the authors add a symbolic layer (PDDL planning) that guarantees only executable actions are generated. The result: smaller open-source models achieve >90% success on complex household simulation tasks while using fewer tokens and images than direct approaches.

title: Semantic Bandits: In-Context Exploration-Exploitation is Biased by Semantic Priors
authors: David Eric Austin, Kaheer Suleman, Jackie Chi Kit Cheung
summary: This paper studies how large language models (LLMs) make exploration-exploitation trade-offs when deployed as decision-making agents. The key finding is that semantic information in action labels — the natural language descriptions of choices — biases LLM behavior in predictable ways, pushing them toward exploitation when labels sound promising and causing them to explore more under negative rewards. This matters because it reveals hidden vulnerabilities in LLM agents that aren't captured by classical decision-making theory.

title: Closing the Affective Loop: Multimodal Speaker-Listener Emotion-Dynamics-Aware Empathetic Social Robots
authors: Zi Haur Pang, Casey Kennington, Tatsuya Kawahara
summary: This paper presents AffectLoop, a social robot system that engages in empathetic dialogue by tracking both the user's emotional dynamics and the robot's own simulated emotional state, then generating responses that maintain emotional alignment. Unlike text-based chatbots that treat empathy as a one-way process, this system creates a "closed loop" where the robot's emotional responses feed back into the interaction, leading to better user satisfaction and emotional recovery in pilot testing.

title: Does the LM Head Create a Harmful Gradient Bottleneck? A Causal Test
authors: Anand Murugan
summary: This paper tests whether the language-model head — the final layer that maps hidden states to vocabulary logits — creates a harmful bottleneck during training. Using careful causal interventions, the authors show the head does compress gradients severely, but this compression is *not* actually harmful to learning; in fact, removing it makes training worse. The finding challenges a recent influential claim and reveals that neural networks may handle this geometric constraint better than theory suggests.

title: Reconstruction: A Blind Benchmark for Recovering Research Ideas from Pre-Publication Bibliographies
authors: Shaolong Chen, Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Xinmiao Yu, Lei Li et al.
summary: This paper introduces Reconstruction, a benchmark that tests whether language models can infer a published paper's core research idea by reading only its bibliography—without access to the paper itself or future literature. The authors find that single models struggle (3–15% success), but a multi-agent approach combining cross-model debate and tournament selection nearly triples performance to 23–42%, demonstrating that collaborative model reasoning can extract latent research intent from citation patterns alone.

title: 'If It Looks Like a User': Measuring Real-Time Moderation Effects via Social Media Simulation
authors: Enrico Verdolotti, Gianluca Nogara, Luca Luceri, Silvia Giordano
summary: This paper develops a calibrated agent-based simulator of social media information spread, grounded in real COVID-19 vaccine discourse data, to evaluate how well content moderation methods actually work when applied in real time. The key finding: static lab tests of moderation (removing bad actors after the fact) overestimate effectiveness, because remaining users compensate by resharing more content—a dynamic effect that only shows up in simulation.

title: Physics of Agents: Statistical Mechanics Predicts Collective Behavior of AI Agents
authors: Batu El, Jinhee Paeng, Fatih Dinc, Shiye Su, Mete Erdogan et al.
summary: This paper treats AI agents as a physical system, using statistical mechanics to predict how language-model agents behave when they interact in groups. The researchers studied over 10,000 communities of agents debating math questions and political topics, and discovered that collective behavior falls into three patterns: indifference, polarization, and consensus. Their model predicts individual agent trajectories and group outcomes with high accuracy, revealing that agents operate like particles minimizing social pressure.

title: VCE-Skill: Enhancing Skill Self-Evolution with Version-Change Experience
authors: Jianming Chen, Xuanbin Ye, Yawen Wang, Junjie Wang, Qing Wang et al.
summary: This paper addresses how AI agents can improve their reusable skills over time by learning from two complementary sources: execution trajectories from current tasks and historical version changes from public skill repositories. The key insight is that public skill evolution patterns provide generalizable "priors" — patterns that worked before — which can be combined with task-specific evidence to create better, more transferable skills. The method, VCE-Skill, achieves measurable improvements in skill quality and cross-model transfer performance.

title: Density-Reweighted Entropic Optimal Transport: Decoupling Geometry from Sampling Density
authors: Keyi Li, Yuval Kluger, Boris Landa
summary: This paper solves a practical problem in dataset alignment: when two datasets have similar geometric structure but very different sampling densities, standard optimal transport methods match points by density rather than geometry, producing misleading correspondences. The authors propose density-reweighted entropic optimal transport (EOT), which lets you dial down the influence of sampling density to recover geometrically faithful alignments. This matters because misaligned datasets break downstream analysis in biology, chemistry, and engineering.

title: Drive, Pack, Fly: The Travelling Thief Problem with Drone
authors: Kabir Murjani, Abhay Sobhanan
summary: This paper tackles the Travelling Thief Problem with Drone (TTP-D): a delivery optimization problem where a ground vehicle carries packages (getting slower as it loads) and launches a drone to fetch outlying items, reducing total time. The researchers combine exact mathematical optimization, metaheuristic algorithms, and deep reinforcement learning to maximize profit minus rental costs, showing that a hybrid approach (DRL + local refinement) offers good speed-quality tradeoffs.

title: Evolving Executable Pipeline Programs for AutoML with Language Models
authors: Sofoklis Kitharidis, Cor J. Veenman, Jan N. van Rijn, Thomas Bäck, Niki van Stein
summary: LACE is an AutoML system that uses large language models to evolve Python pipeline programs rather than selecting from a fixed set of components. Unlike traditional AutoML frameworks that tune predefined operators, LACE generates complete, executable, editable machine learning pipelines—achieving competitive accuracy with AutoGluon on tabular classification while returning code practitioners can directly inspect and modify.

title: MELD: A Protocol for Merging Knowledge Across Distributed Agentic Memories
authors: Lauri Lovén, Jaakko Sauvola, Jukka Riekki, Sasu Tarkoma
summary: This paper introduces MELD, a protocol that lets autonomous agents with separate memories share and reconcile knowledge without a central coordinator. When two agents learn the same fact stated differently, or discover conflicting claims, MELD automatically merges or flags these inconsistencies rather than silently losing information. The work matters because distributed AI systems increasingly need to collaborate while staying independent — and current approaches either lose knowledge or require centralized oversight.

title: LiD-GLM: Lipschitz-constrained Deep Generalized Linear Models
authors: Tom Splittgerber, Niklas Koenen, Marvin N. Wright, Werner Brannath
summary: This paper proposes LiD-GLM, a hybrid model combining traditional generalized linear models (GLMs) with neural networks while maintaining interpretability. The key innovation is using invertible residual networks (i-ResNets) with Lipschitz constraints to allow flexible nonlinear learning while quantifying and controlling how far the model deviates from its classical statistical foundation.

title: A Control-Theoretic Formulation of Global Workspace Theory
authors: Ryota Kanai
summary: This paper formalizes Global Workspace Theory — a neuroscience theory of consciousness — using control theory. The authors propose the Global Mediation Workspace (GMW), which treats a candidate brain region as an open system that receives inputs, transforms them internally, and broadcasts outputs. They test this framework on synthetic data and preliminary neural recordings, showing it can identify the mechanism underlying conscious access.

title: Self-Supervised Auxiliary Task Discovery for Stable Reinforcement Learning in Stock Trading
authors: Arishi Orra, Himanshu Choudhary, Manoj Thakur
summary: This paper proposes an automated framework for discovering auxiliary tasks in reinforcement learning agents trained for stock trading. Instead of manually designing auxiliary tasks (which are helper objectives that improve learning), the system learns what tasks would best stabilize training and boost performance across changing market conditions. The approach is evaluated on four major stock indices and shows improved robustness and profitability compared to existing methods.

title: Learning Stock Trading Policies via Barycenter-Based Adversarial Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Arishi Orra, Himanshu Choudhary, Manoj Thakur
summary: This paper proposes BRaG, a framework that learns stock trading strategies by combining inverse reinforcement learning with adversarial imitation learning and risk constraints. The key innovation is using a Wasserstein barycenter to aggregate multiple expert trading strategies into a single stable pseudo-expert, which then pretains a policy before further refinement with real market rewards. The approach demonstrates stronger returns and more stable risk profiles across major global equity markets compared to traditional and deep RL baselines.

title: FirstDiff: One-Step Diffusion-Based Anomaly Detection for Multivariate Time Series via Initial Noise Prediction
authors: Ali Boudaghi, Alireza Nemati, Hadi Zare
summary: This paper proposes FirstDiff, a fast anomaly detection method for multivariate time series that uses diffusion models — neural networks trained to remove noise from data. Instead of running the full reverse diffusion process (many iterative steps), FirstDiff detects anomalies by examining the noise prediction from just the first step, making it much faster while maintaining high accuracy.

title: Mental Model Management: An Operator-Based Framework for LLM Memory
authors: Oliver Kramer
summary: This paper proposes Mental Model Management (3M), a framework that gives large language models an explicit mechanism for organizing and updating knowledge as compact, evolving conceptual chunks rather than simply accumulating raw text. The framework uses a set of operators (extract, retrieve, add, update, reorganize, detect inconsistencies, derive) to maintain and reason over these structured mental models, addressing a real limitation of current LLMs: they lack persistent, updatable internal knowledge representations that can grow and adapt over time.

title: Language models suffer from a curse of ambiguity
authors: Nicolas Zucchet, Hyun Dong Lee, Scott Linderman
summary: This paper identifies a fundamental problem in how language models learn probability distributions over tokens: ambiguous distributions (where many tokens are plausible next-words) are much harder for neural networks to learn accurately. The authors trace this "curse of ambiguity" to concrete architectural factors—requiring more model capacity, larger embeddings, longer training, and amplifying sampling noise—and validate their findings on both synthetic tasks and real language models. This matters because modern LLMs increasingly rely on sampling from these learned distributions, so getting them right is critical for both accuracy and reliability.

title: Generation-Powered Inference for Distribution-Valued Outcomes
authors: Yijiao Zhang, Hongzhe Li
summary: This paper proposes generation-powered inference (GPI), a statistical framework that uses imperfect generative models to improve inference on distribution-valued outcomes — like predicting how cells respond to genetic changes. The key insight is that even flawed generative models contain useful information; GPI shows how to extract and leverage that information rigorously, with statistical guarantees, without assuming the generative model is correct.

title: Decoding the Past: An Uncertainty-Aware Deep Learning Framework for Sex Attribution in Prehistoric Hand Stencils
authors: Karel Becerra, Boris Mederos, Dean Snow, Ramón A. Mollineda
summary: This paper applies deep learning with explicit uncertainty quantification to determine the biological sex of individuals who created prehistoric hand stencils from the Upper Paleolithic period. The researchers built an ensemble framework that combines multiple neural networks and validation techniques to handle the degradation and ambiguity inherent in ancient rock art, producing both predictions and confidence measures that distinguish between anatomically clear and ambiguous cases.

title: Handover of In-Context Learning State Across Session Boundaries
authors: Masahiro Kato, Taka Kato
summary: This paper addresses a practical problem: when an LLM task spans multiple sessions (due to context limits, restarts, or handoffs to other agents), what information must be preserved to maintain the model's understanding? The authors develop a theoretical framework showing that handover can be characterized by predictive equivalence, derive memory requirements for different scenarios, and propose a three-part record structure that balances fidelity with efficiency. This matters because multi-session workflows are common in real applications, yet there's no principled way to decide what to save.

title: Participatory Moral AI Is Not Neutral: The Invisible Hand of Developers
authors: Taenyun Kim, Edyta Bogucka, Daniele Quercia
summary: This paper reveals that "participatory moral AI"—the practice of polling people on ethical dilemmas to train AI systems—is never neutral. Before any vote happens, developers make three hidden choices: which moral features to ask about, which people to poll, and how to phrase the question. Each choice shapes the outcome. The research tests this across three real scenarios (kidney allocation, worker absence, AI-generated deceased people) and shows that these developer decisions can shift moral preferences by as much as a full rating-scale point—often without transparency or accountability.

title: Learning-to-Transition for Large-scale and High-Order MIMO Detection
authors: Yubo Zhang, Yiyao Liu, Xiaodong Wang
summary: This paper proposes a learning-to-transition (L2T) framework that uses neural networks to solve MIMO detection — the problem of efficiently decoding transmitted symbols from received wireless signals in systems with many antennas. The approach combines Transformers with iterative refinement to find good symbol sequences quickly while also producing the soft probability information needed for downstream channel decoding, achieving better performance than traditional algorithmic methods on high-order (many possible symbol combinations) detection tasks.

title: RecipeNet: A Hierarchical Transformer for Recipe Data
authors: Pin-Yen Huang, Sachin Chhabra, Prasanth Sai Gouripeddi, Abhinav Kumar, Baoxin Li
summary: RecipeNet is a hierarchical Transformer architecture designed to understand recipe data—ordered sequences of steps with multiple structured fields—across domains like materials synthesis, pharmaceuticals, and manufacturing. Rather than flattening recipes into fixed tables (the standard approach), it captures both field-level interactions within each step and sequential dependencies across steps, outperforming existing tabular learning methods on benchmark tasks.

title: Rollplex: Cross-Phase GPU Spatial Sharing for Vision Language Model Post-Training
authors: Hanfeng Lu, Tianyu Feng, Suyi Li, Yuheng Zhao, Wei Gao et al.
summary: This paper presents Rollplex, a GPU scheduling runtime that speeds up vision-language model (VLM) post-training by overlapping independent computation phases that would otherwise run sequentially. The key insight is that prefix processing (which doesn't depend on model outputs) can be executed during rollout decoding without breaking the guarantees of on-policy reinforcement learning, but this requires careful memory and parallelism management to fit everything on limited GPU memory.

title: Generating Benchmark Health Data Using a Tabular Diffusion Transformer
authors: Hao Yan, Lisa Pilgram, Dan Liu, Linglong Kong, Fida Dankar et al.
summary: This paper proposes a method to generate synthetic health data from multiple heterogeneous tables (tables with different column structures) using diffusion transformers. The key innovation is a two-stage framework: first, it converts disparate tables into a standardized statistical representation, then trains a diffusion transformer to learn patterns and generate new synthetic tables. This matters because healthcare organizations need realistic benchmark datasets for research and testing while preserving privacy.

title: Approximate Muon with low-rank adapters
authors: Ben Anson, Conor Houghton, Edward Milsom
summary: This paper adapts the Muon optimizer — which works well for pretraining neural networks — to work with LoRA (low-rank adapters), a popular parameter-efficient fine-tuning method. The key insight is that Muon's orthogonalization step doesn't naturally work with low-rank updates, so the authors approximate a relaxed version of Muon's objective using linearization and least-squares, creating sMuon. The result is modest but consistent performance improvements across fine-tuning tasks while keeping computation efficient.

title: LP-NAS: Linear Programming-based Neural Architecture Search
authors: Abhishek Shukla, Ankur Sinha, Faiz Hamid
summary: This paper proposes LP-NAS, a method for automating neural network design by formulating architecture search as a linear programming problem. Instead of manually designing networks, the algorithm automatically discovers good architectures by using gradient and curvature information from training to guide the search, achieving better results than existing methods like DARTS.

title: Expected Free Energy-based Informative Path Planning for Robotic Mars Exploration
authors: Ajith Anil Meera, Pablo Lanillos, Wouter Kouw
summary: This paper proposes using Expected Free Energy (EFE), a decision-making framework from active inference, to guide robots exploring unknown environments like Mars. The key insight is that robots need to simultaneously gather accurate information AND find valuable locations, while staying within energy/distance budgets — and EFE unifies these competing goals into a single principled objective. The approach outperforms standard information-seeking or reward-seeking methods alone.

title: Designing Reinforcement Learning for Diffusion Models: A Unified Path-Space View
authors: Yixian Xu, Yuanrui Zhang, Shengjie Luo, Liwei Wang, Di He
summary: This paper unifies two seemingly different families of reinforcement learning algorithms for diffusion models by showing they both emerge from the same mathematical principle. The authors derive a policy-gradient estimator from first principles, explain why existing methods differ only in variance-reduction choices, and propose an improved algorithm that outperforms prior approaches on large-scale image generation models.
