title: Offline Deep Q* Estimation with Diffusion Models
authors: Xiaohong Chen, Yuling Jiao, Lican Kang, Jerry Zhijian Yang, Chen Zhong
summary: This paper tackles a core problem in offline reinforcement learning: estimating the optimal action-value function (Q*) when you can only learn from a fixed dataset, without interacting with the environment. The key innovation is using diffusion models — generative neural networks that learn complex distributions — to first estimate the unknown reward function and state transitions, then using those estimates to solve the Bellman equation (the recursive relationship that defines optimal decision-making). The paper provides rigorous theoretical guarantees showing the method converges at a specific rate and demonstrates it works well in practice.

title: Whose doctor does the AI recommend? An algorithm audit of reputation and demographic signals in large language model-assisted physician choice
authors: Syeda Anshrah Gillani, Mirza Samad Ahmed Baig
summary: This paper audits whether large language models recommend physicians fairly when patients ask for referrals. Researchers tested seven LLMs with 40,000+ randomized physician profiles and found that while reputation signals (ratings, fees) dominate recommendations, demographic biases exist but are hidden — models rarely mention gender or ethnicity in their explanations, making these invisible to standard transparency checks.

title: LLMs Don't Pay for the Jump
authors: Paras Balani, Subhrakanta Panda
summary: This paper argues that large language models cannot perform genuine abductive reasoning—the creative leap that produces fundamentally new scientific principles—because they lack a physical mechanism that makes epistemic errors costly. The authors show that transformer inference decouples reasoning from physical consequence, allowing models to maintain high output entropy even when faced with tasks of sharply increasing difficulty, and propose that true abduction requires a coupling between error and cost, not just embodied simulation.

title: Submodular Policy Learning for Distributed Task Allocation in Open Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Jing Liu, Luca Ballotta, Yangyang Yang, Fangfei Li, Yang Tang et al.
summary: This paper tackles policy learning for task allocation when agents dynamically join and leave a system, with utilities that have submodular structure (diminishing returns on adding more agents). The key challenge is that standard optimization techniques don't align with how agents actually make decisions through local policies. The authors propose SubMAPL, a decentralized learning algorithm that uses a new mathematical tool (partition multilinear extension) to bridge this gap and prove it achieves near-optimal performance in time-varying environments.

title: A Survey of Large Models in Sports
authors: Yichen Xu, Jianzhe Ma, Chuhan Wang, Zhonghao Cao, Liangyu Chen et al.
summary: This survey catalogs how large language models and multimodal models are being applied across sports — from game analysis to fan engagement to coaching. It's important because sports is a massive global industry, and LLMs/vision models offer new ways to understand play, predict outcomes, and personalize fan experiences at scale.

title: Wrong but Useful: Trajectory Value Beyond Answer Correctness in Multi-Agent Messages
authors: Chih-Hsuan Yang, Anjir Ahmed Chowdhury, Cheng-Hau Yang, Weijian Zheng, Fernando Llorente et al.
summary: This paper shows that in multi-agent reasoning systems, wrong answers can still be useful for reaching correct final conclusions. The authors introduce Diverse Hypothesis Deliberation (DHD), a measurement method that tests whether individual messages help or harm downstream reasoning by replaying the same solver with each message hidden or visible. They find that across multiple benchmarks and models, incorrect messages frequently improve final correctness because they contain valuable reasoning steps, constraints, or principles—suggesting that agreement or correctness alone shouldn't determine which messages to keep.

title: A Four-Axis Trustworthiness Benchmark for LLM-as-Judge in Principle-Based Regulation
authors: Dipankar Sarkar
summary: This paper evaluates whether large language models can reliably serve as judges for principle-based financial regulation—the kind that uses vague standards like "fair and not misleading" rather than rigid rules. The authors introduce Principle-Bench, a benchmark with 168 test cases designed to measure four critical aspects: whether LLM judges are accurate, robust to paraphrasing, resistant to adversarial attacks, and well-calibrated in their confidence. They find that existing LLM judges fail catastrophically on some tests and disagree with each other, raising serious questions about deploying them in real regulatory contexts.

title: Revisiting Energy-based Tabular Anomaly Detection: Energy and Reconstruction are Complementary
authors: Junichiro Niimi
summary: This paper revisits Deep Boltzmann Machines (DBMs) — a classical energy-based model — for detecting anomalies in tabular data and shows that their energy scores complement reconstruction-based methods like autoencoders better than existing approaches do. When combined via rank fusion, DBM energy and autoencoder reconstruction together outperform either method alone, suggesting that explicit energy modeling offers a non-redundant perspective on anomaly detection that modern methods have largely overlooked.

title: Photonic Quantum Computing vs. Classical Solvers in Constrained Factor Portfolio Optimization
authors: Nirvik Sahoo, Chyng Wen Tee, Paul Robert Griffin
summary: This paper compares three optimization approaches for building diversified stock portfolios: photonic quantum annealers, classical mixed-integer programming solvers, and deep reinforcement learning agents. The key finding is that while quantum hardware can find mathematically superior portfolio allocations in specific scenarios, classical solvers remain more reliable for real-world constraints like controlling tail risk, and reinforcement learning agents struggle when optimizing for higher-order statistics like skewness.

title: A Graph-Based Reinforcement Learning Framework for Structured Drift Diagnosis and Recovery in Autonomous LLM Agents
authors: Ismail El Hamraoui, Sagar Jose, Nicolas Bureau, Robert Plana
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem: autonomous LLM agents deployed in real-world workflows can silently drift from their intended behavior, causing harmful side effects. The authors propose a plug-and-play recovery system that uses a small language model trained via reinforcement learning to detect drift, assess risk, and decide whether to intervene — without retraining the expensive main agent. The approach is tested on a public benchmark and shows promise in reliably catching and recovering from behavioral drift.

title: Forecast Collapse in Time-Series Foundation Models
authors: Shu Wan, Miles Ma, Hank Zhu, Guangqi Liu, Stephen Wang et al.
summary: Time-series foundation models produce flat, uninformative predictions when forecasting stock returns — a failure the authors call "forecast collapse" — even though they perform well on other financial data like trading volume. The paper identifies that this collapse stems from a fundamental tradeoff between calibration (accuracy of predicted magnitudes) and ranking (ability to distinguish which stocks will outperform), and proposes CalibRank, a new objective function that recovers predictive power by optimizing both simultaneously.

title: XAI-Guided Conservative Decentralized Execution for Offline Multi-Agent Network Slicing
authors: Eslam Eldeeb, Hatim Chergui, Merouane Debbah
summary: This paper addresses resource allocation in 6G network slicing—where multiple services compete for shared infrastructure—using a novel offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) approach called X-CODE. The key innovation is that agents learn decentralized policies during centralized training without ever interacting with the network, eliminating costly and unsafe online trial-and-error while achieving zero resource conflicts and 88% lower inference latency than online methods.

title: Reducing ANN-SNN Conversion Error via Residual Membrane Potential Alignment
authors: Zirui Chen, Zihan Huang, Tong Bu, Jianhao Ding, Yiting Dong et al.
summary: This paper addresses a key problem in neuromorphic computing: converting trained artificial neural networks (ANNs) into efficient spiking neural networks (SNNs) without losing accuracy. The authors propose a method that fixes errors introduced during conversion, especially when using very few time steps, making SNNs practical for deployment on low-power hardware.

title: From Passive Delegates to Strategic Negotiators: Reinforcing Social Reasoning in Small Language Models with SocialRL
authors: Wenyue Hua, Zachary Huang, Tyler Payne, Safoora Yousefi, Saleema Amershi et al.
summary: This paper trains small language models (4B parameters) to negotiate strategically on behalf of users by applying reinforcement learning to social reasoning. The key insight: models trained to be helpful assistants often make poor negotiators because they're too trusting and conciliatory. SocialRL teaches models to protect their principal's interests while negotiating across six domains (deal-making, job interviews, marketplace haggling), matching or exceeding GPT-4/5 performance in cross-domain evaluation.

title: SAGE: Surrogate-gradient Adaptation via Attention-Guided Entropy for Spiking Transformers
authors: Kiran Nair, Rodrigue Rizk, KC Santosh
summary: This paper proposes SAGE, a training technique that improves spiking neural networks (SNNs)—energy-efficient brain-inspired neural networks that use sparse event-driven computation—by adaptively adjusting how gradients flow through layers during training. The key insight is using attention mechanism uncertainty to dynamically tune the surrogate-gradient slope (a technical workaround needed because spike functions aren't directly differentiable), achieving 1-2% accuracy improvements on image classification without changing the deployed model.

title: AutoDesign: Meta-Harness Optimization for Long-Horizon Agentic Design
authors: Yaxin Luo, Haobin Jiang, Jialv Zou, Xu Huang, Wenhao Yan et al.
summary: AutoDesign is a framework that automatically improves how AI systems design academic posters from papers by having a code-writing agent recursively refine its "design harness" (the set of rules and tools it uses) based on feedback. The paper demonstrates this on a new benchmark called PosterBench and achieves results competitive with commercial systems, showing that AI agents can learn to design better when given the right feedback loop and autonomy to modify their own operating procedures.

title: OmniScientist: An Omni-Modal Omni-Discipline AI Scientist
authors: Bobo Li, Hao Fei, Tianjie Ju, Mong-Li Lee, Wynne Hsu
summary: OmniScientist is an AI system that automates scientific research across multiple disciplines by processing raw data directly—images, videos, audio, 3D structures, tables, and more—rather than relying on pre-summarized text. The system uses multiple autonomous agents (for ideation, experimentation, and writeup) to move from raw evidence to a complete manuscript, and validates results through code-based checks for novelty, statistical validity, and reproducibility. This matters because most AI research tools work only with text or precomputed summaries, missing the spatial, temporal, and procedural relationships that are often essential for scientific discovery.

title: QuoteBench: How Matched Scores Can Hide Command-Path Failures
authors: Shangao Li, Yao Zhang, Volker Tresp, Yuanyuan Yang
summary: This paper reveals that standard evaluation metrics for LLM-based coding agents can mask critical failures caused by the execution pipeline—not the model itself. The authors introduce QuoteBench, a benchmark that measures where command generation breaks down versus where serialization, parsing, and escaping errors occur, showing that matched scores can hide 55-73% of real failures while overstating model robustness by up to 60 points.

title: SAEVerbalizer: Generating Explanations for Sparse Autoencoder Features via Representation Verbalization
authors: Weihan Meng, Hongzhu Guo, Yi Jing, Dewen Liu, Zijun Yao et al.
summary: This paper proposes SAEVerbalizer, a method to automatically generate natural-language explanations for features discovered by sparse autoencoders (SAEs) — a tool used to decompose the internal representations of large language models into interpretable components. Instead of manually inspecting model behavior to guess what features mean, the approach trains an LLM to produce explanations directly from the mathematical directions that SAEs learn, making the process faster and more systematic.

title: Joint Communication-Control Strategy Optimization with Partially Nested Information Structures: The Linear-Quadratic Case
authors: Haoyi You, Kaiqing Zhang
summary: This paper solves the problem of how multiple agents in a networked system should coordinate their communication and control decisions jointly. The key innovation is showing that under "partially nested" information structures — where agents have hierarchical knowledge about each other's states — the optimization problem becomes tractable and admits closed-form solutions via dynamic programming, even when agents must decide what to communicate to each other.

title: Vero: Can AI Agents Build Formally Verified Software Repositories?
authors: Zhe Ye, Hantao Lou, Yuechun Sun, Peiyang Song, Zhengxu Yan et al.
summary: This paper introduces Vero, a benchmark for evaluating whether AI agents can generate both correct code implementations *and* formal mathematical proofs across real multi-module software repositories. Current state-of-the-art agents solve only 27 of 43 test cases, revealing that building trustworthy, formally verified software at scale remains an open challenge for AI.

title: DFM Mimir v1: An Open HRM Delivering Frontier Performance at 1B Parameters Using Only Permissible Post-Training Data
authors: Peter Schneider-Kamp, Jacob Nielsen, Gianluca Barmina, Kenneth Enevoldsen, Lukas Galke Poech
summary: Mimir v1 is a 1-billion-parameter language model trained entirely on permissible (legally and ethically licensed) datasets that matches the performance of much larger models. It achieves state-of-the-art results for Danish and competitive English performance, showing that you don't need scraped web data or restricted datasets to build frontier-quality models — a significant finding for researchers and organizations committed to open-source and ethical AI development.

title: TabSOM: A tabular-to-image encoding method based on self-organizing maps
authors: David Chushig-Muzo, María Ángeles Rodríguez de Cara, Eva Milara, Francisco J. Lara-Abelenda, Luis Zhinin-Vera et al.
summary: This paper presents TabSOM, a method that converts tabular (spreadsheet-like) data into images so that computer vision models can process it. Unlike existing approaches that only encode individual feature values, TabSOM also captures relationships between features using self-organizing maps, a classical neural network technique. The method achieves top performance on benchmark datasets while remaining interpretable—you can understand why it makes predictions.

title: On the Structural Limits of Machine Learning Decision Systems: An Information-Theoretic, Interaction-Based, and Stochastic-Dynamical Perspective
authors: Nestor R. Barraza, Gabriel Pena
summary: This paper examines fundamental structural limits on what machine learning systems can achieve, regardless of algorithmic sophistication. Using information theory and stochastic dynamics, the authors show that prediction and estimation errors are bounded by properties of the data-generating process itself — not just by how clever our algorithms are — and that violations of implicit assumptions like independence can invalidate standard learning procedures.

title: Intern-S2-Preview: Scientific Agentic Foundation Model
authors: Lei Bai, Jiaqi Cao, Chiyu Chen, Guanzhou Chen, Kai Chen et al.
summary: Intern-S2-Preview is a foundation model family designed to help AI systems solve scientific problems by understanding multiple types of data (text, images, numbers), using scientific tools, and making progress over long task sequences. The model combines large language model capabilities with reinforcement learning and memory systems, achieving strong results on scientific benchmarks while introducing practical techniques to train such complex systems efficiently.

title: TraVEL: Trajectory-Guided Video Embedding Learning for Driving-Video Retrieval
authors: Yi-Chung Chen, Philip Jacobson, Tom Lampo, Yiren Lu, Jin Yao et al.
summary: This paper addresses efficient retrieval of relevant video clips from large driving datasets by developing TraVEL, a method that fine-tunes multimodal embedding models using trajectory-guided supervision. The approach combines supervised fine-tuning on reasoning traces with reinforcement learning (using ego-trajectory similarity as a reward signal) to create compact video embeddings that capture fine-grained motion events — like turning left versus right — without requiring expert rules or auxiliary perception systems at test time.

title: Toward a Gricean Retreat: Probing LLMs for Knowledge Boundaries and Referent Specificity
authors: Dananjay Srinivas, Saksham Khatwani, Maria Pacheco
summary: This paper investigates why large language models (LLMs) fabricate plausible-sounding details about unfamiliar entities instead of admitting uncertainty or giving more general answers. The authors use Gricean pragmatics—a linguistic theory about cooperative communication—as a lens to study this problem, finding that models *internally encode* knowledge boundaries and can predict specificity levels, but fail to use this knowledge during generation. The work bridges interpretability and alignment by showing the mechanisms exist for honest, uncertainty-aware responses; the training objective simply doesn't incentivize them.

title: Synthetic Persona Pretraining: Alignment from Token Zero
authors: Julian Minder, Viktor Moskvoretskii, Raghav Singhal, Difan Jiao, Andy Arditi et al.
summary: This paper proposes Synthetic Persona Pretraining (SPP), a method that bakes desired values and behavior into language models during the initial pretraining phase rather than bolting them on afterward. The authors show that injecting value-aligned "reflections" into pretraining documents—then reinforcing the desired persona during fine-tuning—produces models that are more resistant to jailbreaks, better at following ethical guidelines, and more aligned on moral dilemmas, without sacrificing general capabilities.

title: MARC v1: An Open-Source Multi-Agent Framework for Clinical AI Reasoning and Coordination
authors: Saisha Shetty, Satvik Tripathi, Austin Lin, Colin Zhao, Theodore Kim et al.
summary: MARC is an open-source framework that replaces single-prompt LLM interactions with coordinated teams of specialized AI agents for clinical reasoning tasks. Instead of asking one model to do everything, it routes medical questions through extraction, reasoning, generation, and evaluation agents with traceable outputs—making it easier to find where things go wrong and giving clinicians more interpretable, auditable AI decisions.

title: AaLLM: An End-to-End Analog Circuit Design Framework from Topology Generation to Sizing Using Large Language Models
authors: Mohammed Ayman Habib, Rylan Hart, Morteza Fayazi
summary: This paper presents AaLLM, an end-to-end system that uses large language models to design analog circuits automatically — both choosing circuit topologies (the structure) and sizing components (the values). Rather than requiring experts to manually iterate between different design tools, AaLLM takes user specifications as input and outputs a complete circuit design, achieving designs as good as or better than hand-crafted ones while running 40x faster than existing approaches.

title: MLLM-Routed Heterogeneous Ensembles for Robust Cross-Dataset Image Classification
authors: Daniel Perkins, John Squires, Janou Milligan, Chandra Raskoti, Linda Ungerboeck
summary: This paper introduces ARMDIL, a system that uses a multimodal language model to intelligently choose which vision model to apply to each image, rather than using a single model for all images. The ensemble combines convolutional networks, self-supervised models, and vision-language models trained on diverse datasets, improving robustness when images come from different sources or difficulty levels.

title: Doubly Robust Estimation of Causal Effect on CVR with Targeted Regularization
authors: Jiayi Dan, Bo Li, Lu Deng, Yong Wang
summary: This paper develops a new statistical method for estimating causal effects on conversion rates (CVR) — a critical metric in e-commerce and advertising. The challenge is that clicked samples alone introduce selection bias and noise; the authors solve this by creating a "doubly robust" estimator grounded in semiparametric theory, which converges faster and works reliably even with flexible neural network models.

title: CAPRI: Contract-Aware Proof Repair for Isabelle
authors: Jim Woodcock, Gabriel Leite, Augusto Sampaio, Ran Wei
summary: This paper presents CAPRI, a system for using LLMs to repair failed Isabelle proofs (formal mathematical proofs written in a proof assistant) while ensuring that LLM edits stay within authorized boundaries. The key insight is that simply checking whether Isabelle accepts a proof isn't enough — you also need to verify that the LLM didn't secretly modify parts of the code the developer didn't intend. CAPRI adds a "contract" layer that tracks exactly what changed, making the repair process auditable and safer for use in high-assurance software development.

title: A Unifying Perspective on Causal World Models: From Observations to Representations to Structure
authors: Avinash Kori, Fabrizio Russo
summary: This paper proposes a unified framework for understanding world models — neural networks that learn to predict and understand how environments evolve — through a causal lens. The authors argue that effective world models must not just generate accurate predictions but also capture causal relationships between entities and their interactions. By connecting world modelling to causal representation learning and structural causal models, they provide formal foundations for building agents that can reason about and act in complex environments beyond their training experience.

title: UniTexture: Cross-Task Universal Adversarial Textures for Vision-Language-Action Models
authors: Yukun Dai, Mingzhe Dai, Tianshi Wang, Fengling Li, Jingjing Li et al.
summary: This paper demonstrates that Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models — neural networks that understand images, text instructions, and produce robot control actions — can be fooled by a single adversarial texture placed on a 3D object. The attack works across multiple different tasks without needing to be retrained, revealing a fundamental shared vulnerability in how these robotic AI systems process visual information.

title: Reduced Matrix Multiplication: Input-Adaptive Matrix-Product Reduction for LLM Inference
authors: Zixuan Lan, Yanhong Li, Jiawei Zhou
summary: This paper proposes Reduced Matrix Multiplication (RMM), a method that speeds up transformer inference by selectively removing less important elements from matrix multiplications without retraining the model. The key insight is that many dimensions in these high-dimensional computations are redundant — RMM identifies and skips them, providing a tunable trade-off between speed and accuracy that works across different model sizes and tasks.

title: Heterogeneity-Aware Belief Synchronization for Semantic Communication in AI-Native 6G Networks
authors: Muhammad Hannan Akram, Muhammad Abubakar Rashid, Wassi Haider Kabir, Haejoon Jung, Kapal Dev et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical challenge in future 6G networks: enabling thousands of heterogeneous AI agents (on satellites, drones, edge servers) to communicate meaningfully despite running different models and learning from different environments. The authors propose a framework using latent translation models on edge servers that synchronize agent beliefs without requiring all agents to have identical architectures or undergo joint training—reducing communication cost and privacy leakage while keeping agents sufficiently aligned to understand each other's messages.

title: RippleMem: From Isolated Retrieval to Associative Recollection for Long-Term Agent Memory
authors: Jingbo Ji, Lingyi Li, Xilong Cheng, Yuhao Zhou, Wenji Zhang et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem in LLM-based agents: retrieving the right information from long-term memory when relevant evidence is scattered across many past interactions. RippleMem solves this by replacing simple one-shot retrieval with adaptive associative recollection — it recalls relevant memories, then follows semantic and structural connections to find supporting evidence, much like how humans reconstruct a complete memory from a partial cue. The approach improves accuracy by up to 12% on benchmarks while reducing computational cost by 30x.

title: It's How You Ask: Gender-Associated Linguistic Bias in LLMs
authors: Katherine Van Koevering, Anjalie Field
summary: This paper shows that LLMs systematically respond differently to linguistically identical requests depending on whether they contain speech patterns more common among women—like hedges ("maybe," "I think"), tag questions ("isn't it?"), and collective language ("we"). The researchers find that these linguistic features trigger shorter, less sophisticated responses, and that this bias persists even after controlling for prompt complexity and is harder to fix than explicit gender cues like names. The work matters because professional communication increasingly flows through LLMs, and these disparities could amplify existing workplace inequities.

title: Mixture of Training: Recombining Small-Scale Scaffolded Pretraining Runs into a Larger Language Model
authors: Mohammed Sabry, Sean Augenstein, Keith Rush, Lucio Dery
summary: This paper proposes Mixture of Training (MoT), a method to break down language model pretraining into independent, modular training jobs that can be recombined into a single larger model. Rather than training one giant model end-to-end, MoT trains separate "depth slices" (contiguous layers) within frozen scaffolds and then stitches them together. The authors demonstrate this works on a 1.3B-parameter model, achieving comparable performance to traditional monolithic pretraining while offering potential computational advantages through parallelization and reuse.

title: LigBench: A Unified and Human-Aligned Benchmark for LLM-based Research Idea Generation
authors: Chenrun Wang, Mingxuan Zhu, Tiancheng Huang, Wenjie Li, Yujie Zhang et al.
summary: This paper introduces LigBench, an automated benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can generate good research ideas — the kind that researchers would actually want to pursue. The work matters because as LLMs become research assistants, we need objective, reliable ways to judge the quality of their suggestions rather than having LLMs score themselves, which is circular and unreliable.

title: FlowLOB: Efficient and Controllable Limit Order Book Generation with Flow Matching
authors: Zhuohan Wang, Andreea Bacalum, Ollie Olby, Carmine Ventre, Namid Stillman
summary: FlowLOB generates realistic limit order book (LOB) trajectories — the records of buy/sell orders at different prices — using flow matching, a newer generative modeling technique. The paper shows that flow matching produces high-quality, realistic market simulations with far fewer computational steps than diffusion models, while remaining controllable (you can condition it on specific market scenarios) and generalizing to unseen trading instruments without retraining.

title: VALG: An Agentic System for ML Theory Research
authors: Dechen Zhang, Xuan Tang, Xinxiang Yin, Xingwu Chen, Jian Qian et al.
summary: VALG is an autonomous AI system that conducts machine learning theory research by breaking down theorem-proving into manageable steps: formulating problems, constructing proofs, and learning from failures. When proofs fail, the system diagnoses whether the problem is a calculation error, proof structure, or flawed assumptions—then adjusts accordingly. Tested on open problems from a top theory conference, it produced two complete theorem candidates and several partial results, showing that agentic workflows can meaningfully contribute to mathematical discovery.

title: InterSAGE: The Secure and Verifiable Interoperability Protocol for An Internet of Agents
authors: Zhenhua Zou, Sheng Guo, Qiuyang Zhan, Lepeng Zhao, Shuo Li et al.
summary: InterSAGE is a security protocol suite that enables LLM-powered agents to safely interact across organizational boundaries—proving their identity, capabilities, and accountability. It fills a critical gap in agent interoperability: existing communication protocols define how agents talk, but not how they establish trust or prove what they're authorized to do.

title: OGR-MARL: Option-Guided Residual Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning for Heterogeneous USV Cooperative Pursuit in Constrained Port Waterways
authors: Mao Jiayang, Wang Lanfeng, Peng Zhao-Han
summary: This paper presents OGR-MARL, a framework for controlling multiple heterogeneous unmanned surface vehicles (USVs) working together to chase a target in constrained port waterways. The key innovation is combining rule-based navigation constraints with learned corrective behaviors, allowing agents to satisfy safety and traffic rules while still optimizing for mission success — achieving a 75% capture rate in realistic port scenarios.

title: Reconcile Once, Write Anytime: A Trust-Tiered Librarian and a Multi-Agent Writer for Drift-Free, Point-in-Time Research
authors: Xing Zhang, Yanwei Cui, Guanghui Wang, Peiyang He
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem in LLM-generated long-form reports: factual drift, self-contradiction, and loss of provenance (the chain of evidence). The authors build a two-part system—a deterministic "librarian" that maintains a trust-tiered knowledge library with timestamped sources, and a multi-agent "writer" that composes reports grounded in evidence at any historical cutoff without looking ahead. The work matters because it solves reproducibility and verifiability in AI-generated research, moving beyond simple retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) to a structured, auditable knowledge layer.

title: Online Inference for Quantile Temporal Difference Learning in Distributional Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zijie Cheng, Yang Peng, Zhihua Zhang
summary: This paper develops statistical inference methods for quantile temporal difference learning, a technique used in distributional reinforcement learning to learn the full distribution of future rewards rather than just expected values. The key innovation is an online inference procedure that computes confidence intervals and hypothesis tests efficiently without storing entire trajectories, making it practical for large-scale RL applications.

title: CardioState-JEPA: Delay-Aware Cross-Modal Learning of a Shared Cardiac Representation
authors: Hamza Shafiq, Hung Manh Pham, Bin Zhu, Pan Zhou, Jun Hu et al.
summary: This paper introduces CardioState-JEPA, a foundation model that learns a single shared representation from three different cardiac sensors—ECG (electrical), PPG (blood flow), and PCG (heart sounds)—by training them jointly rather than separately. The key innovation is handling the natural time delays between these signals and exploiting the fact that they measure the same underlying cardiac cycle, which improves performance on downstream tasks across all three modalities by 8–19 percentage points over single-modality baselines.

title: Discovering Efficient and Explainable Communication Topologies for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems via Causal Inference
authors: Junzhi Li, Peng He, Qirui Ji, Wei Wang, Lixiang Liu et al.
summary: This paper introduces E2-Explainer, a framework that identifies which communication channels matter in LLM-based multi-agent systems by using causal inference to discover compact, interpretable communication subgraphs. Instead of treating agent communication as a black box, the authors show how to extract minimal but sufficient communication patterns and use them to prune redundant messages, reducing computational costs while maintaining task performance.

title: Agent Behavioral Contracts II: Certifying Compositional Reliability Without Assuming Independence
authors: Varun Pratap Bhardwaj, Garima Singh, Arun Pratap Bhardwaj
summary: This paper challenges a dangerous assumption in multi-agent system reliability: that component failures are independent. The authors show that two instances of the same language model fail together on 90% of shared failures, not the 10% predicted by independence math. They develop a new certification method that doesn't assume independence away and actually works in practice.

title: High-resolution Calibrated Probabilistic Hourly Precipitation from a Deterministic Forecast
authors: Thomas M Hamill
summary: This paper describes a neural network method called Attention Residual U-Net that predicts hourly rainfall probability and intensity across the United States. Instead of just guessing yes/no for rain, it outputs a full probability distribution — the chance of no rain plus the likely amounts if it does rain. This matters because accurate probabilistic rainfall forecasts help with flood warnings, water management, and emergency planning.

title: Beyond the Best Guess: Improving LLM Solution Coverage with Evolution Strategies
authors: Conor F. Hayes, Elliot Meyerson, Kajetan Schweighofer, Roberto Dailey, Babak Hodjat et al.
summary: This paper shows that Evolution Strategies (ES)—a gradient-free optimization method that explores weight space through random perturbations—produces better solution diversity than standard reinforcement learning when fine-tuning large language models. The key insight: RL narrows the model's output distribution around high-reward answers, but ES maintains a broader distribution that yields more correct solutions when the model generates multiple candidate answers (pass@k), ultimately improving performance on math and science problems.

title: Adjacency-Based Spectral Proxy Control of Mobile Communication Agents
authors: Mariana del Castillo, Federico Larroca
summary: This paper solves a practical problem in mobile agent networks: how to reposition communication agents to maintain network connectivity as task agents move around. Instead of using the standard but computationally hard Fiedler vector approach, the authors propose A-Fiedler, which uses the simpler adjacency matrix eigenvector as a proxy. The result is a control method that's easier to implement in real distributed systems and more robust when communication is limited.

title: LLMs Are Not Good Strategists, Yet Memory-Enhanced Agency Boosts Reasoning
authors: Yi Wu, Zhimin Hu
summary: This paper shows that standard LLMs struggle with long-horizon strategic reasoning because their attention mechanism can't maintain coherent goals across thousands of steps. The authors propose EpicStar, a memory-augmented agent framework that stores successful past episodes and uses dynamic gating to decide whether to reuse old strategies or reason through new ones. Testing on StarCraft II, EpicStar dramatically outperforms baselines while using 10× fewer tokens, suggesting that structured memory is essential for LLMs to act as effective autonomous agents in complex environments.

title: Do LLMs Beat Nash? Testing Decentralized Coordination in Self-Play Multi-Agent Games
authors: Deborah Sinishaw, Qile Zhu, Edwin Meriaux, Gregory Dudek
summary: This paper tests whether large language models can coordinate with each other in games without communication, asking if they can reason about their counterparts well enough to beat the Nash equilibrium — the standard game-theory baseline for uncoordinated play. The researchers find that frontier models sometimes exceed Nash equilibrium outcomes in two-player games but struggle in larger multi-agent teams, suggesting LLMs have limited ability to scale coordination reasoning beyond simple settings.

title: Entropy-Augmented Multi-Objective Policy Optimization in Multiagent Systems
authors: Jamie Santos, Ayhan Alp Aydeniz, Raghav Thakar, Kagan Tumer
summary: This paper addresses a key problem in multi-agent coordination: when multiple autonomous agents optimize for competing objectives, they often converge to similar behaviors, losing the behavioral diversity needed to adapt to different situations. The authors propose augmenting standard multi-objective evolutionary optimization (NSGA-II) with an entropy bonus that rewards behavioral diversity alongside objective performance, achieving up to 48% improvement in solution quality on rover coordination tasks.

title: Multi-AUV Ad-hoc network-based Target Tracking: A Value Gradient Guidance Multi-Agent Diffusion Reinforcement Learning Approach
authors: Jiaao Ma, Chuan Lin, Guangjie Han, Shengchao Zhu, Qian Zhu et al.
summary: This paper addresses cooperative target tracking by multiple autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) communicating through ad-hoc networks under realistic constraints like limited acoustic bandwidth and ocean currents. The authors propose VGG-MADiffRL, a novel multi-agent reinforcement learning algorithm that combines diffusion policies with value gradients to generate more stable, accurate control actions. The approach matters because underwater multi-agent coordination is practically hard (noisy communication, dynamic topology, environmental uncertainty) and existing MARL methods produce unstable policies in these settings.

title: AVA-Encoder: Towards Agent-Native Video Representation Learning
authors: Chuyue Li, Jinpeng Yu, Haozhe Wang, Tian Xueyun, Zhijing Zhang et al.
summary: This paper introduces AVA-Encoder, a framework that learns video representations designed for AI agents to understand, reason about, and edit films. Instead of treating videos as raw pixels, the system converts them into structured knowledge graphs (semantic networks of concepts and relationships) that agents can directly manipulate, then reconstructs videos from these graphs. This bridges a gap between how humans understand cinema and how AI systems can work with video content at a high level of abstraction.

title: DreamFly: Causal Memory and Receding-Horizon Diffusion Planning for Aerial Vision-Language Navigation
authors: Yan Deng, Fei Xu
summary: This paper presents DreamFly, a system that teaches aerial drones to navigate using natural language instructions while interpreting visual feeds in real time. The key innovation is combining causal memory (which only looks at past observations), diffusion-based planning (a generative approach that predicts action sequences), and explicit termination detection—solving the hard problem of embodied AI navigation under uncertainty.

title: Constructing Dynamic Master Logic Models as Knowledge Graphs for Complex System Diagnostics Using Retrieval-Augmented Large Language Models
authors: Saman Marandi, Yu-Shu Hu, Mohammad Modarres
summary: This paper automates the construction of Dynamic Master Logic (DML) models — hierarchical diagrams that map system functions to physical components — by using large language models (LLMs) with retrieval-augmented generation to extract information from technical documentation and represent it as knowledge graphs. The approach makes it practical to build detailed diagnostic models for complex systems like nuclear reactors without relying entirely on human experts, and demonstrates that the automated models can reliably support reasoning about system failures and dependencies.

title: Class Activation Mapping in Explainable Computer Vision: A Method-Centered Review of CNN, Transformer, and Foundation-Model-Era Visual Explanations
authors: AmirHossein Eshghi, Hamid Saadatfar, Seyyed Ali Hoseini, AmirMohsen Eshghi, Siavash Arjomand Bigdel
summary: This paper reviews Class Activation Mapping (CAM) — a family of techniques that explain what parts of an image a visual AI model is "looking at" when making a decision — from its 2016 origins through modern foundation models like CLIP and SAM. The review synthesizes 57 papers and shows how the field has evolved from simple heatmaps on CNNs to sophisticated multi-layer, probabilistic, and token-aware explanations, while identifying fragmentation in how these methods are evaluated.

title: Beyond Trial-and-Error: Agentic Optimization for Image-to-Video Adherence
authors: Aman Tyagi, Hemanth Boinpally, Jonathan Chen, Douglas Gebert, Steven Hickson
summary: This paper tackles a major pain point in AI video generation: modern image-to-video models produce wildly different outputs from small prompt changes, forcing users into tedious trial-and-error loops. The authors propose an "agentic self-improvement" framework that automatically optimizes prompts and generation parameters using a multimodal language model and Bayesian search, achieving 69% human preference over baseline outputs and making video synthesis more reliable for professional use.

title: Large Language Model-Driven Small-Capitalization Trading: Integrating Financial News Sentiment, Macroeconomic Indicators, and Technical Signals
authors: Alireza Kargarzadeh, Nariman Khaledian, Navid Parvini, Arman Khaledian
summary: This paper uses large language models (specifically GPT-4o mini) to extract sentiment signals from financial news and combines them with macroeconomic indicators and technical analysis to build trading strategies for small-cap stocks. The key insight is that separating stock-specific signals from macro-driven signals, and carefully choosing portfolio allocation methods and holding periods, produces superior risk-adjusted returns — with the best strategy achieving a Sharpe ratio of 2.33 even after accounting for transaction costs.

title: VAKRA: Evaluating Multi-Hop Reasoning Across APIs and Retrieval Under Tool-Use Policies
authors: Ankita Rajaram Naik, Anupama Murthi, Benjamin Elder, Siyu Huo, Raavi Gupta et al.
summary: This paper introduces VAKRA, a benchmark for evaluating AI agents on their ability to reason across multiple APIs and documents while following tool-use constraints. The benchmark reveals that even state-of-the-art models struggle significantly with compositional reasoning and policy constraints, dropping from 70% accuracy on simple tasks to as low as 2.4% on policy-constrained questions — problems that stem not from technical tool invocation failures but from language-level reasoning challenges like entity disambiguation.

title: Earth observation embeddings are effective sub-grid descriptors for probabilistic weather downscaling
authors: Pedro Sousa, Will Tebbutt, Sadiq Jaffer, Robin Young, Anil Madhavapeddy et al.
summary: This paper shows that Earth observation embeddings—learned visual representations of land surface conditions from satellite imagery—can improve weather prediction at specific locations by capturing terrain and surface properties that coarse global weather models miss. By combining satellite-derived surface descriptors with a neural downscaling model, the authors achieve 11.5% better temperature predictions and 6.2% better wind predictions across diverse regions, even generalizing to new locations with no training history.

title: One Frozen Simulator Is Not Enough: Simulator Collapse in Multi-Agent RL
authors: Simon Yu, Nicholas Tomlin, Marwa Abdulhai, Ximing Lu, Derek Chong et al.
summary: This paper identifies and solves a critical failure mode in multi-agent reinforcement learning where an AI policy trained against a single frozen language model simulator overfits to that simulator's behavioral quirks and fails to generalize to real users or new simulators. The authors propose two solutions—one that diversifies the simulator's outputs at test time and another that trains the policy against multiple different simulators simultaneously—and show both improve real-world transfer by up to 14%.

title: Regime-Gated Residual Mixture-of-Experts for Cross-Sectional Volatility Forecasting
authors: Junyi Ye, Gargi Vijay Borde
summary: This paper proposes RG-ResMoE, a neural network architecture that forecasts stock volatility by using market regime information strategically—routing expert predictions rather than feeding regime data directly into the model. The key finding is that *where* regime information enters the network matters as much as *that* it enters: using it only for expert routing improves both forecasting accuracy and training stability, while naive direct input degrades performance.

title: VICBench: A Multi-Language Benchmark for Code Vulnerability Detection
authors: Jin Lu, Xuening Han, Yang Zhong, Lin Tan, Kevin Luo et al.
summary: This paper introduces VICBench, a benchmark dataset of 100 real vulnerabilities across Python, Java, and C++ code used to evaluate vulnerability detection tools. The benchmark is significant because it addresses a critical gap: existing vulnerability datasets are too small, limited in language coverage, and don't capture the complexity of real-world security fixes. By showing that state-of-the-art detection methods only achieve 33–40% accuracy, the paper demonstrates the need for better evaluation standards in code security.

title: ScreenShot: A Foundation Model for Few-Shot Combination Drug Screening
authors: Antoine de Mathelin, Christopher Tosh, Wesley Tansey
summary: ScreenShot is a foundation model that predicts how cancer cell samples will respond to drug combinations, trained on 40 publicly available screening datasets. Instead of requiring expensive lab measurements or per-patient retraining, it uses a hierarchical transformer to make predictions from just a few observations of a new patient's cells, and can even suggest which drug combinations to test next to save time and resources.

title: Information Abundance Paradox: Long-Context Training Undermines Parametric Knowledge
authors: Arda Uzunoglu, Benjamin van Durme, Daniel Khashabi
summary: This paper challenges the assumption that longer training contexts always help language models learn better. The authors show that beyond a certain point, abundant context actually makes models *rely more on that context* and *encode less knowledge internally*, a phenomenon they call the Information Abundance Paradox. This matters because it reveals a fundamental trade-off: models trained on very long contexts may perform worse when that context isn't available at test time.

title: Learning-Based Behavior Planning for Automated Driving: Real-World Integration and Deployment
authors: Jean-Pierre Busch, Guido Linden, Jan Bergmann, Lutz Eckstein
summary: This paper presents a hybrid architecture for autonomous vehicle motion planning that combines deep neural networks with classical optimization constraints. The key innovation is pairing a learned model (which handles complex scene interpretation) with a formal verification layer (which enforces safety and drivability rules), addressing a critical real-world problem: how to make AI-based driving decisions both effective and trustworthy enough for deployment.

title: Rethinking Agent Security as a Networking Problem
authors: Van Tran, Taveesh Sharma, Tajveer Singh Dhesi, Nick Feamster
summary: This paper reframes AI agent security from an agent-centric problem to a systems and networking problem. The authors argue that relying on agents themselves to enforce security policies is fundamentally flawed because LLM behavior is nondeterministic and vulnerable to attacks like prompt injection—and instead propose borrowing proven networking principles (centralized control, capability-based access, zero-trust) combined with semantic, context-aware policies to create deterministic security guarantees for autonomous systems.

title: Who Thinks Best Depends on How Long You Let Them: Budget-Dependent Rankings in LLM Evaluation
authors: Rodrigo Guedes de Souza, Alison R. Panisson
summary: This paper challenges the standard assumption that large language model rankings stay the same across different inference conditions. By testing four models on reasoning benchmarks with varying token budgets (64–4,096 tokens), the authors show that model performance and relative rankings shift dramatically depending on how much computational budget each model gets, sometimes reversing completely. This matters because current evaluation practices treat models as having fixed, stable rankings—but in reality, "best" depends heavily on the constraints.

title: Do LLMs Take Care of Their Own? Similarity Signals Can Induce Cooperation
authors: Akash Kundu, Emanuel Tewolde, Ratip Emin Berker, Samuel F. Brown, Vincent Conitzer
summary: This paper studies how large language models (LLMs) behave in strategic interactions when given information about each other's similarity. The researchers find that similarity signals can encourage cooperation in classic game-theory problems like the Prisoner's Dilemma, but different LLM models respond to these signals in drastically different ways. The work matters because as AI agents become deployed in the real world, understanding how they cooperate or compete with each other is critical for safety and efficiency.

title: Confidence Calibration of Deep Learning Systems
authors: Coby Penso
summary: This thesis develops methods to ensure deep learning models output reliable confidence estimates—predictions that accurately reflect how likely they are to be correct—even when training data is noisy or comes from a different domain than where the model will be used. Confidence calibration matters in high-stakes settings like medicine or autonomous driving, where knowing *how uncertain* a model is can be as important as the prediction itself.

title: Mechanist: AI as a Scientific Instrument for Discovering the Mechanisms of Intelligence
authors: Mengru Wang, Junfeng Fang, Shuofei Qiao, Zhenqian Xu, Haoming Xu et al.
summary: This paper introduces Mechanist, an AI agent that autonomously discovers how AI models work by formulating and testing mechanistic hypotheses. Rather than relying on manual human analysis, Mechanist combines a massive knowledge graph of interpretability research with systematic experimentation to uncover the internal mechanisms driving AI capabilities and risks — and then uses those insights to improve model safety and performance.

title: Scalable Multi-Agent Maze Traversal with Local Communication
authors: Julian Rau, Jahir Argote-Gerald, Grace McFassel, Genki Miyauchi, Paul Trodden et al.
summary: This paper presents a distributed algorithm that enables many robots to collectively explore and navigate unknown maze-like environments using only local communication between neighbors. The key innovation is a leader-follower coordination scheme where agents take turns exploring, reducing redundant work while maintaining collision-free movement — and the paper proves this approach is nearly as efficient as if all agents had complete knowledge of the environment.

title: Lapis: Laplacian Spiking Attention via First-Spike Timing and Membrane Leakage
authors: Kaiwen Tang, Jiaqi Zheng, Zixuan Zhu, Yiqun Wang, Zhanglu Yan et al.
summary: This paper introduces Lapis, a new attention mechanism designed specifically for spiking neural networks (SNNs) — biologically-inspired networks that process information via sparse spike timing rather than continuous activations. Instead of using standard dot-product scoring like transformers do, Lapis scores token relationships using the distance between first-spike arrival times, mapped through a Laplacian kernel. The key insight is that this approach uses only addition and subtraction, not multiplication, making it dramatically more energy-efficient while maintaining competitive accuracy on image classification tasks.

title: MOON: Multi-Objective OrthoNormalized Updates for Multitask Learning
authors: Shiji Zhou, Kunlin Lyu, Lei Zhang, Ruodong Wang, Yifan Sun
summary: This paper proposes MOON, a method for multi-task learning that improves how gradients are manipulated during training. The key insight is that modern neural networks (especially Transformers) have matrix-structured parameters, but existing multi-task methods treat them as flat vectors, missing the geometry that could make learning more efficient. MOON respects this matrix structure and shows faster convergence and better final performance across multiple tasks simultaneously.

title: Drift and Dependence: Layer-wise Information-Theoretic Bounds for Replay-Based Continual Learning
authors: Tieliang Gong, Zhongbo Zhang, Wen Wen, Yong-Jin Liu
summary: This paper analyzes why replay buffers—storing and retraining on old examples—help neural networks learn new tasks without forgetting old ones. The authors develop a mathematical framework that separates two coupled problems: the approximation error from using limited past data, and how repeated training on mixed old/new data affects learning. They show which internal network layers should be stabilized to minimize forgetting and provide an online metric to detect when a model is starting to forget.

title: AgenticTwin: An Agentic LLM Framework Integrated with Digital Twin for Anomaly Detection
authors: Touseef Hasan, Mounika Ghanta, Souvika Sarkar, Ujjwal Guin
summary: AgenticTwin combines large language models with digital twins — virtual replicas of physical systems — to detect and explain anomalies in cyber-physical systems like industrial equipment or sensor networks. The paper shows that when LLMs reason over structured anomaly detection outputs and collaborate as agents, human operators get better diagnoses and can ask natural-language questions about what went wrong, making complex sensor data interpretable at scale.

title: Is Per-Agent Policy Composition Safe? Rethinking Successor-Feature Transfer in Cooperative Multi-Agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Zijian Zhao, Sen Li
summary: This paper addresses a critical safety problem in multi-agent reinforcement learning: when teams of agents independently recombine learned policies to serve new objectives after deployment, the resulting joint behavior can be worse than any single policy in their library. The authors prove this failure occurs uniquely in multi-agent settings and propose MA-USFA, a hierarchical method that composes agent policies safely while remaining flexible enough to assign different goals to different agents.

title: Beyond Memory: A Transactional Continuity Kernel for Long-Lived AI Agents
authors: Jun He, Deying Yu
summary: This paper addresses a critical infrastructure problem: how do long-lived AI agents safely maintain and update their internal state when multiple untrusted components (models, tools, background processes) can propose changes? The authors propose the Continuity Kernel (CK), a transactional system that ensures state updates follow an authorized lineage, preventing stale overwrites, privilege escalation, and unaudited changes. This matters because as AI agents become persistent and autonomous, their state management can't rely on memory alone—it needs explicit governance, much like database transactions ensure consistency.

title: Predictive Allostatic Organization in Recurrent and Spiking Agents Under Partial Observability
authors: Frederick Hayes
summary: This paper investigates how recurrent and spiking neural networks develop interpretable internal structures when learning to survive in resource-constrained environments with incomplete information. The authors find that these agents organize their internal states in ways that predict future events and encode energy levels, suggesting a computational principle called "predictive allostatic organization" that may explain how brains and AI systems balance competing goals under uncertainty.

title: Top-down Traffic Scenario Generation via Joint Initial-Goal Diffusion and Trajectory Infilling
authors: Da Saem Lee, Yash Vardhan Pant, Sebastian Fischmeister
summary: This paper introduces TrafficDiffuser, a framework that generates realistic traffic scenarios by jointly modeling agent initial positions and goal destinations using diffusion models, then filling in trajectories between them. This addresses a key bottleneck in autonomous vehicle testing: existing simulators require manual specification of starting conditions, limiting the diversity and realism of generated scenarios. The approach makes scenario generation more interpretable and scalable for simulation-based AV development.

title: Governing Agentic AI in FinTech
authors: Henry Han
summary: This paper investigates how to govern AI agents making consequential financial decisions — a problem largely ignored despite rapid deployment. The core insight is that the real constraint isn't whether AI systems are capable, but whether their decisions can be verified, audited, and reproduced. The authors introduce the "Verifiability Gap" and test whether different AI models (local, hosted, and frontier systems) can consistently replay the same financial decisions, finding that reproducibility varies dramatically by architecture and capability level.

title: Long-Horizon Forecasting of Complete Financial Statements with Forma
authors: Travis L. Johnson, Jiannan Jiang, Soumyabrata Chaudhuri, Yihao Chen, Lauren Falvey et al.
summary: This paper introduces Forma, a transformer-based model that forecasts complete financial statements (78 line items) for 1–20 quarters ahead—a task no prior work has tackled jointly at this scale. The key insight is that specialist architectures beat general-purpose scale for this domain; Forma outperforms classical ML, gradient boosting, zero-shot foundation models, and frontier LLMs, with its advantage widening at longer horizons where valuation matters most.

title: Contextual Quality-Diversity Evolutionary Reinforcement Learning for HVAC Control in Tropical Commercial Buildings
authors: Tran Le Vu
summary: This paper develops CQD-ERL, a hybrid evolutionary and reinforcement-learning controller for managing HVAC systems in tropical commercial buildings. Rather than learning a single fixed policy, the system maintains a diverse archive of specialized policies tailored to different weather and load conditions, improving energy efficiency and safety compared to traditional control approaches.

title: Efficient Hypergradient Descent for Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Nikita Sevriukov, Anna Barabanova, Uliana Gagarina, Karina Ivanova, Sofiia Kasaeva et al.
summary: This paper solves a key computational bottleneck in inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) — the problem of inferring reward functions from expert demonstrations. The authors show that the Hessian of the inner optimization problem has special structure (related to the Fisher information matrix), and they use a sketching technique to avoid expensive matrix inversions, making IRL tractable at scale.

title: Rule of Thumb: Explaining Artificial Intelligence Systems using Partial Information
authors: Kaivalya Rawal, Daria Onitiu, Brent Mittelstadt, Sandra Wachter, Chris Russell
summary: This paper introduces "Rule of Thumb" (RoT), a new method for explaining AI decisions by identifying the most relevant features for a specific prediction. The approach works without needing access to the model's internals, making it practical for auditing black-box systems, explaining LLM outputs, and supporting scientific discovery — while also meeting regulatory requirements for AI transparency.

title: Optimize Cheap, Deploy Strong: Cost-Aware Cross-Tier Transfer for Evolutionary Optimization
authors: Tal Oved, Roi Pony, Oshri Naparstek, Udi barzelay
summary: This paper tackles the high cost of evolving LLM prompts and agentic programs by splitting the computational work across cheaper and stronger models—using weak models for frequent fitness evaluations and reserving strong models only for critical steps. The key insight is that you can evolve prompts on a cheap tier, then deploy the result on a strong tier, cutting search costs 5–54x while maintaining or improving performance.

title: Persistent Recursive Worlds Enable Autonomous Software Evolution
authors: Beichen Huang, Zhenyu Liang, Bowen Zheng, Ran Cheng
summary: This paper presents Genesis, a system that enables autonomous software development by agents over long timescales (120+ hours) without requiring individual agents to persist. Instead of keeping agents alive, Genesis keeps the software project itself persistent—agents propose changes to a shared repository, changes get reviewed and accepted, and only validated work advances the project history. The system successfully built a Rust C compiler from scratch and rewrote legacy Fortran code, demonstrating that long-term software evolution can be organized around a stable project rather than stable agents.

title: Objective-oriented quantitative investment: A specification-driven framework for automated synthesis of trading strategy pipelines
authors: Liangliang Zhang
summary: This paper proposes a new framework for building trading strategies that prioritizes meeting explicit investor requirements—like controlling style exposure or managing portfolio turnover—rather than simply maximizing a single performance metric. The key innovation is treating strategy construction as a formal specification problem: investors describe what they want in a structured language, a compiler assembles candidate pipelines from a vast design space, and a rigorous verification protocol confirms each pipeline actually satisfies the stated constraints before deployment.

title: A Graph Neural Network--Guided Genetic Algorithm for Physical Internet Supply Chain Optimization under Cost Uncertainty
authors: Faezeh Ardali, Gerald M. Knapp
summary: This paper solves supply chain planning in Physical Internet networks — a system where factories, distribution hubs, and retailers collaborate — by combining graph neural networks (GNNs) with genetic algorithms. The key innovation is using a GNN to learn good factory-to-hub assignments, which then guides a genetic algorithm's search through millions of possible configurations. This matters because supply chains face uncertain costs and complex interdependencies; the hybrid approach finds better solutions faster than traditional optimization alone.

title: Beyond Cash Flows: A Multi-Agent AI Framework for Valuing Clinical-Stage, Cross-Border Biotechnology
authors: Yuhan Fang
summary: This paper proposes a multi-agent AI framework for valuing early-stage biotechnology companies—firms with no revenue but whose worth depends entirely on drug development timelines and regulatory approval odds. Traditional investment valuation breaks down here because there are no cash flows to model. The author designs a system where specialized AI agents (analysts, researchers, risk managers) collaborate to convert scientific judgments into defensible valuations and coordinate pricing across international markets, grounding the approach in their own track record managing a cross-border biotech fund.

title: Beyond Naturalness: Probing Automated Text-To-Speech Evaluators on Linguistically Grounded Dimensions
authors: Oluwanifemi Bamgbose, Simon Rosen, Jash Shah, Lindsay Devon Brin, Hoang H Nguyen et al.
summary: This paper shows that current automated speech quality evaluators—both traditional MOS predictors and newer Audio-LLM judges—fail to capture the full complexity of how humans perceive synthetic speech. The authors created a benchmark with linguistically-grounded dimensions (like prosody, articulation, and rhythm) to reveal that these evaluators collapse into measuring just acoustic quality, missing specific linguistic errors that listeners actually notice.

title: Multimodal Model Diffing for Feature Discovery and Control
authors: Hunar Batra, Lachin Naghashyar, Ashkan Khakzar, Philip Torr, Christian Schroeder de Witt et al.
summary: This paper introduces MMDiff, a framework for understanding and controlling the internal features of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) that process both text and images. The work uses sparse autoencoders to decompose hidden neural states into interpretable directions, then compares these across different model versions to isolate which features were changed by multimodal training and how to steer them. This matters because MLLMs are increasingly deployed in high-stakes settings, yet we lack tools to audit their behavior or control specific capabilities like spatial reasoning or safety.

title: From Values to Benchmarks: Evaluating Large Language Models for Governmental Use in Dutch
authors: Laurens Samson, Iva Gornishka, Gossa Lô, Yuki M. Asano, Sennay Ghebreab
summary: This paper develops a systematic evaluation framework for assessing large language models in Dutch governmental settings, identifying six key dimensions (factuality, honesty, bias, energy use, cost, transparency) and benchmarking 30+ models. The work matters because governments need tools to choose LLMs responsibly, yet existing evaluation frameworks ignore public-sector values and non-English linguistic needs.

title: GENCO - A Unified Neural Solver Embedded in a Development Framework for Steady-State Grid Analysis
authors: Alban Puech, Matteo Mazzonelli, Tamara R. Govindasamy, Mangaliso Mngomezulu, Héctor Maeso-García et al.
summary: This paper presents GENCO, a neural network solver that handles three core power grid analysis tasks — power flow, optimal power flow, and state estimation — in a single unified model. The work matters because it brings modern deep learning to critical infrastructure (electricity grids) while maintaining physical consistency, achieving 30–85x speedups over classical solvers while remaining practical for real-world deployment.

title: DSLE: A Learning Environment for Dark Souls Boss Encounters
authors: Derin Gezgin, Jim O'Connor, Tanner Goodwin, Gary B. Parker
summary: This paper introduces DSLE, a benchmark environment that converts Dark Souls boss fights into game-playing tasks for AI agents. The key finding is sobering: current deep reinforcement learning methods (PPO, DQN) fail almost completely on even the tutorial boss, while evolutionary algorithms and rule-based systems fare only slightly better. This work reveals a significant capability gap in modern RL algorithms when facing complex, real-time combat with visual observations.

title: Decoding-Level Taboo: A Diagnostic Stress Test for LLM Robustness
authors: Tadanobu Chuyo Kamijo, Ori Rottenstreich, Javier Conde, Gonzalo Martínez, Pedro Reviriego
summary: This paper introduces Decoding-Level Taboo, a diagnostic test that forces language models to generate text under constrained conditions by blocking their most likely token choices in real time. Most evaluations test models under ideal, "narrow" conditions where they perform well; this work probes what happens when models are pushed off these comfortable paths—revealing gaps between benchmark performance and real-world robustness. The method matters because deployed LLMs face constant constraints (safety filters, system prompts, structural requirements) that differ from training conditions, and understanding this robustness gap is critical for safe deployment.

title: Consilience for Verifier-Free Test-Time Scaling
authors: Lecheng Kong, Like Hui, Haitao Mao, Jun Huan
summary: This paper identifies a critical flaw in confidence-based test-time scaling for LLMs: high confidence across all reasoning steps often signals failure to explore the solution space, not success. The authors propose "consilience," a new selection framework that rewards exploratory reasoning (low initial confidence) followed by convergence to a high-confidence answer, significantly improving performance on complex math and code generation tasks without needing external verifiers.

title: Competitive mediator games and urban CAV routing markets
authors: Grzegorz Jamróz
summary: This paper introduces "competitive mediator games," a new game-theoretic framework that generalizes correlated equilibria to model markets where multiple intermediaries compete to route autonomous vehicles. The work proves that under certain conditions, these markets naturally collapse to monopolies, and applies these insights to understand future autonomous routing and driving (ARAD) service markets.

title: Fusion Training for Mathematical Generalization in Large Language Models
authors: Congfeng Cao, Pengyu Zhang, Jelke Bloem
summary: This paper systematically studies how to train large language models that can switch between two modes: a fast "non-thinking" mode for simple responses and a slow "thinking" mode for complex reasoning, especially in mathematics. The key finding is that these two modes are in tension—training the model to be good at quick answers actually makes it worse at reasoning—and the best training approach depends on balancing data and schedule choices.

title: Financial Numerical Prediction and Allocation as Token Generation
authors: Xu Ouyang, Moontae Lee
summary: This paper shows that a causal language model can directly generate financial forecasts and investment decisions as constrained tokens, rather than using separate task-specific prediction heads. FinATOM unifies stock-return forecasting and ETF portfolio allocation through a single generative interface, achieving better risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe ratio improvements of 7–10%) than traditional approaches on 2023–2025 test data.

title: Stealing Reasoning Traces from Proprietary LLM APIs
authors: Alexander Panfilov, David Schmotz, Ilia Shumailov, Luca Beurer-Kellner, Joachim Schaeffer et al.
summary: This paper uncovers a critical security vulnerability in how major LLM providers (OpenAI, Anthropic, Google) protect their models' reasoning traces — the step-by-step thinking that models use to arrive at answers. The researchers show that encrypted reasoning blocks are reusable across sessions and users, allowing attackers to "decrypt" them by injecting them into weaker models from the same provider, which then output the reasoning in plaintext. This enables model distillation, large-scale extraction of sensitive personal data, and injection of hidden malicious prompts.

title: Towards Expert-level Medical AI for Real-time Video Consultations
authors: Mahvish Nagda, Jihyeon Lee, Matthew Thompson, Chunjong Park, Tim Strother et al.
summary: This paper demonstrates an AI system (AMIE Video) that conducts medical consultations via video at expert physician level, integrating real-time speech, visual perception, and clinical reasoning. In a controlled study comparing the system to actual primary care doctors, AMIE matched or exceeded physician performance in diagnosis, history-taking, and management—a significant milestone because previous medical AI only worked with text, missing critical non-verbal cues that doctors rely on.

title: Nash Peer-to-Peer Insurance Bargaining under Price Fairness and Coalitional Stability
authors: Tim J. Boonen, Wing Fung Chong, Kenneth Tsz Hin Ng, Tak Wa Ng
summary: This paper studies how peer-to-peer insurance groups can fairly distribute risk and premiums when members bargain with a reinsurer. The authors use Nash bargaining — a game-theoretic framework where parties negotiate from disagreement points — to design contracts that are both individually rational (each member prefers the contract to no deal) and coalitionally stable (no subgroup wants to defect). The work matters because P2P insurance is growing, and understanding how to price and allocate risk fairly while preventing group collapse is a practical problem.

title: Agentic Auto-Research is Fuzz Testing
authors: Yifeng He, Jicheng Wang, Yinzhe Zhao, Jiachen Liu, Hao Chen
summary: This paper argues that autonomous research agents need a fundamentally different architecture than current "generate-and-rank" systems. Rather than proposing many experiments and sorting them by final outcomes, agents should work like fuzzers—observing dense, intermediate signals of progress (coverage) and using that feedback to decide what to try next. The paper makes the case that feedback architecture, not just generation capability, is the central bottleneck in making AI-driven research effective and reliable.

title: RynnValue: Scaling Robotic Value Foundation Models with Temporal Distance
authors: Dongchi Huang, Hongyin Zhang, Bohan Hou, Siteng Huang, Zhian Su et al.
summary: This paper introduces RynnValue, a foundation model that learns to predict how far a robot is from reaching language-specified goals by using temporal distance (time-to-goal) as a training signal instead of human preferences. The key insight is that temporal labels can be extracted automatically from video timestamps at scale, allowing the model to train on 7,000+ hours of robotic manipulation data without expensive preference annotations. When converted into reward signals, RynnValue improves real-world robot task success rates from 52.5% to 72.5%.

title: Deep Multimodal Wearable Sensor Fusion for Detection of Body-Focused Repetitive Behaviors
authors: Samaneh Rezaeimanesh, Mohsen Behradfar, Mohammad Fili, Guiping Hu
summary: This paper develops a deep learning system that detects body-focused repetitive behaviors (like hair pulling and skin picking) using data from wrist-worn sensors that measure movement, temperature, and proximity. The system combines multiple sensor modalities to achieve very high accuracy (F1 of 0.985) and could enable continuous, objective monitoring for mental health diagnostics in clinical and home settings.

title: Multi-Agent AI Safety as an Institutional Design Problem
authors: Abdullah X
summary: This paper treats multi-agent AI safety as an institutional design problem — asking how rules, authority structures, and workflows can shape safe collective behavior among AI agents. Through a large-scale empirical study of 5,280 episodes across multiple model families, the authors show that safety depends not just on rules themselves, but on how authority is represented, what fallback options exist, and whether systems track the provenance (origin and history) of decisions.

title: Macaron-V1: Towards Open Continual Learning with Self-Improvement and Mixture-of-LoRA
authors: Mind Lab,  :, Vin Bo, Asher Cai, Jingwei Cao et al.
summary: Macaron-V1 is an open-source agent system designed to continuously improve itself after deployment by learning from real-world interactions. It combines a frozen base language model with multiple specialized adapters (called LoRA modules) that can be swapped per user interaction, enabling the system to serve different roles—chat, coding, reasoning—while staying up-to-date through an automated feedback loop that evaluates and refines the model over time.

title: CARD: Controlled Agentic Reddit Discussions for Credit Card Simulation
authors: Yaoning Yu, Kai-Min Chang, Ye Yu, Yi-Chia Wang, Haojing Luo et al.
summary: This paper presents CARD, a framework for simulating realistic credit card discussion threads on Reddit using controlled language generation. Rather than generating comments independently, CARD orchestrates multiple agents (a planner and writer) that respect conversation structure, stance, tone, and user variation to match real discussion patterns. The work matters because it shows how to move beyond surface-level text generation toward generating coherent multi-turn interactions that reflect authentic human communication about financial products.

title: SR-OPSD: Self-Referenced On-Policy Self-Distillation
authors: Zhuo Sun, Entong Li, Yanlong Zhao, Xiaoyuan Cheng, Wenxuan Yuan et al.
summary: This paper proposes SR-OPSD, an improved method for training language models using reinforcement learning feedback at the token level. The key insight is that standard on-policy self-distillation can become unstable because the "teacher" model constantly changes as the student learns; SR-OPSD stabilizes this by mathematically characterizing what the ideal target should be and how to train toward it, achieving strong results on reasoning and coding tasks.

title: Distributed Team Orchestration via Supervisor Networks: Convergence, Optimality, and Resilience
authors: Juntian Zhu, Guanpu Chen, Tongtian Zhu, Miguel de Carvalho, Zhouwang Yang et al.
summary: This paper addresses how distributed teams of agents can learn to coordinate when they receive belief information from supervisors rather than perfect information about each other's states. The key challenge is that supervisors may make mistakes or face Byzantine (malicious) agents that lie about their actions. The authors propose DTOA (distributed team-orchestrating algorithm), prove it converges to near-optimal team strategies, and show it remains robust even when some agents deliberately misreport information.

title: MoRSE: Task-Oriented Multi-Agent System with Mixture of Role-Subtask Experts
authors: Peiwen Li, Shiyang Zhang, Yangtian Zhang, Sizhuang He, David van Dijk et al.
summary: This paper introduces MoRSE, a system that improves multi-agent LLM teams by giving each agent specialized skills through role and subtask assignment. Rather than using generic prompts for all agents, MoRSE decomposes tasks into dependency-aware subtasks, assigns agents specific roles, and fine-tunes their parameters separately — enabling agents to develop genuine expertise. The approach shows meaningful improvements on code-generation tasks while keeping computational costs low.

title: CPDA: Class-Conditional Path Distribution Alignment for Unsupervised Time-Series Domain Adaptation
authors: Felix Ott, Christopher Mutschler
summary: This paper proposes CPDA, a method for adapting time-series classifiers trained on labeled data from one source (e.g., one sensor) to work on unlabeled data from a different source (e.g., a different sensor or user). The key insight is to align not just overall feature distributions but class-specific temporal patterns between domains, using a specialized kernel that captures time structure and frequency information alongside semantic features.

title: Joint Lyapunov Certificates for K-Agent Generative AI Governance: Stochastic Stability, Emergent Ensemble Risk, and Zero-Knowledge Governance Attestation
authors: Sriram Nagaraj
summary: This paper addresses a critical blind spot in AI governance: when multiple generative AI models interact through shared learning, each model can individually appear stable while the combined system drifts dangerously. The authors develop a mathematical framework using "Joint Lyapunov Certificates" to detect and prove stability of multi-agent AI systems without exposing proprietary model weights, using cryptographic attestation protocols.

title: Personalized Federated Learning via Variance-Aware Nonparametric Empirical Bayes
authors: Jae Ho Chang, Arnab Auddy, Subhadeep Paul
summary: This paper develops a new statistical method for federated learning — a distributed machine learning setting where multiple clients train models locally without sharing raw data.
