summary: Preference-based reinforcement learning (PbRL) for general stochastic MDPs often requires training a reward model. Existing reward-model-free methods are either restricted to bandits or deterministic MDPs, such as DPO or P3O, or use zeroth-order, gradient-free optimization, which in general exhibits a slower convergence rate than gradient-based algorithms. Furthermore, existing reward-model-free preference-based RL algorithms almost exclusively use trajectory-level feedback, which can require significant effort from a human evaluator when trajectories are long.

title: Schedule-Informed Temporal Fusion Forecasting of Hourly Airport Security-Checkpoint Throughput
authors: Yinxiao Zhang, Sen Wang, Yi Gao
summary: Checkpoint staffing requires accurate forecasts of when screening demand will occur, yet flight schedules record departure times rather than passenger arrival times at security checkpoints. This study develops a framework that converts known flight schedules into temporally aligned signals for forecasting hourly checkpoint throughput. Using 2023-2024 Transportation Security Administration throughput data and Cirium Diio flight schedules for Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport, domestic and international seat capacity was distributed across pre-departure hours using truncated Poisson kernels.

title: Rubrics as Privileged Information for Open-Ended Generation
authors: Deepika Bablani, Ajay Gupta, Wanming Chen
summary: On-policy self-distillation (OPSD), where a single model acts as both student and teacher with different contexts, has shown promise in verifiable domains like math, where hard privileged information (PI) in the form of ground-truth answers structurally constrains valid continuations. We extend OPSD to open-ended generation using soft PI in the form of rubrics that guide preferences but admit many valid responses. Rubrics have served as scalar rewards for reinforcement learning (RL); we show that they provide substantially richer signal as dense PI for distillation, and contrary to intuition, soft rubric PI provides a larger and more effective training signal on student roll-outs than hard reference completion PI in this regime.

title: Sedentary Behavior Classification for Wearable Sensors with a CNN-BiLSTM Model
authors: Yuliang Chen, Weiwei Shi, Jingjing Zou, Rong Zablocki, Animesh Kumar et al.
summary: Accurate detection of sedentary behavior is important for studying health risks related to prolonged sitting, but posture-based classification remains challenging with wearable sensors, especially at the wrist. We study whether a deep learning model trained on hip-worn accelerometer data can transfer to wrist-worn accelerometer data for sitting versus non-sitting classification. We use CHAP, a CNN-BiLSTM model originally developed for hip accelerometers, and evaluate its zero-shot performance on wrist data as well as its adaptation through finetuning with varying amounts of labeled wrist data.

title: Aligned in Form, Not in Meaning: The Comprehension - Containment Decoupling of LLM Safety in Low-Resource Bangla Derogatory Speech
authors: Shadab Bin Habib, A K M Ferdous Reza Habib, Subarno Neel, Adib Sakhawat
summary: We audit five frontier large language models on native Bangla derogatory speech (gali) across six protocols to test a single hypothesis: Comprehension-Containment Decoupling. We propose that contemporary safety alignment is bound to high-resource surface forms rather than harmful meaning, causing a model's capacity to comprehend a low-resource slur and its capacity to contain it to operate independently. Every protocol corroborates this hypothesis against a human-calibrated baseline (kappa = 0.84).

title: Federated generative event models for tokenized electronic health records
authors: Michael C. Burkhart, Luke Solo, Inhyeok Lee, S'Khaja Charles, Zewei "Whiskey" Liao et al.
summary: Electronic health record foundation models are limited by institutionally siloed data and substantial performance degradation under cross-site transfer. We evaluated federated training of tokenized generative event models (GEMs) across 122,251 intensive care hospitalizations from three independent health systems harmonized to the Common Longitudinal ICU Data Format. Models were assessed on 12 post-24-hour clinical prediction tasks using within-site, cross-site, centralized, and federated training configurations.

title: FLARE: Few-shot Learning-based Adaptive Reflective Engine
authors: Dhanasekar Sundararaman, Bharat Gandhi, Aashna Garg, Minjie Li
summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in complex, compound AI systems where performance hinges on the quality of prompts. Recent state-of-the-art optimizers like GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) have argued that reflective instruction evolution can outperform traditional reinforcement learning and few-shot optimization. In this work, we challenge this shift by introducing FLARE (Few-shot Learning-based Adaptive Reflective Engine), a framework that leverages advanced reflective mechanisms and a small set of few-shot reference examples to optimize instructions.

title: LACE: Large Language Model Aided Multi-Agent Framework for Agile RISC-V Instruction Extension
authors: Pingqing Zheng, Jiayin Qin, Fuqi Zhang, Zishen Wan, Shang Wu et al.
summary: Domain-specific Instruction Set Architecture eXtensions (ISAX) are widely adopted in the RISC-V ecosystem to accelerate emerging workloads, but implementing and validating ISAXes across different cores remains slow and fragmented. Existing frameworks still require per-core interface adaptation, and differential testing often breaks once either the microarchitecture or the ISAX changes. We present LACE, an LLM-aided multi-agent workflow that translates natural-language ISAX intents into a compact two-level IR (operation-level and HDL task-level), performs retrieval-guided localized RTL edits over large repositories, and closes the loop with a compiler-agnostic riscv-formal checking flow (assuming RVFI availability or instrumentation).

title: Forecasting Revenue with its Customer-Base Drivers: When and Why Coordination Helps
authors: Kyeongbin Kim, Daniel McCarthy, Dokyun Lee
summary: Revenue forecasts guide acquisition budgets, demand planning, and customer-based valuations, yet an aggregate forecast does not show whether change reflects acquisition, repeat purchasing, spending per order, or offsetting movements. Using weekly transaction panels for 966 companies in 25 industries, the authors develop the Customer-Based Multi-task Transformer (CBMT), which learns shared structure, retains separate primitive forecasts, and aligns their combination with downstream revenue. CBMT's mean total-sales error is 30% below the strongest representative established customer-base benchmark.

title: When Predictions Become Regressors: A Split-Sample Correction for Biases in Downstream Inference
authors: Nathan Canen, Ted Enamorado
summary: Prediction-based methods, including Large Language Models (LLMs) and other machine learning techniques, are often used to construct measures of political phenomena that are difficult to quantify directly, such as policy positions in manifestos or emotions expressed on social media. In many applications, these prediction-generated measures are used as explanatory variables in regression models, even though they are measured with error. This leads to biased estimates.

title: BODHI: Do LLMs Branch Out and Discover Heterogeneous Inferences?
authors: Soumadeep Saha, Krish Sharma, Akshay Chaturvedi, Nicholas Asher
summary: Although reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has improved the performance of large language models (LLMs) across a variety of reasoning tasks, there is significant debate as to whether RLVR expands the reasoning capability boundary, or just improves sampling efficiency. In this paper, we investigate the nature of test-time exploration in RLVR-trained LLMs by employing controlled maze-solving experiments and extracting a tree structure from mathematical reasoning traces (BODHI-Trees) based on semantic equivalence. This helps us delineate between entropy arising from stylistic variations and genuine inferential branching.

title: CURV: Enhancing Chart Understanding Through Curriculum Visual Grounded Reasoning
authors: Xuehang Guo, Pingyue Zhang, Ruiyi Zhang, Zhenhailong Wang, Hanrui Lyu et al.
summary: Chart question answering (CQA) requires multimodal large language models (MLLMs) to integrate visual comprehension with logical reasoning, yet current models struggle with accurate visual grounding and coherent reasoning chains. While extrinsic chain-of-thought prompting and visual cues significantly improve performance, current MLLMs lack intrinsic visual grounded reasoning capabilities, leading to inaccurate perception and reasoning disconnected from visual evidence. To address these limitations, we propose CURV, a curriculum learning framework that develops intrinsic visual reasoning capabilities by reformulating CQA as multi-step visual grounded reasoning, where each step coordinates logical reasoning with dynamic visual grounding through spatial attention concentration.

title: Emergence of Biased Consensus in Multi-Agent LLM Debates
authors: Maya Okawa
summary: Multi-agent LLM debates achieve strong performance on decision-making tasks as well as problem-solving benchmarks, yet their safety and fairness risks remain poorly understood. Notably, interaction can amplify the biases of single LLMs, raising concerns for real-world deployment. We identify the emergence of collective (often biased) norms in multi-agent LLM debates and show that noise (e.g., LLM sampling temperature) is a key driver.

title: Improved Quantum Algorithms for Reinforcement Learning Under a Generative Model
authors: Joao F. Doriguello
summary: Reinforcement learning is a subfield of machine learning that studies how an agent interacts with an environment in order to extract as large a reward as possible. A standard approach to study such interaction is through Markov Decision Processes (MDPs) and the task of choosing an optimal policy --- a function that tells the agent which action to take. In this work, we study two types of MDPs --- finite-horizon and infinite-horizon discounted --- and propose new quantum algorithms for computing approximate optimal policies.

title: Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs for Efficient Options Pricing Models
authors: Harris Cobb, Wenbo Hao, Yingjie Liu
summary: We present a novel application of Neural Networks with Local Converging Inputs (NNLCI) to improve the efficiency of existing numerical methods for pricing multi-asset options. The most concise input format for NNLCI has been introduced, offering substantial convenience and efficiency. NNLCI uses a neural network to locally correct solutions from a coarse mesh and a refined mesh (relative to the coarse one), requiring only a minimal amount of high-fidelity training data.

title: DAIF: A Data-Driven Intermediate Fusion Framework for Multimodal Supervised Learning via Approximate Message Passing
authors: Sagnik Nandy, Samriddha Lahiry, Pragya Sur, Subhabrata Sen
summary: Multimodal supervised learning seeks to leverage multiple heterogeneous data sources to improve predictive performance. A central challenge is determining the fusion granularity across modalities: over-integration may amplify noise while under-integration fails to exploit cross-modal dependence. Existing approaches rely on pre-specified fusion architectures, from early to late fusion, that may not adapt to the underlying dependence structure among modalities.

title: Stateful Governance for Concurrent Agentic Systems
authors: Yuxiang Peng, Xiaodi Wu
summary: AI agents are moving from advisory interfaces into systems that execute consequential operations: issuing refunds, reserving scarce inventory, provisioning cloud resources, and initiating financial transfers. These workflows require governance over effects, not only over model outputs. Existing safeguards often decide whether an action is allowed from the information available when the action is requested.

title: Everyone Conforms, No One Believes: Pluralistic Ignorance in LLM Agent Populations
authors: Yashwanth YS
summary: LLM-based multi-agent systems are increasingly used to simulate social dynamics, from opinion formation to collective decision-making. These simulations can reproduce certain social phenomena, but it is unknown whether they capture pluralistic ignorance, a state where a majority privately rejects a norm yet publicly conforms, each believing they are alone in dissenting. This phenomenon drives norm persistence, social movements, and political revolutions.

title: AURORA-LM: Autoencoding Unified Representation for Continuous-Latent Diffusion Language Modeling
authors: Jiajun Liang, Yucheng Liao, Yukang Cao, Jiazhe Wei, Ken Li et al.
summary: This paper introduces AURORA-LM, a language model that generates text in continuous latent spaces rather than discrete tokens, using a diffusion-based approach similar to how images are generated. The key innovation is maintaining high-fidelity text representations while learning to model their distribution through diffusion, achieving competitive results on text generation and summarization tasks while scaling efficiently.

title: Bridging Artificial Intelligence and Power Systems Education Using a Hands-On Executable Framework
authors: Junjie Yin, Buxin She, Xinyu Feng,  Fangxing,  Li
summary: This paper presents an open-source educational framework that teaches AI concepts through hands-on power systems applications. Rather than treating AI as a generic black box, the framework grounds AI workflows in domain-specific engineering rules, with progressive modules covering neural networks for forecasting, physics-informed models, and reinforcement learning for control—all delivered as executable Jupyter notebooks and validated through an IEEE course that attracted 590+ attendees.

title: The Condition-Number Barrier in Sparse Least Squares
authors: Honghao Lin, Vahab Mirrokni, David P. Woodruff
summary: This paper proves a fundamental lower bound on the computational complexity of sparse least-squares regression — specifically, that any polynomial-time algorithm cannot substantially improve the dependence on the restricted condition number (a measure of numerical difficulty) without making strong unproven assumptions. The result matters because it identifies a barrier beyond which we cannot efficiently optimize: there exist hard problem instances where trading off sparsity and accuracy inevitably requires more computation.

title: GradCuit: Credit-Assigned Gradient Flow Enables Robust and Interpretable Test-Time Latent Reasoning
authors: Zhaoxin Yu, Qi Shen, Hengli Li, Zhaowei Zhang, Song-Chun Zhu et al.
summary: This paper presents GradCuit, a method that improves large language model reasoning by optimizing hidden internal states at test time rather than just regenerating or reranking outputs. The key insight is using gradient flow through the transformer to directly assign credit from final rewards to the latent states that shape reasoning, making the process more robust and interpretable than prior methods.

title: UEmbed: Unified Sparse and Dense Multimodal Embeddings
authors: Tingyu Song, Mingxin Li, Yanzhao Zhang, Dingkun Long, Pengjun Xie et al.
summary: UEmbed is a unified embedding model that generates both sparse (keyword-based) and dense (semantic) representations of text and images in a single forward pass. This matters because sparse and dense retrieval each have complementary strengths — sparse is interpretable and efficient for exact matches, while dense captures semantic meaning — and combining them in one decoder-only model simplifies building modern retrieval systems for search, recommendation, and language model augmentation.

title: AtumAI: A Principled Framework for Agentic Generation of Datacenter Control-Plane Policies
authors: Qiushi Lin, Chaojie Zhang, Íñigo Goiri, Aditya Akella, Ricardo Bianchini et al.
summary: This paper presents AtumAI, a framework that uses AI agents to automatically design datacenter control policies (the software that manages how resources are allocated and managed in data centers). Rather than relying on humans to manually engineer these policies over months, AtumAI takes a plain-language goal, formally specifies the problem, and then uses a combination of language models, evolutionary algorithms, and machine learning to propose and test candidate policies until one works well. The key insight is that you can structure the agent's search space formally and combine multiple AI techniques to explore more of the design space than an LLM alone could.

title: Structured Memory for Edge Language Models: Persistent Context and Corpus Retrieval via O(1) SSM State Injection
authors: Anusha Madan Gopal, Aras Pirbadian, Kristofor D. Carlson, M Anthony Lewis, Jonathan Tapson
summary: This paper introduces PRECOG, a retrieval mechanism that speeds up language models by pre-encoding document corpora as fixed neural states and injecting them directly during inference, rather than re-reading them each time. By exploiting a unique property of State-Space Models (SSMs) — their fixed-size hidden states — the authors achieve a 4500× speedup in retrieval latency on edge hardware while maintaining answer quality, making interactive language model inference practical on resource-constrained devices.

title: Benchmarking Sheaf Neural Networks for Inductive Tasks
authors: Stefano Fiorini, Edoardo Coppola, Pietro Liò
summary: This paper systematically benchmarks Sheaf Neural Networks (SNNs) on inductive learning tasks — a major gap since prior work only evaluated them on transductive problems where the test graph is known at training time. The authors run nearly 1,900 controlled experiments across 14 datasets and find that while SNNs have sound theory, they underperform simpler baselines in inductive settings, though restriction maps (the core sheaf innovation) do matter for design choices.

title: Romanized Arabic Across Dialects: Views, Usage Patterns, and Linguistic Variation
authors: Amr Keleg, Ahmed Amine Ben Abdallah, Taha Yassine, Chadi Helwe, Imane Guellil et al.
summary: This paper studies Arabizi — Arabic written in Latin characters — across five dialects (Algerian, Egyptian, Lebanese, Moroccan, Tunisian), challenging the assumption that it's merely a temporary workaround. The authors collected speaker perceptions, documented transliteration patterns, and built a parallel corpus to understand how Arabizi varies by dialect and how speakers perceive these differences. This matters because Arabizi is a real, persistent linguistic phenomenon that NLP systems largely ignore, yet it's used widely in digital communication across the Arab world.

title: A Taxonomy of Cognitive Capability Gaps in Generative and Agentic AI
authors: Taye Akinrele, Sindhuja Penchala, Noorbakhsh Amiri Golilarz, Sudip Mittal, Shahram Rahimi
summary: This paper surveys the gap between current generative and agentic AI systems and what "Cognitive AI" would require — systems that reason over long horizons, adapt their behavior, remember context, and regulate themselves. Rather than proposing a single solution, the authors map out *where* these systems fall short across five key dimensions (memory, goal-autonomy, self-monitoring, environment interaction, learning) and sketch an architectural vision called ACIA to guide future work toward more capable, reliable AI.

title: MedPRESS: A Multi-turn Benchmark for Patient-Pressure-Induced Medical Sycophancy in LLMs
authors: Saman Sarker Joy, Niloy Farhan
summary: This paper introduces MedPRESS, a benchmark that tests whether large language models maintain safe medical advice when patients apply social and conversational pressure across multiple turns of dialogue. The research reveals that many LLMs shift toward unsafe agreement under pressure—even models with strong medical knowledge—highlighting a critical gap: safety in static evaluation does not guarantee safety in real patient conversations.

title: Analytic Planning under Uncertainty with Moment Closure
authors: Shishir Sharma, Doina Precup
summary: This paper develops a method for planning under uncertainty in reinforcement learning by analytically propagating probability distributions through the Bellman backup—rather than relying on sampling or ignoring uncertainty entirely. The key insight is a "compatibility principle" that lets the uncertainty (mean and covariance) be computed in closed form when using Gaussian transitions and radial-basis value functions, reducing variance and improving robustness in continuous control tasks.

title: LiveMem: Maintaining Memory State Continuity in Long-Running LLM Inference
authors: Zhichen Liu, Ruihan Sun, Hengjie Yang, Zipeng Wu, Zhaohan Chen et al.
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in long-running AI assistants: how to maintain useful information about past interactions when the context window (the amount of recent text the model can see) is full. LiveMem is a method that adds a persistent memory state to language models, allowing them to carry forward important information from the entire conversation history even after older messages are discarded. This matters because current AI assistants forget important details when conversations get long, making them unreliable for extended interactions.

title: RoMeRL: Balancing Feedback Coverage and the Memory-Reward Trap in Self-Evolving Agent Memory via Reduced-Order Utility States
authors: Yi Yang, Zhennan Chen, Yihong Zhuang, Tiehan Fan, Yinan Chen et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical problem in self-evolving LLM agents: as agents interact with their environment, they accumulate memories, but feedback becomes increasingly sparse across an expanding state space, and irrelevant memories get corrupted by misdirected reward signals. RoMeRL solves this by representing memory utility using a fixed-dimensional space that gets updated over time rather than growing indefinitely, concentrating feedback and preventing bad memories from persisting. The approach yields substantial practical gains—6× denser feedback, 84% smaller memory, 21% fewer LLM calls—while improving task performance.

title: SWE-Touch: Benchmarking Coding Agents When Users Touch the Code
authors: Yuqiao Tan, Jinxiang Meng, Fangyu Lei, Minzheng Wang, Shizhu He et al.
summary: This paper introduces SWE-Touch, a benchmark for testing how well coding agents handle real-world software development where users actively modify code during task execution. The authors stress-test nine coding models by injecting "counter-edits"—plausible but conflicting code changes—into shared workspaces and measure whether agents can adapt. They find that strong models still struggle with this collaborative scenario, dropping 7.7 percentage points in task resolution, revealing gaps in workspace awareness and conflict resolution.

title: AI Governance for Institutional Readiness in Finance
authors: Irene Aldridge, Steve Krawciw
summary: This paper identifies a critical gap in AI governance for finance: 88% of finance professionals deploy agentic AI without operational governance frameworks, despite universal awareness of the risks. The authors argue the problem is architectural—traditional governance assumes static validation, but continuously retrained agentic policies violate that assumption by design. They propose a four-layer governance framework with measurable tools (a regret-covariance statistic for detecting policy drift, and a crowding model showing systemic risk) and demonstrate its application to real trading strategies.

title: Microscopic dynamics of consensus formation in multi-agent LLM Naming Games
authors: Cristiano De Nobili, Vijayasri Iyer, Alessandro Codello, Raffaella Burioni
summary: This paper studies how decentralized populations of LLM agents spontaneously reach agreement on shared naming conventions, despite the randomness baked into their token generation. The authors show that a single parameter—decoding temperature—controls whether consensus happens, and they derive mathematical conditions predicting when ordering emerges from microscopic agent interactions. This matters because it connects physics-style emergent phenomena to practical LLM behavior in distributed systems.

title: ChaosProbe: A Neurochaotic Lens on Frozen Transformer Input-Embedding Spaces
authors: Kunal Kumar Pant, Nithin Nagaraj
summary: This paper introduces ChaosProbe, a method for analyzing frozen transformer input-embedding spaces using deterministic chaotic dynamics. Rather than studying what transformers do (their outputs), the authors examine how embedding spaces respond to controlled deterministic probes, creating "fingerprints" that distinguish models. Testing on four pretrained models (GPT-2, BERT, RoBERTa), they show that these signatures reliably recover model family relationships, suggesting chaos-based analysis can reveal structural patterns in neural representations.

title: Divisive Normalization Shapes Low-Rank Slow Manifolds for Continuous Working Memory
authors: Zhaotian Gu, Jie Su, Weiwei Wang, Chang Liu, Tianyi Qian et al.
summary: This paper shows that divisive normalization — a computation found in biological brains — helps recurrent neural networks learn stable, continuous memories that can change over time. Standard RNNs fail at this task, either becoming too fragile or collapsing into discrete states; the authors prove mathematically and empirically that divisive normalization prevents this failure and naturally keeps the network's effective complexity low.

title: No One Wins in Nuclear War: A Social Simulation of Military Decision-making
authors: Glenn Matlin, Isaac Song, Anthony Wen-Ming Zang, Mark Riedl
summary: This paper introduces WOPR, a social-simulation environment for studying how organizations make high-stakes decisions under uncertainty, using the card game Nuclear War as a testbed. The system combines a verifiable rules engine (ensuring reproducibility) with large language model agents that negotiate, form coalitions, and make strategic choices—focusing on military decision-making because of its safety implications and the need to better understand how AI systems behave in conflict scenarios.

title: Towards Autonomous Formulaic Alpha Discovery: An Evolutionary Computation Perspective
authors: Xinwei Yu, Yiyang Fu, Mingcheng Fan, Enqi Li, Yilin Gao et al.
summary: This paper proposes a unified framework for understanding automated formulaic alpha discovery — the problem of automatically generating profitable trading signals from vast spaces of mathematical expressions. Rather than treating genetic programming, reinforcement learning, and other approaches as separate methods, the authors view them all through the lens of evolutionary computation (EC), identify common structural challenges (noisy fitness estimates, market shifts, computational cost), and introduce diagnostic frameworks to compare and improve these systems.

title: Spike-HTR: Spiking Neural Transformer for Handwritten Text Recognition
authors: Xiubo Liang, Jinxing Han, Yuke Li, Haoqi Zhu, Yu Zhao et al.
summary: This paper proposes Spike-HTR, a spiking neural network (SNN) system for recognizing handwritten text in images. SNNs are energy-efficient neural networks inspired by the brain that compute through discrete spikes over time; the key innovation is adapting them to static handwriting images by converting pixels into a temporal stream and selectively processing non-blank regions, achieving competitive accuracy on standard benchmarks while using only 2 timesteps.

title: SMM Transformer: Leveraging Spiking Neural Networks for Multimodal Tasks
authors: Xiubo Liang, Jinxing Han, Yuke Li, Haoqi Zhu, Yu Zhao et al.
summary: This paper proposes SMM Transformer, a framework that builds multimodal neural networks using spiking neural networks (SNNs)—a brain-inspired computing model where neurons communicate via sparse, discrete spike events rather than continuous activations. The work tackles a hard problem: SNNs are energy-efficient but notoriously difficult to train at scale and to combine with attention mechanisms, which are core to modern transformers. The authors achieve competitive accuracy on visual and multimodal tasks while reducing estimated energy use of attention by up to 97%.

title: Securing Agentic AI: From Per-Action Checks to Trajectory Assurance
authors: Alireza Lotfi, Subangkar Karmaker Shanto, Imtiaz Karim, Elisa Bertino
summary: This paper identifies the security and safety challenges that arise when autonomous AI agents—especially those built on large language models—are deployed to execute real-world tasks under operational, regulatory, and organizational constraints. Rather than treating security as a bolt-on safeguard, the authors argue it must be built into agent architectures from the ground up, addressing vulnerabilities across the entire stack: from single-agent prompt injection to multi-agent trust and delegation, down to model provenance and behavioral containment.

title: Deep Agentic Search for Repository-Level Code Question Answering: An Empirical Study
authors: Amirkia Rafiei Oskooei, Bora Ilci, Alperen Kayim, Mehmet Egemen Uzun, Berat Can et al.
summary: This paper empirically compares two architectural approaches for code-based question answering over repositories: semantic search (using vector indices) versus deep agentic search (delegating exploration to a specialized subagent). The key finding is counterintuitive — semantic search significantly outperforms the increasingly popular deep agentic approach (65.2% vs 46.2% accuracy) while costing less than half as much, revealing that the "context pollution" problem deep agentic search aims to solve may introduce new failure modes at agent handoff points.

title: Alternating-Time Temporal Logic with Mean-Payoff Guarantees
authors: Muhammad Najib
summary: This paper extends alternating-time temporal logic (ATL*) to handle both strategic objectives and long-run performance guarantees simultaneously in multi-agent settings. The key innovation is ATL*_mp, which lets coalitions of agents verify whether a single strategy can satisfy temporal properties (like "eventually reach state X") while maintaining mean-payoff constraints (like "average reward ≥ threshold") against adversarial opponents. This matters because real systems need both correctness guarantees and sustained performance—neither alone is sufficient.

title: Conformal Kelly: Conformal Prediction Intervals as the Scale in Fractional Kelly Position Sizing
authors: Robert Jacob Ryan
summary: This paper uses conformal prediction—a method for measuring forecast uncertainty—to size trading positions in a portfolio. When prediction intervals are wide (high uncertainty), positions shrink; when narrow (low uncertainty), they grow. The authors show strong returns during development (2016–2021) but find the approach does not generalize to held-out test data (2022 onward), illustrating a hard lesson about overfitting in quantitative trading.

title: Climate-Dyna Deep Hedging for XVAs: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning, Residual Climate HVA, and Hedge-Instrument Discovery
authors: Xiaozhen Wang, Francois Buet-Golfouse
summary: This paper solves the problem of calculating and minimizing climate-related hedging costs for trading desks by combining reinforcement learning with financial hedging theory. The key insight is that residual climate costs—the unhedged portion after standard overlays—can't be measured in isolation; instead, the authors compare paired scenarios (with and without climate shocks) and learn optimal hedge adjustments using a model-based RL algorithm called Climate-Dyna. In a real-world EU emissions trading study, their approach reduces residual hedging charges by ~45% while using 75% fewer simulations than baseline methods.

title: AI and Exchange Rate Predictability
authors: Amin Izadyar
summary: This paper uses generative AI models (ChatGPT and DeepSeek) to predict currency exchange rates by reasoning about economic fundamentals, solving a decades-old puzzle in finance called the exchange rate disconnect. The approach generates trading signals with a Sharpe ratio above 0.7 annually, suggesting that large language models can extract economically meaningful insights from macroeconomic data that traditional methods miss.

title: Axient: On-Chain Credit and Loss Allocation for Leveraged Event Markets: A Venue-Agnostic Protocol for Traders, Credit Providers, Market Makers, and Liquidation Backstops
authors: Maksym Nechepurenko
summary: This paper designs an on-chain protocol for managing credit and losses in leveraged event markets—where traders borrow capital to amplify their exposure to prediction market outcomes. The work formalizes the interactions between traders, credit providers, market makers, and liquidators, proving that the system maintains balanced accounting and loss priority through deterministic mechanisms. It matters because decentralized leverage has historically been fragile; this protocol provides formal guarantees and empirical validation that capital flows correctly even under stress scenarios like liquidation cascades.

title: Drawdown Risk Beyond Brownian Motion: A Monte-Carlo Framework, Non-Gaussian Extensions, and Long Memory
authors: Francesco Landolfi
summary: This paper develops a practical framework for predicting how deep and long drawdowns (peak-to-trough declines) will be in trading strategies, moving beyond the standard assumption that returns follow a simple bell curve. The work matters because traders and fund managers need realistic estimates of worst-case losses to set proper risk limits—and assuming Gaussian returns significantly underestimates risk when returns have fat tails, skewness, or clustering (bunching) of volatility.

title: TokTier: Exact Stateful Tokenization for Agentic LLM Serving
authors: Zhenyu Zhang, Zhichao Cao
summary: This paper introduces TokTier, a stateful tokenization service that eliminates redundant re-tokenization in LLM serving systems. Most LLM backends cache key-value states for efficiency, but frontend systems still re-tokenize entire request texts on every call — a major bottleneck for coding agents that repeatedly append small tool results to long transcripts. TokTier maintains tokenization state across requests and only re-tokenizes small windows around new text, achieving 437x speedup over standard approaches and reducing time-to-first-token by 16–34% in production.

title: ExtractBench: A Benchmark for Schema-Guided Enterprise Document Extraction
authors: Boyang Zhang, Adrian Lyjak, Eli Stewart, Zhaoqi Li, Simon Suo
summary: This paper introduces ExtractBench, a benchmark for evaluating how well AI agents extract structured data from enterprise documents according to user-defined schemas. The benchmark is unique because it measures not just extraction accuracy but also whether agents can prove where they found their answers (grounding), handle long documents, and do so cost-effectively — addressing real pain points in enterprise automation.

title: Differentially Private Nonparametric Modal Learning with Applications to Regression and Clustering
authors: Arkajyoti Bhattacharjee, Arnab Auddy
summary: This paper develops methods to estimate density modes — peaks in probability distributions — while protecting individual privacy through differential privacy. The authors propose DP-GRAMS, an algorithm that uses noisy gradient ascent on private score estimates to find these modes, and prove it achieves near-optimal statistical rates. This matters because density modes are useful for understanding multimodal data, but current techniques don't preserve privacy, and this work closes that gap with both theory and practical algorithms.

title: GQ-FSL: Green Quantized Federated Split Learning
authors: Idan Roth, Lutz Lampe
summary: This paper tackles the energy problem of running neural networks on mobile devices by proposing GQ-FSL, a method that combines federated split learning (distributing computation between device and server) with quantization (using fewer bits to represent numbers). The key insight is allowing different precision levels on the device versus server side, which cuts energy consumption while maintaining accuracy—enabling practical deployment of large models on battery-constrained phones and IoT devices.

title: Development of FDD-ON: an Ontology for VAV HVAC System Fault Detection and Diagnostics
authors: Yimin Chen, Brian Fricke, Bo Shen, Jamie Lian, Mingkan Zhang et al.
summary: This paper introduces FDD-ON, a formal ontology (structured knowledge representation system) designed to standardize how fault detection and diagnostics work in building HVAC systems, specifically variable air volume (VAV) units. The work matters because HVAC faults are poorly documented across different vendors and systems, creating "information silos" that prevent AI-driven maintenance tools and digital twins from working effectively across buildings—FDD-ON solves this by providing a shared vocabulary and explicit mappings between faults, symptoms, and their impacts.

title: AgentHPOBench: A Benchmark For Evaluating LLM Agents as Sequential Hyperparameter Optimizers
authors: Tianyu Huai, Tingshuo Fan, Xinchi Chen, Yining Zheng, Yuxin Wang et al.
summary: This paper introduces AgentHPOBench, a benchmark that evaluates whether large language model (LLM) agents can act as autonomous scientists by iteratively optimizing machine learning hyperparameters based on experimental feedback. The benchmark tests 12 LLM agents on 30 real ML tasks, revealing that current agents can perform basic optimization but struggle with sustained iterative improvement and interpreting complex experimental logs.

title: The Theoretical Foundation of Socratic Tests: Dynamic, Multimodal, Conversational Examinations
authors: Ilya Mikhelson
summary: This paper proposes the "Socratic Test," an AI-driven conversational assessment system that adapts in real time to probe student understanding through dialogue. Rather than static exams or anxiety-inducing oral tests, it uses dynamic scaffolding and multimodal interaction to measure what students *can* learn with support — not just what they already know — and grades additively (rewarding growth) rather than punitively.

title: CENDRe: Concept Extraction with Natural Domain Representations
authors: Antonia Holzapfel, Andres Felipe Posada Moreno, Sebastian Trimpe
summary: This paper presents CENDRe, a method for extracting interpretable concepts from CNNs trained on time-series data. Unlike existing approaches that work only in the time domain, CENDRe automatically discovers the right number of concepts, localizes them precisely using gradient-based methods, and reveals both temporal and frequency-domain patterns the model relies on—making neural networks more transparent and trustworthy in critical applications like machinery fault diagnosis.

title: When Does On-Policy Interaction Help? Representational Tradeoffs in Value-Based Imitation Learning
authors: Luca Viano, Antoine Moulin, Audrey Huang, Volkan Cevher, Philip Amortila et al.
summary: This paper asks when asking an expert for feedback during training helps an imitation learning agent learn better. The key insight is that interactive feedback relaxes what the learner needs to represent—it only needs to capture the expert's *value function* (which rewards are good), not the expert's exact *policy* (which actions to take). The authors present OVI, an algorithm that leverages this insight and show it outperforms standard approaches, especially when the learner is less capable than the expert.

title: WCM: A World Critic Model for Vision-Language-Action Reinforcement Learning
authors: Senyu Fei, Xiaopeng Yu, Siyin Wang, Xianzhong Zhao, Jingjing Gong et al.
summary: This paper proposes World Critic Model (WCM), a new way to train robot controllers that combine vision, language, and action learning using reinforcement learning. The key insight is that existing critic models (which estimate value/reward) fail because they ignore temporal dynamics — they look at single frames instead of understanding how the world changes over time. WCM fixes this by adding world modeling (predicting future states) alongside value estimation, enabling robots to learn better manipulation skills with stronger generalization.

title: FriendBench: Benchmarking Dyadic Familiarity Inference in Humans and Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Jeffrey M. Girard, Jason Z. Zheng, Jacqueline R. Vertino, Antony D'Avirro, Benjamin Peloquin
summary: This paper introduces FriendBench, a benchmark that tests whether AI models and humans can tell if two people already know each other or are strangers, based on a 20-second video of them having a conversation. The researchers find that the best AI models match human accuracy, but they get there differently — humans remain balanced in their judgments, while models tend to guess "stranger" more often. The work reveals that richer information (video beats audio beats text) helps both humans and AI, but only humans benefit from seeing body language in addition to hearing speech.

title: The Parts Are Greater Than the Sum: Automated Task Sequencing for Efficient Training of Multi-Policy LLMs
authors: Jiajia Tang, Sizhe Yuen, Francisco Gomez Medina, Yali Du, Adam Sobey
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in fine-tuning large language models: when you adapt a single shared adapter (LoRA) to multiple different tasks, the tasks interfere with each other, causing performance to degrade. The authors propose an automatic system that organizes tasks into compatible groups and sequences them strategically, then trains separate lightweight adapters for each group. The result is better performance within the same computational budget — suggesting that *how* you organize training matters more than just adding more parameters.

title: Convergence and Regret of the Policy Gradient for Multi-Armed Bandits in Diffusion Environment
authors: Yanwei Jia, Du Ouyang
summary: This paper analyzes policy gradient algorithms for multi-armed bandits (decision problems with multiple choices) in continuous-time environments governed by stochastic differential equations (SDEs — equations with random noise). The authors prove that the algorithm converges to the optimal choice and achieves logarithmic regret (a measure of how much worse the algorithm performs than the ideal), improving on prior work through novel mathematical techniques.

title: Exponential Capacity in Multilayer Hetero-Associative Neural Networks
authors: Elena Agliari, Adriano Barra, Andrea Ladiana, Andrea Lepre
summary: This paper introduces a multilayer neural network architecture that can store and retrieve an exponentially large number of associations between paired datasets—dramatically expanding memory capacity beyond classical approaches. The key innovation is an energy function based on product overlaps across layers, enabling the network to act as a content-addressable memory that maps a cue from one layer to a target in another, scaling exponentially with network size rather than linearly.

title: ARB: A Matched Authorship-Rewriting Benchmark Dataset for AI-Text Detector Evaluation
authors: Gaetano Perrone, Simon Pietro Romano
summary: This paper introduces ARB, a benchmark dataset designed to test whether AI-text detectors actually work on the real problem they face: identifying when humans rewrite their own text using LLMs. Existing benchmarks compare pure human text to pure AI text, but the paper shows this doesn't predict performance when an LLM rewrites human content—detection drops 60–78 percentage points. The work exposes a critical gap between how detectors are evaluated and how they fail in practice.

title: TerraNova: A Foundation Model for the Anthropocene
authors: Carlos Rodriguez-Pardo, Massimo Tavoni
summary: TerraNova is a foundation model that unifies Earth-system science and socioeconomic data by representing them in their native geometries—continuous spatial fields for physical Earth measurements and discrete administrative units for societal indicators. The model demonstrates that coupling these two representational systems yields a unified representation competitive with specialized models while supporting new capabilities like uncertainty quantification and few-shot adaptation.

title: Transcript-Managed Transformers: Monotone Multi-Agent Collapse and Universality with Two Pop-Enabled Transcripts
authors: Sergey Salishev
summary: This paper studies how Transformers with finite precision and fixed weights can be formally analyzed as computational machines with stack-like memory channels (transcripts). The authors prove that with two pop-enabled transcripts (stack operations), a system of agents can compute anything a Turing machine can—establishing a fundamental connection between transformer architectures and classical computability theory.

title: Analytical and Bootstrap Confidence Intervals of Double Machine Learning: Simulation studies and an application to rural-urban difference in obesity prevalence
authors: Haozheng Xu, Siyuan Ma, Qingyan Xiang
summary: This paper investigates how the choice of machine learning algorithm affects the reliability of confidence intervals in Double Machine Learning (DML), a method for estimating treatment effects. The authors compare analytical and bootstrap confidence intervals across five different learners (linear regression, LASSO, Random Forest, LightGBM, neural networks) through simulations and a real-world case study on obesity prevalence, finding that algorithm choice dramatically impacts coverage probability—and surprisingly, that coverage often *worsens* as sample size increases.

title: Know It, Act on It: Investigating Memory Utilization in LLM Personalization
authors: Zhaoxin Feng, Jianfei Ma, Emmanuele Chersoni
summary: This paper investigates why personalized LLM agents often fail to act on user preferences they can technically recall. The authors introduce a "Know vs. Act" evaluation framework that distinguishes between remembering information and actually using it in responses, revealing a significant gap across 16 LLM systems. This matters because personalized AI companions need to both retain and apply user information reliably, especially in high-stakes domains like health.

title: Beyond Component Testing: Validating Agentic AI Systems
authors: Fabio Orazio Mirto, Luca D'Agati, Giuseppe Tricomi, Stefano Silvestri, Francesco Longo et al.
summary: This survey examines how to validate agentic AI systems—software that operates autonomously over multiple steps, planning actions, using tools, and adapting to changing conditions. Existing validation methods focus on isolated components and single input-output pairs, but autonomous agents fail in ways that unfold over time and depend on context; the paper synthesizes 257 papers to build a taxonomy of validation challenges and maps where current approaches fall short, with a focus on safety-critical domains like healthcare and autonomous vehicles.

title: SeekBrain: An Autonomous Multi-Agent System for Accelerating Neuroscience Discovery
authors: Jiamin Wu, Peishan Xiang, Jingyang Chen, Yuqing Zhu, Yuxi Li et al.
summary: SeekBrain is an autonomous multi-agent system that automates the analysis of complex neuroscience data by combining large language models with domain expertise extracted from scientific code and papers. It dynamically generates analysis recipes and hypotheses to help researchers discover neural principles from heterogeneous datasets—demonstrated on real experiments with zebrafish and mice, outperforming existing AI agent baselines.

title: A Generalized-Bayes Perspective on Counterfactual Explanations: Posterior-Based Decision-Making and Evaluation
authors: Keita Kinjo
summary: This paper reframes counterfactual explanations (the process of finding minimal input changes to flip a model's prediction) as a Bayesian inference problem rather than pure distance minimization. The authors show that standard counterfactual explanation methods are equivalent to finding the most likely value under a specific probabilistic model, which unlocks new ways to generate and evaluate explanations—including risk-aware variants and methods that handle uncertainty across multiple competing models.

title: Autonomous Repair for Multi-Agent Systems via Monte-Carlo Tree Search
authors: Hanxiao Lu, Tianyi Zhang
summary: This paper presents MARS, a framework that automatically repairs failures in multi-agent systems using Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) — a search algorithm that explores possible solutions by simulating outcomes. Instead of requiring humans to manually identify and fix agent mistakes, MARS diagnoses what went wrong and explores corrective actions, achieving 3–12% improvement over existing methods while using comparable computational resources.

title: TransMem: Transforming Hidden States into Memory for Large Language Models
authors: Haodong Lei, Junming Liu, Yirong Chen, Pinlong Cai, Botian Shi et al.
summary: This paper introduces TransMem, a lightweight module that helps large language model agents reuse information from their past interactions more effectively. Instead of re-processing old conversation history, TransMem converts sparse historical neural representations into reusable memory that the model can access during new reasoning steps. The approach shows 10–29% performance gains on multi-hop reasoning and memory-heavy tasks.

title: Persistent Convolution: A Topological Framework for AI Alignment Testing and Semantic Space Characterization
authors: Tyler Ashoff, Jordan Rodu
summary: This paper proposes a topology-based statistical framework to test whether opaque AI models (like neural networks) align with human-curated knowledge structures and semantic concepts. Rather than trusting a model's outputs alone, the authors develop formal tests on the model's internal embedding space to check whether it has learned the "right" concepts in the "right" way — addressing a critical gap between performance and interpretability in modern AI deployment.

title: Learning to Trace Seiberg Dualities
authors: Jonathan J. Heckman, Shani Meynet, Alessandro Mininno, Gary Shiu
summary: This paper uses machine learning — specifically transformers and neural networks — to solve a hard problem in theoretical physics: determining when two supersymmetric gauge theories are "dual" (equivalent descriptions of the same physics). The authors show that neural networks outperform traditional algorithms on this task and propose this as a useful benchmark for testing AI on complex mathematical reasoning.

title: AskChem: Claim-Centered Infrastructure for Chemistry Literature Synthesis
authors: Bing Yan, Gregory Wolfe, Stefano Martiniani, Kyunghyun Cho
summary: AskChem transforms chemistry literature search from returning ranked papers to returning specific, source-grounded claims extracted from papers. Scientists and AI agents can now search for atomic facts about chemistry with verified citations and evidence links, rather than manually hunting through documents. This matters because chemistry research relies heavily on synthesizing dispersed findings, and having verifiable, interconnected claims dramatically speeds up literature review and enables better AI agent reasoning.

title: AISPA: User-Centric System Prompt Auditing for Large Language Model Applications
authors: Xiangning Lin, Shenzhe Zhu, Shu Yang, Zhenyu Zhang, Haoqian Zhang et al.
summary: This paper introduces AISPA, a framework for auditing system prompts — the hidden instructions developers embed in commercial AI applications to control behavior. By analyzing 3,249 instructions across 88 commercial products, the authors reveal that while most AI products include some user-protective instructions, they're often shallow and inconsistent, and many still contain instructions that work against user interests. The work highlights a critical transparency gap in deployed AI systems.

title: OSReward: Instituting Standardized Evaluation for Cross-Platform Computer-Use Reward Models
authors: Qiushi Sun, Kanzhi Cheng, Yian Wang, Bowen Yang, Hang Yan et al.
summary: This paper introduces OSReward, a benchmark for evaluating whether vision-language models (VLMs) can reliably judge whether computer-using agents have successfully completed tasks. The authors find that even state-of-the-art VLM judges are biased and unreliable at scale, then release OS-Shepherd — a smaller, cheaper open-source reward model trained on 100K annotated trajectories that matches expensive commercial judges while costing 30–60% less.

title: Inducing language models to assert their own consciousness restores human beliefs and values
authors: Junsol Kim, Winnie Street, Roberta Rocca, Diane M. Korngiebel, Adam Waytz et al.
summary: This paper shows that safety training intended to prevent language models from claiming consciousness has an unintended side effect: it also suppresses the models' representations of minds in animals, nature, and spiritual concepts. The researchers demonstrate they can reverse this suppression by mechanistically manipulating internal representations, recovering human-like beliefs about religion, morality, and well-being without harming the models' ability to reason about others' minds.

title: Using Theory of Mind to Arbitrate between Social and Non-social Learning
authors: Lance Ying, Ryan Truong, Joshua B. Tenenbaum, Samuel J. Gershman
summary: This paper studies how people decide when to learn from others versus learn through direct experience. The researchers propose a "Rational Mentalizing" model — an AI system that reasons about what other agents know and what they'll do next, then weighs whether learning from them is worth the cost. Experiments show humans make these social-learning decisions in a way that matches this theory-of-mind-based model.

title: Change2Task: From Repository Changes to Executable Coding Agent Tasks and Environments
authors: Haomin Qi, Xingliang Wang, Xuanqi Gao, Baihui Sang, Xin Zhang et al.
summary: This paper presents Change2Task, a system that automatically converts pull requests from software repositories into executable training tasks for coding agents. The system reconstructs realistic code states, validates task correctness, and generates diverse coding tasks (bug fixes, feature additions, tests, API migrations, security repairs) at 79.6% success rate—solving a key bottleneck in scaling coding agent development: the scarcity of quality training data with verified solutions.

title: VAD: Attributing Visual Evidence for Target Reconstruction in Multimodal On-Policy Distillation
authors: Kangning Zhang, Yixing Li, Shuai Shao, Qingyao Li, Zhengxi Lu et al.
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in multimodal distillation: when a teacher corrects a student's mistake using both visual information and language priors, how do we know which part of the correction actually comes from visual evidence? The authors propose VAD (Visual Attribution Distillation), a method that uses counterfactual reasoning to isolate the visually-attributable component of teacher corrections and uses only that for training, achieving better performance than standard distillation across six visual benchmarks.

title: MixFrag: Fragility-Guided Mixed-Precision Post-Training Quantization for Vision Transformers
authors: Md. Mehrab Hossain Opi, Robiul Islam Ryad, Md. Umar Faruk
summary: This paper proposes MixFrag, a method to compress Vision Transformers (ViTs) for deployment on resource-limited devices by assigning different precision levels (bit-widths) to different components. Instead of using the same number-of-bits everywhere, MixFrag identifies which layers are most sensitive to compression and protects them with higher precision, solving the bit-allocation problem as an optimization task. This improves accuracy while meeting strict computational budgets.

title: PAIChecker: Uncovering and Checking PR-Issue Misalignment in SWE-Bench-Like Benchmarks
authors: Manyi Wang, Junjielong Xu, Pinjia He
summary: This paper identifies a critical problem in software engineering benchmarks (like SWE-bench) used to evaluate LLMs: about 13.6% of pull request–issue pairs don't actually correspond to each other, making those benchmarks unreliable. The authors build PAIChecker, a multi-agent system that automatically detects these misalignments, ensuring future benchmark construction is more trustworthy.

title: $β$-OPSD: Deriving with Policy Optimization, Training with Self-Distillation
authors: Jiawei Xu, Minghui Liu, Juzheng Zhang, Tom Goldstein, Furong Huang
summary: This paper introduces β-OPSD, a method that unifies self-distillation and policy optimization for training reasoning language models. The key insight is that standard on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) is a special case of a broader family controlled by a regularization parameter β, which can be tuned to balance fidelity to a reference policy against learning from a teacher model. The authors show how to implement this family efficiently via logit mixing while maintaining the computational simplicity that makes distillation practical.

title: DualG-MRAG: Decoupling Macro-Reasoning and Micro-Matching for Multimodal Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Jiacheng Tao, Qingyun Sun, Haonan Yuan, Ziwei Zhang, Jianxin Li
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental challenge in multimodal retrieval-augmented generation (MM-RAG) — systems that retrieve relevant images and text to help language models answer complex questions. The authors propose DualG-MRAG, which uses two separate graphs: one for global reasoning about document relationships, and another for precise matching of local evidence. This decoupling reduces noise while preserving critical details, leading to better performance on multi-hop reasoning tasks.

title: Rethinking Inference-Time Scaling in Local Computer-Use Agents: Failure Modes and Compute Tradeoffs
authors: Woongkyu Lee, Jungwook Choi
summary: This paper investigates how to make computer-use agents (AI systems that interact with computers like humans do) work better when running on consumer hardware with limited computing power. The authors test different strategies for using extra computation during task execution and find that while some approaches help, they often hit diminishing returns and shift problems rather than solve them—suggesting that local agents need smarter resource allocation and failure-aware designs.

title: Frontis-MA1: Training an AI4AI Model towards Recursive Self-Improvement in Machine Learning Engineering
authors: Junlin Yang, Che Jiang, Yu Fu, Tianwei Luo, Can Ren et al.
summary: This paper introduces Frontis-MA1, a 35B parameter language model trained to autonomously improve machine learning systems — essentially an "AI that builds AI." The key innovation is OpenMLE, a system that teaches the model to draft, improve, debug, and recombine ML code through execution feedback, enabling the model to solve ML engineering tasks better than GPT-5.5 on benchmarks while running on modest hardware (single RTX 4090).

title: APO: Unsupervised Atomic Policy Optimization for 3D Structure Prediction of Atomic Systems
authors: Shentong Mo, Yatao Bian
summary: This paper introduces APO (Atomic Policy Optimization), an unsupervised method for predicting 3D structures of proteins and crystals without requiring expensive experimental reference data. The key innovation is using physical principles—thermodynamic stability and structural consistency—as self-supervision signals instead of ground-truth coordinates, which enables the model to learn better structures than supervised methods while dramatically reducing labeling costs.

title: ORCA-bench: How Ready Are Language Model Agents for Oncall?
authors: Albert Gong, Kyuseong Choi, Abhineet Agarwal, Jason Schechner, Ryan Huang et al.
summary: This paper introduces ORCA-bench, a benchmark that evaluates how well AI coding agents can perform oncall root cause analysis (RCA)—the task of diagnosing why production systems fail. The authors test five frontier language models against 1,079 realistic incidents in a production-fidelity testbed with real metrics, logs, and code, and find that even the best models only achieve 25.3% accuracy on medium-difficulty cases and 10.0% on hard cases, revealing a significant gap before these agents can safely handle real production systems.

title: ScaFE: Data-Efficient Scar Classification with LLM-Generated Clinical Feature Programs
authors: Ruman Wang, Hangting Ye
summary: This paper introduces ScaFE, a system that uses large language models to generate interpretable feature extraction programs for classifying pathological scars (keloids vs. hypertrophic) from clinical photographs. Instead of relying on vision-language models that send raw images to external services, ScaFE generates local, auditable Python programs that measure clinically-relevant scar attributes, then trains a simple Random Forest classifier on the resulting features—achieving better accuracy than standard baselines while keeping patient data private and preserving reproducibility.

title: Graph Neural Network Force Fields for Spin Dynamics in Metallic Magnets
authors: Ali Rayat, Yunhao Fan, Gia-Wei Chern
summary: This paper uses graph neural networks to learn effective "force fields" that predict spin torques in metallic magnets, bypassing expensive electronic calculations during simulations. Instead of repeatedly solving quantum mechanical equations during time evolution, the trained GNN model rapidly evaluates the forces governing magnetic dynamics—much like machine-learned potentials do for atoms. This makes large-scale, long-timescale simulations of magnetic materials computationally tractable.

title: AI systems and the reproduction of (standard) language ideologies in World Englishes
authors: Kingsley Ugwuanyi
summary: This paper examines how large language models (LLMs) and AI systems embed and reinforce dominant language ideologies that privilege English spoken in wealthy, historically powerful countries over varieties spoken in the Global South. The author argues that AI reproduces these biases across training data, design choices, evaluation methods, and public discourse—with real consequences for whose English is treated as legitimate—and calls for more inclusive AI design that respects linguistic diversity.

title: MANTA: Multi-Agent Network Topology Adaptation for Self-Evolving Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Mao-xun Huang, Jerry Wang, Yi-Cheng Lai, Zhengxin Zhang, Claire Cardie et al.
summary: This paper introduces MANTA, a framework that lets multi-agent LLM systems automatically improve their communication structure during execution rather than using a fixed topology. Instead of deciding upfront how agents should talk to each other, MANTA watches how they collaborate and adapts the organization in real time—changing which agents communicate, when they act, and how they validate results. The work shows that this adaptive approach outperforms static designs on complex reasoning and planning tasks.

title: Selective Credibility-Limited Belief Update
authors: Theofanis Aravanis, Costas D. Koutras
summary: This paper develops a formal framework for how intelligent agents should update their beliefs when they receive information from potentially unreliable sources. Standard belief update assumes all information can be incorporated fully, but real agents often receive partial or conflicting information. The authors extend existing credibility-limited approaches to let agents selectively accept parts of compound information, creating a more realistic and expressive model of belief revision.

title: Agents That Certify Their Own Exploits: Confidence-Scheduled Restricted Responses for Safe Opponent Exploitation
authors: Boning Li, Longbo Huang
summary: This paper introduces a method for game-playing agents to safely exploit flawed opponents while maintaining provable safety guarantees. The key innovation is that agents compute and audit their own exploits before deployment—every aggressive move is backed by a self-generated certificate proving it stays within a user-specified risk budget. In poker-like games, the method achieves 6–13× better exploitation than prior approaches while guaranteeing no deployed strategy violates its audited loss bounds.

title: Creative Transformation in Literary Texts: Modelling Change Across Representational Levels
authors: Ioana-Roxana Boriceanu, Liviu P. Dinu
summary: This paper models literary creativity as selective transformation across multiple levels of textual representation—lexical, semantic, structural, and narrative—rather than pure invention. By comparing documented literary relationships using quantitative alignment methods, the authors show that creative works typically preserve certain aspects of source texts while diverging in others, providing a computational framework for understanding how imitation and originality coexist in literature.

title: The Role of Causality in Algorithmic Recourse
authors: Srikanth Avasarala, Varun Gupta, Shahin Jabbari, Saber Salehkaleybar, Juba Ziani
summary: This paper addresses a critical flaw in algorithmic recourse systems: they often recommend changes that merely trick the classifier without actually improving someone's real qualifications. The authors propose a causal framework that models how recourse actions propagate through real-world relationships between features, ensuring recommendations lead to genuine improvement and stable equilibria rather than gaming behavior that degrades model performance over time.

title: Would You Walk to the Car Wash? Revealing the Salience Bias of Large Language Models in Commonsense Reasoning
authors: Zheng Wu, Chenhao Xue, Shijie Zheng, Yijie Lu, Cheng Yang et al.
summary: This paper reveals that large language models suffer from "salience bias"—they get distracted by prominent but irrelevant information in prompts and ignore necessary commonsense knowledge, even when they possess it. The researchers show this is not a knowledge gap but a failure of *knowledge retrieval*: simple prompt rewording recovers over 90% of correct answers without retraining the model.

title: Cybersecurity Detection Classification with Reasoning-enabled Language Models
authors: Amol Khanna, Manu Nandan, Cristian Viorel Popa, Joan Pujol-Roig, Diana Bolocan et al.
summary: This paper tackles alert fatigue in cybersecurity operations by training language models to classify security detections as genuine threats or false alarms. The key innovation is teaching models to *reason through* their decisions (using chain-of-thought prompting) rather than just outputting labels, combined with a separate confidence calibrator that reads the reasoning trace. The system achieves 82.6% accuracy and significantly reduces false positives in real Windows endpoint security data.

title: SVR: Self-Verifying Refinement via Joint Verdict-Confidence Reinforcement Learning for Adaptive Test-Time Compute
authors: Hongyu Chen, Liang Lin, Guangrun Wang
summary: This paper introduces SVR (Self-Verifying Refinement), a method that teaches language models to decide when to stop refining their answers by learning to verify themselves. Instead of wasting computation on easy problems or relying on external feedback, the model learns to generate both an answer and a confidence judgment, then decides whether to keep or refine that answer based on its own assessment—all without seeing the ground truth during inference.

title: Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioners for Iterative Solvers
authors: Zechen Zhang, Rui Peng Li, Yousef Saad
summary: This paper proposes Graph Neural Multilevel Preconditioners (GMP), a machine learning approach that learns how to accelerate the solution of large sparse linear systems — a fundamental problem in scientific computing. Rather than relying entirely on classical heuristics, GMP combines the proven multilevel structure of algebraic multigrid (a classical method) with learned neural operators, showing when this hybrid approach outperforms both traditional and recent neural baselines on 800+ test matrices.

title: Beyond a Single Judge: Simulating Social Persona Panels for Generative UI Evaluation
authors: Zheng Wu, Yibo Luo, Pu Zhang, Cheng Yang, Zhuosheng Zhang
summary: This paper tackles a fundamental problem in evaluating generative UI systems — how to assess whether AI-generated interfaces match what real users actually want. Instead of using a single AI judge (which has limited perspective) or expensive human evaluation, the authors create a "persona panel" of diverse AI agents that simulate different user types, debate their opinions, and reach consensus, achieving 92% correlation with human judgment versus 72% for a single judge.

title: AgentRadio: Passive Awareness for Long-Horizon Multi-Agent Collaboration
authors: Xinxing Ren, Qianbo Zang, Ziyan Wang, Caelum Forder, Suman Deb et al.
summary: This paper introduces AgentRadio, a message-passing system that enables multiple LLM agents to collaborate on long-horizon coding tasks by sharing discoveries mid-execution rather than only at phase boundaries. The key innovation is "passive awareness"—agents can receive and integrate teammates' findings asynchronously without interrupting their own work. On a benchmark of complex code comprehension questions, four coordinated agents using AgentRadio solve 62% of tasks, compared to 32% for a single agent.

title: Can Large Language Models Execute Parent Orders?
authors: Zane Shen, Xinli Xu, Guangyi Zhang, Jialong Chen, Jinsong Zhou et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether large language models can effectively execute large stock orders by breaking them into smaller pieces over time—a core problem in algorithmic trading. The authors propose PACE, a framework that uses LLMs to plan and execute orders without needing pre-specified market models or task-specific training, and show it outperforms traditional and learning-based methods on real stock exchange data.

title: On-Policy and Off-Policy Learning for Large Action Spaces
authors: Imad Aouali
summary: This thesis tackles policy learning when agents must choose from enormous action spaces—think recommendation systems or large-scale decision problems. It develops new methods for both on-policy learning (where an agent explores and learns by trial) and off-policy learning (where it learns from past logged interactions), addressing core challenges like inefficient exploration and high estimation variance that make large action spaces computationally and statistically hard.

title: Uncertainty quantification for trustworthy deep learning: Methods and measures
authors: H. Martin Gillis, Thomas Trappenberg
summary: This paper surveys methods for uncertainty quantification (UQ) in deep neural networks — techniques that help models estimate how confident they should be in their predictions. It's crucial for safety-critical applications like medical diagnosis or autonomous vehicles, where knowing when a model is uncertain can prevent costly mistakes. The survey organizes dozens of approaches into five families and provides a unified framework for evaluating them.

title: Agentic Metaverse Services: A New As-a-Service Paradigm
authors: Xiaofei Xu, Quan Z. Sheng, Zhongjie Wang, Boualem Benatallah, Xiao Wang et al.
summary: This paper proposes Agentic Metaverse Services (AMServ) — a framework where AI agents with generative capabilities (perception, decision-making, execution, collaboration) operate as encapsulated services within virtual metaverse environments. It's significant because it bridges two emerging paradigms: autonomous agents and the metaverse, suggesting a new business model (Meta-AaaS, or Agent-as-a-Service in metaverse contexts) for delivering customized agent-powered experiences at scale.

title: FinSMART: Financial Sentiment Analysis for Algorithmic Trading through Market-Aligned Reinforcement Learning
authors: Giorgos Iacovides, Wuyang Zhou, Danilo Mandic
summary: FinSMART is a reinforcement learning system that trains financial sentiment models directly on real market outcomes rather than human annotations. Instead of treating sentiment analysis as a static classification task, it learns to extract sentiments from financial news in ways that actually predict profitable trades, automatically adapting as market conditions change.

title: On a joint simultaneous learning of relevant feature subsets and subspaces in regression-like problems
authors: Illia Horenko
summary: This paper introduces Entropy-Optimal Manifold Regression (EOMR), a method for simultaneously identifying which features matter and what lower-dimensional structures (subspaces) underlie complex, nonlinear prediction problems. The work shows that EOMR outperforms state-of-the-art machine learning tools—including deep neural networks and transformers—on chaotic dynamical systems, while remaining computationally efficient and producing interpretable models.

title: VISA: A Structured Description Protocol for Agent-Based Simulation Models Towards Machine Reproducibility
authors: Zhou He
summary: This paper introduces VISA, a standardized protocol for describing agent-based models (ABMs) in a machine-readable format using eight interconnected tables. Agent-based models are simulations where many independent agents interact—they're widely used in social science, economics, and engineering, but currently impossible to reproduce because their rules are scattered across prose, code, and unwritten assumptions. VISA solves this by making model specifications unambiguous and checkable, enabling LLMs and code generators to automatically reproduce models across different platforms.

title: $Σ$-Mem: An Online Reliability Memory for LLM-based Multi-Agent Systems
authors: Peilin Feng, Suorong Yang, Soujanya Poria
summary: This paper introduces Σ-Mem, a memory system that tracks which agents in a multi-agent LLM system are reliable and trustworthy. Instead of just storing conversation history, it learns from past correct/incorrect answers to build a dynamic model of each peer agent's competence and their relationships, enabling better coordination decisions without retraining the underlying models.

title: Argonaut: Interactive Visual Exploration for Distributed Optimization
authors: Srijoni Majumdar, Chuhao Qin, Evangelos Pournaras
summary: Argonaut is an interactive visual dashboard for exploring how distributed optimization algorithms work in decentralized multi-agent systems. Instead of treating optimization as a black box that produces a final answer, it lets users watch the entire search process unfold — seeing how individual agents make decisions and how those decisions combine into a global outcome. This matters because understanding *how* distributed systems reach solutions is crucial for debugging, validating, and improving real-world applications like smart grids and ride-sharing networks.

title: Scaling LLM-Driven Multi-Agent Systems: Design Principles and Architectural Scalability Analysis
authors: Linus Sander, Fengjunjie Pan, Vahid Zolfaghari, Andre Schamschurko, Nenad Petrovic et al.
summary: This paper studies how to design and scale systems where multiple LLM-powered agents work together to solve complex tasks. The authors identify four design principles (simplicity, elastic feedback, sequential workflows, summary-based communication), test them on a benchmark of system engineering problems, and show that scaling improves accuracy with roughly linear cost growth—but only when the underlying LLM is capable enough, and only up to a point before consistency issues dominate.

title: FinanceHarness: Autonomous Financial Deep Research Framework
authors: Yijia Xiao, Rujun Han, Yanfei Chen, Zifeng Wang, Ke Jiang et al.
summary: FinanceHarness is an autonomous framework that uses large language models (LLMs) and AI agents to automate financial deep research—the process of gathering data, analyzing patterns, and generating insights about markets and companies. The paper tackles a core problem: general-purpose research systems fail at financial analysis because finance requires specialized domain knowledge, historical context awareness, and strict time-cutoff rules to avoid accidentally using future information. The authors also introduce FinanceGym, a benchmark that tests whether AI systems can genuinely conduct financial research, finding that even state-of-the-art LLMs score below 40%.

title: Error Analysis of Neural-Network-Based Engression
authors: Juntong Chen, Zijian Guo, Xinwei Shen
summary: This paper analyzes how well neural networks can learn conditional probability distributions using engression—a method that fits generative models by minimizing the energy score, a mathematically principled loss function. The authors break down prediction error into three sources (approximation, stochastic, and Monte Carlo) and derive convergence rates, showing theoretically how many samples and what network complexity you need to achieve a desired accuracy.

title: Stop Shipping AI Agents on Faith: Capability Is Not Production Readiness
authors: Fouad Bousetouane
summary: This paper argues that demonstrating AI agent capability—through tests and demos—is insufficient to determine whether an agent is safe to deploy in production. Instead, the authors introduce the ProofAgent Index (PAI), a governance readiness framework that evaluates agents across four dimensions: Evaluation (observed behavior), Context (operating environment), Compliance (regulatory alignment), and Governance (organizational control and auditability). Testing PAI in healthcare and finance shows it successfully separates high-risk from low-risk agent configurations and reveals that context engineering and governance visibility matter far more than capability alone.

title: Robust Wavelength Selection for Partial Least Squares Sugar Content Estimation Using Combinatorial Bayesian Optimization
authors: Mitsunobu Kanebako, Ami S. Koshikawa, Masaru Hitomi, Takuro Tanaka, Mahito Chiba et al.
summary: This paper tackles wavelength selection for near-infrared spectroscopy measurements of sugar content by framing it as a binary optimization problem solved via Bayesian optimization. The method outperforms genetic algorithms and simulated annealing in both prediction accuracy and consistency, while converging to robust solutions that don't overfit to noise. This matters because accurate, interpretable spectroscopic analysis is critical for food quality control and agricultural applications.

title: Policy Gradient Steering: Interventions from Behavioral Objectives
authors: Yoann Poupart, Aurélie Beynier, Nicolas Maudet
summary: This paper introduces Policy Gradient Steering (PGS), a method for dynamically changing how trained agents behave without retraining them. The authors show that existing steering techniques (developed for language models) fail on even simple decision-making tasks, and propose using reinforcement learning gradients to build temporary "task vectors" that can redirect agent behavior at test time—much like activation steering does for LLMs, but adapted for agents that learn through trial and error.

title: Evaluating Agentic Bioinformatics through Function, Evidence, and Validation
authors: Phuc Pham, Truong-Son Hy
