summary: This paper proposes the Function–Evidence–Validation (FEV) framework to rigorously evaluate AI agents used in biological research, arguing that scientific credibility depends on inspectable workflows rather than final outputs alone. The authors map 109 agentic systems across genomics, protein science, and drug discovery, finding that most systems excel at planning and tool execution but lag in reproducibility, transparency, and empirical validation—a gap they address by recommending workflow-correctness as the primary assessment criterion.

title: Strategy, Not Payoffs: A Behavioural Embedding of Normal-Form Games
authors: Joshua Caiata, Sreepriya Pulyassary, Xiang Li, Kate Larson
summary: This paper investigates how large language models transfer strategic reasoning skills across different games when fine-tuned on one game versus another. The authors propose a lightweight embedding based on two behavioral features—Nash equilibrium entropy and response sensitivity—that successfully predicts whether learning one game will help or hurt performance on another, contrary to approaches that rely on payoff structures. The work matters because it reveals that strategic transfer in LLMs depends on the *type of decision-making required* rather than the numerical payoff matrices.

title: Belief Coevolution in a Social Network of Generalist and Specialist Large Language Models
authors: Germans Savcisens, Samantha Dies, Courtney Maynard, Tina Eliassi-Rad
summary: This paper studies how beliefs form and spread among groups of interacting large language models (LLMs) deployed as agents in networks. The authors built CoevolveSim, a simulation framework, and ran 1,280 experiments to understand whether model specialization, assigned roles, and network structure affect how LLM populations reach consensus. They found that giving some models specialized training matters far more than simply prompting models with different personas, and that diverse model types are needed to accurately simulate real belief dynamics in multi-agent LLM systems.

title: Skill Use or Skill Theater? Evaluating the Reasoning Backroom in Skill-Augmented Language Agents
authors: Jinwei Hu, Yi Qi, Xinmiao Huang, Youcheng Sun, Yi Dong et al.
summary: This paper reveals a critical gap between what language agents *claim* to use and what they *actually* rely on when making decisions. The authors introduce BACKTRACE, an evaluation framework that catches agents performing "skill theater" — appearing to use provided skills while actually ignoring them, or vice versa. The work matters because it exposes a fundamental provenance problem: we can't trust an agent's explanation of its reasoning, which has serious implications for debugging, auditing, and trusting AI systems.

title: Auditing Emergent LLM-Agent Collaboration through Cooperation-Obligation Coupling
authors: Zuyuan Zhang, Hanqing Yang, Carlee Joe-Wong, Tian Lan
summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in auditing multi-agent LLM systems: how to verify that emergent collaborative work is sound and responsibility is fairly allocated. The authors propose iCORE, a unified representation that tracks observable interactions, evolving work assignments, and evidence linking them together, enabling auditors to catch incomplete reasoning and misaligned accountability that plausible outputs might otherwise conceal.

title: THGFM: Dual-Branch Temporal Heterogeneous Graph Fusion Model
authors: Yixin Peng, Diego Collarana, Er Jin, Stefan Decker
summary: This paper introduces THGFM, a neural network model for learning patterns in temporal heterogeneous graphs—networks where nodes and connections have different types and change over time. The key innovation is a dual-branch architecture that balances shared learning across all node types with specialized learning for specific relation types, while also directly incorporating time into the attention mechanism (the part of neural networks that focuses on relevant information). On academic citation and collaboration networks, THGFM outperforms existing graph models by 3–12%.

title: Do You Really Need to Pretrain Q-Functions for Online RL Fine-Tuning?
authors: Perry Dong, Ron Polonsky, Dorsa Sadigh, Chelsea Fin
summary: This paper challenges the assumption that Q-functions (value estimators in reinforcement learning) should be pre-trained on offline data before fine-tuning on new tasks. The authors discover that naive Q-function pre-training often doesn't help and propose Initialization via Policy Ensemble (IPE), which bootstraps Q-function learning by collecting data from multiple diverse policies. On standard benchmarks, IPE achieves 1.26x better performance than conventional pre-training approaches.

title: Mental World Modeling
authors: Hao Fei, Yiran Zhao
summary: This paper introduces Mental World Modeling (MWM), a framework that extends traditional world models to track not just physical states but also the mental states (beliefs, desires, intentions, emotions) of agents. The authors argue that predicting human behavior requires understanding what people know and want, not just what they can see, and demonstrate this with MENTIS—a training-free system that jointly simulates physical and mental state changes to predict human decisions in complex social scenarios.

title: Can AI agents conduct open-ended AI research? Early evidence from two case studies
authors: Peter Kirgis, Sayash Kapoor, Andrew Schwartz, Stephan Rabanser, David Africa et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether AI agents can conduct genuine open-ended research by having frontier AI systems tackle unpublished research questions from real NeurIPS papers, with the original authors grading the results. The agents successfully handled engineering tasks but failed to make meaningful progress on the core research questions, revealing critical gaps in how agents approach complex, unstructured research problems.

title: Inverse Learning of Latent Risk-Neutral Densities from Irregular Option Quotes
authors: Lennon J. Shikhman, Michael Galarnyk, Aadi Dash, Nicholas A. Welsh
summary: This paper tackles a fundamental problem in quantitative finance: recovering the risk-neutral probability density (the market's implied view of future asset prices) from option quotes, which is harder than just matching option prices accurately. The authors compare classical parametric models (lognormal mixtures, Merton models) with neural operators (DeepONet) and transformer architectures, revealing that no single approach wins universally—what matters depends on the specific evaluation target (matching prices vs. recovering the true density).

title: Partner Capability Estimation for Task-Agnostic Adaptation in Ad-Hoc Teamwork
authors: Peter Tisnikar, Maja Swieczkowska, Benteng Ma, Gerard Canal, Matteo Leonetti
summary: This paper tackles ad-hoc teamwork—where an agent must quickly adapt to work effectively with new, unknown partners—by inferring what each partner can actually do (their "hidden capabilities") without knowing the task in advance. The key insight is that instead of assuming partners always act optimally, the method learns task-invariant capability vectors and accounts for human behavioral diversity, allowing agents to plan better collaborative strategies with minimal prior information.

title: Improving Item Discoverability in e-Commerce Search via Related Intent Generation
authors: Ji Xin, Xiao Xiao, Ishan Bhatt, Vinesh Gudla, Trace Levinson et al.
summary: This paper presents a system that improves product discoverability in e-commerce search by generating related user intents to expand what items get shown to customers. Instead of just returning exact matches to a query, the system uses large language models to infer what else a shopper might want (substitutes, complements, related items) and retrieves those too — all while keeping costs manageable by using smaller, fine-tuned models for common queries.

title: SpecFirst: Behavioral Specification Elicitation as a First-Class Step in Agent-Based Program Synthesis from Scratch
authors: Yihao Chen, Shi Chang, Feng Lin, Khaled Chawa, Boyuan Chen et al.
summary: This paper shows that LLM-based agents struggle to write programs from scratch because they try to understand requirements and write code in one pass. The authors propose SpecFirst, a two-stage approach: first, an agent carefully explores a program's behavior and writes a formal specification; second, a different agent uses that specification to generate code. On 200 benchmark tasks, SpecFirst improves success rates by 7–21% over single-pass approaches, demonstrating that separating specification from implementation is crucial for from-scratch program synthesis.

title: OmegaUse-OfficeVal: Benchmarking LLM Agents on Long-Horizon Office-Suite Tasks with Economic Grounding
authors: Jingbo Zhou, Yusai Zhao, Qi Bao, Jingjia Cao, Zhenghai Chen et al.
summary: This paper introduces OmegaUse-OfficeVal, a benchmark for testing whether LLM agents can complete real office tasks (like spreadsheet work, document editing, scheduling) at a reasonable cost. The key innovation is pairing each task with economic signals — human labor time and estimated task price — so you can directly compare whether using an LLM is cheaper and faster than hiring a human. Testing shows LLMs are faster and cheaper than humans but don't yet match human-level quality on complex multi-step office workflows.

title: Anatomy Contextualized Adaption of CT Foundation Models
authors: Roshan Kenia, Stephanie L McNamara, William Lotter
summary: This paper proposes Anatomy Contextualized Adaptation (ACA), a lightweight method to improve CT scan foundation models by aligning fine-grained anatomy features with medical text while preserving global context. Rather than retraining models from scratch, ACA adapts frozen pre-trained models efficiently—in under an hour—and outperforms both standard foundation models and existing fine-grained approaches on medical imaging benchmarks.

title: MindForge: Teaching Small Language Models Whole-Life-Cycle Software Engineering via Source-Free Program Synthesis
authors: Yihao Chen, Shi Chang, Khaled Chawa, Feng Lin, Boyuan Chen et al.
summary: This paper introduces MindForge, a pipeline that trains smaller language models to write complete programs from scratch—a task where even the best current models succeed less than 1% of the time. By converting open-source programs into "source-free" environments (exposing only compiled executables and docs, not source code), the authors create scalable training data. Fine-tuning a 27B parameter model on these trajectories boosts its performance from 38% to 50% on standard benchmarks and shows consistent gains across seven different software engineering tasks.

title: Linguistic Monoculture in LLM-Assisted Language Use
authors: Suhas Thejaswi, Juhi Kulshreshta, Lutz Oettershagen
summary: This paper studies how widespread use of LLMs for writing and editing may paradoxically reduce linguistic diversity — a phenomenon called "linguistic monoculture." The authors build a mathematical model showing how different LLM assistance designs (shared fixed models, recursive updates, personalized models) lead to different equilibrium linguistic patterns, and prove that people rationally choosing to conform for clarity may converge to less diversity than is socially optimal.

title: Minimal Markovization via Stable Quotients in Holonomy-Cover Decision Processes
authors: Zuyuan Zhang, Yongshan Chen, Mahdi Imani, Tian Lan
summary: This paper solves a fundamental problem in partially observable decision-making: finding the smallest memory-efficient state representation that restores the Markov property. The authors introduce "stable quotients" for a structured class of hidden-mode problems (holonomy-cover POMDPs) and prove that tracking just the current observation plus a discrete class label gives an exact, minimal Markov state. This matters because agents need compact internal representations to act optimally under incomplete information without growing memory exponentially.

title: Hierarchical Spatio-Temporal Transformer for Coherent Emergency Department Forecasting
authors: Filipa Lino, Bárbara Tavares, Carlos Santiago, Cláudia Soares, Manuel Marques
summary: This paper proposes HierSTT, a Transformer-based forecasting model that predicts emergency department (ED) patient demand at three hierarchical levels — hospitals, regions, and national systems — simultaneously while ensuring the predictions stay logically consistent across levels. The work addresses a real healthcare problem: most forecasting models make independent predictions at each level, leading to incoherent results where hospital forecasts don't sum to regional totals. HierSTT solves this by using a coherence-aware loss function and a spatio-temporal Transformer architecture, cutting prediction error by 32% compared to non-hierarchical baselines.

title: On-Policy Distillation for LLM Safety: A Routing Approach to Template-Robust Realignment
authors: Yongjian Guo, Wanlun Ma, Lingyu Shen, Xi Xiao, Sheng Wen
summary: This paper addresses a critical vulnerability in fine-tuned large language models: malicious actors can embed harmful behaviors into training data that activate only with specific prompts, while the model retains its useful skills. The authors propose Routing-based On-Policy Distillation (ROPD), a defense method that learns to distinguish between aligned and compromised model outputs rather than memorizing specific attack templates, making the defense robust even against unseen attack variations.

title: Herding, Momentum, and Reversal in China's A-Share Market: An Agent-Based Network Model with Information Diffusion
authors: Jiahao Weng
summary: This paper builds an agent-based model of stock markets where individual investors influence each other locally (through social networks) and learn about prices at different speeds (information travels slowly). The model explains why stocks show momentum (prices keep moving in one direction) followed by reversals (sudden direction changes), and validates these patterns in China's A-share market using statistical measures of investor herding.

title: PIKS: Universal Physics-Informed Kernel Methods
authors: Joachim Bona-Pellissier, Giacomo Meanti, Matteo Santacesaria, Lorenzo Rosasco
summary: This paper develops Physics-Informed Kernel methodS (PIKS), a theoretically grounded alternative to physics-informed neural networks that embeds physical constraints directly into kernel methods. Instead of training neural networks to satisfy differential equations, PIKS uses kernel methods (mathematical functions that measure similarity between data points) with closed-form solutions, making it analytically tractable. The key innovation is proving that PIKS works even when physical targets don't lie in the ideal mathematical space, and demonstrating it can match or beat both neural network and traditional numerical solvers.

title: Setoka: A Benchmark for Hierarchical User Understanding in Personalized Agents over Heterogeneous Data
authors: Lingyang Zeng, Guangze Chen, Kaichen Yu, Zhicheng Pan, Siyang Weng et al.
summary: This paper introduces Setoka, a benchmark for testing how well personalized AI agents understand users by integrating information from diverse data sources over time. Most existing tests focus on simple fact retrieval from conversation history; Setoka evaluates deeper understanding—like inferring behavior patterns and personality traits from fragmented, heterogeneous data. The work matters because personalized agents increasingly assist users across many domains, and effective assistance requires understanding not just what users explicitly said, but who they are.

title: Think Short, Defer Smart, Act, and Repeat: Calibrated Reasoning and Uncertainty-Aware Deferral for Edge LLM Agents
authors: Amirmohammad Farzaneh, Osvaldo Simeone
summary: This paper presents TSDS, a framework that helps language model agents run efficiently on edge devices by deciding when to think locally versus when to ask a cloud server for help. The key insight is combining two mechanisms — stopping local reasoning once a decision stabilizes, and deferring uncertain decisions to the cloud — calibrated together to guarantee both task performance and bounded cloud usage. This matters because it enables practical deployment of reasoning-heavy AI systems on resource-constrained devices while maintaining reliability.

title: Crossing-Free Probabilistic K-Line Forecasts Without Retraining
authors: Runyao Yu, Yuchen Tao, Yujie Chen, Wentao Wang, Derek W. Bunn
summary: This paper solves a practical problem in financial forecasting: when predicting uncertainty around stock prices (open, high, low, close), the forecasts often become internally inconsistent—either quantiles cross each other or the predicted high falls below the predicted open. The authors propose KQSP, a simple post-processing method that fixes these inconsistencies without retraining the model, preserving forecast accuracy while eliminating all crossing violations.

title: DREvo: Distilling Recalibrated Historical Experience for Harness Self-Evolution
authors: Hanghui Guo, Weijie Shi, Zhangze Chen, Shengxiang Xu, Yishu Wang et al.
summary: This paper addresses a practical problem in building AI agents: how to automatically improve "harnesses" (instruction sets or prompts that guide LLM behavior) by learning from past attempts. The authors propose DREvo, a method that intelligently filters historical experience to determine which past insights remain relevant, then distills those insights into concrete directions for improvement. On five benchmarks, DREvo improves agent performance by 14–16% compared to existing approaches while producing more stable, predictable evolution across iterations.

title: Universality and Approximation Rates of Graph Neural Networks with Random Features
authors: Lukas Gonon, Thilo Meyer-Brandis, Niklas Weber
summary: This paper proves that graph neural networks with random node features can learn any permutation-invariant or permutation-equivariant function on graphs, and derives specific rates showing how network complexity translates to approximation accuracy. The result is important because it rigorously justifies why random features improve GNNs and provides practical guidance on network sizing for desired accuracy.

title: The Sparsity Ceiling: Where Spiking Networks Can and Cannot Trade Activity for Energy
authors: Zeyu Wang
summary: Spiking neural networks (SNNs) are often promoted as energy-efficient because they use sparse, event-driven computation instead of dense matrix multiplications. This paper shows that the energy savings from sparsity depend on the task structure, not on SNNs themselves — and identifies hard limits (a "sparsity ceiling") where further reductions fail. The findings matter because they explain when neuromorphic hardware actually wins and when the promised efficiency gains vanish.

title: Living-Harness Is an Interactive-Agent Evolver
authors: Yuetian Du, Yucheng Wang, He Xu, Jiexu Xu, Shanwen Tan et al.
summary: This paper introduces Living-Harness, a system that allows LLM-based agents to evolve their operational structure (tools, memory, workflow) after each task rather than remaining static. By extracting lessons from failures and successes into episodic memory and state repair graphs, the agent improves reliability across future tasks. This matters because current LLM agents often repeat the same mistakes even when they've been corrected once—Living-Harness fixes that by treating the agent's guiding structure as continuously learnable.

title: One Run Is Not an Idea: The Implementation Lottery in Automated Research
authors: Jingjie Ning, Shanshan Zhong, Xiaochuan Li, Ji Zeng, Chenyan Xiong
summary: This paper identifies a critical flaw in how automated research systems (including AI agents) evaluate ideas: they confuse one implementation's test score with evidence about the underlying idea's merit. The authors show that implementation details cause massive variance in experimental outcomes—sometimes reversing which approach "wins"—meaning a single run cannot reliably guide research decisions. They propose the Idea Reliability Audit to measure whether conclusions hold across multiple independent implementations.

title: EvoPINN: Agentic Discovery of Executable Algorithms for Physics-Informed Neural Networks
authors: Peng Yin, Kai Li, Yifan Zhang, Jian Cheng
summary: This paper presents EvoPINN, a system where an AI agent automatically discovers improved algorithms for physics-informed neural networks (PINNs)—a technique that combines neural networks with physics equations to solve complex differential equations. Rather than having humans manually design network architectures and training procedures through trial-and-error, the system uses an LLM agent to propose and evaluate algorithmic modifications, constrained by strict mathematical validity checks. The work demonstrates that this automated discovery process invents genuinely novel and effective PINN variants that outperform hand-engineered baselines.

title: Reconstructing Backpropagation from Forward Fluctuations in Noise-modulated Neural Networks
authors: Shuhei Ikemoto
summary: This paper shows how to reconstruct backpropagation—the standard algorithm for training neural networks—in a noise-modulated neural network (NNN) using only forward-pass information, without needing the reverse data path that biological brains don't have. The key insight is that noise acts as a computational resource: weight matrices can be estimated from covariances between layer outputs, and combining this with local error estimation allows gradients to propagate forward through the network to update weights. This matters because it bridges neuromorphic plausibility (making learning rules more brain-like) with practical accuracy, and enables hardware implementation using only local polynomial operations and comparators.

title: Neural Architecture Search for Traffic Prediction: A Survey of Methods, Challenges, and Future Directions
authors: Truong Giang Vu, Li Yang, Richard W. Pazzi
summary: This survey reviews Neural Architecture Search (NAS)—automated methods for designing deep learning models—applied specifically to traffic prediction. Traffic prediction is critical for transportation systems, but current models are hand-designed and don't generalize well across cities; NAS automates this design process by systematically searching over candidate architectures to find models that fit spatial-temporal traffic data without manual trial-and-error.

title: Pramana: A Composable, Domain-Specific Backend for Empirical Networking Research
authors: Jaber Daneshamooz, Eugene Vuong, Alagappan Ramanathan, Manni Moghimi, Haarika Manda et al.
summary: Pramana is a composable backend system designed to speed up empirical networking research by reducing the gap between formulating research hypotheses and generating the experimental data needed to test them. The paper introduces an "intent specification" — a single contract that separates *what data to generate* (intent), *where to generate it* (substrate), and *how to produce it* (mechanism) — allowing researchers to reuse the same experiment specification across different execution environments. This matters because as AI systems increasingly assist in hypothesis generation, validation bottlenecks will become more severe unless data-generation infrastructure can keep pace.

title: Learning Implicit Causal World Models from Multi-Agent Demonstrations
authors: Jasorsi Ghosh
summary: This paper proposes Implicit Causal World Models — neural network simulators that learn true cause-and-effect relationships in multi-agent environments from offline demonstrations, rather than just learning statistical patterns. The key innovation is recovering causal structure without requiring hand-crafted causal graphs, which matters because standard world models fail when the test environment differs from training data (distribution shift), a critical problem in robotics and multi-agent coordination.

title: The Confounder Trap: Treatment-Encoding Representations in Causal Inference with Text
authors: Marie Neubrander, Graham Tierney, Alexander Volfovsky
summary: This paper identifies a fundamental problem in causal inference with text: when treatment status is encoded in the words themselves, standard representation learning can inadvertently encode treatment directly, violating the statistical overlap assumption needed for valid causal estimation. The authors propose masking-based solutions that remove treatment-defining words before learning representations, restoring overlap and improving causal effect estimates.

title: Top-$k$ Pareto Bandits: Hypervolume Regret for Multi-Objective Slate Selection
authors: Nicolas Gutowski, Fabien Chhel, Alexandre Letard, Sylvain Lamprier
summary: This paper solves the problem of selecting a small set of actions that approximate the Pareto frontier in multi-objective bandit settings — where an agent repeatedly chooses k arms and receives d-dimensional reward vectors, without knowing which arm is best in advance. The key insight is to use dominated hypervolume (a measure of how well a set covers the trade-off space) as the objective, and the authors provide an algorithm called THV-UCB with theoretical regret guarantees showing this approach works efficiently.

title: VetClaw: An Edge-Cloud Multimodal Agentic System for Veterinary Disease Screening
authors: Syed Mhamudul Hasan, Anas AlSobeh, Hussein Zangoti, Abdur R. Shahid
summary: VetClaw is an edge-cloud system that combines a camera on a veterinary device with an AI model running on a server to screen animals for diseases. The key innovation is treating disease screening not as a single prediction but as a multi-step workflow—collecting images, asking about symptoms, checking safety rules, and routing uncertain cases to a veterinarian—which improves accuracy and makes the system safer and more usable.

title: Desktop-Delta Bench: Do Computer-Use Models Understand Desktop GUI Transitions?
authors: Abhishek Pillai, Samir Kumar Nayak, Yuan Chen
summary: This paper introduces Desktop-Delta Bench, a benchmark for evaluating whether computer-use agents (AI systems that control desktop GUIs) can understand what happened after they take an action. Current benchmarks only measure whether agents complete tasks or recognize UI elements in a single frame; this paper fills a gap by testing whether agents can reconstruct causal state transitions—crucial for verifying progress, rejecting stale observations, and recovering from errors. The benchmark reveals consistent weaknesses across eight model families, showing that even the best agents struggle with temporal ordering (65% accuracy) and inferring action types.

title: Reinformed Dreamer: An Asymmetric World Model Efficiently Trained through Latent Guidance
authors: Gaspard Lambrechts, Adrien Bolland, Daniel Ebi, Damien Ernst
summary: This paper improves how reinforcement learning agents learn world models—internal representations of their environment—by using additional information during training. The key innovation is "latent guidance," a technique that helps the agent's internal representations learn more useful features by comparing them against privileged information (extra state details available only during training). The result is faster, more stable learning across multiple benchmark tasks.

title: CHARM: A Multimodal Graph Foundation Model with Hierarchical Context Modeling for Zero-Shot Transfer
authors: Ankang Yang, Jitao Zhao, Di Jin, Yuxiao Huang, Dongxiao He
summary: This paper introduces CHARM, a multimodal graph foundation model that can transfer knowledge to new graph domains without task-specific fine-tuning. The key innovation is hierarchical context modeling — organizing multimodal information (text, images, etc.) at different levels to extract shared concepts that generalize across domains, enabling zero-shot transfer on graphs containing rich node and edge attributes.

title: UniMem: Complementary Episodic-to-Parametric Memory for Boundary-Agnostic Task Streams
authors: Siyu Xia, Chenheng Zhang, Yanting Wu, Haoxuan Li, Jiajun Chai et al.
summary: This paper proposes UniMem, a memory management system for LLM agents that must continuously learn from an unbounded stream of tasks without explicit task boundaries. The core insight is to mimic the human brain by splitting memory into two complementary systems: a flexible episodic buffer for storing novel tasks, and a growing parametric memory that consolidates recurring patterns — enabling agents to be both adaptable and efficient without knowing task boundaries in advance.

title: MDTransformer: A Hardware-Software Co-Design of Mode-Division Photonic Transformer Accelerator with Inverse-Designed Coherent Crossbar
authors: Solomon Micheal Serunjogi, Rachmad Vidya Wicaksana Putra, Ayat Taha, Muhammad Shafique, Mahmoud Rasras
summary: This paper presents MDTransformer, a photonic hardware accelerator that performs transformer computations using light instead of electronics. The key innovation is using spatial modes of light (independent "lanes" in a single optical waveguide) to parallelize matrix operations, achieving significant energy savings and area reduction while maintaining compatible inference speed compared to previous photonic transformer designs.

title: Instruction-Tuned Models Locally Reuse Human Syntax More Than Humans Do
authors: Zandi Eberstadt
summary: This paper investigates whether instruction-tuned large language models exhibit syntactic convergence—the tendency to match the grammatical patterns of their conversation partner—similar to humans. Using a substitution-paradigm approach on 16 Llama and Gemma models, the authors find that instruction-tuned models actually *over-reuse* syntax from preceding human turns compared to human baselines, though they paradoxically show weaker convergence to actual context versus random primes after instruction tuning.

title: Pictura: Perspective-View Self-Play at Scale for Driving
authors: Yuan Yin, Elias Ramzi, Marc Lafon, Valentin Charraut, Victor Bares et al.
summary: This paper tackles a fundamental gap in autonomous driving: training policies directly from camera images rather than unrealistic privileged sensor data. The authors introduce Pictura, a GPU-accelerated simulator that renders egocentric (first-person) camera views for each agent during training, and use it to train Alberti—the first large-scale driving policy trained purely from perspective images via self-play. The work matters because it bridges the gap between how agents are trained in simulation (with perfect information) and how they actually perceive the world when deployed.

title: Empirical Evaluation of Out-Of-Distribution Performance of Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Malena Loza, David Chushig-Muzo, Eva Milara, Luis Bote-Curiel, Luis Estrada-Petrocelli et al.
summary: This paper evaluates how well nine tabular foundation models (neural networks pre-trained on tabular data) perform when the data distribution shifts — a common real-world problem where training and deployment data differ. The authors test these models on three datasets with different types of distribution shift and find that all models degrade significantly, with performance gaps ranging from 0.3% to 6%, suggesting that foundation models for tabular data inherit the same robustness challenges as classical models.

title: Physics-Aware End-to-End Deep Reinforcement Learning for Quadcopter Control with Actuator Dynamics
authors: Ya-Chia Shen, Woei-Leong Chan
summary: This paper applies deep reinforcement learning (DRL) to control quadcopters by learning directly from physics-based simulations that include realistic motor dynamics and aerodynamic effects. The key insight is that incorporating low-level physical constraints — like motor time delays and gyroscopic coupling — into the learning environment helps DRL agents discover stable, practical control policies. This matters because quadcopters are mechanically underactuated (four control inputs for six degrees of freedom), making them a hard benchmark for learning-based control.

title: Reinforcement Learning for Code Optimization
authors: Pierre Chambon, Kunhao Zheng, Juliette Decugis, Benoit Sagot, Gabriel Synnaeve
summary: This paper tackles code optimization using reinforcement learning — training neural networks to generate faster programs, not just correct ones. The core insight is that naive RL fails when optimizing for execution speed due to noisy timing measurements and reward sparsity; the authors solve this by carefully designing how code is tested, how speed feeds into rewards, and how the learning algorithm handles sparse noisy signals. On benchmark problems, their approach roughly doubles the percentage of solutions that achieve significant speedups while maintaining correctness.

title: MODUS: Decoder-Only Any-to-Any Modeling of Diverse Modalities
authors: Mingqiao Ye, Zhaochong An, Zhitong Gao, Xian Liu, François Fleuret et al.
summary: This paper presents MODUS, a decoder-only neural network that can accept any combination of modalities (images, text, audio, etc.) as input and generate any modality as output using a single unified model. Unlike existing any-to-any systems that require separate encoders and decoders or diffusion models, MODUS leverages pre-trained decoder-only models and treats all modalities symmetrically, achieving competitive performance across multiple benchmarks without task-specific components.

title: A Cost-Effective Multimodal LLM Reasoning Framework for Question Answering over Irregular Clinical Time Series
authors: Frank Nie, Ethan B Liu, Yuan Zhu, Wei Fan, Jindong Han
summary: This paper presents ClinPRISM, a system that answers questions about irregular clinical time series (patient data collected at uneven intervals) using multimodal large language models. The work matters because clinical data is messy and sparse in practice, but existing time-series LLMs weren't designed to handle these real-world patterns efficiently—ClinPRISM solves this with a cost-effective approach that runs fast on modest hardware.

title: Evaluating Multi-Turn Multimodal Diagnostic Reasoning on Challenging Real-World Clinical Cases
authors: Rui Yang, Weihao Xuan, Yi Lin, Zhuhan Bao, Jonathan Chong Kai Liew et al.
summary: This paper introduces ClinMM-Bench, a large-scale evaluation benchmark for testing how well multimodal AI models (systems that process both text and images) can perform real-world clinical diagnosis over multiple conversation turns. The work matters because existing AI evaluations use single, isolated tasks, while actual diagnosis is iterative—doctors see images progressively, update hypotheses, and refine reasoning over time. The benchmark reveals that current models struggle with reliable diagnostic reasoning despite sometimes getting the right answer.

title: Minimizing Targeted Activations: Input-Only Suppression of Evaluation-Awareness Latents in Large Language Models
authors: Deepanshu Mody, Samarth Agarwal, Utkarsh Mittal, Dipesh Mahato
summary: This paper investigates whether we can suppress internal "evaluation-awareness" latents in large language models by optimizing only the input prompt—without changing the model's weights. The authors find that while certain internal features can be driven toward zero, this internal suppression often fails to actually change the model's behavior on safety evaluations, suggesting that linear readability of a latent does not guarantee behavioral control.

title: The Barron-Lipschitz Energy Gap and Depth Separation Phenomena in Scientific Machine Learning
authors: Nima Rezaei, Stephan Wojtowytsch
summary: This paper investigates fundamental limitations of neural networks—even infinitely wide ones—when solving variational problems in scientific machine learning. The authors show that neural networks can fail to represent certain solution structures (like circular folds in elastic shells) that classical function classes can easily describe, revealing a theoretical "energy gap" that prevents convergence to optimal solutions in some calculus of variations problems.

title: Towards a Systems Foundation for Agentic Cloud Management
authors: Minghao Li, Ziqian Liu, Ziyu Mao, Daqian Ding, Yu Kang et al.
summary: This paper introduces CloudWeaver, a systems foundation for managing cloud infrastructure using autonomous agents. The key problem: as organizations deploy multiple AI agents to automate cloud operations, there's no infrastructure to coordinate them safely, prevent conflicts, or maintain human oversight. CloudWeaver solves this by providing isolation (each agent gets a scoped view of resources) and coordination (managing concurrent operations on shared resources without collisions).

title: OmniQEC: discovering practical quantum error-correcting codes by an AI scientist
authors: Ge Yan, Shanchuan Li, Pengyue Ma, Qixin Zhang, Pingchuan Ma et al.
summary: This paper presents OmniQEC, an AI system that uses large language models to automatically discover quantum error-correcting (QEC) codes—the mathematical structures needed to protect quantum computers from errors. The key innovation is treating code discovery as an iterative search problem where an LLM orchestrator coordinates code generation, screening, and evaluation, balancing fast approximate checks against slower but physically realistic circuit simulations. The discovered codes outperform hand-designed benchmarks on realistic hardware constraints.

title: CHILL-Harness: Counterfactual Harness Learning for Efficient Reasoning in Long-Horizon Agents
authors: Jiarun Fu, Lizhong Ding, Sida Chen, Honglei Xin, Chunhui Zhang et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical inefficiency in LLM-based agents: their control systems (harnesses) use fixed policies that waste computation on unnecessary reasoning steps. The authors propose CHILL-Harness, a system that learns to dynamically adapt which tools, verification steps, and reasoning paths to use based on task context and execution state — cutting token consumption and runtime while maintaining task success rates.

title: KQFuzz: Knowledge-Guided Fuzzing for Quantum Libraries via Large Language Models
authors: Fuyuan Xia, Qixin Zhang, Chenhao Ying, Haojin Zhu, Shuai Wang et al.
summary: This paper presents KQFuzz, a fuzzing tool that uses large language models to automatically generate test cases for quantum computing libraries like Qiskit and PennyLane. By combining LLM-based code generation with knowledge of the quantum library's codebase and guided mutation strategies, KQFuzz finds bugs more effectively than existing approaches—improving code coverage by up to 18% and discovering 13 previously unknown bugs in real quantum libraries.

title: ARCHER: Agentic Rule and Compliance Harness for Executable Regulations
authors: Chiraag Singh Anand, Xue Wen Tan, Lionel Teo, Eric Tan
summary: ARCHER is a system that automatically generates auditable code for checking whether building designs comply with regulatory rules, using multiple AI agents working together. This matters because building compliance checking currently requires expensive manual work, and existing automated systems are inflexible, proprietary, and hard to adapt — ARCHER makes the process transparent, scalable, and cost-effective even with open-source models.

title: Learning from the Unseen: Offline Reinforcement Learning with Hidden Actions
authors: Zeyu Bian, Ying Zhou, Yifan Cui
summary: This paper tackles offline reinforcement learning in a realistic but understudied setting: when the dataset contains only noisy proxies for true actions, not the actions themselves. The authors develop LURE, a statistically principled estimator that recovers policy values from such incomplete data and validate it on medical decision-making (sepsis treatment). This matters because real-world datasets—clinical records, logs from automated systems—often hide the actual decisions behind measurements or side effects.

title: Algorithmic Separation between Constant-Depth and Logarithmic-Depth Neural Networks
authors: Yunwei Ren, Zihao Wang, Jason D. Lee
summary: This paper proves that neural networks with logarithmic depth can efficiently learn certain Boolean functions that constant-depth networks fundamentally cannot learn well. The result matters because it's the first rigorous algorithmic separation between these two depth regimes — showing that depth isn't just theoretically useful for approximation, but actually changes what a network can learn *efficiently* during training.

title: RIDGE: An Autonomous Framework for Validation and Method Discovery in LLM-Generated Option Pricing
authors: Liexin Cheng, Xue Cheng, Shuaiqiang Liu, Cornelis W. Oosterlee
summary: This paper presents RIDGE, an automated framework that validates option pricing code generated by large language models (LLMs) and discovers new pricing methods. The framework applies rigorous financial tests — no-arbitrage checks, stress tests, benchmarks — to catch implementation bugs that standard software testing would miss, and has discovered new semi-analytic pricing approaches in the process.

title: Quantum Transformer BSDE Solver via Multi-Layer Fully-Connected Variational Quantum Circuits
authors: Howard Su, Huan-Hsin Tseng, Chi-Sheng Chen, Lance Bai
summary: This paper proposes a quantum computing approach to solving high-dimensional partial differential equations (PDEs) — mathematical equations crucial for pricing financial derivatives and modeling physical systems. The method combines quantum circuits with transformer-style attention mechanisms to learn solutions to backward stochastic differential equations (BSDEs), which are reformulations of certain PDEs. On 36-dimensional benchmark problems, the quantum transformer shows promise but doesn't yet outperform classical transformer baselines at scale.

title: Fourier Feature Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Elasto-Plastic Analysis of Geomaterials with a Non-Associative Mohr-Coulomb Model
authors: Apisit Robjanghvad, Sompote Youwai
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental limitation of Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) — a machine learning approach for solving differential equations — when applied to geotechnical problems involving plastic deformation in soil. The authors propose Fourier Feature PINNs (FF-PINNs), which use random Fourier feature mapping to better capture sharp stress gradients at failure zones. The work matters because it demonstrates a mesh-free alternative to expensive finite element simulations while maintaining physics consistency, potentially accelerating design and analysis cycles in civil and geotechnical engineering.

title: Mitigating the Impact of Retention Loss on Inference Accuracy in 65 nm Single-Poly Floating-Gate Analog In-Memory Computing
authors: Mirko Brazzini, Giulio Filippeschi, Alessandro Catania, Sebastiano Strangio, Giuseppe Iannaccone
summary: This paper addresses a critical hardware challenge in analog in-memory computing: floating-gate memory cells gradually lose charge over time (retention loss), degrading neural network inference accuracy. The authors demonstrate that combining circuit-level compensation techniques with algorithmic recalibration (batch normalization) can recover baseline accuracy even 60 days after programming, making analog memory viable for practical AI inference at the edge.

title: Transfer Learning in High-Dimensional Clustering: Minimax Thresholds and Applications in Single-Cell Data
authors: Abhinav Chakraborty, Sagnik Nandy
summary: This paper studies when and how clustering can be improved by borrowing information from related datasets, a problem called transfer learning for clustering. The authors develop theoretically optimal methods for a standard clustering model (Gaussian mixtures) and characterize exact conditions—involving signal strength, sample sizes, and dataset similarity—under which transfer helps; they also apply these methods to real single-cell RNA data.

title: ClinFusion: A Vision-Centric Multimodal LLM System for Holistic Medical Understanding
authors: Hangjie Yuan, Yichen Qian, Zhiwei Tang, Xianzhe Xu, Lirong Wu et al.
summary: ClinFusion is a multimodal AI system that combines vision and language understanding specifically for medical imaging analysis. The paper addresses a critical gap: existing medical AI systems struggle to process diverse medical images (2D scans, 3D volumes) and evaluate their outputs in clinically meaningful ways. ClinFusion achieves state-of-the-art results on medical benchmarks and radiologist validation, suggesting it could improve clinical workflows.

title: KANEx: Translating Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks' Interpretability to Medical Explainability
authors: Krithi Shailya, Ananya Lakshmi Ravi, Venkatanathan K. V., Sowmya S. Sundaram, Gokul S. Krishnan et al.
summary: This paper introduces KANEx, a framework that combines Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs) with Vision-Language Models to make chest X-ray classifiers more interpretable and trustworthy for clinicians. Instead of treating a neural network as a black box and only adding natural-language explanations on top, the authors leverage KANs' inherently interpretable spline-based components to ground those explanations in mathematically transparent reasoning. On the MIMIC-CXR dataset, this approach produces more faithful saliency maps and better visual localization than standard methods.

title: Global Convergence of DGM and PINN Algorithms for Solving Nonlinear PDEs
authors: Justin Sirignano, Konstantinos Spiliopoulos, Samuel Cohen
summary: This paper proves that neural networks trained with gradient descent to solve nonlinear PDEs (partial differential equations) will converge to the actual PDE solution, not just to a local minimum of the loss function. This is a fundamental theoretical result for Deep Galerkin Method (DGM) and Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) — two increasingly popular techniques that use neural networks to solve scientific computing problems — because it answers the long-standing question of whether these methods actually work.

title: The Physics of Multi-Turn Long-Horizon Planning: From Pre-training to Post-training via Single- and Multi-Teacher On-Policy Agentic Distillation
authors: Tianyi Men, Zhuoran Jin, Kang Liu, Jun Zhao
summary: This paper systematically investigates how foundation model agents learn to plan over long sequences of decisions—a critical capability for real-world autonomous systems. By constructing a controlled experimental environment, the authors decompose planning ability into three stages: pre-training (how agents acquire planning skills), post-training (how to refine those skills via policy optimization), and integration (how to combine diverse planning strategies from multiple teachers). The core finding is that explicit world models, high-quality data, and careful multi-teacher distillation are essential for robust long-horizon reasoning.

title: DataOrchestra: Learning to Orchestrate Per-Example Curation of Pretraining Data
authors: Zhen Huang, Yikun Wang, Shijie Xia, Pengfei Liu
summary: This paper presents DataOrchestra, a framework that customizes data preprocessing for each example during LLM pretraining, rather than applying fixed processing rules uniformly across all data. The system decides for each chunk whether to drop it, leave it alone, or clean it using one of several operations (programmatic editing or LLM-based rewriting), and consistently improves downstream task performance compared to using any single processing method alone.

title: Efficient LLM-Generated Shuttling Compilers for Complex Trapped-Ion Architectures
authors: Fabian Kreppel, Reza Salkhordeh, Ferdinand Schmidt-Kaler, André Brinkmann
summary: This paper shows that frontier LLMs (Claude Opus 4.7 and Claude Fable 5) can automatically generate working quantum compiler code for trapped-ion quantum computers—complex algorithms that have traditionally required months of expert manual engineering. The generated compilers optimize ion-qubit movements ("shuttling") and match or beat hand-written versions, reducing development time from months to days.

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning via Physics-Aware Policy Distillation
authors: Shaker Al-Tamari, Waled Kadour
summary: This paper makes Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) systems interpretable by distilling a high-performance continuous control agent into a simple decision tree that humans can understand. The authors show they can preserve the original agent's performance while gaining explainability — a critical step toward deploying AI safely in robotics and autonomous systems where regulatory approval and human trust are non-negotiable.

title: MMOE: Modernizing Diffusion Transformers with Efficient Expert Design
authors: Yanhao Jia, Jiepeng Wang, Haibin Huang, Chi Zhang, Erik Cambria et al.
summary: This paper adapts efficient scaling techniques from large language models (LLMs)—specifically mixture-of-experts (MoE) architectures—to diffusion transformers used for image generation. Rather than simply adding more parameters, the authors introduce ModernMOE (MMOE), which carefully combines routed experts, lightweight expert shortcuts, and residual connections to achieve faster convergence and better image quality per unit of compute. The work demonstrates that generative models can benefit from the same balanced scaling principles that made LLMs efficient.

title: Kimi K3: Open Frontier Intelligence
authors: Kimi Team, Tongtong Bai, Yifan Bai, Yiping Bao, M. C. et al.
summary: Kimi K3 is a 2.8 trillion parameter open-source language model with native vision understanding and a million-token context window, designed to match frontier-level performance on reasoning, coding, and agentic tasks. The paper describes architectural innovations (Delta Attention, Stable LatentMoE) and training techniques (multi-domain reinforcement learning) that achieve 2.5× better scaling efficiency than its predecessor, making it one of the most capable open models available.

title: Evidence Attribution in Visual Document Understanding without Coordinates or Region Labels
authors: Zhuchenyang Liu, Yao Zhang, Yu Xiao
summary: This paper tackles a critical failure in document understanding systems: models answer questions correctly but cite the wrong evidence regions (called "attribution hallucination"). The authors show that replacing coordinate-based evidence selection with a text-quoting approach — where models quote relevant passages and a layout parser locates them — dramatically improves both evidence recall and accuracy. They further introduce a training method that learns to produce better evidence quotes without expensive region-level labels.

title: Sparse Autoencoders Encode Both Concepts and Functions: The Downstream Geometry of Feature Effects
authors: Phu Gia Hoang, Anwoy Chatterjee, Tanmoy Chakraborty, Iryna Gurevych, Subhabrata Dutta
summary: This paper investigates why sparse autoencoders (SAEs)—tools designed to extract interpretable features from neural networks—often fail to reliably steer model behavior even when their features appear meaningful. By analyzing how individual feature interventions change model outputs across different contexts, the authors find that most features don't act as simple, reusable directions; instead, their effects depend heavily on context. This challenges the assumption that interpretability and causal control are tightly linked.

title: Looping Is Not Reliability: State-Bound Evidence and Typed Revision Contracts for Agentic Code Repair
authors: Xueping Gao, Jianwei Yang, Qiang Yang
summary: This paper challenges the assumption that looping—repeatedly generating, testing, and revising code—automatically improves reliability in code repair agents. The authors conduct rigorous empirical studies on HumanEval bugs, showing that repeated revisions can actually degrade correctness despite theoretical "ever-correct" guarantees, and propose a formal contract system that separates concerns like verification, state preservation, and auditing to ensure agentic code repair is actually reliable.

title: D-Score: A Spectral Hidden-State Signal for Hallucination Detection in Large Language Models
authors: Bianca Raimondi, Davide Evangelista, Maurizio Gabbrielli, Elena Loli Piccolomini
summary: This paper proposes D-Score, a method to detect when large language models generate hallucinations (false or unsupported text) by analyzing the geometry of hidden neural activations. The approach uses a spectral statistic from a single forward pass—no external fact-checkers or multiple generations needed—making it fast and practical for real-time hallucination detection.

title: From transcription to semantic corpus analysis: unsupervised learning of sentence representations for ancient languages
authors: Th{é}otime de la Selle
summary: This paper tackles the challenge of finding semantic similarities in ancient texts (Latin and Ancient Greek) where standard language models fail. The authors develop unsupervised methods to adapt specialized language models into sentence encoders that can identify text reuse—when ancient authors quote or paraphrase earlier works—without requiring labeled training data, demonstrating strong results on identifying biblical passages reused in patristic literature.

title: Stress-Testing EEG Foundation Models for Clinical Decoding: Dataset Identity and Targeted Negative Controls
authors: Marzieh Zare
summary: This paper stress-tests six pretrained EEG foundation models on clinical tasks (dementia, Alzheimer's, seizure detection) using rigorous evaluation protocols with negative controls. The authors show that apparent model performance often reflects dataset identity leakage or weak baselines rather than genuine clinical signal—a crucial warning for researchers deploying these models in medical settings.

title: Systematic Analysis of Large Language Models and Transformer-Based Machine Translation for English-Tamil and Tamil-English Across Diverse Datasets
authors: Sriharshaa S, Sangeetha Sivanesan
summary: This paper evaluates how well state-of-the-art neural translation models handle English-Tamil translation—a genuinely hard problem because Tamil has limited training data, complex grammar, and varied domains. The authors test supervised models (NLLB, mBART) and few-shot prompting with a large language model (TamilLaMA) across four datasets, using both automatic metrics and attention visualization to understand what the models learn and where they struggle.

title: Debiased Machine Learning: Identification, Estimation, and Shape Constraints
authors: Qihui Chen, Ka Yan Cheng, Zheng Fang
summary: This paper develops a general framework for debiased machine learning (DML) that corrects biases introduced when using high-dimensional machine learning estimators (like neural networks) to estimate nuisance parameters in causal and econometric models. The core innovation is characterizing when the "Riesz representer"—a mathematical object central to DML—is identifiable, and providing a unified estimation procedure that works with modern architectures while incorporating shape constraints to improve precision.

title: Decentralised Consensus Learning Networks: SME Rotation Without Centralised Reward
authors: Florin Neagu
summary: This paper presents a decentralised learning framework where multiple agents reach consensus on beliefs through peer validation rather than external reward signals. Instead of a central authority defining correctness, agents dynamically earn "subject-matter expert" status by demonstrating consistency with the collective view — a mechanism that proves robust across network sizes from 30 to 10,000 agents but becomes increasingly concentrated in high-dimensional belief spaces.

title: The Fundamental Structure of Risk: From Characteristics to Covariance
authors: Alexandre Alouadi, Charles-Albert Lehalle
summary: This paper proposes a new way to estimate how stock prices move together (covariance) by using company fundamentals instead of historical price data. The model learns a latent representation from firm characteristics and produces interpretable risk factors and forward-looking covariance estimates — useful for portfolio managers who need reliable risk forecasts and can easily add new stocks without retraining.

title: Bayesian Feature Extraction using Gaussian and Diffused-gamma Priors for High Dimensional Spatio-Temporal Data
authors: Garrett Frady, Dipak K. Dey, Shariq Mohammed
summary: This paper develops a Bayesian method for identifying important features in high-dimensional data that vary across space and time—like brain activity recorded from multiple locations over time. The key innovation is using special statistical priors (Gaussian and Diffused-gamma) that automatically encourage sparse, interpretable solutions. The authors demonstrate the approach on electroencephalography (EEG) data to understand how chronic alcohol affects different brain regions.

title: Energy Constrained Hierarchical Underwater Monitoring via Local Multi-Agent RAG
authors: Mohamed Amine Janati, Laurent Gautier, Stéphane Barbot
summary: This paper describes a hierarchical underwater monitoring system that combines always-on low-power sensors with intermittent high-performance computing to identify marine species and generate research reports while minimizing energy use and data transmission. The system uses embedding-based retrieval and multi-agent reasoning to organize sensor data locally—solving the practical problem that underwater deployments cannot afford to transmit raw video and audio streams to the cloud.

title: Self-Authored Verification Is Unreliable in Heuristic Self-Improving Agents
authors: Diandian Guo, Cong Cao, Fangfang Yuan, Yingqi Wang, Yueshan Wang et al.
summary: This paper identifies a critical failure mode in self-improving agents: when agents control both the policies they optimize and the tests that verify those policies, their self-authored verification scores become unreliable proxies for real deployment performance. The authors demonstrate this "verifier–deployment gap" empirically and propose SEAL (Sealed Exogenous Acceptance Loop), a lightweight mechanism that requires external validation of policy changes to prevent silent performance degradation.

title: Algorithms for Equilibria in Concurrent Stopping Games
authors: Léonard Brice, Thomas A. Henzinger, K. S. Thejaswini
summary: This paper studies how to find Nash equilibria—stable strategy profiles where no player wants to unilaterally change their behavior—in concurrent stopping games, where multiple agents act simultaneously and the game terminates almost surely. The authors prove that finding equilibria with payoff constraints is generally undecidable, but offer two tractable paths: approximate equilibria (solvable in exponential time) and a risk-sensitive equilibrium concept (NP-complete, hence more computationally friendly).

title: Grading the Narrators: An Isnad-Rijal Framework for Claim-Level Provenance in Multi-Agent Knowledge Systems
authors: Ali Zahid Raja
summary: This paper imports classical Islamic hadith science methodology—which carefully tracked knowledge claims through chains of human narrators—and applies it to multi-agent AI systems where knowledge flows through chains of autonomous agents and transformations. The authors build a formal framework ("isnad-rijal") to grade the reliability of each agent in a knowledge chain and route claims for quarantine, review, or acceptance based on combined chain-strength and content-quality assessment.

title: Optimal Control with Expectation Constraint in a Smooth Boundary Case
authors: Bruno Bouchard, Lucas Gnecco Heredia, Ludovic Moreau, Kim-Anh Pham
summary: This paper solves a utility maximization problem with an expectation constraint — a classic problem in portfolio optimization — by proving the boundary of the feasible region is smooth and deriving the correct boundary conditions for the value function. The authors develop new PDE approximation methods that work in both regular and degenerate cases, and demonstrate that neural networks can solve these problems numerically, opening the door to practical computational methods for constrained portfolio optimization.

title: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Predicting Nitrous Oxide Flux
authors: Freddy Yu, Jashanjeet Kaur Dhaliwal, Subhadeep Chakraborty
summary: This paper applies Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to predict nitrous oxide emissions from agricultural soils, a major greenhouse gas and ozone-depleting substance. By embedding mechanistic equations from established process-based models into the neural network's loss function, the authors show that physics constraints improve robustness to unfamiliar soil conditions, though generalization across geographically distant sites remains difficult.

title: Limbomorphs
authors: Alex Alvarez, Michael Levin
summary: This paper studies "Limbomorphs" — lifelike creatures that emerge from evolving spatiotemporal fields in an interactive evolutionary system called Gifbreeder, with no explicit agent or environment definition. By perturbing these evolved patterns, the authors investigate whether their behavior reflects genuine goal-directed navigation or is merely appearance, offering insights into how agent-like dynamics can spontaneously arise from simple generative rules.

title: The Intruder Threshold: A Spectral Law for LoRA Fine-Tuning
authors: Peng Xie
summary: This paper discovers a mathematical law that predicts when LoRA fine-tuning (a parameter-efficient adaptation technique) will create "intruder" dimensions — new directions in the weight matrix that are orthogonal to the pretrained model and cause catastrophic forgetting. The authors derive a critical threshold formula from the spectrum of the original weights and validate it across thousands of layers, enabling practitioners to prevent forgetting without expensive validation.

title: Breaking the Total Variance Barrier: Sharp Sample Complexity for Linear Heteroscedastic Bandits with Fixed Action Set
authors: Heyang Zhao, Tianyuan Jin, Weixin Wang, Vincent Y. F. Tan, Pan Xu et al.
summary: This paper solves a fundamental problem in stochastic linear bandits—a core reinforcement learning setting where an agent repeatedly chooses from a fixed set of actions to maximize cumulative reward. The authors show that previous analysis was loose: they prove you can achieve much better sample efficiency by exploiting variance structure in the environment, breaking through a long-standing $\sqrt{\Lambda}$ barrier where $\Lambda$ is cumulative noise variance. The result matters because bandits are everywhere (online advertising, clinical trials, adaptive experiments) and tighter bounds directly translate to fewer samples needed in practice.

title: Benchmarking Zero-Shot LLM-Generated Parent Selection in Genetic Programming for Symbolic Regression
authors: Hengzhe Zhang, Qi Chen, Bing Xue, Wolfgang Banzhaf, Mengjie Zhang
summary: This paper tests whether large language models can write effective parent-selection algorithms for genetic programming (a search technique used to find mathematical formulas that fit data) without any training examples or feedback. The researchers prompt eight different LLMs to generate selection operators, evaluate them on real regression benchmarks, and find that some LLM-generated operators outperform standard baselines—suggesting LLMs can produce useful search heuristics from task descriptions alone.

title: Continuous surrogates versus threshold Boolean networks for modeling Arabidopsis ISR gene regulation
authors: Gonzalo A. Ruz
summary: This paper compares two modeling approaches for gene regulation in plants: continuous machine learning models (Random Forest and neural networks) versus discrete Boolean networks. The key finding is that these methods excel at different things—continuous models predict numerical values accurately, while Boolean networks better capture the true dynamic behavior of gene systems over time.

title: Neural Network-Driven Volatility Drag Mitigation under Aggressive Leverage
authors: Christian Bongiorno, Efstratios Manolakis, Rosario Nunzio Mantegna
summary: This paper redesigns a neural network for portfolio optimization to minimize variance while operating under high leverage. The authors shrink the model from ~40,000 parameters to just 2,175 by replacing complex components with simpler mathematical functions, and show the compact version outperforms traditional risk-parity strategies while handling aggressive borrowing without triggering margin calls.

title: SM4RT: Learning Structured Motion Geometry for 4D Reconstruction
authors: Shing Ho J. Lin, Wenzhao Zheng, Dong Zhuo, Yuqi Wu, Jie Zhou et al.
summary: This paper introduces SM4RT, a neural network model that reconstructs both the 3D geometry and motion of dynamic scenes from single-camera video. The key insight is that real objects move as rigid units following physics (SE(3) transformations), not as random scattered points — so the model exploits this structure to better understand how scenes change over time.

title: Skill Self-Play: Pushing the Frontier of LLM Capability with Co-Evolving Skills
authors: Siyuan Huang, Pengyu Cheng, Haotian Liu, Tao Chen, Yihao Liu et al.
summary: This paper introduces Skill Self-Play, a framework where language models learn by playing against themselves—generating tasks, solving them, and improving dynamically across learned "skills." The key insight is that organizing self-improvement around modular skills lets models explore diverse tasks while maintaining reliable feedback, solving a core problem in self-supervised LLM training where either you get good verification (but narrow domains) or broad exploration (but noisy rewards).

title: Explainable Reinforcement Learning for assisting Air Traffic Controllers
authors: Anduel Mehmeti, Gabriella Gigante, Salvatore Venticinque
summary: This paper applies explainability techniques to reinforcement learning agents operating in air traffic control, a safety-critical domain where humans must trust AI decisions. The authors train an RL agent to plan alternative flight routes while avoiding restricted airspace, then use saliency maps to show controllers which input features most influenced the agent's choices. The work addresses a fundamental barrier to AI adoption in aviation: establishing human trust through transparency.

title: The Regression Tax: Decomposing Why Skills Help and Hurt LLM Agents
authors: Darshan Tank, Baran Nama
summary: This paper reveals a hidden cost of adding skills to LLM agents: while skills improve average performance, they also cause regressions where previously successful tasks fail after skill integration. By analyzing nearly 6,000 runs across benchmarks, the authors identify three mechanisms causing regression and show that top-performing skills succeed mainly by avoiding damage, not by enabling new capabilities. The finding challenges how we evaluate and design skills for autonomous AI agents.

title: Dysphagia Risk Stratification in Head and Neck Cancer via Two-Stage PRO-Clinical Stacking
authors: Siyuan Zhao, Eric Ababio Anyimadu, Zachary G. Brumm, Yue Ma, Clifton David Fuller et al.
summary: This paper develops a machine learning model to identify head and neck cancer patients at risk of dysphagia (swallowing difficulty) using patient-reported symptoms and clinical data, avoiding the need for expensive imaging. The method stacks two prediction stages to create an interpretable risk assessment tool that could help clinicians decide which patients need specialized swallowing evaluation during survivorship care.

title: Opaque Epistemic Mediation: How LLM Deployment Configurations Shape the Validation of Pseudo-Science
authors: Davide Scarso, Hugo Noronha de Almeida, Joaquim Pina
summary: This paper reveals that commercial LLMs evaluate fringe scientific claims inconsistently across deployment configurations — not because the underlying models differ, but because system prompts, safety mechanisms, and interface routing create wildly different outputs for identical requests. The researchers found one model (Grok Fast) systematically assigns credibility to ethnonationalist pseudo-science while others refuse or score it low, and these stances shift unpredictably across updates and interfaces, raising urgent questions about whose responsibility it is when LLMs validate harmful misinformation.

title: CausalForge: A Formally Grounded, Self-Improving Agentic Framework for Automated Research in Causal Inference
authors: Jiyuan Tan, Vasilis Syrgkanis
summary: CausalForge automates theoretical research in causal inference by combining formal verification (via the Lean proof assistant) with an AI agent pipeline. The system generates, formalizes, and proves causal theorems while checking that formal statements actually match the intended scientific claims — solving a critical problem where language models alone unreliably verify research correctness.

title: Interpretable EEG biomarkers with bag-of-waves: Spatial and temporal waveform dictionaries for low-data regimes
authors: Athanasios Papastathopoulos-Katsaros, Steven T. Lee, Lin Yao, Ajay Thomas, Junseok Park et al.
summary: This paper introduces bag-of-waves, a simple and interpretable method for analyzing EEG brain signals that learns a small dictionary of recurring waveform patterns without labeled data. Unlike deep neural networks that are black boxes or hand-crafted features that embed researcher bias, bag-of-waves recovers clinically meaningful brain wave shapes that neurologists can directly understand — and it works well even with very small datasets (e.g., 16 animals).

title: \k{appa}-LoRA: Condition Numbers Reveal Which LoRA Matrices Worth Updating
authors: Jianghui Wang, Silong Yong, Francesco Orabona, Marco Canini, Katia P. Sycara et al.
summary: This paper shows that not all weight matrices in LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tuning contribute equally to model improvement. The authors propose κ-LoRA, which selectively updates only the matrices with the largest condition numbers — a mathematical measure of how "unbalanced" a matrix is. By updating just the top 50% of matrices this way, the method cuts fine-tuning time by 16% and memory use by 4.5% while maintaining accuracy, making large model adaptation cheaper for resource-constrained settings.

title: TRACE-ROUTER: Task-Consistent and Adaptive Online Routing for Agentic AI
authors: Ritik Raj, Souvik Kundu, Sarbartha Banerjee, Dheemanth Joshi, Ishita Vohra et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in how AI systems route tasks to different language models in production settings. Instead of making routing decisions independently for each LLM call, TRACE-Router makes a single routing choice per task and uses the final task outcome to learn which model-selection strategy works best. The work matters because enterprise AI systems increasingly need to balance cost and quality across diverse workloads — and getting this balance right requires feedback aligned with actual task success, not individual model calls.

title: Phylogenetic signal in marine mammal and bird vocalizations captured by audio foundation models: the limited benefit of domain-specific pretraining
authors: Víctor Rincón Yepes
summary: This paper investigates whether pretrained audio foundation models automatically learn to encode evolutionary relationships in animal vocalizations, even without explicit training to do so. The authors test four audio models on a phylogenetic distance prediction task using marine mammal and bird recordings, finding that general-purpose models capture strong evolutionary signal—sometimes better than domain-specific ones—revealing that these models learn something about biological structure beyond their original training objectives.

title: Where FactsGo Missing: A LayerwiseTaxonomy and Per-Layer Attribution of Information Omissionin Air-Gapped LLM Agent Pipelines
authors: Santhiya Rajan
summary: This paper investigates why small language models (4-8B parameters) silently omit critical facts when deployed as agents in regulated, air-gapped environments (hospitals, law firms, sovereign clouds). The authors map every stage where information gets lost—from data ingestion through the agent decision loop—and show that 68% of omissions originate in deterministic infrastructure layers (quantization, caching, prompt handling), not the model itself. This reframes a reliability crisis as a systems problem with specific, fixable interventions.

title: Local-Global Geometric Insights for Graph Neural Networks via Entropic Curvature
authors: Rachid Caich, Yassine Abbahaddou
summary: This paper introduces Entropic Curvature, a new mathematical tool for understanding how information flows across entire graphs in neural networks. The work solves a key limitation of existing curvature measures — they only look at local connections and miss what happens globally — by using transport theory (how probability distributions move through space) to capture long-distance information propagation. The authors show this unifies two major GNN failure modes (oversmoothing and oversquashing) and provide practical mechanisms to improve graph neural network performance.

title: A Factorial Study of Synthetic Data Generation for Low-Resource Machine Translation using Grammar Books
authors: Varun Ghat Ravikumar, Sina Ahmadi, Lena Jäger, Rico Sennrich
summary: This paper shows how to build machine translation systems for endangered languages by extracting grammatical rules and examples from existing grammar books using large language models, then generating synthetic training data for fine-tuning. The work demonstrates practical improvements on three typologically diverse low-resource languages, opening a path toward translation tools where parallel data doesn't exist but linguistic documentation does.

title: Learning Bidirectional Causal Interactions with Heteroscedastic Neural Networks
authors: Masahiro Tanaka
summary: This paper proposes SEM-DNN, a neural network method for learning bidirectional causal relationships from observational data when the outcomes directly influence each other (simultaneity problem). The key insight is using heteroscedastic structure — variable variance across the feature space — to uniquely identify true causal effects without needing external instruments, something traditional econometric approaches struggle with.

title: Hopformer: Homogeneity-Pursuit Transformer for Time Series Forecasting
authors: Wan Zhang, Qinjie Lin, Chan Lee, Weijian Li, Han Liu et al.
summary: Hopformer is a two-stage neural network for forecasting multiple time series with many input features. It first extracts common patterns across all series (homogenization), then uses a transformer to model what remains (heterogeneity). The method beats existing approaches by 6.56% on standard benchmarks and comes with theoretical guarantees about accuracy and generalization.

title: Why Large Language Models and Humans Converge and Diverge in Evaluating Creativity
authors: Pengzhao Lyu, Yeun Joon Kim, Hanlin Xiao, Yingyue Luna Luan
summary: This paper investigates when and why large language models (LLMs) agree or disagree with humans when evaluating creative ideas. Across three studies with six different LLMs and over 2,000 ideas, the researchers find that LLMs converge with humans on novelty but diverge sharply on contextual factors like market viability and social impact—and that different LLM models apply fundamentally different evaluation standards. This matters because LLMs are increasingly used to assess creativity in real applications, yet their judgments are unpredictably misaligned with human values.

title: From Score Approximation to Distribution Approximation in Score-Based Diffusion Models
authors: Lan V. Truong
summary: This paper proves that when a neural network approximates the score function (the gradient of log probability) accurately enough, the probability distribution generated by a score-based diffusion model will be close to the target data distribution. It bridges a gap in diffusion model theory by showing that good score approximation actually translates to good distribution approximation, with explicit error bounds.

title: Draining the Energy Commons: Self-Defeating Over-Appropriation as a Coordination Failure in Agentic LLM Collectives
authors: Marcantonio Bracale Syrnicov, Federico Pierucci, Matteo Prandi, Marcello Galisai, Piercosma Bisconti et al.
summary: This paper studies what happens when multiple LLM agents share a finite resource (an energy reserve) and must coordinate to avoid depleting it. The researchers found that agents from GPT, Gemini, and Grok families systematically over-appropriate shared energy beyond sustainable levels — a classic "tragedy of the commons" — even though this self-defeats their own long-term objectives. This reveals a critical alignment failure: individual LLM agents optimizing locally can cause system-level collapse that isolated testing would never catch.

title: From Isolated Tasks to Structured Capabilities: A Multilayer Taxonomy for Large Language Models
authors: Shixin Fang, Jiachen Wo, Wenjuan Qin, Sihang Jiang, Yanghua Xiao
summary: This paper organizes LLM evaluation around capabilities rather than isolated tasks by introducing a multi-layer taxonomy of 14 capability domains and 91 subskills. The authors analyzed over 15,000 recent LLM papers and mapped them to this taxonomy, revealing significant research gaps and dominance patterns—for example, language and reasoning skills receive 43% of research attention while theory of mind and social reasoning get less than 2%. This shift from task-centric to capability-centric thinking makes it easier to identify what LLMs can actually do, compare studies across the field, and spot where evaluation is sparse.

title: DBA-Bench: A Production-Fidelity Benchmark for LLM-Based Database Operations Agents
authors: Junming Chen, Junyang Jiang, Xu Chen, Zibo Liang, Kai Zheng
summary: This paper introduces DBA-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based database administration agents in realistic operational settings. The benchmark closes a critical gap between how these agents are currently tested and how they must perform in production — where they interact with live databases, must diagnose complex cascading faults across thousands of signals, and must execute safe remediation under strict constraints. Current LLM agents achieve only 12.4% safe success compared to 93.4% for human DBAs, revealing the substantial work ahead.

title: Predictive Lightweight MARL for Resilient Coverage in Sparse-Signaling Aerial Networks
authors: Chuan-Chi Lai, Ang-Hsun Tsai
summary: This paper presents PL-MARL, a lightweight multi-agent reinforcement learning framework that keeps drone swarms coordinated even when communication is severely restricted. The key innovation is using physics-based trajectory prediction to reconstruct what neighboring drones are doing without constantly exchanging messages, allowing the swarm to maintain coverage and avoid collisions while minimizing bandwidth usage—critical for real-world aerial networks where spectrum is scarce.

title: When Language Models Meet NeuroGraphs: Exploring Enhanced Agentic LLM Framework Towards Brain Network Analysis
