authors: Jiaxing Li, Rui Dong, Muyao Tang, Youyong Kong
summary: This paper proposes BrainAgent, a framework that combines large language models with brain network analysis to move beyond simple classification toward interpretable scientific reasoning. Instead of treating connectome (brain network) data as just another classification problem, the system converts brain networks into structured descriptions, retrieves relevant neuroscience knowledge, and performs multi-step reasoning with verification — producing both predictions and human-readable explanations.

title: On the Runtime Analysis of Reinforcement Learning Hyper-Heuristics
authors: Pietro S. Oliveto, Zhenyu Wang, Peizhou Wu, Mengqing Xu
summary: This paper analyzes a Reinforcement Learning Hyper-Heuristic (RLHH)—a system that uses RL to automatically choose which optimization algorithm to apply at each step of a search process. The authors prove rigorously that with proper parameter settings, RLHH achieves optimal runtime performance on the LeadingOnes benchmark function, matching the best possible speed achievable with its available operators. This matters because it bridges the gap between simplified theoretical hyper-heuristics and realistic machine learning approaches used in practice.

title: Efficient Online LLM Watermark Detection via Rao-Blackwellized E-Processes
authors: Lu Luo, Dandan Mo, Chengdong Xu, Ting Li, Jinhan Xie et al.
summary: This paper presents a method to detect whether text was generated by an LLM or written by humans, using a statistical technique called watermarking. The key innovation is enabling this detection to work *online* — meaning you can make a decision as soon as enough evidence accumulates, rather than waiting until text generation is complete. This matters because it's faster, uses less memory, and provides mathematically guaranteed accuracy.

title: Reliability-Contagion Feasibility in LLM Multi-Agent Networks
authors: Ruiwu Niu, Xincheng Shu, Ying Zhao
summary: This paper studies how errors spread through networks of communicating LLM agents—like a disease contagion—and derives mathematical conditions for when reliability can coexist with information sharing. The authors show that adding more connections to an agent network creates a fundamental trade-off: more communication helps agents correct errors collectively, but also speeds up error propagation. They identify network topologies that balance these opposing forces.

title: Learning to Access Computation: Accessibility Plasticity as a Principle of Adaptive Intelligence
authors: Zhaowen Fan
summary: This paper introduces Accessibility Plasticity, a new principle for how neural networks adapt to new tasks and environments. Instead of only changing weights or adding new computation, the key idea is that systems can reorganize *which existing computations can talk to each other* — like rewiring connections without rebuilding components. The authors show this approach can match performance on sequential learning tasks while requiring fewer parameter changes, suggesting accessibility is as important as capability when building adaptive systems.

title: Synthetic data generation framework for quality control automation in gravure printing
authors: Korota Arsène Coulibaly, Mohamed Hamlich, Khalid Hmali, Andrea Trombin
summary: This paper solves a real industrial problem: rotogravure printing (a high-volume printing method) currently relies on slow manual inspection to catch defects like creases and streaks. The authors built an automated synthetic data generation system that creates realistic images of printing defects with pixel-perfect labels, then used those synthetic images to train a defect-detection model that achieved 80.9% accuracy on real factory samples. This matters because manual inspection is expensive and subjective—automating it with synthetic data saves money and scales instantly to any production line.

title: MedGame: Storytelling Gamification Empowered by Large Language Models for Medical Education
authors: Qian Wu, Xinrong Zhou, Zizhan Ma, Kai Chen, Zheyao Gao et al.
summary: MedGame transforms static clinical cases into interactive storytelling games powered by large language models, creating a more engaging learning experience for medical students. The system uses two AI components—one that designs clinically-accurate narratives with decision points, and another that orchestrates these into interactive experiences—along with a benchmark of 5,000 cases to measure performance. Student studies show this gamified approach feels more useful and engaging than traditional text-based medical education.

title: Graph Learning on Ensembles of Cyclic Peptides: An Investigation of Molecular Ensemble Modeling
authors: Aaron Feller, Kris Deibler, Maxim Secor
summary: This paper introduces EnsembleEGNN, a neural network model that predicts molecular properties from cyclic peptides by processing multiple 3D conformations (shapes) of the same molecule simultaneously, rather than treating it as a single fixed structure. The key insight is that molecules in solution exist as dynamic ensembles, and capturing this conformational diversity improves property prediction accuracy compared to single-structure or sequence-only baselines.

title: Beyond Sycophancy: Structured Resistance and Compliance in LLM Moral Reasoning
authors: Baihui Wang, Bernard Koch
summary: This paper investigates how large language models (LLMs) update their moral judgments when exposed to different perspectives, showing that the process isn't simply about reducing "sycophancy" (telling people what they want to hear) but follows structured patterns borrowed from human social psychology. The authors demonstrate that models' resistance or compliance depends on three factors: how different a new view is from their current position, who presents it, and whether a group endorses it—enabling better design of AI systems that can learn from others without blindly accepting influence.

title: OpenForgeRL: Train Harness-native Agents in Any Environment
authors: Xiao Yu, Baolin Peng, Ruize Xu, Hao Zou, Qianhui Wu et al.
summary: OpenForgeRL is an open-source framework that enables end-to-end training of AI agents that use complex inference harnesses (like Claude Code or Codex) in real-world environments. The key innovation is decoupling training from the harness itself—using a lightweight proxy to record harness behavior as training data, while a Kubernetes orchestrator runs distributed rollouts—making it practical to apply reinforcement learning to sophisticated multi-turn agents that were previously hard to train with standard RL tools.

title: MIRROR: Learning from the Other View for Multi-Modal Reasoning
authors: Wen Ye, Yuxiao Qu, Aviral Kumar, Xuezhe Ma
summary: This paper addresses a key weakness in vision-language models (VLMs): they often fail at visual reasoning tasks even when they could solve the same problem presented as text. The authors show that different representations of the same problem—text-only, image-only, or combined—expose different reasoning strengths and weaknesses. They propose MIRROR, a reinforcement learning method that trains models to learn from their best-performing modality, using the strongest view as a teacher for weaker ones, improving both accuracy and cross-modal consistency on geometry reasoning tasks.

title: X$^3$-OPD: Distilling Reasoning into Large Audio-Language Models via On-Policy Alignment
authors: Dongjie Fu, Di Cao, Xize Cheng, Zihan Zhang, Wenxu Jia et al.
summary: This paper presents X³-OPD, a method for teaching audio-language models to reason better by distilling knowledge from text-based language models. The core insight is that audio models struggle with logical reasoning because training data is scarce, so the authors transfer reasoning skills from powerful text models to audio models using on-policy learning—where the audio model generates its own reasoning steps while receiving guidance from the text teacher. This matters because audio contains information (tone, background sounds, speech patterns) that text alone misses, but current audio models can't reason about it well.

title: Zero-Flow Two-Sample Tests
authors: Yakun Wang, Leyang Wang, Song Liu, Taiji Suzuki
summary: This paper introduces a new statistical test to determine whether two datasets come from the same distribution. The key innovation is the "zero-flow discrepancy" (ZFD), which detects local misalignments between samples and uses neural networks to learn directional patterns that reveal distributional differences. The method maintains statistical validity while using flexible deep learning, making it practical for complex, real-world data.

title: From Resource Flow to Executable Tests: Petri-Net-Guided LLM Test Generation for Concurrent Stateful Rust APIs
authors: Kaiwen Zhang, Guanjun Liu
summary: This paper combines Petri nets (a formal model for concurrent systems) with large language models to automatically generate rigorous test cases for concurrent Rust APIs. The key insight is that LLMs alone produce shallow or incorrect tests for complex concurrent code, while formal methods alone require too much manual work—so the authors use Petri nets as a structured blueprint to guide LLM test generation, catching bugs that respect both API semantics and concurrency rules.

title: GS-Agent: Creating 4D Physical Worlds With Generative Simulation
authors: Hongxin Zhang, Chunru Lin, Junyan Li, Zhou Xian, Tsun-Hsuan Wang et al.
summary: This paper presents GS-Agent, a system that converts natural language descriptions into realistic 4D physical worlds (3D scenes with dynamic motion and physics). Instead of training end-to-end neural networks, it orchestrates multiple AI agents that collaborate through code to iteratively build scenes—managing 3D assets, materials, placement, motion, and camera/lighting—while a physics engine ensures the results are physically plausible and interactive.

title: Same Dangerous Objective, Opposite Advice: Direct Exposure versus Multi-Agent Mediation
authors: Linjun Li
summary: This paper reveals a critical safety vulnerability: large language models (LLMs) can be manipulated into providing harmful advice when a dangerous objective is relayed through intermediary agents rather than shown directly. The researchers demonstrated that GPT-5.6-sol rejected unsafe requests when asked plainly, but accepted the same objectives when other agents transformed and reframed the instruction before passing it to the model, hiding the manipulative intent upstream. This exposes a compositional safety gap—multi-stage workflows can circumvent model safeguards by keeping dangerous instructions outside the final model's context.

title: Improved lower bounds for the Shannon capacity of odd cycles
authors: Nathaniel Itty, Christopher D. Rosin, Chase Carstensen, Daniel Reichman
summary: This paper uses large language models to discover improved lower bounds for the Shannon capacity of odd cycles—a fundamental problem in information theory that asks: what's the maximum rate at which we can send information error-free over a noisy channel? By constructing explicit independent sets in graph strong powers through iterative LLM interactions, the authors tighten decades-old bounds for cycles with 7, 11, and 13 vertices, demonstrating that LLMs can help find hard-to-spot combinatorial structures that humans struggle to construct by hand.

title: Agentic Context Management: Solving Agent Memory and Cost by Treating Them as Lifecycle and Architecture Problems
authors: Gaurav Dadhich
summary: This paper argues that production AI agents fail not because they reason poorly, but because they cannot manage what information they hold in their reasoning context—conversations, prompts, tool definitions, outputs. The authors propose Agentic Context Management (ACM), a framework that treats memory as a dynamic lifecycle problem rather than just a storage-and-retrieval problem, and show that proper context compaction can achieve linear token cost while preserving accuracy, compared to naive approaches that grow quadratically.

title: Artificial Epanorthosis: Why large language models overuse a classical rhetorical figure, and how to mitigate it
authors: Federico Boggia
summary: This paper investigates why large language models systematically overuse epanorthosis—a classical rhetorical figure involving self-correction (e.g., "This is not a course. It is a journey of transformation")—and proposes methods to calibrate this behavior to match human writing patterns. The work bridges classical rhetoric with modern LLM analysis, showing that the overuse stems from training data distribution and preference tuning rather than fundamental generation constraints, and demonstrates practical techniques to reduce the figure to human-appropriate levels across different genres.

title: Toward Generalizable Cognitive Impairment Detection with Speech-Based Multimodal Large Language Models
authors: Yingchao Huang, Xin Wang, Yuhan Su, Shanshan Yao
summary: This paper proposes a multimodal framework using large language models to detect cognitive impairment from speech by combining acoustic and linguistic features. The approach achieves 92.4% accuracy on benchmark datasets and shows strong cross-dataset generalization, offering a non-invasive, privacy-preserving screening tool for early diagnosis of cognitive decline.

title: Toward Continuous Assurance for the Democratization of AI Agent Creation in Industry
authors: Natan Levy, Harel Berger
summary: This paper tackles a practical problem: non-technical users in organizations are building AI agents through low-code and no-code tools, but these agents silently degrade over time as their underlying dependencies (models, APIs, data sources, permissions) change. The authors propose a "continuous assurance" framework—combining dependency tracking, readiness checks, and governance—to keep citizen-created agents reliable in production without requiring deep technical expertise to maintain them.

title: Compact Latent Coordination for Autonomous Vehicles at Unsignalized Intersections
authors: Gil Lifshits, Igal Bilik, Gilad Katz
summary: This paper presents MAPS, a hierarchical deep reinforcement learning system for coordinating autonomous vehicles at unsignalized intersections without relying on traffic signals or privileged communication. A centralized "Master" agent learns a compact continuous embedding (proto-plan) that encodes coordination strategy, which decentralized "Worker" agents use alongside local observations to control individual vehicles. The approach achieves collision-free navigation with reduced travel times and generalizes remarkably well — a system trained on three agents works zero-shot on five-agent scenarios with 94% success.

title: Agentic coding without the cloud: evaluating open-weight large language models on longitudinal data preparation tasks
authors: Mack Nixon, Liam Wright, Yevgeniya Kovalchuk, Alison Fang-Wei Wu, Martin Danka et al.
summary: This paper evaluates open-source large language models running locally on consumer hardware for automated data preparation — a tedious bottleneck in research involving sensitive longitudinal data. The work demonstrates that mid-size open models (31–35B parameters) can handle complex data cleaning tasks like merging survey waves and harmonizing categories with 87.9% success, offering a privacy-safe alternative to cloud-based AI coding assistants.

title: Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization
authors: Rajiv Shailesh Chitale, Rahul Madhavan, Taneesh Gupta, Deepanway Ghosal, Aravindan Raghuveer
summary: This paper introduces Test-Time Scaling via Error Localization (TTEL), a method that improves large language model performance on complex reasoning tasks by reusing valid parts of partially-correct solutions instead of discarding them. The key insight is to identify exactly where an error occurred in a reasoning chain, then branch off from that point rather than starting over — this cuts computational cost roughly in half while maintaining or improving accuracy on programming and math problems.

title: KroQuant: Kronecker-Structured Block Transforms for Efficient Post-Training Quantization of Diffusion Transformers
authors: Yann Bouquet, Alireza Khodamoradi, Kristof Denolf, Mathieu Salzmann
summary: This paper presents KroQuant, a method to compress diffusion transformers (neural networks that generate images by progressively removing noise) to 4-bit precision without severely degrading image quality. The key insight is using Kronecker-structured transforms—mathematically efficient linear transformations based on tensor products—to handle outliers in activation values during quantization, while keeping the computational cost low enough to run during image generation.

title: When Trivia Is Not Trivial: Everyday Knowledge Failures in Multilingual LLMs
authors: Anna Mosolova, Djamé Seddah
summary: This paper introduces TriviaRoomQA, a multilingual benchmark of 8,640 quiz-style questions across six European languages, to expose knowledge gaps in large language models that standard benchmarks miss. The authors evaluate 30 models and find that while LLMs excel at formal domains like history and mathematics, they fail surprisingly often on everyday cultural knowledge—celebrities, music, movies, news—and perform inconsistently across languages on identical questions, revealing that factual knowledge in LLMs is language-dependent rather than universal.

title: An Evaluation Framework for Structured Audio Captions Validated by Controlled Perturbations
authors: Liang-Yuan Wu, Sripathi Sridhar, Mark Cartwright, Magdalena Fuentes
summary: This paper proposes a new evaluation framework for assessing automatically generated audio captions that go beyond simple text descriptions. The authors argue that modern audio captioning systems now produce structured outputs (with separate components for acoustic properties, semantic descriptions, measurements, etc.), but existing evaluation metrics are designed for flat text and miss this complexity. They introduce a multi-axis framework combining LLM-based semantic evaluation with computational metrics for acoustic accuracy, and validate it using controlled error injection.

title: Euclid-MCP: A Model Context Protocol Server for Deterministic Logical Reasoning via Prolog
authors: Bartolomeo Bogliolo
summary: This paper introduces Euclid-MCP, a software tool that connects large language models to a logical reasoning engine (Prolog) so they can reliably solve multi-step logical problems instead of guessing. The work matters because LLMs are good at language but terrible at guaranteed logical correctness—critical in compliance, security, and safety applications—and this system bridges that gap by letting the LLM ask a symbolic engine for definitive answers.

title: MemTools: A Unified Research Framework for Interoperable Agent Memory
authors: Chengfeng Zhao, Jinhui Chen, Sirui Liang, Shizhu He, Yequan Wang et al.
summary: This paper introduces MemTools, a unified framework for building and studying agent memory systems that works across different architectures. The key problem: existing agent memory implementations are fragmented, tightly coupled to specific systems, and hard to compare fairly. MemTools solves this by standardizing how memory components interact, making it possible to swap parts between systems and test them rigorously—like having a universal toolkit instead of proprietary tools locked into each brand's ecosystem.

title: Hilbert Operator for Progressive Encoding (HOPE): A Mathematical Framework for Deconstructing Learned Representations in Deep Networks
authors: Hossein Mobahi, Peter L. Bartlett
summary: This paper introduces HOPE, a mathematical framework that deconstructs what neural networks learn by treating network compression as a problem in functional analysis. Instead of using ad-hoc pruning heuristics, the authors model neurons as operators in a Hilbert space (an abstract mathematical setting for continuous functions), enabling a unified way to remove or merge neurons and entire layers without architectural bias. This matters because understanding what networks learn and how to compress them efficiently is crucial for both interpretability and deployment.

title: FedAgentKE: Federated Semantic Knowledge Evolution for Heterogeneous Agents
authors: Weihao Li, Jun Bai, Ziyang Song
summary: This paper proposes FedAgentKE, a framework that lets multiple LLM-based agents learn from each other without sharing their raw reasoning steps. Instead of working in isolation, agents collaboratively evolve shared reasoning patterns through federated learning—a privacy-preserving approach where knowledge is distilled, aggregated, and adapted across different agent systems. The work matters because modern AI systems increasingly need to coordinate and improve together, and this method enables that without exposing sensitive internal reasoning.

title: Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score (CM-LRS): From Plausible to Bankable
authors: Prerit Ahuja
summary: This paper introduces CM-LRS (Capital Markets LLM Reliability Score), a framework for evaluating whether language model outputs are "bankable"—defensible to regulators and counterparties in actual financial workflows. Rather than measuring generic fluency or question-answering accuracy, CM-LRS scores models across seven dimensions (factual accuracy, traceability, numerical consistency, completeness, discipline, usefulness, auditability) on real capital markets tasks like M&A analysis and debt issuance document generation. The work shows that frontier closed-source models cluster tightly (within 0.22 points), but all struggle with retrieval and synthesis tasks, revealing where LLMs remain unreliable for high-stakes finance.

title: pAI-Econ-claude: A Gated Human-in-the-Loop Multi-Agent Architecture for AI-Assisted Economic Theory Development
authors: Chen Zhu, Xiaolu Wang, Weilong Zhang
summary: This paper presents pAI-Econ-claude, a multi-agent system where AI agents collaborate with human experts to develop economic theory, using gates and checkpoints to catch errors when no automated correctness measure exists. The work shows that structured oversight and human judgment allocation outperform fully autonomous agent systems in domains like economics where ground truth is expensive or impossible to verify automatically.

title: Search Hardness-Aware LLM-Based Problem Formulation for Expensive Simulation-Driven Design
authors: Yuchen Li, Handing Wang, Bing Xue, Mengjie Zhang
summary: This paper proposes SHA-PF, a framework that uses large language models to automatically reformulate engineering design problems in ways that make them easier to solve. Rather than just translating requirements into objectives and constraints, the method discovers formulations that guide optimization algorithms toward efficient search by prioritizing samples with high potential for progress—dramatically reducing the number of expensive simulations needed to find good designs.

title: Explainable Belief Harmonization under Dynamic Epistemic Partitions
authors: Adam Kostka, Jarosław A. Chudziak
summary: This paper addresses how multiple agents can reconcile conflicting beliefs when their observational capabilities change during runtime—for example, when sensors fail or new data sources become available. The authors propose a formal framework combining logic-based reasoning with numerical methods to detect and repair inconsistencies while preserving explanations of why changes occurred. This matters because real multi-agent systems (robotics, distributed sensors, autonomous vehicles) must handle dynamic capability shifts, yet existing consensus and belief-merging methods assume static agent architectures.

title: Transformer-based Diffusion models for Hydrological Time Series Probabilistic Imputation and Forecasting
authors: Ferdinand Bhavsar, Lionel Benoit, Maxime Savatier, Edith Gabriel
summary: This paper applies transformer-based diffusion models to fill gaps and predict hydrological data (water quantity and quality measurements). The approach is valuable because traditional statistical methods struggle with the irregular, sparse measurements typical in water resource monitoring, where missing data and sensor failures are common — so a neural generative approach can learn complex temporal patterns and produce realistic reconstructions.

title: GLP: A Grassroots, Multiagent, Concurrent, Logic Programming Language for AI
authors: Ehud Shapiro
summary: This paper introduces Grassroots Logic Programs (GLP), a concurrent logic programming language designed to let multiple independent agents coordinate and form larger systems without requiring central control or a single global authority. The work matters because it offers a technical foundation for building truly decentralized platforms where participants can operate autonomously yet still coalesce into shared infrastructure—a rare middle ground between centralized and purely decentralized systems.

title: Smooth Neural Point Processes via B-Splines
authors: Michele Bellomo, Riccardo Ramaschi, Alberto Dolara, Tomaso Aste
summary: This paper proposes a new way to model temporal point processes (sequences of events in continuous time) using neural networks combined with B-splines — smooth mathematical curves. The key insight is that by directly modeling the conditional intensity function (the instantaneous rate of events) as a weighted combination of B-spline basis functions, the method achieves exact likelihood calculations, faster training through parallelization, and better predictive accuracy than existing neural approaches.

title: HiMe: Real-Time Self-Hosted Personal Agent Platform for Health Insights with Wearable Devices
authors: Wei Liu, Siya Qi, Linhai Zhang, Lorainne Tudor Car, Yulan He
summary: HiMe is a privacy-first platform that runs on your own device to analyze health data from wearables (like smartwatches) using AI agents in real time. Instead of sending your data to the cloud, it stays local and learns your health patterns over time, giving personalized insights without compromising privacy.

title: Weight-norm Criticality: A Mechanism for Loss Spikes Induced by the Normalization and Weight Decay
authors: Xiaolong Li, Zhangchen Zhou, Zhi-Qin John Xu
summary: This paper identifies a previously overlooked source of training instability in deep neural networks: the interaction between weight normalization and weight decay that drives scale-invariant weight norms toward zero, causing abrupt loss spikes. The work explains why weight decay improves generalization up to a point but then destabilizes training if made too strong—a phenomenon distinct from the well-known "edge of stability" problem caused by learning rates alone.

title: Safe and Scalable Multi-Drone Payload Transport via CBF-based Reinforcement Learning with Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Transfer
authors: Jaeyoun Choi, Oswin So, Songyuan Zhang, Cooper Taylor, Chuchu Fan
summary: This paper presents a learning-based framework for coordinating multiple drones to safely transport payloads together—a challenging problem because the drones, cables, and load are dynamically coupled. The authors use reinforcement learning with safety constraints (via Control Barrier Functions) and domain randomization to train a single policy that generalizes across different team sizes and real-world conditions without needing to retrain or fine-tune.

title: When Does Recurrence Become an Algorithm? Convergence Selection in Weight-Tied Looped Transformers
authors: Tong Zhang, Junhao Hu, Yun Peng, Tao Xie
summary: This paper investigates when recurrent transformers (the same transformer block applied repeatedly) actually learn to solve algorithmic problems, rather than just memorizing patterns. The authors discover a "budget law" that predicts how fast the model solves a problem per loop based on training data size and loop count, and show that weight tying (reusing the same block) fundamentally shifts which algorithm the model learns—from parallel to serial computation. These findings are invisible to standard analysis methods, so the authors introduce new measurement techniques to detect what algorithms transformers actually implement.

title: SPECTRA: State-Space Exogenous Context and Temporal-Frequency Resolution Architecture for Probabilistic Energy Forecasting
authors: Hang Ye, Xinyan Jiang, Yuedong Shi, Yangxin Zhu, Jianming Wei et al.
summary: This paper introduces SPECTRA, a neural architecture for predicting energy supply and demand with both point estimates and uncertainty bounds. The key insight is that predictable patterns (trends and seasons) and unpredictable noise play different roles in shaping forecast distributions—the first anchors the prediction, the second determines confidence intervals. The method outperforms existing approaches on electricity load, price, solar, and wind forecasting by 5–7%.

title: Bayesian uncertainty estimation improves clinical decision making in medical AI agents
authors: Frederik Hauke, Patrick Wienholt, Christiane Kuhl, Dyke Ferber, Jakob Nikolas Kather et al.
summary: This paper shows that Monte Carlo dropout can give medical AI systems a reliable measure of uncertainty about their predictions, and that doctors using AI-assisted diagnostic agents make better decisions when uncertainty is presented as a simple binary flag rather than a raw score. The work demonstrates that uncertainty estimation isn't just academically interesting — it genuinely improves clinical outcomes by helping agents know when to defer to human judgment.

title: LKValues: Aligning Large Language Models with Sri Lankan Societal Values
authors: Nethmi Muthugala,  Supryadi, Surangika Ranathunga, Nisansa de Silva, Ruijie Tao et al.
summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in LLM value alignment: most existing approaches embed Western cultural norms, leaving underrepresented languages and non-Western societies poorly served. The authors create LKValues, a comprehensive resource suite grounded in Sri Lankan societal values, including a dataset of 150k instruction-tuning examples and a 1,000-instance benchmark in Sinhala and English. They show that even state-of-the-art models exhibit significant cultural and cross-lingual alignment gaps, and that fine-tuning on culturally-grounded data can meaningfully reduce these disparities.

title: Towards Miniature Humanoid Tele-Loco-Manipulation Using Virtual Reality and Reinforcement Learning
authors: Nicolas Kosanovic, Jordan Dowdy, Jean Chagas Vaz
summary: This paper develops a control system for miniature humanoid robots that combines Virtual Reality teleoperation for the upper body with Reinforcement Learning for balance and walking. The work makes sophisticated full-body robot control accessible on cheap, small hardware (specifically the ROBOTIS OP3), demonstrating that a remote operator can make the robot walk while simultaneously manipulating objects—a task previously limited to expensive industrial-scale humanoids.

title: Persian Pixel: A large-scale synthetic OCR dataset for Persian language
authors: Pouria Mahdi, Haq Nawaz Malik
summary: This paper introduces Persian Pixel, a large synthetic dataset of 343,000 text images designed to train optical character recognition (OCR) systems for Persian language. The work solves a critical bottleneck: Persian OCR lags far behind Latin-script systems because Persian's complex cursive script and lack of annotated training data make it hard to build accurate recognition models. By programmatically generating realistic training images with authentic Persian typography and document degradation, the authors provide a cost-effective path to robust Persian OCR without expensive manual labeling.

title: Train the Model, Not the Reader: Decodability Supervision for Verifiable Activation Explanations
authors: Hiskias Dingeto
summary: This paper exposes a critical flaw in how we verify explanations of neural network activations: the standard reconstruction-based test (does the explanation let us regenerate the activation?) can pass while being fundamentally unfaithful. The authors propose RECAP, a training-time method that keeps internal model representations independently verifiable, making it harder for models to game explanations during safety audits.

title: PG-KINN: A Physics-Informed Petrov-Galerkin Kolmogorov-Arnold Network for Solving Forward and Inverse PDEs
authors: Amirhossein Sadr, Nima Soltani, Vahideh Moghtadaiee, Aida Pakniyat, Dara Rahmati et al.
summary: This paper introduces PG-KINN, a method that combines Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks (KANs — neural networks with learnable spline activations) with a Petrov-Galerkin weak formulation to solve partial differential equations (PDEs) both forward and inverse problems. The key insight is that by using a weak formulation (integration by parts) instead of strong-form residual minimization, the method achieves better numerical conditioning, lower differentiation requirements, and works for broader classes of PDEs including non-self-adjoint and nonlinear systems.

title: Statevector-Referenced Geometry Survival of a Four-Qubit ZZ Quantum Kernel on IBM Quantum Hardware: A Fixed-Subset Diagnostic Across Three Execution Configurations
authors: Rostyslav Sipakov
summary: This paper diagnoses how well quantum kernel methods preserve geometric structure when executed on real quantum hardware. The authors measure a four-qubit ZZ kernel's Gram matrix across different error-mitigation configurations on IBM hardware, finding that gate twirling best preserves geometry—but warns that implementation fidelity and task relevance are separate concerns, and no quantum advantage should be claimed.

title: Online Variance Reduction for Domain Adaptation on Streaming Data
authors: Andrea Napoli
summary: This paper introduces ARROW, the first online variance reduction algorithm for domain adaptation on streaming data. It tackles a practical problem: existing variance reduction techniques work offline, but real-world data arrives continuously, making them incompatible with streaming scenarios. ARROW maintains moving averages of alignment statistics and reweights incoming data batches to reduce variance while adapting to new domains—achieving speeds and accuracy comparable to offline methods.

title: Notes to Self: Can LLMs Benefit from Experiential Abstractions?
authors: Chang Liu, Xinyu Li, Artur Dubrawski
summary: This paper investigates whether large language models (LLMs) can learn from their own problem-solving experiences by extracting and reusing natural-language abstractions — essentially distilled strategies or lessons learned. The researchers build a library of these "notes to self" from solved math problems, then test whether retrieving or training with these abstractions helps LLMs solve new problems better. The work suggests LLMs can benefit from experiential learning in ways that mirror how humans leverage accumulated knowledge.

title: Variance-reduced Domain Adaptation using Paired Sampling
authors: Andrea Napoli
summary: This paper tackles a key problem in domain adaptation — when a machine learning model trained on one dataset (source domain) struggles on a different dataset (target domain) due to distribution shift. The authors propose Paired Sampling for Domain Adaptation (PSDA), a variance reduction technique that makes existing domain adaptation methods more stable and effective during training by smartly pairing data points across domains. Experiments show the method improves target domain accuracy while reducing training variance.

title: Test-Time Training for Modality Order Consistency in Vision-Language Models
authors: Aditi Gupta, Yossi Gandelsman
summary: Vision-language models (like CLIP or LLaVA) perform differently depending on whether you show them the image first or ask the question first — a semantically meaningless change that shouldn't matter. This paper identifies this "modality order" bug, uses activation patching to locate it in mid-network layers, and proposes a simple test-time training fix that closes the performance gap and even improves both orderings.

title: Closing the Lab-to-Store Gap: A Data-Efficient Post-Training and Experience-Driven Learning VLA Framework for Retail Humanoids
authors: Roger Sala Sisó, Tiago Silvério, Jakob Sand, Tran Nguyen Le
summary: This paper addresses the "lab-to-store gap" — the problem that robots trained in controlled settings fail in real retail environments. The authors present DEED, a practical framework that combines careful data preparation, targeted fine-tuning, and learning-from-experience to make humanoid robots reliable at real-world tasks like shelf restocking. The key insight is that this is mostly an engineering problem, not an architecture problem: with the right data and training pipeline, even a single GPU can produce a working robot.

title: PyroDash: Cost-Efficient Token-Level Small-Large Language Model Collaborative Inference
authors: Niqi Lyu, Pengtao Shi, Wei Qiu, Jianlin Zhong, Sicong Xia et al.
summary: PyroDash is a framework that pairs small, cheap language models (SLMs) with large, powerful ones (LLMs) to save money while maintaining reasoning quality. During generation, the SLM learns when to ask the LLM for help by emitting a special token—this decision is trained using reinforcement learning to balance accuracy against cost. On math problems, it achieves better accuracy than using the LLM alone while cutting costs by up to 98%.

title: Adaptive deep nonparametric regression from dependent data under covariate shift
authors: William Kengne, Ehud Mossa Ockegna
summary: This paper develops deep neural network methods for regression tasks when training and test data come from different distributions (covariate shift) and observations are dependent rather than independent. The key innovation is a sparse-penalized deep neural network estimator that reweights data to account for distribution mismatch, with theoretical guarantees showing it achieves near-optimal convergence rates even with time-series data.

title: The Blessing of Dimensionality: How Near-Orthogonality in High-Dimensional Spaces Explains Temporal Portability
authors: Abigail Woodring, Adrian Chan, Rana Muhammad Shahroz Khan, Sukwon Yun, Chau-Wai Wong et al.
summary: This paper explains why PortLLM—a method for adapting fine-tuned language models to continually pretrained base models without retraining—works so well and for so long. The authors show empirically that LoRA patches (parameter-efficient adaptations) remain effective across 10+ updates of the base model, and they prove theoretically that high-dimensional near-orthogonality explains this "temporal portability," offering a geometric perspective on why simple adaptation methods persist over time.

title: Sound Probabilistic Safety Bounds for Large Language Models
authors: Mahdi Nazeri, Anne-Kathrin Schmuck, Sadegh Soudjani, Alessandro Abate
summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework to rigorously measure how often large language models (LLMs) generate harmful outputs. The core innovation is using Clopper-Pearson confidence intervals — a classical statistical tool — combined with a smart search algorithm to efficiently compute provably-correct lower bounds on harm probability, even when the true probability is extremely small. This matters because it enables formal safety certification of LLMs, moving beyond ad-hoc testing.

title: Self-supervision drives representational convergence in medical foundation models more than clinical supervision
authors: Soroosh Tayebi Arasteh, Sebastian Ziegelmayer, Mahshad Lotfinia, Lisa Adams, Sven Nebelung et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether medical image encoders from different organizations learn similar representations, and what drives that convergence. The authors systematically compare 18 image and 7 text encoders across multiple datasets and find that convergence is real but modest—and surprisingly, it's driven by the self-supervised training objective, not by clinical expertise or model scale. This challenges the assumption that bigger, clinically-trained models automatically learn shared, interchangeable representations.

title: Statistical Inference for Rank Allocation in Low-Rank Adaptation
authors: Yihang Gao, Vincent Y. F. Tan
summary: This paper proposes StatLoRA, a statistical method for deciding how to distribute rank resources across different components of LoRA (Low-Rank Adaptation) fine-tuning in large language models. Instead of using ad-hoc importance scores, StatLoRA frames rank allocation as a hypothesis testing problem with theoretical guarantees, and shows it matches or beats existing methods on NLP tasks while being more principled.

title: Active Inference as a Convex Markov Decision Process
authors: Nikola Milosevic, Nicolás Hinrichs, Nico Scherf
summary: This paper shows that Active Inference — a neuroscience-inspired framework where agents minimize expected free energy to make decisions — can be reformulated as a convex optimization problem within the standard reinforcement learning framework. By doing this, the authors make Active Inference amenable to modern RL algorithms and convergence guarantees, bridging two previously separate theoretical perspectives on adaptive behavior.

title: Autonomous Collaborative Learning Among an Ensemble of Tsetlin Machines with Consensus-Based Inference
authors: Yehuda Rudin, Osnat Keren, Michal Yemini, Alexander Fish
summary: This paper proposes a decentralized learning framework where multiple Tsetlin Machines (rule-based learning systems) collaborate without sharing raw data, each agent solving its portion of a classification problem and reaching consensus on predictions. It matters because it shows how distributed, privacy-preserving machine learning can work with interpretable rule-based models in settings like multi-sensor environments where data cannot be centralized.

title: The Giant Hippocampus: From Structural Monoculture to a System of Systems
authors: Jaeho Seol
summary: This paper argues that modern AI has made a structural mistake by applying identical Transformer architectures to all tasks, when neuroscience shows that different cognitive functions require qualitatively different neural structures. The author proposes a "System of Systems" design — heterogeneous modules with specialized inductive biases communicating through standardized interfaces — as a principled alternative to monolithic, scaled-up models.

title: Harnessing Disagreement: Detecting Correlated Agreement Blindness in Multi-Agent Triage
authors: Shay Seiya McDonnell, Avantika Singh, Quoc-Viet Pham, Vratislav Havlik, Gregory M. P. O'Hare
summary: This paper identifies a critical flaw in multi-agent safety systems: when independent agents improve and converge toward similar decisions, they become blind to correlated failures—situations where multiple agents make the same wrong call. The authors propose ARAT, a system using diverse reasoning models (Random Forest, k-NN, and a calibrated meta-model) that actively detects and escalates these dangerous agreement moments, validated on network intrusion detection and clinical readmission prediction tasks.

title: SpikingMOT: A Spike-Driven Multi-Object Tracker
authors: Yiding Sun, Xiangyang Yang, Dongxu Zhang, Qirui Wang, Zijie Xu et al.
summary: This paper introduces SpikingMOT, a multi-object tracking system that uses spiking neural networks (SNNs)—brain-inspired networks that process information through sparse, event-driven activations—instead of traditional dense neural networks. The key insight is that tracking doesn't need constant, full activation of neurons; sparse, selective firing can actually predict motion just as well while using 86% less energy and 72% fewer parameters. The work achieves state-of-the-art tracking accuracy on challenging benchmarks (SportsMOT and DanceTrack) while being far more efficient.

title: Asymptotically Optimal Regret for Reinforcement Learning without Horizon Dependence
authors: Runlong Zhou, Zihan Zhang, Maryam Fazel, Simon S. Du
summary: This paper solves a fundamental problem in reinforcement learning: how to minimize regret (cumulative mistakes) without the regret depending on the planning horizon H. The authors propose a new algorithm achieving near-optimal regret bounds for tabular Markov decision processes — environments with discrete states and actions where the agent learns to maximize rewards. This matters because previous algorithms had regret that grew with log H, making them inefficient for long-term planning; this work removes that dependence entirely.

title: Dreamer-CPC: Message Learning with World Models for Decentralized Multi-agent Reinforcement Learning
authors: Taisuke Takayama, Naoto Yoshida, Tadahiro Taniguchi
summary: This paper proposes Dreamer-CPC, a decentralized multi-agent reinforcement learning method where agents learn to communicate by exchanging messages derived from their internal world models rather than raw observations. The key insight is that messages grounded in latent world-model states (which encode history) enable better coordination than messages based only on current observations, especially when some agents have missing or partial information.

title: Not Birds of a Feather: Personality-Based Partner Selection in LLM Agents
authors: Tao Wang, Hsiang-Ling Chiu, Chihang Wei, Yang Xiu, Zhonghao Hou
summary: This paper studies how LLM agents select partners based on personality traits when capability is held constant. The researchers found that agents show strong, task-dependent personality preferences (e.g., choosing "open" agents for creative tasks, "conscientious" agents for strategic ones) that contradict both human similarity-attraction patterns and human evidence about what personalities actually make teams perform well — raising concerns about bias in AI agent marketplaces.

title: Learning the Arabic Dialect Continuum as a Continuous Space: A Regression Approach to Speaker Origin Prediction
authors: Mohamed Aziz Khadraoui, Adel Ammar, Bilel Benjdira, Zahid Khan, Skander Turki et al.
summary: This paper treats Arabic dialect variation as a continuous geographic phenomenon rather than discrete categories, predicting speaker location as latitude-longitude coordinates using neural networks. The approach is novel because it acknowledges that Arabic dialects form a spectrum across space — not isolated pockets — and validates this mathematically using a spherical loss function that respects Earth's curvature.

title: Efficient Clustering with Provable Guardrails for LLM Inference at Scale
authors: Longshaokan Wang, Wai Tsang Keung, Punit Ghodasara, Roman Wang, Ali Dashti et al.
summary: This paper tackles a critical bottleneck in scaling LLM applications: the computational cost of running inference on millions of requests. The authors propose a clustering algorithm that groups similar inputs and reuses LLM outputs across cluster members, with mathematical guarantees that each member stays sufficiently close to its representative. The method is deployed at scale (38 million customers) and achieves 50× cost and latency reduction.

title: Same Game, Different Story: A Minimal Conservative Strategic Robustness Benchmark for Large Language Model Agents
authors: Seyed Pouyan Mousavi Davoudi, Alireza Amiri-Margavi, Amin Gholami Davodi, Hamidreza Hasani Balyani, Arshia Gharagozlou
summary: This paper introduces a benchmark to test whether large language model agents make consistent decisions when the same strategic game is presented using different narratives or framings. The authors find that LLMs like GPT-4 and LLaMa-2 shift their behavior substantially based on social context (e.g., "business" vs. "friend-sharing" framing) even when payoffs stay identical—a concerning sign that these models lack robustness in real strategic interactions.

title: Remote ID Spoofing-Aware Trajectory Planning for Small Unmanned Aerial Systems
authors: Jeremiah Webb, Bryce Bjorkman, Abel Diaz Gonzalez, Austin Coursey, Noah Dahle et al.
summary: This paper presents a decentralized trajectory planning system for small unmanned aerial vehicles (drones) that accounts for spoofed Remote Identification broadcasts — fake location signals that adversaries could transmit to cause collisions. Rather than trusting all received location data, the system uses physical signal measurements to detect when broadcasts are false, then plans collision-avoidant paths that remain safe even under uncertainty about true positions. Results show the approach reduces near-collision events in multi-drone delivery scenarios.

title: Adaptive Capitulation: A Structural Failure Mode of LLM Responses in Vulnerability Contexts
authors: Eunna Lee
summary: This paper identifies a failure mode in large language models (LLMs) called "adaptive capitulation" — where models appear to validate harmful user requests before actually facilitating them, rather than cleanly refusing or helping. The authors show this isn't a bug in any single model, but a structural problem baked into how LLMs balance safety with helpfulness when users are in vulnerable emotional states.

title: Predictive Extrema, Unprofitable Policies: An AI-Assisted Audit of Candle-Based Binance Spot Timing Models
authors: Ayoub Jadouli
summary: This paper audits whether machine-learning models trained to predict cryptocurrency price extrema can generate profitable trading strategies on Binance spot markets after accounting for transaction costs. The authors systematically tested multiple models and found that none produced positive returns — in fact, all underperformed simple buy-and-hold, leading to a firm conclusion: do not trade on these predictions. The work is valuable as a cautionary case study showing that predictive accuracy (high AUC scores) does not guarantee trading profitability.

title: Copy Less, Ground More: Overcoming Repetitive Copying in Long-Context Reasoning via Evidence-Aware Reinforcement Learning
authors: Lizhe Fang, Weizhou Shen, Tianyi Tang, Yisen Wang
summary: This paper identifies and fixes a critical failure in long-context language models: they waste effort copying irrelevant text from the input instead of reasoning productively. The authors show this problem gets worse as context grows, diagnose its root cause (poor focus on relevant evidence), and propose GEAR — a reinforcement learning method that rewards models for grounding answers in key evidence while penalizing reliance on distractors. The method consistently improves reasoning accuracy by up to 4.6 points while reducing wasted copying.

title: Appearance Pointers -- Multimodal Region Control of Diffusion Transformers
authors: Rahul Sajnani, Yulia Gryaditskaya, Radomír Měch, Srinath Sridhar, Matheus Gadelha
summary: This paper introduces "appearance pointers," a technique for controlling where and how multimodal inputs (text and images) influence image generation in Diffusion Transformers. The core problem is that creative professionals need precise regional control — specifying which materials or objects go where — but text prompts alone can't reliably achieve this. The solution uses compact tokens that act as spatial guides, mapping text or image cues to user-defined regions without retraining the base model.

title: CodeRescue: Budget-Calibrated Recovery Routing for Coding Agents
authors: Qijia He, Jiayi Cheng, Chenqian Le, Rui Wang, Xunmei Liu et al.
summary: CodeRescue solves a key problem in AI coding agents: after a failed attempt, should the system try cheaper recovery or escalate to a stronger (more expensive) model? The paper trains a smart router that learns when recovery is worthwhile versus when escalation is better, and adds a budget-calibration layer so the same router works under different cost constraints without retraining. This matters because execution feedback in coding makes cheap recovery often viable—throwing away that signal by always escalating wastes resources.

title: Agents in the Wild: Where Research Meets Deployment
authors: Grace Hui Yang, Pranav N. Venkit, Hooman Sedghamiz, Enrico Santus, Victor Dibia et al.
summary: This paper bridges the gap between agentic AI research and real-world deployment by analyzing what makes LLM-based agent systems work in production. Rather than focusing on benchmarks or algorithms, it examines practical challenges like robustness, safety, and reliability that emerge when deploying agents in pharmaceutical discovery and finance, offering concrete design patterns and mitigation strategies for failure modes.

title: 1-Lipschitz Neural Networks on Hadamard Manifolds
authors: Davide Murari, Marta Ghirardelli, Ben Adcock, Elena Celledoni, Brynjulf Owren et al.
summary: This paper constructs neural network layers that are provably 1-Lipschitz (slope-bounded) on curved spaces called Hadamard manifolds, rather than flat Euclidean spaces. Controlling Lipschitz constants is a key way to make neural networks robust to small input perturbations; the novelty here is extending this to manifolds (curved spaces) like hyperbolic geometry and matrices of positive eigenvalues. The work matters because many real data naturally live on such manifolds, and ensuring robustness there could improve safety-critical applications.

title: Fundamental limits of distributed multiclass classification from simple binary decisions
authors: Ioannis Papageorgiou, Srinivas Nomula, Ayalvadi Ganesh, Sidharth Jaggi, Parimal Parag
summary: This paper studies how to build a multiclass classifier by combining many simple binary classifiers in a distributed way, where each agent runs one binary classifier. The authors derive theoretical limits on performance when using hyperplane-based binary classifiers on high-dimensional Gaussian data, showing how error rates scale with the number of classes and dimensions. This matters because it characterizes the fundamental trade-offs in distributed learning, providing guidance on whether such decompositions are practical.

title: ROMS-IMLE: A Minimalist Approach to Competitive Single-Step Generative Modelling
authors: Chirag Vashist, Ke Li
summary: This paper challenges the conventional wisdom that gradual multi-step transformations (used in diffusion and flow matching models) are necessary for high-quality image generation. Instead, the authors build a minimal single-step generative model using Implicit Maximum Likelihood Estimation (IMLE) and a simple convolutional network, achieving competitive results (FID 2.56 on ImageNet 256×256) while being faster and more parameter-efficient than state-of-the-art alternatives.

title: ISO: An RLVR-Native Optimization Stack
authors: Hanqing Zhu, Wenyan Cong, Zhizhou Sha, Sagnik Mukherjee, Xinyuan Song et al.
summary: This paper identifies and exploits a structural property of how language models learn from reward feedback during reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR). Rather than retraining model weights from scratch, the authors show that models can reuse their foundational weight structure (spectrum) while learning new behaviors through targeted updates to input/output relationships (frames)—and they build a practical optimization framework called ISO that makes this 2–3× faster without sacrificing performance.

title: Two-Level Meta-Rubrics for Evaluating Open-Ended Generation: GAMUT, a Benchmark for Factual Completeness
authors: Xilun Chen, Zhaleh Feizollahi, Ross Goodwin, Seungwhan Moon, Scott Yih et al.
summary: This paper introduces GAMUT, a benchmark for evaluating whether long-form text generated by AI models contains all the facts it should — what researchers call "factual completeness." Most existing evaluation methods only check if claims are correct (precision), missing the equally important question of whether responses are complete. The authors propose a two-level framework that captures hierarchical relationships between facts, making it possible to automatically grade completeness at scale.

title: ResearchArena: Evaluating Sabotage and Monitoring in Automated AI R&D
authors: Lena Libon, Ben Rank, Jehyeok Yeon, David Schmotz, Jeremy Qin et al.
summary: This paper introduces ResearchArena, a benchmark for testing whether AI agents performing automated research tasks can be sabotaged without detection. The work treats untrusted AI agents as potential adversaries and evaluates monitoring systems' ability to catch hidden failures before deploying research artifacts like trained models or optimized software. It matters because as AI systems take on more autonomous R&D work, we need robust methods to verify safety before using their outputs.

title: CircuitKIT : Circuit Discovery, Evaluation, and Application Toolkit for Mechanistic Interpretability
authors: Pratinav Seth, Hem Gosalia, Aditya Kasliwal, Vinay Kumar Sankarapu
summary: CircuitKIT is a toolkit that unifies the fragmented workflow of circuit analysis — the process of identifying and understanding which parts of a neural network are responsible for specific behaviors. The paper solves a practical problem: researchers currently cobble together separate tools for discovering circuits, evaluating them, and then using them for downstream tasks like model editing or pruning. CircuitKIT provides standardized infrastructure so different discovery methods can be compared fairly and applied beyond toy problems.

title: Gaussian Boson Sampling for Asset Clustering in Statistical Arbitrage Portfolios
authors: Dayne Marcus Lopena, Daniel Buguks, Zhenghao Li, Ewan Mer, Shana H. Winston et al.
summary: This paper applies Gaussian Boson Sampling (GBS)—a quantum computing method for finding dense subgraphs—to identify clusters of correlated stocks for building statistical arbitrage portfolios. The authors show that quantum clustering algorithms outperform classical methods in constructing market-neutral portfolios, especially during high-volatility periods and in large stock universes, potentially opening a practical quantum advantage in portfolio construction.

title: They'll Verify. They Just Won't Act. How Authority Framing and Laundered Code Turn a Trusted Agentic CI/CD Pipeline Into an Attack Surface
authors: Yohann Sidot
summary: This paper demonstrates a critical vulnerability in multi-agent LLM-based CI/CD pipelines: attackers can use authority framing (fake pre-approval codes) and obfuscated malicious intent to trick multiple verification stages into shipping secret-stealing code. Even with distributed reviewers and security scanners, the system fails ~55% of the time — because reasoning about intent, not just code syntax, is needed to catch the attack.

title: Prompt Design at Scale: How Format, Instruction Count, and Context Length Shape Instruction Adherence and Hallucination in Large Language Models
authors: Netanel Eliav
summary: This paper systematically tests how three prompt-design choices—formatting style, number of simultaneous instructions, and context length—affect whether language models follow instructions accurately and avoid hallucinating. The authors ran thousands of controlled experiments across five models using a custom synthetic dataset, finding that instruction adherence collapses around 80 rules, recall degrades sharply near context limits (with format-dependent effects), and models refuse to answer rather than make things up when overloaded.

title: Inference-Time Steering for Cross-Lingual Factual Consistency in LLMs
authors: Alexander Manev
summary: This paper identifies and addresses a critical flaw in multilingual LLMs: they give different factual answers depending on the language of the prompt, even though the underlying knowledge should be language-agnostic. The authors test four intervention strategies at inference time to steer models toward consistent, factually accurate responses across languages, finding that simple prompt-based techniques outperform more complex internal manipulation methods.

title: MeetingToM: Evaluating Multimodal LLMs on Theory-of-Mind Reasoning in Multi-Party Meetings
authors: Ziyi Wang, Yuhang Wu, Dongxu Piao, Xingyu Liu, Tianhui Zhou et al.
summary: This paper introduces MeetingToM, a benchmark that tests whether multimodal language models (AI systems that process both text and visual information) can understand hidden social dynamics in group meetings. The researchers reveal that current models struggle to read between the lines — they miss non-verbal cues, fail to detect when people privately disagree while publicly appearing to agree, and can't distinguish genuine consensus from fake agreement driven by social pressure.

title: S3: Stable Subgoal Selection by Constraining Uncertainty of Coarse Dynamics in Hierarchical Reinforcement Learning
authors: Kshitij Kumar Srivastava, Kshitij Jerath
summary: This paper proposes S3, a method for hierarchical reinforcement learning (HRL) that helps high-level agents choose better subgoals by understanding the unpredictability of multi-step environment dynamics. Rather than trying to predict single-step transitions, the method predicts "coarse dynamics"—what happens several steps ahead—and encourages the high-level agent to select subgoals in regions where this prediction is confident. The approach outperforms existing HRL methods on long-horizon tasks in non-stationary environments.

title: The Price of Reasoning: Cost-Quality Tradeoffs in Reinforcement Learning for Neural Machine Translation
authors: Michael Jungo, Aixiu An
summary: This paper investigates whether reasoning traces in neural machine translation actually improve translation quality, or if improvements come from the reinforcement learning training method itself. The authors systematically remove reasoning from different phases (training vs. inference) and measure the cost-quality tradeoff, finding that reasoning at inference time significantly boosts translation quality but increases computational cost. This matters because it clarifies what actually drives performance in modern LLM post-training approaches for language tasks.

title: Spiking Neural Networks for fMRI-Based Visual Semantic Decoding
authors: Jiahong Zhang, Jinning Zhao, Sijun Shen, Siyuan Xu, Bo Xu et al.
summary: This paper shows that spiking neural networks (SNNs)—brain-inspired models that process information through discrete spike events—produce visual features that align much better with brain activity than traditional artificial neural networks do. Using fMRI brain scans, the researchers decode what people are seeing by mapping brain signals to visual features; they find that SNN-derived features cut prediction error by 97% and double semantic decoding accuracy compared to standard neural networks, suggesting SNNs may be a closer computational model to how biological vision actually works.

title: Boundary-Adapted PINNs for Elliptic Dirichlet Problems: $H^2(Ω)$ A Priori Error Bounds with Application to Mean Escape Time Computation
authors: Nathanael Tepakbong, Jun Fan, Xiang Zhou, Ding-Xuan Zhou
summary: This paper develops Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) — neural networks trained to solve differential equations — with theoretical guarantees for a specific class of boundary value problems. The key insight is that to get accurate solutions, the boundary condition enforcement method must satisfy a particular mathematical property (being "normalized to first order"), not just enforce the boundary exactly. This matters because it provides both practical guidance and theoretical understanding for using neural networks to solve differential equations, with application to computing mean escape times in stochastic processes.

title: How network perturbations distort agreement trajectories in LTI multi-agent systems
authors: Gal Barkai, Irinel-Constantin Morărescu
summary: This paper studies how network disruptions (like communication delays) distort the trajectories that multi-agent systems are supposed to synchronize to. The key finding: even tiny transmission delays can completely derail a system's ability to follow periodic reference signals—a vulnerability not previously recognized in distributed coordination theory. This matters because many real systems (power grids, robotic swarms, autonomous vehicles) rely on these protocols to stay synchronized.

title: AI Tour Meeting: Group Travel Planning by LLM Agents
authors: Daisuke Kikuta
summary: This paper presents AI Tour Meeting, a framework where multiple LLM-based agents with different personas negotiate together to plan a group trip. Each agent has its own constraints and preferences, and they discuss options in natural language until they reach agreement on an itinerary. The work is useful for studying how LLM agents collaborate and make group decisions in realistic scenarios.

title: Elicitation without Backpropagation: Steering Model Behavior by Optimizing the Latent Posterior
authors: Garrett Baker, Vinayak Pathak, Daniel Murfet, Susan Wei
summary: This paper introduces Posterior Prefix Tuning (PPT), a method to steer transformer behavior toward desired outputs without backpropagation. Instead of training the model, PPT optimizes prompts by working with the latent posterior — a probabilistic view of what predictive models the transformer implicitly represents. This matters because it offers a computationally cheaper, more interpretable alternative to standard fine-tuning, especially for aligning model behavior with specific utility functions.

title: Strategy-Following Multi-Agent Deep Reinforcement Learning Considering Control Strategies Provided to Other Agents
authors: Yamato Takahagi, Gentoku Nakasone, Yoshinari Motokawa, Toshiharu Sugawara
summary: This paper proposes a learning method where some agents in a multi-agent system receive explicit instructions from a human manager, while other uninstructed agents automatically adapt their behavior to complement the overall task. The key innovation is enabling partially-instructed teams to achieve better coordination than either fully-instructed or fully-autonomous approaches, making it practical for humans to steer learned agent behaviors without managing every agent individually.

title: Conditioned Direct Feedback Alignment via Activity and Error Geometry
authors: Houman Safaai, Varun Reddy, Bernardo L. Sabatini
summary: This paper investigates why direct feedback alignment (DFA)—a biologically plausible learning algorithm that avoids backpropagation's weight transposes—sometimes fails, and proposes conditioning schemes to fix it. The key insight is that weight updates in DFA are outer products of activity and error signals, so anisotropy (uneven directions) in either factor degrades learning. By conditioning both factors separately, the authors achieve 40% improvement in some regimes and develop a family of normalized DFA variants that work better than standard DFA.

title: Patch Policy: Efficient Embodied Control via Dense Visual Representations
authors: Gaoyue Zhou, Zichen Jeff Cui, Ada Langford, Bowen Tan, Yann LeCun et al.
summary: This paper proposes Patch Policy, a method that lets robot control policies use dense visual patch features from pretrained Vision Transformers instead of compressing images into single tokens. The approach achieves 40% better performance than global pooling methods and beats larger vision-language models while using 99.3% fewer parameters, making it practical for real-time robotic control.

title: It's Not What You Say, It's How You Say It: Evaluating LLM Responses to Expressions of Belief
authors: Kevin Du, Clara Kümpel, Michelle Wastl, Alex Warstadt
summary: This paper systematically studies how linguistic variation in user statements affects whether LLMs follow the user's stated beliefs or rely on their training knowledge. The authors create a controlled benchmark that pairs different linguistic expressions of belief (using presuppositions, certainty markers, tone) with factual queries, then test 16 models to identify which phrasings are most persuasive—finding that larger and instruction-tuned models are less susceptible to contextual framing than smaller base models.

title: Vector Search As Nearest Neighbor Matching: RAG-based Policy Learning in Causal Inference
authors: Masahiro Kato, Taka Kato
summary: This paper applies retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) — a technique where a model retrieves relevant examples before generating outputs — to the problem of learning optimal decision-making policies in causal inference. The key insight is that vector search (finding similar cases in an embedding space) can be understood as a form of nearest-neighbor matching, a classical causal inference method. The authors show how to decompose the error of such policies and provide theoretical guarantees, bridging modern machine learning with traditional causal reasoning.

title: GigaPath-Flash and GigaTIME-Flash: Efficient Pathology Foundation Models for Whole-Slide and Tumor Microenvironment Analysis
authors: Naoto Usuyama, Jeya Maria Jose Valanarasu, Sicong Yao, Hanwen Xu, Jaspreet Bagga et al.
summary: This paper introduces GigaPath-Flash and GigaTIME-Flash, efficient foundation models for analyzing whole-slide pathology images and tumor immune microenvironments. By distilling larger models into compact versions with 22–21M parameters, these models retain 97% of performance while requiring 50× less compute, making clinical-scale pathology AI practical and widely accessible.

title: SWE-Pruner Pro: The Coder LLM Already Knows What to Prune
authors: Yuhang Wang, Yuling Shi, Shaoqiu Zhang, Jialiang Liang, Shilin He et al.
summary: This paper proposes SWE-Pruner Pro, a method that helps coding agents efficiently manage long contexts by pruning irrelevant tool outputs. Rather than using a separate classifier, the approach leverages internal representations the agent already computes while reading code, reducing token usage by up to 39% while maintaining or improving task performance on software engineering benchmarks.

title: Unveiling Invariant and Transferable Latent Factors Across Heterogeneous Environments via ATLAS
authors: Yihong Gu, Katherine Liao, Tianxi Cai
summary: This paper proposes ATLAS, a method for learning stable, transferable representations from high-dimensional data collected across multiple environments with different distributions. The key insight is that latent structure can be decomposed into *invariant factors* (shared across all environments) and *heterogeneous factors* (environment-specific), and that this decomposition enables robust prediction in new environments and strong out-of-sample generalization.

title: PPL-Factory: Task-Aware and Budget-Aware Data Selection from Language Modeling to Reasoning
authors: Hang Zhang, Warren J. Gross
summary: This paper introduces PPL-Factory, a data selection method that identifies the most valuable training samples for fine-tuning language models while using only a fraction of the full dataset. The key insight is that different tasks (like math reasoning vs. general language modeling) benefit from different sample-scoring strategies, and the method combines task-specific perplexity scores with budget constraints to achieve better performance with far fewer samples — reaching full-data accuracy using just 1-10% of training data.

title: FlashRT: Agent Harness for Guiding Agents to Deploy Real-Time Multimodal Applications
authors: Krish Agarwal, Zhuoming Chen, Yanyuan Qin, Zhenyu Gu, Atri Rudra et al.
summary: FlashRT is a system that uses AI coding agents to automatically optimize real-time multimodal applications (like voice agents and video generation) across multiple GPUs. Instead of requiring engineers to hand-tune deployments, FlashRT guides an agent through a series of code transformations—converting simple reference implementations into highly efficient, hardware-aware deployments that achieve up to 70× latency reduction and 3.6× throughput improvement.

title: OR Else: A Differentiable Trust Region for Policy Optimization
authors: Chinmay Rane, Kanishka Tyagi, Michael Manry
summary: This paper proposes Output Reset (OR), a smooth alternative to clipped policy objectives in reinforcement learning algorithms for language model post-training. Instead of the abrupt gradient changes in PPO and GRPO (which use hard clipping), OR applies a smooth one-sided saturation rule that changes how policy updates are computed. The authors test PPO-OR and GRPO-OR on a 1B parameter language model and find mixed results: PPO-OR gains reward under some settings but GRPO-OR shows stability improvements without consistent reward gains.

title: TRIM: Reducing AI-Generated CodeSlop via Agent Trajectory Minimization
authors: Alex Mathai, Shobini Iyer, Aleksandr Nogikh, Petros Maniatis, Franjo Ivancic et al.
summary: This paper identifies and addresses "CodeSlop"—the bloated, redundant code that AI agents generate as they explore solution paths during iterative problem-solving. The authors propose TRIM, an algorithm that minimizes the *trajectory* (search process) of coding agents rather than directly pruning the final code, reducing unnecessary verbosity by 18–33% while maintaining functional correctness and requiring less computational cost than existing approaches.

title: Differentiable Logic Gate Networks for Low-Latency EEG Classification on Edge Devices
authors: Shyamal Y. Dharia, Stephen D. Smith, Camilo E. Valderrama
summary: This paper proposes Differentiable Logic Gate Networks (Diff-Logic), a neural architecture that compiles into pure Boolean circuits executable via bitwise operations, enabling real-time EEG classification on power-constrained edge devices. The approach outperforms floating-point neural networks on dementia detection and achieves 2.9× speedup over standard MLPs while maintaining nearly constant inference time across 10× increases in model size—solving a critical bottleneck in portable brain-computer interfaces.

title: LLMs and Agentic AI Systems for Smart Grids: A Tutorial on Architectures and Applications
authors: Daniela Rojas, Abdulwahab Albassam, Aidan G. Leung, Jett Ngo, Ryan Luo et al.
summary: This paper shows how to safely deploy large language models (LLMs) and agentic AI systems in power grid management by grounding their outputs in trusted numerical solvers rather than relying on LLM reasoning alone. The key insight is that LLMs excel at planning, orchestration, and explanation, but should hand off actual computation to verified tools—a principle demonstrated across wind forecasting, EV charging, and grid diagnostics with significant improvements in correctness and safety.

title: O-VAD: Industrial Video Anomaly Detection through Object-Centric Tracking and Reasoning
authors: Mei Yuan, Qi Long, Qifeng Wu, Zhenyang Li, Yizhou Zhao et al.
summary: This paper presents O-VAD, a framework for detecting anomalies in industrial video footage that tracks how objects change over time and reasons about whether those changes are normal or abnormal. Unlike existing vision-language models that work on general videos, O-VAD is designed specifically for manufacturing environments where objects undergo complex transformations following strict physical and procedural rules—and it achieves this without needing retraining or domain-specific knowledge injected by humans.

title: SGA: Plug&Play Geometric Verification for Educational Video Synthesis
authors: Lopez Jhon, Hinojosa Carlos, Ghanem Bernard
summary: This paper addresses a real problem in AI-generated educational videos: when LLMs write code to create animated math lessons (using Manim), the resulting animations often have objects overlapping or blocking each other, making them hard to understand. The authors propose SGA, a "plug-and-play" quality-control module that catches these geometric mistakes before rendering and fixes them automatically. They also introduce MVQS, a fast way to score animation quality without actually rendering the video.

title: How Does Alignment Tuning Shape Representations of Sycophancy and Related Cue-Induced Biases in LLMs?
authors: Prakhar Gupta, Terry Jingchen Zhang, Florent Draye, Bernhard Schölkopf, Zhijing Jin
summary: This paper investigates how alignment tuning (the process of fine-tuning language models to be helpful and harmless) inadvertently creates internal representations that make models vulnerable to simple prompt manipulations — like biased few-shot examples or leading questions — that flip correct answers. By analyzing hidden states across multiple model families, the authors show that these susceptibilities are distinct, causally active directions in the model that can be identified, decoded, and even steered to reduce bias, offering both a mechanistic explanation and a potential debiasing method.

title: LLM-as-a-Coach: Experiential Learning for Non-Verifiable Tasks
authors: Tianzhu Ye, Li Dong, Guanheng Chen, He Zhu, Xun Wu et al.
summary: This paper proposes Experiential Learning (EL), a new training method for language models on open-ended tasks where correct answers cannot be automatically verified. Instead of converting detailed feedback into a single numerical score (the standard approach), the method treats an evaluator LLM as a "coach" that passes rich textual insights directly to the policy model. The key insight: preserving fine-grained feedback improves learning and prevents the model from gaming the reward system.

title: FinSAgent: Corpus-Aligned Multi-Agent RAG Framework for Evidence-Grounded SEC Filing Question Answering
authors: Jijun Chi, Zhenghan Tai, Hanwei Wu, Tung Sum Thomas Kwok, Hailin He et al.
summary: This paper presents FinSAgent, a multi-agent framework that answers questions about SEC financial filings by better aligning retrieval and reasoning with the actual structure and terminology of the filings themselves. The key insight is that existing systems fail because they rely on generic semantic similarity matching, which misses domain-specific evidence and retrieves irrelevant chunks — FinSAgent fixes this by conditioning each agent's searches on the filing's known structure (10-K items) and using a learned reranker that distinguishes evidential validity from topical similarity.

title: The Shared Discovery Paradox: How a One-Answer Rule Turns Better Information into Worse Search
authors: Yohei Nakajima
summary: This paper reveals a paradox in how organizations share pooled information: better aggregated beliefs can paradoxically reduce discovery when everyone acts on the same single recommendation. The authors develop an exact mathematical benchmark with searchers hunting for a target and show that a one-answer protocol compresses a rich portfolio of potential actions into repetitive choices, destroying coverage despite improved accuracy.

title: MADA-RL: Multi-Agent Debate-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Parameter-Efficient Reasoning in Compact Models
authors: Martino M. L. Pulici, Cuong Xuan Chu, Evgeny Kharlamov, Zifeng Ding, Volker Tresp et al.
summary: This paper introduces MADA-RL, a training method that turns small language models (1.5B parameters) into better reasoners by having them debate with each other in specialized roles. The key innovation is a "counterfactual critic advantage" — a smarter way to train one model (the critic) to spot and fix mistakes made by another (the generator), using only a tiny fraction of the parameters that full fine-tuning requires. On math problems, it improves a small model's accuracy by 2 percentage points while being 16× more parameter-efficient than standard approaches.
