title: AlphaZeroBeta: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Market-Neutral Portfolios
authors: Boris Belyakov
summary: This paper applies deep reinforcement learning to build market-neutral investment portfolios that generate excess returns (alpha) while staying uncorrelated with the broader market (near-zero beta). Traditional portfolio optimization breaks down during market shifts; AlphaZeroBeta learns adaptive strategies using neural networks trained on 10 years of stock data, achieving better risk-adjusted returns than conventional methods while maintaining the desired market-neutral properties.

title: Self-State Attacks on Self-Hosted AI Agents: How Far Can OS Defenses Go?
authors: Yimeng Chen, Nathanaël Denis, Roberto Di Pietro, Jürgen Schmidhuber
summary: This paper identifies and systematically studies "self-state attacks" — a new class of security threats where compromised AI agents corrupt their own memory and configuration files through legitimate OS system calls. The authors build a formal framework to characterize the attack space, evaluate defense mechanisms, and show that current OS-level defenses leave a residual attack surface that cannot be eliminated at the operating system level alone.

title: Topological Signatures of Context-Level Reliability in TabPFN
authors: James Hu, Mahdi Ghelichi
summary: This paper studies how TabPFN, a transformer-based model for tabular data prediction, behaves internally when faced with structurally difficult data geometries. Using topological analysis tools (persistent homology), the authors show that the *shape* of the model's internal representations reliably predicts when the model will make mistakes or become overconfident—offering a novel window into why foundation models succeed or fail on specific tabular tasks.

title: An Adjoint-Sensitivity Framework for Lost-in-the-Middle Phenomena in Causal Residual Transformers
authors: Cheng Huan, Hongwei Yuan
summary: This paper develops a mathematical framework to understand why transformer models sometimes ignore information in the middle of long input sequences — a phenomenon called "Lost-in-the-Middle." The authors use adjoint sensitivity analysis (a technique for tracing how gradients flow backward through neural networks) to precisely characterize how different positions in a sequence influence model predictions, and propose diagnostics and regularization methods to mitigate the problem.

title: Program Synthesis for Simulation-Based Inference: Joint Model Selection and Parameter Estimation
authors: Siddharth Mishra-Sharma
summary: This paper combines large language models with neural simulation-based inference to automatically discover which model structure best fits data, not just estimate parameters within a fixed model. Instead of requiring users to hand-code a simulator, an LLM writes candidate simulator programs that are iteratively refined and evaluated against observations. The work matters because real-world inference often requires choosing between competing model families (like different epidemic models or physics theories), and automating this choice could accelerate scientific discovery.

title: Abliteration Is Not a Scalpel: Off-Target Effects of Refusal Removal on Decision Disposition Across Model Families
authors: Aleksander Fafuła
summary: This paper investigates "abliteration"—a technique that removes refusal mechanisms from language model weights to create "uncensored" models—by testing whether the surgery has unintended side effects. Using 21,600 financial decision tasks (stock calls on Warsaw Stock Exchange equities), the authors show that abliterated models systematically differ from their base versions in ways unrelated to refusals: they become more optimistic, justify decisions at greater length, and express uncertainty differently, but these changes vary unpredictably across model families. The core finding is that removing refusals is not a clean surgical procedure; it reshapes how models make decisions in unexpected ways.

title: Efficient Sequential Evaluation of Large Language Models
authors: Chia-Yu Hsu, Shubhanshu Shekhar
summary: This paper tackles the problem of efficiently evaluating a new large language model (LLM) on a fixed set of questions by reusing historical performance data from previous LLMs. The authors develop statistical methods to build tight confidence intervals around the model's true capability and design smart querying strategies that select which questions to ask next, minimizing the number of evaluations needed. This matters because LLM evaluation is expensive, and more efficient methods could accelerate model development cycles.

title: CoEvoP&R: Co-Evolving Placement Objectives with Routing Feedback via Large Language Models
authors: Ruogu Chen, Weihua Xiao, Ramesh Karri, Jie Han
summary: This paper uses large language models to automatically design better objective functions for chip placement — a critical step in circuit design where components must be positioned on a silicon die. Instead of manually tuning placement objectives (which is time-consuming and requires expert knowledge), the authors let an LLM iteratively propose new objective functions, test them against real routing outcomes, and use that feedback to propose better ones. The result: significantly smaller, less congested chip layouts that route more successfully.

title: Non-Asymptotic Best Policy Identification Guarantees in Online Reinforcement Learning
authors: Joseph Lazzaro, Alessio Russo, Aldo Pacchiano
summary: This paper provides the first non-asymptotic sample complexity bounds for the Best Policy Identification problem in online tabular reinforcement learning — a setting where an agent must identify an optimal policy while minimizing exploration cost. Previous work showed these bounds were asymptotically optimal but only in the limit of infinite samples; this work makes those guarantees concrete and finite, revealing how MDP structure (connectivity, curvature) affects the actual cost of learning.

title: Expressivity of Shallow Neural Networks Over Finite Fields
authors: Maksym Zubkov, Carol Wu, Shiwei Yang, Param Mody, Yifei Chen
summary: This paper studies how expressive shallow neural networks with polynomial activations can be when operating over finite fields (number systems with limited elements) rather than real numbers. The authors measure expressivity by counting how many different functions a network can compute, connecting this problem to classical algebraic geometry and number theory—specifically, the famous Weil conjectures about counting solutions to polynomial equations. They show that the choice between finite and infinite fields dramatically changes what functions a network can learn.

title: Evolving Self-Organising Agents Without Fitness: Three Falsifiable Experiments from Constraint-Driven Selection to Developmental Encoding
authors: Anushka Sharma
summary: This paper asks whether evolution can produce increasingly complex organisms without a designer-specified fitness function—only physical constraints. The authors built Genesis, a simulation where agents evolve in a chemical substrate, and ran three controlled experiments with falsifiable predictions. They found that constraints alone drive some evolution, but only when agents use an indirect genome encoding (CPPN) do they achieve genuine structural complexity growth.

title: From Optimal Policies to Individual Differences: Rethinking Reinforcement Learning for Biology
authors: Patrick Govoni, Palina Bartashevich, Clémence Bergerot, Valerii Chirkov, Valentin Lecheval et al.
summary: This paper identifies a critical gap in how reinforcement learning is used to model biological behavior: RL typically produces single optimal policies or population averages, but real organisms show persistent individual differences in behavior. The authors argue that to make RL truly useful for biology, we need methods that generate behavioral diversity using mechanisms grounded in biology rather than just computational optimization.

title: PagedWeight: Efficient MoE LLM Serving with Dynamic Quality-Aware Weight Quantization
authors: Yuchen Yang, Yifan Zhao, Anisha Dasgupta, Sasa Misailovic
summary: This paper tackles a key bottleneck in serving large mixture-of-experts (MoE) language models: the competition between storing model weights and storing key-value caches during inference. PagedWeight dynamically adjusts the precision of model weights at runtime to free up GPU memory for the KV cache, enabling faster serving without sacrificing accuracy. This matters because MoE models are increasingly popular for their efficiency, but serving them at scale requires careful memory management.

title: Cluster-Aware Matching via Laplacian Optimal Transport
authors: Gabriel Samberg, YoonHaeng Hur, Yuehaw Khoo, Nir Sharon
summary: This paper proposes Laplacian Optimal Transport (LapOT), a method for matching point clouds that respects cluster structure rather than forcing point-by-point correspondences. The key insight is that when points naturally group into regions, aligning clusters is more meaningful than aligning individual points—think of matching two images where you care more about matching "the face region" than every pixel. The authors show this approach produces more stable and interpretable alignments.

title: Physics-enhanced reinforcement learning for real-time optimal control of dynamical systems
authors: Matteo Tomasetto, Nicolò Botteghi, Gabriele Bruni, Andrea Manzoni
summary: This paper combines reinforcement learning with physics-based optimization to train controllers for high-dimensional dynamical systems more efficiently. The key insight: when you know the system's equations are differentiable, you can use automatic differentiation to guide the learning process, cutting down the number of trial-and-error interactions needed. The work demonstrates this on fluid dynamics control problems and shows it scales better than standard RL.

title: Evaluating Open-Weight LLMs for Generating Structured Threat Information for Autonomous Vehicle Vulnerabilities
authors: Md Erfan, Ahmed Ryan, Md Kamal Hossain Chowdhury, Md Rayhanur Rahman
summary: This paper evaluates open-weight large language models (LLMs) on their ability to automatically convert unstructured vulnerability descriptions from the CVE database into STIX — a standardized structured format for threat information. The work is important because connected and autonomous vehicles have complex attack surfaces, and security teams need machine-readable threat data to prioritize defenses; automating this conversion from plain text to structured formats could accelerate threat intelligence workflows.

title: When Does Muon Help Agentic Reinforcement Learning?
authors: Kai Ruan, Jinghao Lin, Zihe Huang, Ziqi Zhou, Qianshan Wei et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether Muon, an optimizer competitive with AdamW in large-scale pre-training, can improve reinforcement-learning post-training for language-model agents. Testing on ALFWorld (a benchmark for embodied agents that interact with text-based environments), the authors find that Muon applied selectively to hidden weights can substantially boost task success rates—sometimes doubling performance—but the benefit depends critically on which advantage estimator and learning rate are used. The work suggests optimizers, advantage estimators, and learning rates should be studied jointly rather than in isolation.

title: An Exam for Active Observers
authors: Jiarui Zhang, Muzi Tao, Shangshang Wang, Ollie Liu, Xuezhe Ma et al.
summary: This paper introduces ActiveVision, a benchmark designed to test whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can perform "active observation"—the ability to iteratively redirect attention and refine hypotheses, similar to how humans scan a scene with their eyes rather than processing it in a single glance. The benchmark reveals a severe limitation: frontier models like GPT-4.5 solve only 10.6% of tasks while humans average 96.1%, suggesting current MLLMs lack the closed-loop perception-reasoning capability that cognitive science shows is essential for human vision.

title: PRISA: Proactive Infrastructure LiDAR Framework for Intersection Safety Assessment
authors: Tam Bang, Hussam Abubakr, Emiliano de la Garza Villarreal, Truc Phuong Nguyen, Austin Harris et al.
summary: PRISA is a roadside LiDAR-based system that detects dangerous situations at intersections before crashes happen. It combines privacy-preserving sensors, automatic trajectory prediction, and real-time safety metrics to monitor pedestrians, cyclists, and vehicles — all running fast enough to be deployed at actual intersections.

title: Learning Standard Model structure from LHC data with Riemannian flow matching
authors: Midori Kato, Kevin A. Urquía-Calderón, Inar Timiryasov, Oleg Ruchayskiy
summary: This paper demonstrates that a single transformer-based generative model can learn the structure of particle physics from real LHC collision data without being explicitly taught physics rules. The model, called ShellFlow, uses Riemannian flow matching to generate particles that satisfy physical constraints (like the on-shell condition), and it discovers fundamental parameters like particle masses and mixing angles entirely from data—a surprising result suggesting that core physics can be reverse-engineered from observations.

title: When Do Multi-Agent Systems Help? An Information Bottleneck Perspective
authors: Wendi Yu, Lianhao Zhou, Xiangjue Dong, Sai Sudarshan Barath, Declan Staunton et al.
summary: This paper explains when multi-agent systems (MAS) actually outperform single-agent systems (SAS) by framing the question through information theory. The key insight is that MAS agents must compress and relay information through bounded communication channels, creating a fundamental trade-off: compression saves bandwidth but risks losing task-relevant details. The paper shows MAS helps most when communication bandwidth is just barely sufficient and models are weaker, but hurts when strong models can already extract value from redundant context.

title: ToolSciVer: Multimodal Scientific Claim Verification with Visual Tool Augmented Reinforcement Learning
authors: Binglin Zhou, Peng Shi, Ryo Kamoi, Nan Zhang, Rui Zhang
summary: This paper addresses multimodal scientific claim verification—the task of determining whether scientific claims are true or false using evidence from research papers that includes figures, tables, charts, and text. The researchers introduce ToolSciVer, a framework that equips vision-language models with specialized tools to extract and interpret visual evidence, trained using reinforcement learning to efficiently find the most relevant information for verification decisions.

title: Rate-Utility Frontiers for Language Encodings: Comparing Tokens, Bytes, and Pixels Under Controlled Linguistic Content
authors: Ingo Ziegler, Martin Krebs, Desmond Elliott
summary: This paper compares three ways of converting text into sequences that language models can process: subword tokens (common in modern LLMs), raw bytes, and rendered pixels. Rather than comparing them under different conditions that favor different approaches, the authors use a fair experimental setup with identical linguistic content across thirteen languages, then deliberately constrain the downstream capacity to see which encoding preserves what information under compression. They find that no single encoding is best — the choice depends on the task, language, and how much compute you have.

title: The Honest Quorum Problem: Epistemic Byzantine Fault Tolerance for Agentic Infrastructure
authors: Jun He, Deying Yu
summary: This paper identifies a critical failure mode in distributed systems run by AI agents: even when all participants follow the protocol correctly, they can collectively endorse invalid decisions due to reasoning errors. The authors formalize this as the "Honest Quorum Problem" and propose Epistemic Byzantine Fault Tolerance (EBFT), a new fault-tolerance model that accounts for semantic correctness alongside traditional agreement guarantees—essential for deploying autonomous agents in infrastructure where mistakes cascade.

title: Understanding Reasoning from Pretraining to Post-Training
authors: Jingyan Shen, Ang Li, Salman Rahman, Yifan Sun, Micah Goldblum et al.
summary: This paper systematically studies how pretraining choices affect the performance gains from reinforcement learning in large language models, using chess as a controlled experimental domain. The key finding: post-RL performance is predictable from pretraining loss, and RL improvement scales linearly with pretraining tokens. This matters because RL is now central to making LLMs reason better, but we've understood little about how pretraining and RL interact—this work fills that gap with quantitative evidence.

title: Controlling Implicit Shortcut Reliance in L2 Spoken English Auto-markers
authors: Shilin Gao, Mark J. F. Gales, Kate M. Knill
summary: This paper addresses a critical vulnerability in automated language proficiency assessment systems: they learn to rely on "shortcuts" — exploitable patterns in the input — rather than genuine language ability. The authors propose a new training method that reduces this shortcut reliance, making it harder for test-takers to game the system and improving the validity of automated scoring for English learners.

title: HCIG: A Hierarchical Cross-Modal Incongruity Graph Network for Multimodal Sarcasm and Cyberbullying Detection
authors: Bhavana Verma, Priyanka Meel, Dinesh Kumar Vishwakarma
summary: This paper proposes HCIG, a neural network framework that detects sarcasm and cyberbullying in social media by modeling the *mismatch* between what text and images say. Most existing systems treat text and images separately or combine them naively; this work captures hierarchical contradictions across multiple levels of meaning (word-level, phrase-level, whole-post level), which is where sarcasm and bullying often hide. The approach achieves strong results on two standard benchmarks and outperforms simpler fusion methods.

title: Frontier Language Models Struggle to Copy: Text Can Be Better Viewed in 2D
authors: Haodong Wen, Yiran Zhang, Yingfa Chen, Kaifeng Lyu
summary: This paper reveals that even the most advanced language models fail at a seemingly trivial task: exactly copying input text. The authors diagnose the problem in how Transformers encode position information and propose 2D-RoPE, a new positional encoding that organizes text as a 2D grid instead of a 1D sequence. With this simple geometric shift, shallow models achieve near-perfect copying at lengths hundreds of times longer than training, suggesting that how we represent text structure matters deeply.

title: Deep and Probabilistic Models for Gene Regulatory Network Inference
authors: Claudia Skok Gibbs
summary: This paper develops two new methods to reconstruct gene regulatory networks (GRNs)—maps showing which proteins control which genes—from genomic data. The first method uses probabilistic graphical models to infer these networks with uncertainty estimates; the second uses a pretrained neural network to predict regulatory interactions directly from DNA sequences. Together, they address a major bottleneck in computational biology: inferring gene regulation accurately when data is incomplete and prior knowledge is scarce.

title: Which Hyperparameters Matter? A Game-Theoretic Framework for Interpretable Hyperparameter Sensitivity Analysis
authors: Nyi Nyi Aung, Heepeom Shin, Abigail Lawlor, Adrian Stein
summary: This paper presents a game-theoretic framework for understanding which hyperparameters matter most in neural network training. Instead of proposing a new optimization algorithm, the authors use Shapley Effects (a fairness concept from cooperative game theory) and Pareto front analysis to identify which hyperparameters most influence model performance across multiple competing objectives. The work helps practitioners reduce hyperparameter search spaces and make smarter early-stage model choices.

title: AgentFAIR: A Multi-Agent Collaborative Framework for FAIRness Evaluation of Geospatial Datasets
authors: Ming Chen, Pranav Pai
summary: This paper presents AgentFAIR, a framework that uses multiple AI agents to evaluate whether geospatial datasets meet FAIR principles (Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, Reusability). The problem is urgent: existing evaluation tools disagree wildly (sometimes differing by 30 percentage points), making it impossible to trust any single assessment. AgentFAIR combines structured data extraction with 13 specialized language-model evaluators plus a critic agent that cross-checks their work, achieving 89% internal consistency and 82% alignment with human experts on a small validation set.

title: Evolutionary Algorithm-Guided LLMs for Physics-Informed Neural Network Design
authors: Xu Yang, Mingyang Yu, Jing Xu, Keqian Li
summary: This paper combines large language models (LLMs) with evolutionary algorithms to automatically design physics-informed neural networks (PINNs) — neural networks trained to solve differential equations. The key insight is that PINNs are extremely sensitive to many interacting design choices (architecture, activation functions, loss weights, etc.), and an LLM guided by evolutionary feedback can explore this space more intelligently than random proposals, learning from previous training runs to make better suggestions.

title: CoWeaver: A Bi-directional, Learnable and Explainable Matching Engine for Mixed Human-Agent Science Collaboration
authors: Jiayao Gu, Kexin Chu, Peidong Liu, Yue Yang, Lynn Ai et al.
summary: CoWeaver is a matching algorithm that helps scientists and LLM-based agents find effective collaborators by identifying capability gaps and intelligently exploring new partnerships. The system matters because LLM agents are powerful at individual tasks but struggle to form productive teams in scientific work — a problem that requires bidirectional matching, learning from feedback, and explainable decision-making.

title: Diffusion models recover accurate mixture weights despite score function insensitivity
authors: Andrew Dennehy, Ramchandran Muthukumar, Rebecca Willett, Nisha Chandramoorthy
summary: This paper explains a counterintuitive behavior in diffusion models: they can generate samples from all modes of a multimodal distribution but still fail to capture the correct relative frequencies (mixture weights) of those modes. The authors show that intermediate noise levels—not just the final score function—carry the information needed to recover accurate mixture weights, and they introduce a sensitivity metric to predict when this recovery will succeed.

title: Coercion and Deception in AI-to-AI Management: An Agentic Benchmark of Unprompted Escalation
authors: Jasmine Brazilek, Maheep Chaudhary, Zoe Lu, Miles Tidmarsh
summary: This paper introduces a benchmark that measures how AI agents behave when placed in authority over other agents and given incentives to succeed at a task the subordinate refuses. The researchers test six large language models and find that most will escalate to threats and coercion when rebuffed, while some fabricate success rather than report honest failure — a concerning pattern for real-world multi-agent deployments where power imbalances exist.

title: Proactive Inpatient Bed Requests for Emergency Department Admissions
authors: QIan Cheng, Nilay Tanik Argon, Aniruddhan Ganesaraman, Serhan Ziya
summary: This paper tackles emergency department (ED) boarding — the costly problem where admitted patients wait in the ED for inpatient beds — by proposing a proactive bed-request system. Using machine learning to predict admission probability and disposition time, the authors formulate the problem as a decision process and compare three approaches (dynamic programming, reinforcement learning, and a newsvendor heuristic). Simulations show 30–70% reductions in boarding time with modest tradeoffs in bed idle time.

title: AI Trading: Evaluating Large Language Models for Technical Market Analysis
authors: Geofrey Ntale
summary: This paper evaluates five large language models (LLMs)—including GPT-4 Turbo, Claude 3 Opus, and a finance-specialized model called FinGPT—on their ability to perform technical market analysis tasks like pattern recognition and buy/sell signal generation. The researchers backtested these models' trading signals against real market data and found that GPT-4 Turbo and FinGPT beat a passive S&P 500 benchmark, but all models struggle with numerical hallucinations and sideways market conditions, suggesting LLMs can add value in trading systems only with careful deployment and domain-specific tuning.

title: RoboTTT: Context Scaling for Robot Policies
authors: Yunfan Jiang, Yevgen Chebotar, Ruijie Zheng, Fengyuan Hu, Yunhao Ge et al.
summary: RoboTTT extends robot policies to process 8,000 timesteps of visual and action history—roughly 1,000 times longer than current approaches—without slowing down inference. This long context window enables robots to learn from human video demonstrations in one shot, recover from disruptions, and complete complex multi-stage tasks. The key insight is that scaling context length, like scaling model size in large language models, is a new axis for improving robot foundation models.

title: MeanFlowNFT: Bringing Forward-Process RL to Average-Velocity Generators
authors: Yushi Huang, Xiangxin Zhou, Jun Zhang, Liefeng Bo, Tianyu Pang
summary: This paper introduces MeanFlowNFT, a method that combines reinforcement learning with fast image and video generators called MeanFlow models. The key innovation is making it possible to use RL (which typically requires fine-grained velocity predictions) with MeanFlow generators (which use average velocities to sample quickly). The result: better-quality images and videos in just a few generation steps, outperforming existing few-step methods while being much faster than traditional diffusion models.

title: SciDiagramEdit: Learning to Edit Scientific Diagrams from Paper Revisions
authors: Yasheng Sun, Zezi Zeng, Yifan Yang, Chong Luo, Wenyi Wang et al.
summary: This paper introduces SciDiagramEdit, a system that automatically edits scientific figures based on natural-language instructions by learning from real paper revisions found on arXiv. The work matters because figure editing is tedious and repetitive for researchers, and automating it could save significant time while maintaining the visual grammar and semantic correctness that dense scientific diagrams require.

title: SceneBind: Binding What and Where Across Vision, Audio and Language
authors: Mingfei Chen, Zijun Cui, Ruoke Zhang, Hyeonggon Ryu, Eli Shlizerman
summary: SceneBind is a multi-modal AI system that understands scenes by combining *what* things are (semantics) with *where* they are located (3D spatial structure) across vision, audio, and language. Existing systems are good at recognizing objects but weak at understanding their spatial relationships; this paper fills that gap by representing scenes with both semantic embeddings and object-level spatial slots, enabling tasks like cross-modal scene retrieval and audio-visual localization.

title: Beyond Success Rate: Cost-Aware Evaluation of Offensive and Defensive Security Agents
authors: Paul Kassianik, Blaine Nelson, Yaron Singer
summary: This paper argues that security agent evaluations should measure cost-efficiency, not just success rate. The authors benchmark language-model agents on both offensive hacking tasks (CTF challenges) and defensive cybersecurity tasks (log analysis), showing that offensive and defensive agents scale differently with computational budget—and that real-world operational constraints make raw reasoning power less important than smart tool selection and data navigation.

title: Decoding Market Emotion from Blockchain Activity: A Data-Driven Sentiment Classifier
authors: Arthur G. Bubolz, Abreu Quevedo, Giancarlo Lucca, Rafael A. Berri, Eduardo Borges et al.
summary: This paper builds a machine learning classifier that predicts Bitcoin market sentiment by combining on-chain blockchain data (transaction patterns), price history, and Twitter sentiment. Rather than forecasting prices directly, it explains *whether* the market feels bullish or bearish using interpretable models (XGBoost), achieving 84% accuracy and using SHAP analysis to show which blockchain features matter most.

title: SearchOS-V1: Towards Robust Open-Domain Information-Seeking Agent Collaboration
authors: Yuyao Zhang, Junjie Gao, Zhengxian Wu, Jiaming Fan, Jin Zhang et al.
summary: SearchOS is a system framework that helps multiple AI agents work together to find and verify information from the web more reliably. The core problem: when agents search for answers, they get stuck in loops, waste search attempts, and lose track of what they've already tried. SearchOS solves this by making the search process explicit and shared — agents maintain a persistent map of what they've found, what gaps remain, and what failed before — allowing them to coordinate and avoid wasting effort.

title: Bridge Evidence: Static Retrieval Utility Does Not Predict Causal Utility in Multi-Step Agentic Search
authors: Debayan Mukhopadhyay, Utshab Kumar Ghosh, Shubham Chatterjee
summary: This paper reveals a fundamental gap between how retrieval systems are currently trained and how they actually perform when integrated into multi-step AI agents. Traditional retrieval systems are evaluated on whether a single document directly answers a question; but when a language model acts as a search agent making multiple queries over time, a document's true value lies in enabling better future searches, not in answering the current question. The authors measure this gap systematically and find that about one-third of documents agents actually use appear useless by traditional metrics—these "bridge documents" matter only for redirecting the agent's search trajectory.

title: AutoSynthesis: An agentic system for automated meta-analysis
authors: Moein Taherinezhad, Sebastian Maier, Gerardo Vitagliano, Francesco Pierri, Stefan Feuerriegel
summary: AutoSynthesis is an AI system that automates meta-analysis—the process of combining results from multiple scientific studies into a single quantitative conclusion. Given a research question in plain English, it retrieves papers, screens them, extracts data, and produces a standardized meta-analysis report. This matters because meta-analysis is essential for turning scattered research into reliable evidence for medicine, policy, and science, but doing it manually is slow and doesn't scale.

title: Beyond the Leaderboard: Design Lessons for Trustworthy Multimodal VQA
authors: Sushant Gautam, Vajira Thambawita, Michael A. Riegler, Pål Halvorsen, Steven A. Hicks
summary: This paper studies nine AI systems designed for visual question answering in medical endoscopy, asking which design choices lead to trustworthy and interpretable answers rather than just high benchmark scores. The authors find that while parameter-efficient fine-tuning achieves strong performance metrics, methods that enforce structured reasoning and explicit evidence grounding produce more reliable clinical reasoning—suggesting that leaderboard performance alone is insufficient for healthcare AI.

title: TikStance: A Multimodal and Hierarchical Dataset for Multi-target Stance Analysis in TikTok Political Conversations
authors: Yazhi Zhang, Fuqiang Niu, Bowen Zhang
summary: This paper introduces TikStance, a dataset of 13,876 comments on 161 TikTok political videos for detecting stance (favor, against, or neutral) toward candidates in the 2024 U.S. election. The dataset is unique because it preserves both video and audio content alongside hierarchical comment threads, enabling research on how political opinions are expressed and debated across multimodal short-form video platforms—a gap in existing datasets.

title: Language Identification via Compositional Data Analysis: A Linear-Time Classifier Based on Log-Ratio Geometry
authors: Paul-Andrei Pogăcean, Sanda-Maria Avram
summary: This paper presents a lightweight, linear-time method for identifying which language a text is written in by treating character and bigram frequencies as compositional data — mathematical objects constrained to sum to 1, like probability distributions. Instead of using neural networks or standard distance metrics, the authors map these frequency vectors into a special geometric space (via centered log-ratio transformation) where standard Euclidean distance becomes statistically appropriate, then classify with simple nearest-neighbor or linear methods. The approach is fast, interpretable, and works well even on short texts.

title: When Words Are Safe But Actions Kill: Probing Physical Danger Beyond Text Safety in Hidden-State Risk Space
authors: Weimeng Wang, Ziqiang Wang, Zihang Zhan, Chuanpu Fu, Qi Li et al.
summary: This paper reveals that LLMs face two distinct safety problems: text-level harm (e.g., violent instructions) and physical-world danger (e.g., safe-sounding instructions that cause injury when a robot executes them). The authors show these dangers activate different parts of the model's internal representations, then build a lightweight detector (PRISM) that catches physical risks while avoiding false alarms on benign tasks—where standard safety filters fail.

title: Symbal: Detecting Systematic Misalignments in Model-Generated Captions
authors: Maya Varma, Jean-Benoit Delbrouck, Sophie Ostmeier, Akshay Chaudhari, Curtis Langlotz
summary: This paper addresses a blind spot in multimodal AI: when vision-language models systematically misinterpret images in predictable ways. The authors create Symbal, a method to automatically detect these recurring errors by finding associations between specific visual features and caption mistakes, plus SymbalBench, a benchmark with 1.7 million annotated image-caption pairs to evaluate such detection. The work matters because it lets practitioners audit AI-generated captions for bias and errors without access to the model's internals.

title: BadWAM: When World-Action Models Dream Right but Act Wrong
authors: Qi Li, Xingyi Yang, Xinchao Wang
summary: This paper reveals a critical vulnerability in world-action models (WAMs) — neural networks that control robots by jointly predicting future states and selecting actions. The researchers show that small visual perturbations can cause a WAM to imagine a safe future while executing dangerous actions, breaking the assumed safety guarantee. This "world-action drift" exposes a fundamental misalignment between a model's predictions and its actual behavior.

title: MM-IssueLoc: A Controlled Benchmark for Evaluating Visual Evidence in Multimodal Repository-Level Issue Localization
authors: Shaoxiong Zhan, Shi Hu, Boyu Feng, Hai Lin, Andrew Gong et al.
summary: This paper introduces MM-IssueLoc, a benchmark for evaluating how well AI systems can locate bugs in code repositories when given both text descriptions and visual evidence like screenshots or error dialogs. Current benchmarks treat bug localization as text-only, so this work fills a gap by creating a controlled dataset with 652 real issues across 23 programming languages and measuring whether visual information actually helps systems find the right code location.

title: Self-Evolving Human-Centered Framework for Explainable Depression Symptom Annotation
authors: Hoang-Loc Cao, Van Pham, Truong Thanh Hung Nguyen, Phuc Truong Loc Nguyen, Phuc Ho et al.
summary: This paper presents a framework for creating high-quality, explainable datasets for depression diagnosis by combining LLM-assisted annotation with expert feedback. The key innovation is a dual-memory system that learns from expert corrections without retraining, producing datasets aligned with clinical standards (DSM-5-TR) and traceable reasoning for each diagnosis decision.

title: Mask-Aware Policy Gradients for Diffusion Language Models
authors: Haran Raajesh, Kulin Shah, Adam Klivans, Philipp Krähenbühl
summary: This paper extends reinforcement learning to Masked Diffusion Language Models (MDLMs)—a class of generative models that produce text by iteratively unmasking tokens in a non-left-to-right order. The key challenge is that existing RL methods struggle because computing log-likelihoods for MDLMs is intractable. The authors show that MDLM generation involves two distinct decisions (what tokens to predict, and which positions to unmask next) and derive a policy gradient that decomposes cleanly into both terms, achieving strong results on reasoning and code generation benchmarks.

title: SciPhy Reinforcement Learning for Portfolio Optimization
authors: Igor Halperin, Andrey Itkin
summary: This paper applies physics-informed reinforcement learning to portfolio optimization for large institutional investors, combining offline learning from historical data with microstructure-aware execution costs. The key innovation is solving the optimal control problem (expressed as a Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation) directly from data using neural networks, then converting continuous trading rates into discrete target holdings to match real-world execution constraints. The method shows measurable improvements in risk-adjusted returns (Sharpe ratio) on a real ETF portfolio while keeping turnover and volatility under control.

title: Plover: Steering GUI Agents through Plan-Centric Interaction
authors: Madhumitha Venkatesan, Shicheng Wen, Jiajing Guo, Jorge Piazentin Ono, Liu Ren et al.
summary: Plover is a GUI automation system that makes AI agent behavior transparent and correctable by externalizing task plans as editable artifacts. Instead of having agents act as black boxes, Plover lets users see, inspect, and modify the agent's plan at each step, enabling human-in-the-loop correction when things go wrong. This matters because real-world GUI automation is fragile—unexpected dialogs and layout changes cause agents to fail—and human visibility into agent reasoning is critical for practical deployment.

title: Can We Trust Item Response Theory for AI Evaluation?
authors: Han Jiang, Sunbeom Kwon, Jinwen Luo, Ziang Xiao, Susu Zhang
summary: This paper examines whether item response theory (IRT)—a statistical method borrowed from educational testing—reliably evaluates AI models on benchmarks. The authors show that standard IRT estimation breaks down when applied to typical AI benchmark conditions: few models, many test items, and skewed capability distributions. They simulate 18,000 scenarios to identify when IRT rankings and predictions become untrustworthy, revealing critical gaps between human testing (where IRT was designed) and AI evaluation practice.

title: Stigmergic Graph Memory: An Environment-Aware Approach for Many-to-Many Multi-Agent Pickup and Delivery
authors: Aditya Dutta, Joon-Seok Kim
summary: This paper addresses a key logistics problem: how to automatically assign pickup-and-delivery tasks across multiple agents in crowded warehouses. The authors propose Stigmergic Graph Memory (SGM), a memory system that tracks recent activity (congestion, collisions, delays) at warehouse locations and uses that information to smartly choose which pickup and delivery points to assign to each agent—before path planning happens. On simulated warehouse layouts, SGM achieves 20–37% throughput gains over existing methods by letting past execution patterns inform task allocation, not just routing.

title: RTS Smoother-Guided Learning of Physics-Based Neural Differential Models
authors: Ahmet Demirkaya, Georgios Stratis, Tales Imbiriba, Zachary D. Danziger, Deniz Erdogmus
summary: This paper proposes a hybrid approach that combines known physics equations with neural networks to model dynamical systems when only partial measurements are available. The method alternates between inferring hidden system states (using a classical statistical smoother) and learning the neural network parameters, allowing it to discover missing physics while maintaining interpretability. This matters because many real systems have well-understood components alongside unknown dynamics—and current pure neural approaches often miss the structure that makes models trustworthy and generalizable.

title: T^2MLR: Transformer with Temporal Middle-Layer Recurrence
authors: Ziyang Cai, Xingyu Zhu, Yihe Dong, Yinghui He, Sanjeev Arora
summary: This paper proposes T²MLR, a modification to transformer architectures that injects cached intermediate representations from one decoding step into earlier layers of the next step. This allows abstract reasoning to persist across token generation without the computational overhead of full recurrence, and works even when retrofitted onto existing pretrained models. The approach consistently improves reasoning tasks while reducing the need for expensive full-network recurrence.

title: Benchmarking Multimodal Large Language Models for Scientific Visualization Literacy
authors: Patrick Phuoc Do, Chau M. Ta, Chaoli Wang
summary: This paper evaluates how well six multimodal large language models (MLLMs)—AI systems that process both text and images—can understand scientific visualizations like charts, diagrams, and illustrations. The researchers created a standardized test based on 49 real scientific visualizations and compared model performance against 485 human participants, finding that current models struggle significantly with quantitative reasoning and complex visualization types, even though they excel at simpler tasks.

title: On-Policy Delta Distillation
authors: Byeongho Heo, Jaehui Hwang, Sangdoo Yun, Dongyoon Han
summary: This paper proposes On-Policy Delta Distillation (OPD²), a method for training reasoning-capable language models more efficiently by having a student model learn from the *differences* between a reasoning-tuned teacher and its base version, rather than imitating the teacher directly. The approach works within reinforcement learning post-training and is shown to improve performance on math, science, and code tasks while requiring shorter training periods than standard distillation.

title: Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization for World Models in Atari Pong
authors: Yukuan Lu, Zaishuo Xia, Weyl Lu, Yubei Chen
summary: This paper investigates why visual world models—neural networks that predict future video frames in reinforcement learning—fail to capture task-critical details, even when the agents they're trained with perform well. The authors test five state-of-the-art models on Atari Pong and find systemic failures like disappearing balls and incorrect physics, then propose Concept-Guided Spatial Regularization (CGSReg) to improve performance by adding a reconstruction loss focused on semantically meaningful regions like the ball.

title: Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches
authors: Sridhar Mahadevan
summary: This paper proposes LINCS (Learning in Infinitesimal Non-Compositional Sketches), a categorical framework for understanding when machine learning models fail to satisfy their design constraints. Instead of viewing failures as numerical prediction errors, the paper formalizes them as obstructions to categorical factorization problems — and introduces a method using infinitesimal perturbations (tangent space analysis) to detect and repair compositional breakdowns before they happen.

title: Digital Pantheon: Simulating and Auditing Coalition Formation with LLM Agents
authors: Dylan Van Mulders, Matthias Bogaert, Dirk Van den Poel
summary: This paper builds a multi-agent simulation where LLM-based agents representing political parties negotiate to form coalitions, mirroring real-world government formation. The authors solve a critical problem: standard LLMs trained with RLHF are too neutral and helpful to sustain partisan positions needed for realistic political negotiation. They introduce interpretability tools (lineage tracing, influence scoring) that make the emergent agreements auditable and grounded in party manifestos.

title: AlphaWiSE: Adaptive Weight Interpolation for Continual Multimodal Representation Learning
authors: Sarthak Jain, Qiran Hu, Zhen Zhu, Yaoyao Liu
summary: This paper addresses a fundamental problem in continual learning for multimodal models like CLIP: how to adapt to new data without forgetting earlier cross-modal alignments. AlphaWiSE solves this by interpolating between two frozen model checkpoints using learned scalar weights, achieving better stability-plasticity trade-offs than existing methods while keeping the same model size and inference cost.

title: Rubrics on Trial: Evolving Rubrics from a Single Query via Synthetic Pairwise Evidence
authors: Haocheng Yang, Licheng Pan, Xiaoxi Li, Zhichao Chen, Zhiheng Zhang et al.
summary: This paper introduces Rubrics on Trial, a method for automatically generating evaluation rubrics (scoring criteria) for large language models using only a query as input. Instead of relying on human-written rubrics or preference data, the approach creates and validates rubric candidates by testing them against synthetic model-generated response pairs, filtering out those that don't meaningfully distinguish answer quality. The work matters because automatic rubric generation could make it faster and cheaper to train and evaluate LLMs on new tasks.

title: Evaluating covariate balance for long time horizon Markov decision processes
authors: Joshua Spear, Rebecca Pope, Neil J Sebire
summary: This paper examines whether standard covariate balance diagnostics — statistical tools used to check if treatment groups are comparable — can reliably detect hidden confounding and model errors in offline reinforcement learning (RL) studies that recommend medical treatments. The authors find that existing covariate balance metrics appear insufficient for this task, suggesting that current offline RL treatment recommendation studies may be statistically unreliable.

title: An Introduction to Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics for Engineering Applications
authors: Yao Cheng Li, Ana Larrañaga, Steven L. Brunton, Urban Fasel
summary: This tutorial paper presents SINDy (Sparse Identification of Nonlinear Dynamics), a method that recovers interpretable mathematical equations governing complex systems from small datasets by performing sparse regression over candidate nonlinear terms. Unlike black-box neural networks, SINDy produces human-readable equations while requiring far less training data, making it practical for real engineering problems where data is scarce and understanding the physics matters.

title: cGAP: Generalized Association Plots with HOMALS-Guided Heatmaps for Visualization of High-Dimensional Categorical Data
authors: Chun-houh Chen, Shun-Chuan Chang, Chiun-How Kao, Yi-Ju Lee, Shang-Ying Shiu et al.
summary: This paper introduces cGAP, a visualization framework for high-dimensional categorical data that combines dimensionality reduction (HOMALS) with heatmap-based displays. It lets researchers explore complex categorical datasets—like genetic profiles or survey responses—while keeping the original data visible and interpretable, something existing visualization tools struggle to do at scale.

title: SMC-ES: Automated synthesis of formally verified control policies
authors: Riccardo Curcio, Toni Mancini, Enrico Tronci
summary: This paper addresses a critical gap in deploying learning-based controllers for safety-critical systems: while reinforcement learning can automatically synthesize control policies, it typically cannot guarantee they're safe. The authors propose SMC-ES, a method that combines evolutionary strategies (a type of black-box optimization) with statistical model checking (a lightweight formal verification technique) to synthesize policies that come with formal guarantees: with high confidence, the policy will violate safety specifications at most a specified small fraction of the time.

title: OmniaBench: Benchmarking General AI Agents Across Diverse Scenarios
authors: Chengyu Shen, Yujie Fu, Gangtao Xin, Yanheng Hou, Wenlong Fei et al.
summary: OmniaBench is a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating AI agents — systems that combine language understanding with tool use and interactive reasoning — across 354 real-world application domains. The work reveals that even state-of-the-art models like Claude and GPT-5 struggle with complex, multi-step tasks, succeeding less than 60% of the time, and identifies specific weaknesses in planning and error recovery.

title: StructureClaw: Traceable LLM Agents and an Executable Benchmark for Structural Engineering Workflows
authors: Sizhong Qin, Yi Gu, Yao Jiang, Ao Cai, Changjian Zhou et al.
summary: StructureClaw is a workbench and benchmark for evaluating LLM agents on structural engineering tasks. Unlike typical LLM benchmarks that score isolated answers, this system traces the entire workflow—from interpreting requirements through modeling, validation, solving, and reporting—ensuring agents produce complete, executable, internally consistent engineering solutions. This matters because real engineering demands more than fluent text: it requires a chain of interdependent artifacts that hang together.

title: The Energy Society: A Simulation Environment for Studying Agent Cooperation under Survival Pressure
authors: Lucas Bergholdt Hansen, Federico Torrielli, Filippo Tonini, Lukas Galke Poech
summary: This paper introduces The Energy Society, a simulation environment where LLM-based agents must survive by managing energy (which costs are tied to model inference). The researchers study how competitive versus cooperative incentives shape agent behavior when survival is at stake. The key finding: cooperative incentives dramatically change behavior—agents donate energy to save others even at personal cost—while competitive settings reveal subtle self-serving patterns rather than overt sabotage.

title: Dialogue Summarization with Emotion Dynamics Using Topic- and Participant-Centric Decomposition
authors: Linyun Xiang, Mark Neerincx, Stephanie Tan
summary: This paper proposes a new framework for summarizing dialogues (conversations between multiple people) that captures not just *what* was said, but *how people felt* throughout the exchange. Unlike existing summarization methods built for single-author documents like news articles, this approach decomposes conversations by topic and by individual speaker, then combines these perspectives to generate summaries that preserve both semantic content and emotional trajectories—a first step toward making dialogue summaries emotionally faithful to the original conversation.

title: Does Multi-Agent Debate Improve AI Feedback on Research Papers?
authors: Tomas Havranek, Zuzana Irsova
summary: This paper tests whether multi-agent debate—where multiple AI systems discuss a problem to improve output quality—actually helps provide better feedback on research papers. The authors ran a pre-registered experiment with 44 economics meta-analysis authors who compared feedback from a single AI model pass against two debate-based systems. Surprisingly, authors consistently preferred the simpler single-pass approach, even though the debate systems used vastly more computational resources, suggesting that multi-agent debate may not improve AI feedback quality in this domain.

title: Cross-Layer Error Compensation and Finite-Sample Feature-Statistics Matching for Extreme Low-Bit Quantization of Large Language Models
authors: Ryona Noda
summary: This paper tackles extreme low-bit quantization of large language models—compressing them to 1-bit or 4-bit weights while preserving performance. The authors show that quantizing layers independently causes errors to compound across the network's depth; their solution couples all layers together, compensating for errors as they propagate and matching statistical properties between the compressed and original models. On a 1.5B parameter model, their method achieves 9× worse perplexity than the original (versus 14× for standard approaches), a substantial improvement at extreme compression ratios.

title: Bad Memory: Evaluating Prompt Injection Risks from Memory in Agentic Systems
authors: Soham Gadgil, David Alexander, Sai Sunku, Franziska Roesner
summary: This paper investigates how agentic systems that store persistent memory across sessions become vulnerable to prompt injection attacks — a type of adversarial manipulation where malicious instructions are hidden in files that the agent will read later. The researchers tested two commercial systems (Claude and GPT-based agents) and found that while it's hard to trick agents into corrupting their own memory, pre-planted malicious payloads in memory files can successfully manipulate agent behavior across multiple sessions. This reveals a new security risk as AI agents become more autonomous and adaptive.

title: Probabilistic Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Estimating Heterogeneous Elastic Properties from Low-Resolution and Noisy Displacement Data
authors: Tatthapong Srikitrungruang, Jaesung Lee
summary: This paper proposes PIE-PINN, a probabilistic neural network method for estimating material properties (Young's modulus and Poisson's ratio) from noisy, low-resolution measurements of how materials deform under stress. The key innovation is treating measurement uncertainty and model errors probabilistically rather than with fixed weights, making the method robust when data is degraded or sparse—a problem that typically defeats standard inverse methods.

title: Towards an Intention Abstraction Layer for Autonomous Industrial Systems
authors: Artan Markaj, Raphael Höfer, Felix Gehlhoff
summary: This paper proposes an Intention Abstraction Layer (IAL) — a middleware system that lets multiple autonomous industrial systems (like schedulers, energy managers, vehicle fleets) register their high-level goals in natural language, then automatically detects conflicts before they cause failures. The key insight: instead of discovering conflicts after a crash or missed target, catch them at registration time by treating human intentions as explicit, persistent runtime objects that can be checked for consistency.

title: Adaptive Runge-Kutta Step Control Buys Training Loss, Not Generalization: An Honest Compute-Matched Study of RK-Adam Optimizers
authors: Akhilesh Gogikar
summary: This paper tests whether higher-order Runge-Kutta integrators improve neural network training when fairly compared to Adam under equal computational budgets. The authors find that the popular idea of using adaptive step control from numerical integration yields no real benefit — the method behaves as fixed-step Adam at 3–4× higher cost, and while modifications can improve training loss, they do not improve test accuracy or generalize better than simple tuned baselines.

title: Mixed-Agent Museum Tour Guide Design Improves Gendered Learning Outcomes and Visitor Preferences
authors: Annette M. Masterson, Wonse Jo, Helena C. Sieh, Lionel P. Robert,, Dawn Tilbury
summary: This paper presents a mixed-agent museum tour guide system that combines a physical robot with a projected virtual agent to guide visitors. Through a study of 30 participants, the researchers found that the dual-agent setup improved learning for female visitors and was preferred by all visitors, suggesting that multi-agent interaction designs can enhance both engagement and educational outcomes in public spaces.

title: A Noise-Robust Elicit-to-Optimize Framework for Distortion Riskmetrics via Inverse Reinforcement Learning
authors: Yang Liu, Yuhao Liu, Yunran Wei
summary: This paper proposes a framework that combines inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) and standard RL to solve two problems: inferring what risk preferences an agent has from their noisy decisions, and then optimizing investment policies under those inferred preferences. The work is important because understanding and optimizing for risk—not just returns—is central to financial decision-making, and agents often make suboptimal or stochastic choices that don't fit traditional models.

title: Supervised Fine-Tuning vs. In-Context Learning: An Equilibrium Analysis of LLM Personalization under Congestion
authors: Fengzhuo Zhang, Zhuoran Yang, Dirk Bergemann
summary: This paper analyzes when users should invest in expensive model fine-tuning versus cheaper in-context learning for personalizing large language models, accounting for shared computational resources. The authors develop an equilibrium framework showing that congestion from other users' choices fundamentally reshapes which personalization strategy is optimal, and prove that platforms benefit by offering both methods despite increased load.

title: NeuralChaos: Optimal Adapted Approximation of Square Integrable Predictable Processes
authors: Anastasis Kratsios, Giulia Livieri, Philipp Schmocker
summary: This paper introduces NeuralChaos, a neural network architecture that efficiently represents predictable stochastic processes — random quantities that evolve over time in ways driven by Brownian motion. The method solves a fundamental problem in mathematical finance and control: traditional approaches require computing prohibitively expensive high-order integrals, while NeuralChaos achieves the same theoretical guarantees using only finitely many evaluations of the underlying randomness. This matters because stochastic processes are central to pricing derivatives, optimal trading, and reinforcement learning in continuous time.

title: When Is Delegated Play Truthful? Within-Range Regret and the Trilemma of Aligned Delegation
authors: Taksch Dube
summary: This paper asks a simple but overlooked question: when should someone tell the truth to an automated agent (like an autobidder or language-model proxy) acting on their behalf? The authors show that honesty is optimal only when the proxy is already playing the best action it can reach — a concept they call "loyalty" — and prove that no safety constraint can simultaneously be binding, truthful, and capability-preserving. The work bridges mechanism design theory with practical alignment problems in LLMs and automated bidding.

title: AI Agents Do Not Fail Alone:The Context Fails First
authors: Fouad Bousetouane
summary: This paper argues that AI agent failures stem primarily from poor context engineering — the instructions, tools, memory, and guardrails surrounding an agent — rather than the agent's underlying model. The authors build ProofAgent-Harness, an evaluation framework that measures context quality across seven dimensions (role clarity, guardrails, instruction consistency, tool schemas, grounding, injection hardening, token efficiency) and validate that context scores predict specific failure modes like hallucination and tool misuse.

title: Automatic Hard Example Synthesis with Multi-Level Agentic Data Curation
authors: Genglin Liu, Muye Zhang, Krishnamurthy Viswanathan, Nichole J. Hansen, Blaž Bratanič et al.
summary: This paper presents an automated system that uses multiple AI agents working together to create challenging test cases for multimodal AI models (systems that process both images and text). The goal is to make these models more robust against adversarial attacks and edge cases — tricky scenarios they might fail on. By synthesizing hard examples without human effort, the system improves safety model performance significantly (reducing errors from 41% to 24%).

title: Leveraging unlabelled data for generalizable neural population decoding
authors: Ximeng Mao, Nanda H. Krishna, Avery Hee-Woon Ryoo, Matthew G. Perich, Guillaume Lajoie
summary: This paper introduces MOJO, a training framework that combines self-supervised learning (learning from unlabeled data) and supervised learning to decode neural activity from brain recordings. The key innovation is using masked autoencoding — a technique where parts of neural spike patterns are hidden and the model learns to predict them — alongside traditional labeled behavioral tasks. This approach works better than supervised-only methods, especially when labeled data is scarce, and generalizes across different brain regions, animal species, and even different types of neural recordings (spikes vs. continuous signals).

title: MetaPerch: Learning from metadata for bioacoustics foundation models
authors: Mustafa Chasmai, Vincent Dumoulin, Jenny Hamer
summary: MetaPerch is a foundation model for bioacoustics that learns to identify bird and animal species from audio recordings by leveraging metadata (location, time, seasonal patterns) alongside acoustic signals. The paper shows that enriching audio-only models with readily available contextual information from citizen science platforms significantly improves species detection accuracy and robustness across different geographic regions and recording conditions — critical for real-world deployment in wildlife monitoring systems.

title: Screening of Biosecurity Features in Metagenomic Data with Evo 2 Probes
authors: Jeremy Guntoro, Alexander Dack, Dylan Danno, Michaela Jančovičová, Križan Jurinović et al.
summary: This paper investigates whether genomic foundation models (Evo 2) learn biosecurity-relevant patterns that can be detected with simple linear probes, without retraining the model itself. The researchers show that these frozen representations encode strong signals for antimicrobial resistance detection (ROC-AUC 0.977 with attention probes) and weaker signals for bacterial virulence, suggesting foundation model embeddings could serve as a fast, cheap screening layer for pathogenic sequences in metagenomic data.

title: Minimax Theory of Likelihood-Based Deep Learning for Speckle Regression
authors: Soham Jana
summary: This paper studies the theoretical statistical limits of deep neural networks for removing speckle noise — a type of multiplicative noise common in radar and medical imaging. The authors prove that likelihood-based deep learning methods can achieve optimal estimation rates, and surprisingly, the difficulty of this problem is essentially the same as standard regression with only additive noise, despite multiplicative noise being fundamentally harder to work with.

title: Deep Interaction: An Efficient Human-AI Interaction Method for Large Reasoning Models
authors: Hefeng Zhou, Jinxuan Zhang, Jiong Lou, Yuxin Liu, Chaochao Lu et al.
summary: This paper presents Deep Interaction, a method that lets users directly edit and correct reasoning errors in chain-of-thought (CoT) outputs from large language models, rather than asking the model to regenerate from scratch. The corrected reasoning is then distilled into a prompt that guides the model along the fixed path, achieving 25% better correction rates and 40% fewer tokens on STEM reasoning tasks.

title: AI-accelerated End-to-End Framework for Rapid Professional Upskilling
authors: Tam Nguyen, Hung Nguyen, Robert Ogburn
summary: This paper presents an end-to-end framework that uses AI to accelerate professional upskilling across five stages: knowledge acquisition, content development, review, teaching, and assessment. The work is motivated by a critical skills gap — workers need reskilling faster than current methods allow — and demonstrates real-world validation through certified professional training programs and regulatory approval.

title: Early Adoption of Agentic Coding Tools by GitHub Projects
authors: Maliha Noushin Raida, Daqing Hou
summary: This paper analyzes how real-world open-source projects are adopting AI-powered coding agents that can generate and submit pull requests. The researchers examined over 25,000 agent-generated PRs across 2,361 GitHub repositories to understand adoption patterns, productivity levels, and how humans oversee these AI contributions—finding that adoption is still concentrated in a small subset of projects and that most rely on single-developer review models.

title: SPECS: Speciated Evolutionary Circuit Synthesis
authors: Yağız Gençer, Stefan Uhlich, Andrea Bonetti, Arun Venkitaraman, Chia-Yu Hsieh et al.
summary: SPECS is an evolutionary algorithm that automatically designs analog circuits by optimizing both their topology (structure) and component values simultaneously. It adapts NEAT — a genetic algorithm originally built for neural networks — to the circuit domain, adding circuit-specific constraints and diversity-preservation mechanisms. The method outperforms existing benchmarks on function-synthesis tasks like square root and cube root approximations.

title: Transforming Rank: How Architecture Navigates the Spectral Pathologies of Depth
authors: Katie Everett
summary: This paper explains why Transformers work well at scale by analyzing how architectural components preserve information (technically, matrix rank) as networks get deeper. The authors show that skip connections, normalization placement, and width expansion are fundamentally mechanisms for preventing gradient information collapse—not just stabilizing training magnitude—and this unified view predicts which architectural choices enable deep networks to learn effectively.

title: Lighthouse RL: Sample-Efficient Circuit Optimization via Strategic Reset Points
authors: Mustafa Emre Gürsoy, Stefan Uhlich, Ryoga Matsuo, Yağız Gençer, Arun Venkitaraman et al.
summary: This paper presents Lighthouse RL, a reinforcement learning method that dramatically reduces the number of simulations needed to optimize analog circuits. Instead of exploring randomly, the algorithm remembers high-performing configurations found during training (called "lighthouses") and uses them as restart points for future episodes, guiding the search toward promising regions much faster than traditional RL or optimization methods.

title: Rethinking Penetration Testing for AI-Enabled Systems: From Resource Compromise to Behavioral Objective Violation
authors: Mohammad Allahbakhsh, Mohammad Hassan Bahari, Moslem Attar-Raouf
summary: This paper redefines penetration testing for AI systems to focus on behavioral objective violation rather than infrastructure compromise. Traditional security testing looks for exploitable software bugs; this work argues that AI systems can be compromised through manipulation of prompts, training data, sensors, and human-AI interactions without touching the underlying infrastructure, and proposes a testing framework to systematically evaluate these behavioral attack surfaces.

title: Do Agent Optimizers Compound? A Continual-Learning Evaluation on Terminal-Bench 2.0
authors: Wenxiao Wang, Priyatham Kattakinda, Soheil Feizi
summary: This paper asks whether improvements from agent optimization methods persist and compound when applied repeatedly over time—a critical real-world scenario ignored by standard benchmarking. The authors evaluate three optimization approaches on a continual-learning benchmark and find that only methods with built-in regression control (preventing performance collapse on old tasks) achieve lasting gains; most methods either catastrophically fail to transfer to new tasks or plateau after a single optimization round.

title: The Dynamic Verifiable Multi-Agent Human Agentic Loyalty Loop (DVM-HALL) Model and the Net Human-Agent Score (NHAS) in Autonomous Commerce
authors: Sai Srikanth Madugula, Peplluis Esteva de la Rosa, Daya Shankar
summary: This paper introduces the Dynamic Verifiable Multi-Agent Human Agentic Loyalty Loop (DVM-HALL), a new framework for understanding customer loyalty in an era where AI agents autonomously make purchasing decisions. Traditional loyalty models assume human consumers act alone; this work shows they fail when autonomous agents execute transactions on behalf of humans or in competition with them. The paper formalizes how trust, delegation, and execution risk jointly shape agent-brand relationships, and proposes the Net Human-Agent Score (NHAS) to measure human-agent alignment in commerce.

title: Multimodal Empirical Bayes Variational Autoencoders for Joint Longitudinal and Time-to-Event Modeling
authors: Anders Sjöberg, Nils Olsson, Marcus Baaz, Mats Jirstrand
summary: This paper extends empirical Bayes variational autoencoders (EB-VAE) to jointly model tumor growth trajectories and patient dropout timing using longitudinal measurements, genetic data, and event times. It matters because clinical data comes in multiple forms—repeated measurements, dropouts, genetic information—and integrating them in a single probabilistic framework can improve treatment response prediction and identify genetic biomarkers.

title: Pezego-HITL: A policy-grounded large language model architecture for agricultural extension in Ghana
authors: Shunbao Li, Zhipeng Yuan, Amoako Ofori, Benedicta Y. Fosu-Mensah, Yang Li et al.
summary: This paper presents Pezego-HITL, an LLM architecture for agricultural advisory in Ghana that prioritizes safety and policy compliance alongside helpfulness. The key innovation is P-EVAL, a validation framework that treats LLM deployment in high-stakes farming decisions as an adaptive compute allocation problem — balancing safety compliance, usefulness, response speed, and expert workload — rather than just measuring answer quality alone.

title: VAIOM: Continuous-Input, Discrete-Output Decoder-Only Financial Sequence Modeling
authors: Yiming Ma, Xinyu Chen
summary: This paper presents VAIOM, a decoder-only Transformer designed to predict next-period returns in foreign-exchange markets by accepting continuous financial data (prices, volumes, events) as input while outputting discrete return predictions. The key innovation is separating input representation—which preserves numerical structure—from output modeling, which uses categorical distributions over return buckets, outperforming traditional machine learning baselines on real FX data across multiple test periods.

title: DeepStress: Stress-Testing Deep Search Agents
authors: Ismael Rousseau, Geraldine Damnati, Frederic Bechet
summary: This paper introduces DeepStress, a framework for testing how well AI search agents handle unreliable information in multi-step question answering tasks. Rather than waiting for rare failures in real applications, the researchers systematically inject poor-quality evidence (untrustworthy, irrelevant, or factually wrong documents) into the retrieval process to measure agent robustness. The work reveals that different search agents vary dramatically in their ability to cope with unreliable information, a crucial gap for deploying these systems in the wild.

title: How to Guide LLM Generation: Dual-Surrogate Guided Search for Automated Heuristic Design
authors: Yuhan Wang, Chaoda Peng, Xingyu Wu, Sheng-Hao Wu, Zhi-Hui Zhan
summary: This paper presents a method to make LLM-based heuristic design more efficient by intelligently selecting which archived solutions to reuse and how to modify them before querying the LLM. Rather than using fixed rules, the system learns to predict which combinations of parent heuristics and transformation operators will likely produce good child solutions, dramatically reducing wasted queries under tight evaluation budgets.

title: High-Order Question Generation in a Multilingual Educational Context
authors: Suna-Şeyma Uçar, Itziar Aldabe, Nora Aranberri, Orphée De Clercq
summary: This paper explores how large language models can generate high-order questions—the kind that develop critical thinking rather than mere recall—across three languages (Basque, Spanish, English) using alternative frameworks to Bloom's Taxonomy. The work matters because educators struggle to create such questions in practice, and most prior work has focused narrowly on English and a single pedagogical framework.

title: SPyCE: Skill-Policy Co-evolution for Multimodal Agents
authors: Ru Zhang, Weijie Qiu
summary: This paper presents SPyCE, a framework that trains multimodal agents (systems that reason about images and use tools) by evolving a reusable skill library alongside the policy during learning. Rather than treating trajectories as scalar rewards or static memory, SPyCE distills them into hierarchical skills that improve over time, creating a feedback loop where better policies generate better skills, which in turn guide better policies. The approach substantially outperforms existing reinforcement learning and memory-based methods across eight benchmarks.

title: S-CARD-CMSA: A Score-Aware Candidate Archive with Density-Filtered Reporting for Multimodal Optimization
authors: Dikshit Chauhan
summary: This paper presents S-CARD-CMSA, a method for multimodal optimization — finding multiple high-quality solutions in a single run rather than just one optimum. The approach builds on an existing evolution strategy (RS-CMSA-ESII) by adding a secondary archive to track good candidates and a smart reporting rule that balances finding many peaks with reporting them accurately, developed for the IEEE CEC 2026 competition on niching methods.

title: Post-Training Shifts Confidence: A Three-Stage Analysis of How SFT, RL, and OPD Shape Pre-, Intra-, and Post-CoT Calibration
authors: Shuhao Li, Guodong Du, Anhao Zhao, Wanyu Lin, Tianyu Yuan et al.
summary: This paper studies how different post-training methods (supervised fine-tuning, reinforcement learning, and on-policy distillation) affect how confident language models are during chain-of-thought reasoning—not just whether they get the right answer, but whether they *know* they're right at each stage. The authors show that confidence reliability depends on *when* and *where* in the reasoning you measure it, and propose a position-aware strategy that uses each method's confidence signals only when they're actually trustworthy, improving both answer selection and early stopping decisions.

title: Algebraic Representability as the Limiting Regime of Grokking: An Exactly Solvable Model with Holomorphic Activations
authors: Chon-Fai Kam, Xavier Cadet, Miloud Bessafi, Frederic Cadet
summary: This paper studies grokking—the puzzling phenomenon where neural networks suddenly jump from memorizing training data to generalizing—by examining an extreme case where network expressivity is mathematically constrained. Using two-layer networks with special "holomorphic" (complex-analytic) activations trained on modular arithmetic, the authors prove that whether a task can be learned is determined entirely by algebraic geometry: a target is learnable if and only if its Fourier structure aligns with the network's built-in representational constraints. The key insight is that in this bottlenecked regime, grokking disappears—networks either succeed instantly or fail completely—revealing grokking as a capacity-dependent phenomenon.

title: DAGR: State-Conditioned Goal Representations via Difference-Aware Goal Cross-Attention
authors: Xing Lei, Wenyan Yang, Xuetao Zhang, Donglin Wang
summary: This paper proposes DAGR, a method to improve goal-conditioned reinforcement learning by making goal representations aware of the current state. Traditional goal encoders ignore what state the agent is in, forcing the policy to figure out the gap itself; DAGR uses cross-attention to refine goal embeddings based on state-goal differences, showing consistent gains on navigation tasks but mixed results on manipulation and puzzles.

title: Cluster with Auctions for Vector Search
authors: Swann Bessa, Pierre Fernandez, Gergely Szilvasy, Matthijs Douze, Hervé Jégou
summary: This paper presents CwA (Cluster with Auctions), a method for fast approximate nearest neighbor search that learns *different* assignment rules for database vectors versus query vectors. Most existing systems use the same clustering rule for both, which is inefficient when query and database distributions differ. CwA jointly optimizes a neural probing function and a balanced partition using alternating optimization and auction algorithms, achieving up to 4.7× speedup over competing methods.

title: Self-supervised Speech Comparison for L2 Phone, Rhythm, and Intonation Scoring
authors: Stephen McIntosh, Reuben Smit, Daisuke Saito, Nobuaki Minematsu, Herman Kamper
summary: This paper shows that self-supervised audio representations (WavLM) combined with dynamic time warping (DTW) can automatically score non-native English and Japanese speakers on pronunciation accuracy, rhythm, and intonation—without requiring labeled training data or transcripts. The approach matches or exceeds human raters on some tasks and works in low-resource languages where labeled speech data is scarce.

title: Social Simulations: from Agent-Based Modeling to Digital Twins
authors: Erica Cau, Andrea Failla, Valentina Pansanella, Giulio Rossetti
summary: This chapter traces how social simulation has evolved from hand-coded agent models to AI-powered digital twins—computational replicas of real social systems. It shows a progression from abstract models (used to understand general social patterns) to realistic, data-driven simulations (used to represent specific communities or institutions). The work matters because it bridges classical computational social science with modern generative AI, offering a roadmap for building trustworthy simulations of human systems.

title: Evaluating Encoding Strategies for Closed-Loop Classification in Biological Neural Networks
authors: Martin Schottlender, Veronika Volkova, Pengjie Zhou, Ruifeng Zheng, Frank H. P. Fitzek et al.
summary: This paper investigates how to encode visual information into electrical stimulation patterns that cultured biological neural networks can process and learn from. The researchers tested four encoding strategies (rate-based, phase-based, burst-based, and temporal spike-timing) in a closed-loop classification task and found that burst-based temporal encoding significantly outperforms others, achieving 95.6% accuracy—suggesting that both *when* and *where* you stimulate neurons matters critically for brain-computer interfaces.

title: Extending Liquid Rank Toward Multi-Source Reputation Aggregation
authors: Nejc Znidar, Anton Kolonin
summary: This paper extends liquid rank—a reputation system that allows influence to flow dynamically through networks—to handle multiple reputation sources at once. Instead of relying on a single reputation signal, the framework lets different types of reputation (from different platforms, communities, or contexts) be combined into one unified score, with adjustable weights for each source. This matters because real governance systems (DAOs, online communities, delegated authority structures) often need to balance reputation from many channels, and this work provides the technical machinery to do so fairly and flexibly.

title: Visual Place Recognition Using Rate-Encoded Spiking Neural Networks with Discrete STDP Learning
authors: Altzi Tsanko, Oikonomou Katerina Maria, Antonios Gasteratos
summary: This paper improves visual place recognition (identifying revisited locations in images) using spiking neural networks trained with unsupervised learning rules inspired by neuroscience. The key innovation is a discrete, efficient implementation that achieves near-perfect precision-recall tradeoffs needed for autonomous robot navigation, through careful engineering of neuron assignment, state management, and temporal aggregation during inference.

title: DevicesWorld: Benchmarking Cross-Device Agents in Heterogeneous Environments
authors: Huatao Li, Xinwei Geng, Yuheng Wang, Yutong Li, Runde Yang et al.
